passage.text:
A hare liked to run fast.
He liked to brag, too.
"I am the fastest of all!" he said.
A tortoise was slow.
He walked step by step.
"Let's have a race," said the tortoise.
The hare laughed and laughed.
"You want to race me?"
"Yes, let's race!"
***
A fox said, "Ready, set, go!"
The hare ran off like the wind.
The tortoise plodded along.
Step, step, step.
Soon the hare was far ahead.
He looked back.
He could not see the tortoise at all.
"I have lots of time," said the hare.
"I will take a little nap."
He lay down under a tree.
Soon he was fast asleep.
***
The tortoise did not stop.
Step, step, step.
He went past the sleeping hare.
Step, step, step.
He got close to the finish line.
The hare woke up.
He saw the tortoise at the line!
He ran as fast as he could.
But it was too late.
The tortoise won the race!
"Slow and steady wins the race," said the fox.

cards.q: Who liked to brag about being fast?
cards.note: A hare is a big rabbit with long legs, built for speed.

cards.q: Who said 'Ready, set, go'?
cards.note: The fox starts the race and says the lesson at the end.

cards.q: What did the hare do under the tree?
cards.note: He was so sure he would win that he stopped trying.

cards.q: How did the tortoise move in the race?
cards.note: Slow, but he never stopped; that is what steady means.

cards.q: What happened first in the story?
cards.note: The bragging comes before the race even starts.

cards.q: What happened at the end of the story?
cards.note: The hare woke up too late to catch him.

cards.q: How did the hare feel when he saw the tortoise at the line?
cards.note: He thought the race was his, so seeing the tortoise there was a shock.

cards.q: What does this story teach?
cards.note: Keep going and do not quit, even if you are not the fastest.

cards.q: In the story, what does 'plodded' mean?
cards.note: To plod is to walk slowly with heavy steps; plod across the room together.

cards.q: Which word is in the story?
cards.note: He reads the three words himself; only one of them is in the story.

decks.subject: storytime
decks.title: The Boy Who Cried Wolf
decks.about: Aesop's fable of the bored shepherd boy who yells Wolf! for fun until nobody believes him; in this telling the real wolf only scatters the sheep and nobody gets hurt. It is one of the fables in the NC/CKLA Grade 1 Fables and Stories domain, and the clearest first-grade example of a story with a lesson. It is a public-domain story retold here in first-grade words, three pages long.
decks.tip: Ask: why did nobody come the third time, and what could the boy do to be trusted again?

book.author: Aesop (retold)
book.source: public domain, retold in first-grade words
book.blurb: A boy who tricks the village one time too many.

passage.text:
A boy kept the sheep on a hill.
All day he sat and sat.
It was not much fun.
"I know," he said.
"I will play a trick."
He ran down the hill.
"Wolf! Wolf!" he yelled.
"A wolf is after the sheep!"
The people from the village ran up the hill.
There was no wolf.
The boy just laughed.
***
The next day, the boy did it again.
"Wolf! Wolf!" he yelled.
The people ran up the hill.
There was no wolf.
The boy laughed and laughed.
The people were upset.
"Do not trick us," they said.
"Tell the truth."
***
Then one day, a real wolf came.
It ran at the sheep.
"Wolf! Wolf!" the boy yelled.
"Help! It is a real wolf!"
But no one came.
They thought it was a trick again.
The wolf chased the sheep all over the hill.
The boy felt very sad.
It took all day to get the sheep back.
Tell the truth, so people will trust you.

cards.q: Who kept the sheep on the hill?
cards.note: Someone who looks after sheep is called a shepherd.

cards.q: Where were the sheep?
cards.note: The village is down below, so the people have to run up the hill each time.

cards.q: What did the boy yell to trick the people?
cards.note: That yell is why the story is called The Boy Who Cried Wolf; cried means yelled here.

cards.q: What did the real wolf do to the sheep?
cards.note: In this telling the sheep are only scattered; it takes all day to get them back.

cards.q: What happened first in the story?
cards.note: He was bored, so he played a trick, and then he played it again.

cards.q: What happened at the end of the story?
cards.note: The third time nobody came, and the boy had to gather the sheep himself.

cards.q: How did the people feel when they were tricked again?
cards.note: Ask how he feels when someone tricks him; that is why they stopped coming.

cards.q: What does this story teach?
cards.note: If you tell lies, people stop trusting you, even when you tell the truth.

cards.q: In the story, what does 'village' mean?
cards.note: A village is a small town where the people all know each other.

cards.q: Which word is in the story?
cards.note: He reads the three words himself; only one of them is in the story.

decks.subject: storytime
decks.title: The Fox and the Grapes
decks.about: Aesop's fable of the hungry fox who jumps and jumps for grapes he cannot reach, then sticks his nose in the air and says they were probably sour anyway. It gives first graders a lesson they can spot for themselves, and it explains a saying they will hear for the rest of their lives: sour grapes. It is a public-domain story retold here in first-grade words, three pages long.
decks.tip: Act it out: jump for a toy held up high, miss, then stick your nose in the air and say, I bet they are sour!

book.author: Aesop (retold)
book.source: public domain, retold in first-grade words
book.blurb: A fox who cannot reach the grapes says he never wanted them.

passage.text:
A fox went for a walk one sunny day.
He was very hungry.
Then he saw some grapes.
They hung on a vine, up high.
The grapes were big and ripe.
"Yum!" said the fox.
"Those grapes look so sweet."
"I want them!"
***
The fox ran and jumped.
Up, up, up!
He snapped at the grapes.
Thump!
He fell down.
He missed!
He ran and jumped again.
Up, up, up!
Thump!
He missed again.
"Grr!" said the fox.
He stamped his foot.
***
He tried one more time.
Up, up, up!
Thump!
The grapes were still too high.
At last the fox sat down.
He was hot and tired.
Then he stuck his nose up in the air.
"I never wanted those grapes," he said.
"I bet they are sour."
And off he went.
But he did want them.
Do not pretend you never wanted what you cannot get.

cards.q: Who saw the grapes up on the vine?
cards.note: Real foxes do eat fruit, grapes and berries included, not just meat.

cards.q: Where were the grapes?
cards.note: A vine is a plant that climbs, and grapes grow on it in bunches.

cards.q: What happened each time the fox jumped?
cards.note: Read the up, up, up, thump lines together and jump on every up.

cards.q: What did the fox say about the grapes at the end?
cards.note: Sour means sharp, like a lemon, and he only said it because he could not reach them.

cards.q: What happened first in the story?
cards.note: First he saw the grapes, then he jumped and jumped, then he gave up and walked off.

cards.q: What happened at the end of the story?
cards.note: He never got a single grape; he just stuck his nose in the air and left.

cards.q: How did the fox feel when he kept missing?
cards.note: The story never says the word, so the clues are the Grr and the stamped foot.

cards.q: What does this story teach?
cards.note: Calling something sour grapes means pretending you never wanted the thing you could not get.

cards.q: In the story, what does 'ripe' mean?
cards.note: Ripe fruit is soft, sweet and ready to pick, while a banana with green skin is not ripe yet.

cards.q: Which word is in the story?
cards.note: He reads the three words himself; only one of them is in the story.

decks.subject: storytime
decks.title: The Ant and the Grasshopper
decks.about: Aesop's fable of the ants who work all summer and the grasshopper who sings and plays, told gently: when winter comes the ants share their food, and the grasshopper learns to work and plan ahead. First graders know the pull between playing now and getting ready for later, which makes this an easy lesson to talk about. It is a public-domain story retold here in first-grade words, four pages long.
decks.tip: Ask: what is one thing you can do today to be ready for tomorrow, like packing your school bag?

book.author: Aesop (retold)
book.source: public domain, retold in first-grade words
book.blurb: A busy ant, a singing grasshopper, and a long, cold winter.

passage.text:
It was a warm summer day.
A grasshopper hopped in the grass.
He sang and sang.
"La, la, la!"
An ant went by.
She had a big seed on her back.
"Come and play!" said the grasshopper.
"I can't," said the ant.
"I have work to do."
"I am saving food for the winter."
***
"Winter is a long way off," said the grasshopper.
And he sang some more.
Day after day, the ants worked.
They carried seeds and corn to their nest.
Day after day, the grasshopper played.
"Come and play!" he said.
"We have work to do," said the ants.
The grasshopper just laughed.
***
Then the days got short and cold.
Snow fell on the grass.
The grasshopper was cold and hungry.
He looked for food, but there was none.
He went to see the ants.
Knock, knock!
"Please help me," he said.
"I have no food, and I am so cold."
***
The ants had lots of food.
"Come in," they said.
"We will share with you."
They gave him seeds and corn.
Soon he was warm and full.
"Thank you," said the grasshopper.
"Next summer, I will work, too."
And he did!
He still sang, but he worked, too.
It is smart to work and plan ahead.

cards.q: Who sang and played in the grass?
cards.note: A grasshopper is a green or brown bug with long back legs, made for hopping.

cards.q: What did the ant have on her back?
cards.note: Real ants can carry things much heavier than their own bodies.

cards.q: What were the ants saving food for?
cards.note: In winter there is snow and no food to find, so the ants fill their nest while it is warm.

cards.q: Where did the grasshopper go when snow fell?
cards.note: He knocked and asked the ants for help, even though he had laughed at their work.

cards.q: What happened first in the story?
cards.note: Summer comes first in this story, then winter, so ask him what the grasshopper did all summer.

cards.q: What happened at the end of the story?
cards.note: In the oldest tellings the ants send him away, but here they share and he learns to work.

cards.q: How did the grasshopper feel when the ants shared?
cards.note: He said thank you, so ask him how it feels when someone shares with him.

cards.q: What does this story teach?
cards.note: The ants worked while it was warm, so they had enough to share when it got cold.

cards.q: In the story, what does 'plan ahead' mean?
cards.note: The ants planned ahead when they saved food in the summer for the cold winter.

cards.q: Which word is in the story?
cards.note: He reads the three words himself; only one of them is in the story.

decks.subject: storytime
decks.title: The Crow and the Pitcher
decks.about: Aesop's fable of the thirsty crow who cannot reach the water at the bottom of a pitcher, until she stops to think and drops in stones, one by one, to bring the water up. It shows first graders that a hard problem gets solved by thinking it through and sticking with it, and the trick really works, so they can try it at the kitchen table. It is a public-domain story retold here in first-grade words, four pages long.
decks.tip: Try it: drop pebbles into a glass with a little water in it and watch the water climb, just like in the story.

book.author: Aesop (retold)
book.source: public domain, retold in first-grade words
book.blurb: A thirsty crow, a tall pitcher, and one clever idea.

passage.text:
The sun was hot, and the land was dry.
A crow was very thirsty.
She flew and flew, looking for water.
At last she saw a pitcher.
There was some water in it!
But the water was down low.
She put her beak in.
She could not reach the water.
***
"I will tip it over," said the crow.
She pushed and pushed.
But the pitcher was too heavy.
It did not tip.
"I will break it," she said.
Peck, peck, peck!
But the pitcher was too strong.
It did not break.
The crow sat and thought.
***
Then she saw some little stones.
She had an idea!
She picked up a stone in her beak.
Plop!
She dropped it in the pitcher.
The water came up a little.
She dropped in one more stone.
Plop!
The water came up a little more.
***
Plop, plop, plop!
Stone after stone went in.
Bit by bit, the water came up.
At last it was at the top.
The crow drank and drank.
What a clever crow!
She did not give up.
Think it through, and keep on trying.

cards.q: Who was very thirsty?
cards.note: Crows are some of the smartest birds, and real crows have solved this very puzzle in science tests.

cards.q: What did the crow find with water in it?
cards.note: There was water inside, but it was too far down for her beak to reach.

cards.q: What did the crow drop into the pitcher?
cards.note: Each stone takes up room at the bottom, so the water has to move up.

cards.q: What happened to the water each time a stone went in?
cards.note: Bit by bit, stone by stone, the water rose until it was at the top.

cards.q: What happened first in the story?
cards.note: She found the pitcher, tried to tip it, tried to break it, and only then thought of the stones.

cards.q: What happened at the end of the story?
cards.note: After all that work she finally got her drink, and she drank and drank.

cards.q: What was the crow like?
cards.note: The story calls her a clever crow, because she stopped, thought, and found a better way.

cards.q: What does this story teach?
cards.note: Pushing and pecking did not work, so she thought it through and kept going until it did.

cards.q: In the story, what is a 'pitcher'?
cards.note: A pitcher is a tall jug with a handle and a spout for pouring, like a lemonade jug.

cards.q: Which word is in the story?
cards.note: He reads the three words himself; only one of them is in the story.

decks.subject: storytime
decks.title: Town Mouse, Country Mouse
decks.about: Aesop's fable of the country mouse who goes to town with the town mouse, enjoys a fancy feast until a big dog sends them running to hide, and decides his quiet home is best; in this telling nobody gets hurt. It gives first graders two very different settings to compare and a gentle lesson about what makes a home feel good. It is a public-domain story retold here in first-grade words, four pages long.
decks.tip: Ask: would you rather live in a busy town or on a quiet farm, and why?

book.author: Aesop (retold)
book.source: public domain, retold in first-grade words
book.blurb: Two mice, two very different homes, and one big dog.

passage.text:
Country Mouse lived on a farm.
His home was a little hole under a tree.
It was quiet and calm.
He ate seeds and nuts and corn.
One day, Town Mouse came to visit.
She looked at his food.
"Just seeds and nuts?" she said.
"Come to town with me."
"In town, we eat cake and cheese!"
***
So the two mice went to town.
Town Mouse lived in a big house.
Bang, clang, honk!
Town was very loud.
On the table was a feast.
There was cake and cheese and jam.
"Yum!" said Country Mouse.
The two mice began to eat.
***
Then a big dog ran in.
"Ruff! Ruff!"
"Run!" said Town Mouse.
The mice ran and hid in a hole.
They shook and shook.
At last the dog went away.
The mice were safe.
But Country Mouse did not want more cake.
***
"Is it always like this?" asked Country Mouse.
"Yes," said Town Mouse.
"Then I will go home," said Country Mouse.
"I like my seeds and nuts."
"I like my quiet home."
So he went back to his farm.
He ate his corn and slept well.
A calm, simple home can be best.

cards.q: Who lived in a big house in town?
cards.note: A town is a busy place with lots of houses, people and noise.

cards.q: What did Country Mouse eat at home?
cards.note: Plain farm food, but he liked it; the cake and cheese were in town.

cards.q: Who ran in while the mice were eating?
cards.note: Ruff, ruff: in this telling the mice just run and hide, and nobody gets hurt.

cards.q: What did the mice do when the dog came?
cards.note: They hid in a hole and stayed there until the dog went away.

cards.q: What happened first in the story?
cards.note: The visit to the farm comes first, then the trip to town, then the dog.

cards.q: What happened at the end of the story?
cards.note: He picked his quiet farm over the cake and the noise.

cards.q: How did the mice feel when the dog ran in?
cards.note: They shook and shook, which is how he can tell they were scared even though the story never says it.

cards.q: What does this story teach?
cards.note: Country Mouse had plain food, but his home was calm, and that mattered more to him than cake.

cards.q: In the story, what does 'feast' mean?
cards.note: A feast is lots of good food all at once, like a big holiday dinner.

cards.q: Which word is in the story?
cards.note: He reads the three words himself; only one of them is in the story.

decks.subject: storytime
decks.title: The North Wind and the Sun
decks.about: Aesop's fable of the bragging North Wind and the Sun, who have a contest to see which of them can get a man's coat off: the harder the Wind blows, the tighter the man holds on, but the Sun's gentle warmth does it easily. It gives first graders a clear lesson about being gentle instead of rough, and it is easy to act out. It is a public-domain story retold here in first-grade words, four pages long.
decks.tip: Act it out with a jacket: blow hard while he holds it tight, then be the warm sun and see what he does.

book.author: Aesop (retold)
book.source: public domain, retold in first-grade words
book.blurb: Who can get the coat off, the strong wind or the warm sun?

passage.text:
The North Wind liked to brag.
"I am stronger than you," he said to the Sun.
"Let's find out," said the Sun.
Down below, a man walked on a path.
He had on a big, warm coat.
"Who can get his coat off?" asked the Sun.
"That is easy!" said the Wind.
"I will go first."
***
The Wind blew.
Whoosh!
The man held on to his coat.
The Wind blew harder.
Whoosh! Whoosh!
The man held his coat tight.
The Wind blew as hard as he could.
Leaves flew off the trees.
But the man held his coat tighter and tighter.
At last the Wind gave up.
***
Then it was the Sun's turn.
The Sun did not blow.
The Sun just smiled and shone.
The man felt warm.
He let go of his coat.
The Sun shone some more.
"It is so hot!" said the man.
He took off his coat.
He sat down in the shade to rest.
***
The Sun had won!
The Wind's mouth fell open.
"How did you do that?" he asked.
"I did not blow or push," said the Sun.
"I was just gentle and warm."
"Then the man took off his coat by himself."
The Wind did not brag after that.
Gentle and kind works better than rough and strong.

cards.q: Who said, 'I am stronger than you'?
cards.note: The North Wind is the cold wind that blows down from the north in winter.

cards.q: What did the Wind and the Sun want the man to take off?
cards.note: The coat is the whole contest: whoever gets it off wins.

cards.q: What did the man do when the Wind blew?
cards.note: The harder the wind blew, the tighter he held on, so the Wind only made things worse.

cards.q: What did the Sun do to win?
cards.note: The warm sunshine made the man so hot that he took the coat off by himself.

cards.q: What happened first in the story?
cards.note: The bragging starts it all, before the contest even begins.

cards.q: What happened at the end of the story?
cards.note: The man took his coat off for the Sun, so the Sun won and the Wind stopped bragging.

cards.q: How did the Wind feel when the man took off his coat?
cards.note: His mouth fell open, so ask him to make the surprised face the Wind made.

cards.q: What does this story teach?
cards.note: Pushing hard only made the man hold on tighter, but being gentle got the job done.

cards.q: In the story, what does 'brag' mean?
cards.note: To brag is to tell everyone how great you are, the way the Wind did at the start.

cards.q: Which word is in the story?
cards.note: He reads the three words himself; only one of them is in the story.

decks.subject: storytime
decks.title: The Little Red Hen
decks.about: The folk tale of the hard-working hen whose friends will not help plant, cut or bake, and then all want to eat the bread. Most first graders already know it from kindergarten read-alouds, which makes it a good story to read on their own: a known plot and lines that repeat on every page. It is a public-domain story retold here in first-grade words, four pages long.
decks.tip: Let him be the cat, the dog and the pig and say Not I in a different lazy voice each time.

book.author: a folk tale (retold)
book.source: public domain, retold in first-grade words
book.blurb: Nobody wants to help, but everybody wants bread.

passage.text:
A little red hen lived on a farm.
She lived with a cat, a dog, and a pig.
One day she found some wheat seeds.
"Who will help me plant the wheat?" she asked.
"Not I," said the cat.
"Not I," said the dog.
"Not I," said the pig.
"Then I will do it myself," said the hen.
And she did.
***
The wheat grew tall.
"Who will help me cut the wheat?" she asked.
"Not I," said the cat.
"Not I," said the dog.
"Not I," said the pig.
"Then I will do it myself," said the hen.
And she did.
She took the wheat to the mill.
The mill made it into flour.
***
"Who will help me bake the bread?" she asked.
"Not I," said the cat.
"Not I," said the dog.
"Not I," said the pig.
"Then I will do it myself," said the hen.
And she did.
The bread smelled so good.
***
"Who will help me eat the bread?" she asked.
"I will!" said the cat.
"I will!" said the dog.
"I will!" said the pig.
"No," said the hen.
"You did not help me."
"So I will eat it myself."
And she did.
She ate it with her little chicks.
Yum!
If you want to share, you have to help.

cards.q: Who found the wheat seeds?
cards.note: Everything in the story starts with the hen finding those seeds.

cards.q: What did the cat say when the hen asked for help?
cards.note: The cat, the dog and the pig all say the same two words, every time.

cards.q: Where did the little red hen live?
cards.note: A farm is where wheat can be planted and grown.

cards.q: What did the hen make with the flour?
cards.note: Seeds, then wheat, then flour, then bread: ask him to say the steps in order.

cards.q: What happened first in the story?
cards.note: First seeds, then tall wheat, then flour, then bread.

cards.q: What happened at the end of the story?
cards.note: She shared it with her chicks, not with the friends who would not help.

cards.q: How did the cat, dog and pig act when asked to help?
cards.note: Ask what the three friends could have done differently.

cards.q: What does this story teach?
cards.note: If you want to share the good part, you have to share the work.

cards.q: In the story, what is a 'mill'?
cards.note: A mill grinds wheat seeds into flour; long ago a big wheel did the grinding.

cards.q: Which word is in the story?
cards.note: He reads the three words himself; only one of them is in the story.

decks.subject: storytime
decks.title: The Three Little Pigs
decks.about: The folk tale of three pigs and their houses of straw, sticks and bricks, told gently: the wolf runs out of puff and runs away, and nobody is eaten. Every first grader knows it, and the repeating chant is perfect for practicing reading with expression (RF.1.4). It is a public-domain story retold here in first-grade words, four pages long.
decks.tip: Read the wolf's lines together in a big huffy voice, then ask which house he would build and why.

book.author: a folk tale (retold)
book.source: public domain, retold in first-grade words
book.blurb: Three houses and one puffed-out wolf.

passage.text:
Once there were three little pigs.
It was time to make their own homes.
The first pig made a house of straw.
It was quick to make.
The second pig made a house of sticks.
It was quick to make, too.
The third pig made a house of bricks.
It took a long time.
But it was strong.
***
A wolf came to the straw house.
"Little pig, little pig, let me in!"
"No, no, not by the hair on my chin!"
"Then I'll huff and puff and blow your house in!"
The wolf huffed and puffed.
The straw house fell down.
The first pig ran to the stick house.
***
The wolf came to the stick house.
"Little pig, little pig, let me in!"
"No, no, not by the hair on my chin!"
"Then I'll huff and puff and blow your house in!"
The wolf huffed and puffed.
The stick house fell down.
The two pigs ran to the brick house.
***
The wolf came to the brick house.
"Little pig, little pig, let me in!"
"No, no, not by the hair on my chin!"
"Then I'll huff and puff and blow your house in!"
The wolf huffed and puffed.
The brick house did not fall!
The wolf was all out of puff.
He ran away.
The pigs were safe and snug.
Take your time and do the job well.

cards.q: Who made a house of bricks?
cards.note: The third pig took the longest, and his house was the strongest.

cards.q: What was the first pig's house made of?
cards.note: Straw is dry yellow grass stems; it is quick to build with but very light.

cards.q: What did the wolf do to the straw house?
cards.note: One huff and one puff and the straw house fell down.

cards.q: Which house stayed up?
cards.note: Bricks are heavy blocks of baked clay, far too heavy to blow over.

cards.q: What happened first in the story?
cards.note: All three houses are built on the first page, before the wolf shows up.

cards.q: What happened at the end of the story?
cards.note: In this telling the wolf just runs out of puff and leaves.

cards.q: How did the pigs feel inside the brick house?
cards.note: The story says safe and snug; ask what makes him feel safe and snug at home.

cards.q: What does this story teach?
cards.note: The quick houses fell; the one that took time and work stood up.

cards.q: In the story, what does 'huffed and puffed' mean?
cards.note: Huff and puff together at a tissue and watch it fly, then try it on a book.

cards.q: Which word is in the story?
cards.note: He reads the three words himself; only one of them is in the story.

decks.subject: storytime
decks.title: The Gingerbread Man
decks.about: The folk tale of the cookie who runs away from everyone until a sly fox offers him a ride across the river, told lightly: the fox eats the cookie in one bite and says yum. The repeating chant Run, run, as fast as you can makes it one of the easiest stories to read with expression. It is a public-domain story retold here in first-grade words, four pages long.
decks.tip: Ask: why did the Gingerbread Man trust the fox when he ran away from everyone else?

book.author: a folk tale (retold)
book.source: public domain, retold in first-grade words
book.blurb: A runaway cookie meets a sly fox.

passage.text:
A little old woman made a cookie.
It was a gingerbread man.
She put him in the oven to bake.
When she opened the oven, he jumped out!
He ran out the door.
"Run, run, as fast as you can!"
"You can't catch me, I'm the Gingerbread Man!"
The old woman ran after him.
But she could not catch him.
***
He ran past a cow.
"Stop!" said the cow.
"I want a bite!"
"Run, run, as fast as you can!"
"You can't catch me, I'm the Gingerbread Man!"
The cow ran after him.
But she could not catch him.
***
He ran past a horse.
"Stop!" said the horse.
"I want a bite!"
"Run, run, as fast as you can!"
"You can't catch me, I'm the Gingerbread Man!"
The horse ran after him.
But he could not catch him.
Then he came to a river.
He could not swim.
***
A fox came by.
"Hop on my tail," said the fox.
"I will take you across."
He hopped on.
"The water is deep," said the fox.
"Hop up on my back."
"Now hop up on my nose."
He hopped up on the fox's nose.
Snap!
The fox gobbled him up in one bite.
"Yum!" said the fox.
And that was the end of the Gingerbread Man.

cards.q: Who made the Gingerbread Man?
cards.note: Gingerbread is a cookie made with ginger, a spice; smell some if you have it.

cards.q: What did the Gingerbread Man do when the oven opened?
cards.note: Out of the oven, out the door, and the chase begins.

cards.q: What did the cow want?
cards.note: The cow, the horse and the fox all want the same thing.

cards.q: What did the fox tell the Gingerbread Man to do?
cards.note: Tail, then back, then nose: each hop brings the cookie closer to the fox's mouth.

cards.q: What happened first in the story?
cards.note: Baked, ran, cow, horse, river, fox: ask him to say the order on his fingers.

cards.q: What happened at the end of the story?
cards.note: Snap, one bite, yum; that is how the story has always ended.

cards.q: What was the fox like in the story?
cards.note: The fox did not chase; he was sly and got the cookie to come to him.

cards.q: Where did the Gingerbread Man meet the fox?
cards.note: The river is the problem: a cookie cannot swim, and that is why he needed the fox.

cards.q: In the story, what does 'gobbled' mean?
cards.note: To gobble is to eat something fast and all at once, like a hungry turkey.

cards.q: Which word is in the story?
cards.note: He reads the three words himself; only one of them is in the story.

decks.subject: storytime
decks.title: Goldilocks and the Bears
decks.about: The tale of the girl who tries three bowls, three chairs and three beds in the bears' house, with a gentle ending: Goldilocks says sorry and learns to ask first. First graders know this story well, and the big, middle and little pattern makes every page easy to predict and read. It is a public-domain story retold here in first-grade words, five pages long.
decks.tip: Ask him to retell it on three fingers: three bowls, three chairs, three beds, and what happened to each.

book.author: a folk tale (retold)
book.source: public domain, retold in first-grade words
book.blurb: Three bowls, three chairs, three beds and one sorry girl.

passage.text:
Three bears lived in a house in the woods.
There was a big Papa Bear.
There was a middle-sized Mama Bear.
And there was a wee little Baby Bear.
One morning, Mama Bear made porridge.
It was too hot to eat.
So the three bears went for a walk.
***
A girl named Goldilocks came by.
She peeked in the window.
No one was home.
So she went in.
She saw three bowls of porridge.
She tasted the big bowl.
"Too hot!"
She tasted the middle bowl.
"Too cold!"
She tasted the little bowl.
"Just right!"
And she ate it all up.
***
Then she saw three chairs.
The big chair was too hard.
The middle chair was too soft.
The little chair was just right.
Crack!
It broke.
Then she saw three beds.
The big bed was too hard.
The middle bed was too soft.
The little bed was just right.
Goldilocks fell fast asleep.
***
The three bears came home.
"Someone ate my porridge," said Papa Bear.
"Someone ate my porridge," said Mama Bear.
"Someone ate all of my porridge!" said Baby Bear.
"Someone sat in my chair," said Papa Bear.
"Someone broke my chair!" said Baby Bear.
"Someone slept in my bed," said Papa Bear.
"Someone is in my bed right now!" said Baby Bear.
***
Goldilocks woke up.
She saw the three bears.
"Oh my!" she said.
She jumped out of bed.
She ran all the way home.
"I am sorry," she said to her mom.
"That house was not mine."
Ask before you use what is not yours.

cards.q: Who lived in the house in the woods?
cards.note: Papa Bear, Mama Bear and Baby Bear: big, middle and little.

cards.q: Where was the bears' house?
cards.note: The setting is where a story happens; this one is a house in the woods.

cards.q: What did Goldilocks do with Baby Bear's porridge?
cards.note: Too hot, too cold, just right, and then it was gone.

cards.q: What happened to the little chair?
cards.note: Crack! It was just right, until it was not.

cards.q: What happened first in the story?
cards.note: The hot porridge is why the bears went out, and that is why the house was empty.

cards.q: What happened at the end of the story?
cards.note: She ran home and said sorry to her mom.

cards.q: How did Goldilocks feel when she saw the three bears?
cards.note: Oh my! Ask how the bears felt too, coming home to a stranger in a bed.

cards.q: What does this story teach?
cards.note: Ask before you use what is not yours; the last line says it.

cards.q: In the story, what does 'wee' mean?
cards.note: Wee is an old word for tiny; Baby Bear is the wee one.

cards.q: Which word is in the story?
cards.note: He reads the three words himself; only one of them is in the story.

decks.subject: storytime
decks.title: The Mitten
decks.about: The Ukrainian folk tale of an old man who drops a mitten in the snow and the animals who squeeze in one by one, until his dog barks and they all jump out again. It is a cumulative tale with a line that repeats, which makes it easy to read and great for retelling in order. This retelling follows the traditional public-domain folk tale, not any one picture book, in first-grade words, four pages long.
decks.tip: Count the animals on your fingers as they squeeze in, then ask who jumped out first.

book.author: a folk tale (retold)
book.source: public domain, retold in first-grade words
book.blurb: How many animals fit in one lost mitten?

passage.text:
An old man walked in the snowy woods.
His dog walked with him.
The old man dropped a mitten.
He did not see it fall.
He kept on walking.
A little mouse ran by.
She saw the mitten in the snow.
"This looks snug," she said.
She crept in.
***
A frog hopped by.
"Who is in this mitten?" he asked.
"A mouse," said the mouse.
"Let me in, too!"
"Come in, there is room for one more."
A rabbit hopped by.
"Who is in this mitten?" he asked.
"A mouse and a frog."
"Let me in, too!"
"Come in, there is room for one more."
***
A fox trotted by.
"Who is in this mitten?" she asked.
"A mouse, a frog, and a rabbit."
"Let me in, too!"
"Come in, there is room for one more."
A wolf came by.
Then a big bear came by.
"Let us in, too!"
"Come in, there is room for one more."
The mitten was very, very full.
It was warm and snug.
***
The old man looked at his hands.
"Oh no!"
"I lost my mitten!"
He went back to find it.
His dog ran ahead.
"Woof! Woof!"
Out jumped the bear.
Out jumped the wolf and the fox.
Out jumped the rabbit, the frog, and the mouse.
They all ran off into the woods.
The old man picked up his mitten.
It was stretched, but still warm.

cards.q: Who dropped the mitten in the snow?
cards.note: He did not even notice; he just kept on walking.

cards.q: What did the mouse say when she saw the mitten?
cards.note: The mouse is first in; she gets the whole mitten to herself for a minute.

cards.q: What did the old man's dog do?
cards.note: Woof! Woof! The barking is what sends all the animals running.

cards.q: What happened when the animals heard the dog?
cards.note: Out they came, biggest first, and ran off into the woods.

cards.q: What happened first in the story?
cards.note: Lost mitten, then mouse, frog, rabbit, fox, wolf, bear, then the dog.

cards.q: What happened at the end of the story?
cards.note: The old man got his mitten back, stretched out but still warm.

cards.q: How did the old man feel when he lost his mitten?
cards.note: Oh no! Ask how he feels when he loses a glove or a toy.

cards.q: Where did the mouse find the mitten?
cards.note: Snowy woods in winter; that is why a warm mitten is such a find.

cards.q: In the story, what does 'snug' mean?
cards.note: Snug is warm and cozy with no room to spare, like a sleeping bag zipped up.

cards.q: Which word is in the story?
cards.note: He reads the three words himself; only one of them is in the story.

decks.subject: storytime
decks.title: The Three Billy Goats Gruff
decks.about: The Norwegian folk tale of three goats who must cross a grumpy troll's bridge to reach the green grass on the hill; in this telling the big goat butts the troll into the river, and he simply floats away. Three crossings with the same trip, trap and the same questions make it easy to read with expression and to retell in order. It is a public-domain story retold here in first-grade words, five pages long.
decks.tip: Read the goats in three voices, tiny, middle and big, and stamp out every trip, trap with your feet.

book.author: a folk tale from Norway (retold)
book.source: public domain, retold in first-grade words
book.blurb: Three goats, one bridge, and one very grumpy troll.

passage.text:
Once there were three billy goats named Gruff.
One was little.
One was middle-sized.
One was big.
They wanted the green grass on the hill.
To get there, they had to cross a bridge.
And under the bridge lived a grumpy troll.
***
The little goat went first.
Trip, trap! Trip, trap!
"Who is that on my bridge?" roared the troll.
"It is me, the little goat."
"I will gobble you up!" said the troll.
"Please do not eat me," said the little goat.
"Wait for my brother."
"He is much bigger."
"Then go," said the troll.
And over he went.
***
Next the middle goat went.
Trip, trap! Trip, trap!
"Who is that on my bridge?" roared the troll.
"It is me, the middle goat."
"I will gobble you up!" said the troll.
"Please do not eat me," said the middle goat.
"Wait for my big brother."
"He is much, much bigger."
"Then go," said the troll.
And over he went.
***
Then the big goat went.
Trip, trap! Trip, trap!
The bridge shook.
"Who is that on my bridge?" roared the troll.
"It is me, the big goat!"
"I will gobble you up!" said the troll.
"Come and try!" said the big goat.
Up jumped the troll.
The big goat put down his horns.
Bump!
He butted the troll off the bridge.
***
Splash!
The troll fell into the river.
He floated far, far away.
The big goat trip-trapped over the bridge.
All three goats went up the hill.
They ate and ate the sweet green grass.
Munch, munch, munch!
And the grumpy troll never came back.

cards.q: Who said, 'Who is that on my bridge?'
cards.note: The troll asks the same thing three times, so read it in a big, grumpy voice.

cards.q: What did the goats want to eat?
cards.note: The best grass was on the hill, and the only way there was over the troll's bridge.

cards.q: What did the little goat tell the troll to do?
cards.note: The two smaller goats each send the troll on to a bigger brother, which is a clever way to get across.

cards.q: Where did the troll fall?
cards.note: Splash: in this telling he just floats far away and never comes back.

cards.q: What happened first in the story?
cards.note: Little, then middle, then big: the goats cross from smallest to biggest.

cards.q: What happened at the end of the story?
cards.note: All three goats got to the hill at last and ate the sweet green grass.

cards.q: What was the troll like?
cards.note: The story calls him grumpy, and he roars every time a goat steps on his bridge.

cards.q: Where did the troll live?
cards.note: Most of the story happens on that bridge, so ask him to draw it with the troll underneath.

cards.q: In the story, what does 'butted' mean?
cards.note: Goats butt with their heads and horns; press your forehead gently on his hand to show him.

cards.q: Which word is in the story?
cards.note: He reads the three words himself; only one of them is in the story.

decks.subject: storytime
decks.title: The Enormous Turnip
decks.about: The Russian folk tale of a turnip so enormous that Grandpa, Grandma, a girl, a dog, a cat and at last a tiny mouse all have to pull together to get it out of the ground. The chain repeats and grows by one helper at a time, which makes it easy to read along, to retell in order and to see the lesson that even the smallest helper counts. It is a public-domain story retold here in first-grade words, five pages long.
decks.tip: Line up stuffed animals and act it out, adding one helper at a time until the turnip pops out.

book.author: a folk tale from Russia (retold)
book.source: public domain, retold in first-grade words
book.blurb: A turnip so big that it takes everyone, even a mouse, to pull it up.

passage.text:
Grandpa planted a turnip seed.
"Grow, little turnip, grow!" he said.
"Grow big and sweet!"
The turnip grew and grew.
It grew big.
It grew bigger.
It grew enormous!
One day, Grandpa went to pull it up.
***
Grandpa pulled and pulled.
But the turnip did not come up.
He called Grandma to help.
Grandma pulled Grandpa.
Grandpa pulled the turnip.
They pulled and pulled.
But the turnip did not come up.
Grandma called the girl to help.
***
The girl pulled Grandma.
Grandma pulled Grandpa.
Grandpa pulled the turnip.
They pulled and pulled.
But the turnip did not come up.
The girl called the dog to help.
The dog pulled the girl.
The girl pulled Grandma.
Grandma pulled Grandpa.
Grandpa pulled the turnip.
They pulled and pulled.
But the turnip did not come up.
***
The dog called the cat to help.
The cat pulled the dog.
The dog pulled the girl.
The girl pulled Grandma.
Grandma pulled Grandpa.
Grandpa pulled the turnip.
They pulled and pulled.
But the turnip did not come up!
The cat called a little mouse.
"I can help!" said the mouse.
***
The mouse pulled the cat.
The cat pulled the dog.
The dog pulled the girl.
The girl pulled Grandma.
Grandma pulled Grandpa.
Grandpa pulled the turnip.
They pulled and pulled and pulled.
Pop!
Up came the turnip!
They all fell down in a heap.
"I helped!" said the little mouse.
That night, they all had turnip soup.
Even the smallest helper matters.

cards.q: Who planted the turnip seed?
cards.note: A turnip is a round root vegetable that grows under the ground, like a carrot.

cards.q: Who came to help last?
cards.note: The mouse is the smallest helper of all, and she comes last.

cards.q: What did they all have that night?
cards.note: Turnips are often cooked in soups and stews.

cards.q: What happened when the turnip came up?
cards.note: Everyone tumbled into a heap, so act it out with a tug and a soft landing on a pillow.

cards.q: What happened first in the story?
cards.note: A seed, then an enormous turnip, then one helper after another.

cards.q: What happened at the end of the story?
cards.note: It took every helper, right down to the mouse, to pull it out.

cards.q: How did the mouse feel when the turnip came up?
cards.note: The mouse shouts that she helped, so ask him about a time he helped with a big job.

cards.q: What does this story teach?
cards.note: The turnip only came up when the tiny mouse joined in.

cards.q: In the story, what does 'enormous' mean?
cards.note: Enormous is even bigger than big, so stretch your arms as wide as they will go.

cards.q: Which word is in the story?
cards.note: He reads the three words himself; only one of them is in the story.

decks.subject: storytime
decks.title: Stone Soup
decks.about: The folk tale of three hungry travelers who make soup from a stone, until the whole town has added a carrot, an onion, some beans and more, and everyone sits down to eat together. The same lines repeat as each new food goes in, so the story is easy to predict and read, and it opens a good talk about sharing. It is a public-domain story retold here in first-grade words, four pages long.
decks.tip: Make a pretend pot of stone soup together and ask what he would put in to share.

book.author: a folk tale (retold)
book.source: public domain, retold in first-grade words
book.blurb: One stone, one pot, and a whole town that shares.

passage.text:
Three hungry travelers walked down a long road.
They came to a little town.
"May we have some food?" they asked.
"We have no food," said the people.
They shut their doors.
But the people did have food.
They just did not want to share.
"Then we will make stone soup!" said the travelers.
***
They got a big pot.
They filled it with water.
They made a fire under it.
Then they dropped in one round stone.
The people came out to look.
"What are you making?" asked a girl.
"Stone soup," said the travelers.
"It is very good."
"But it is better with a carrot."
"I have a carrot!" said the girl.
In went the carrot!
***
"It is better with an onion," said the travelers.
"I have an onion!" said a man.
In went the onion!
"It is better with some beans."
"I have beans!" said a woman.
In went the beans!
Then a boy came with potatoes.
A grandma came with salt.
One by one, the people came.
Each one put in a little bit.
The soup smelled so good!
***
At last the soup was ready.
The people got bowls and spoons.
They all sat down at one long table.
There was lots of soup for everyone.
They ate and sang and laughed.
"This is the best soup!" said the girl.
"And it is made from a stone!"
The travelers just smiled.
When everyone shares a little, there is plenty for all.

cards.q: Who came walking down the long road?
cards.note: A traveler is someone on a trip; these three had walked a long road and were very hungry.

cards.q: Where did the travelers make their soup?
cards.note: The setting is a little town where everyone has food but nobody wants to share it.

cards.q: What did the travelers say they would make?
cards.note: Stone soup sounds silly, and that is just what made the people come out to look.

cards.q: What did the girl put in the soup?
cards.note: First a carrot, then an onion, beans, potatoes and salt: each person adds one thing.

cards.q: What happened first in the story?
cards.note: The travelers ask for food first, and the people say they have none.

cards.q: What happened at the end of the story?
cards.note: The whole town sat down at one long table and shared the soup.

cards.q: How did everyone feel at the long table?
cards.note: They ate and sang and laughed: the story shows it without saying the word.

cards.q: What does this story teach?
cards.note: When everyone shares a little, there is plenty for all; the last line says it.

cards.q: In the story, what does 'plenty' mean?
cards.note: Plenty means more than enough, like a pot of soup big enough for a whole town.

cards.q: Which word is in the story?
cards.note: He reads the three words himself; only one of them is in the story.

decks.subject: storytime
decks.title: The Elves and the Shoemaker
decks.about: The Brothers Grimm's tale of a poor shoemaker who finds his shoes finished every morning, and of the thank-you he and his wife make for the two tiny elves who did the work. First graders love the secret night-time helpers and the night-then-morning pattern, and the ending is a gentle lesson in saying thank you. It is a public-domain story retold here in first-grade words, five pages long.
decks.tip: Tap, tap, tap like the elves, then ask how the shoemaker and his wife said thank you.

book.author: the Brothers Grimm (retold)
book.source: public domain, retold in first-grade words
book.blurb: Two tiny elves, a lot of shoes, and a big thank-you.

passage.text:
Once there was a kind shoemaker.
He and his wife were very poor.
One night, he had one last bit of leather.
It was just enough for one pair of shoes.
He cut it out and set it on his bench.
"I will make the shoes in the morning," he said.
Then he went to bed.
***
In the morning, he got a big surprise.
The shoes were all done!
Every stitch was neat and tiny.
A man came in and bought them.
He paid a lot of money.
Now the shoemaker could get leather for two pairs.
That night, he cut it out and went to bed.
In the morning, two pairs of shoes were done!
***
This went on, night after night.
Soon they were not poor at all.
"Who is making our shoes?" asked his wife.
"Let's hide and see," said the shoemaker.
At midnight, two little elves came in.
They had no warm clothes.
Tap, tap, tap went their tiny hammers.
They made shoes all night long.
Then they ran out into the cold.
***
"The elves helped us," said the wife.
"But they looked so cold."
"Let's make them warm clothes to say thank you."
She made two tiny shirts and two tiny coats.
He made two pairs of tiny shoes.
That night, they set the gifts on the bench.
Then they hid to watch.
***
At midnight, the elves came in.
They saw the tiny clothes.
"Are these for us?" they asked.
They put them on.
"Look at us!" they sang.
They danced all over the room.
Then they danced out the door.
The shoemaker and his wife smiled.
When someone is kind to you, say thank you.

cards.q: Who made the shoes at night?
cards.note: The shoemaker and his wife hid and saw them come in at midnight.

cards.q: Where did the shoemaker set the leather?
cards.note: A shoemaker works at a bench, a strong table for cutting and sewing.

cards.q: What was the big surprise in the morning?
cards.note: Every stitch neat and tiny, and nobody saw who did it.

cards.q: What did the shoemaker and his wife make for the elves?
cards.note: Tiny shirts, tiny coats and two pairs of tiny shoes, because the elves looked so cold.

cards.q: What happened first in the story?
cards.note: One last bit of leather, cut out and left on the bench: that is where it all starts.

cards.q: What happened at the end of the story?
cards.note: Warm at last, the elves danced right out the door.

cards.q: How did the elves feel in their new clothes?
cards.note: They sang and danced: the story shows it without saying the word.

cards.q: What does this story teach?
cards.note: When someone is kind to you, say thank you; the tiny clothes were the shoemaker's thank-you.

cards.q: In the story, what does 'midnight' mean?
cards.note: Midnight is twelve o'clock at night, the middle of the night, when everyone is asleep.

cards.q: Which word is in the story?
cards.note: He reads the three words himself; only one of them is in the story.

decks.subject: storytime
decks.title: Little Red Riding Hood
decks.about: The old folk tale of the girl in the red hood and the wolf in Grandma's cap, told gently: Grandma hides in her closet, Red calls for help, a woodcutter chases the wolf far away, and nobody is eaten. The famous What big eyes you have lines are perfect for reading with expression, and the story carries a clear safety lesson about staying on the path and not talking to strangers. It is a public-domain story retold here in first-grade words, five pages long.
decks.tip: Take turns being Red and the wolf on the big eyes, big ears, big teeth page, then ask what Red should have done in the woods.

book.author: a folk tale from Europe (retold)
book.source: public domain, retold in first-grade words
book.blurb: A red hood, a basket, and a wolf in Grandma's cap.

passage.text:
Once there was a girl named Little Red Riding Hood.
She always wore a red cape with a hood.
One day, Mom packed a basket of muffins.
"Take this to Grandma," said Mom.
"She is sick in bed."
"Stay on the path."
"And do not talk to strangers."
"Yes, Mom," said Red.
***
Red went into the woods.
Soon she met a big gray wolf.
"Where are you going?" asked the wolf.
Red forgot what Mom said.
"To see Grandma," she said.
"Pick her some flowers," said the wolf.
So Red left the path to pick flowers.
The wolf ran off to Grandma's house.
***
Grandma looked out her window.
She saw the wolf coming!
She hid in her closet.
The wolf came in.
He put on Grandma's cap.
He got into her bed.
He pulled the covers up to his nose.
Knock, knock!
"Come in, dear," said the wolf.
Red came in with her flowers.
***
"Grandma, what big eyes you have!" said Red.
"All the better to see you with," said the wolf.
"Grandma, what big ears you have!"
"All the better to hear you with."
"Grandma, what big teeth you have!"
Red looked again.
That was not Grandma!
It was the wolf!
"Help, help!" she yelled.
***
A woodcutter was cutting wood near the house.
He heard Red yell and ran in.
The wolf jumped out of bed.
He ran out the door.
The woodcutter chased him far, far away.
The wolf never came back.
Then Grandma came out of her closet.
She was safe!
Red gave her a big hug.
They ate muffins together.
Stay on the path and do not talk to strangers.

cards.q: Who did Red meet in the woods?
cards.note: Red forgot what Mom said and talked to him, and he was a stranger.

cards.q: Where was Red taking the basket?
cards.note: Grandma was sick in bed, so Mom packed a basket of muffins for her.

cards.q: Where did Grandma hide from the wolf?
cards.note: She saw him coming from her window and hid in time; nobody gets eaten in this telling.

cards.q: What did the woodcutter do?
cards.note: He chased the wolf far, far away, and it never came back.

cards.q: What happened first in the story?
cards.note: The basket and Mom's two rules come first: stay on the path, and do not talk to strangers.

cards.q: What happened at the end of the story?
cards.note: Grandma came out of the closet, and they ate the muffins together.

cards.q: How did Red feel when she saw Grandma was safe?
cards.note: She gave Grandma a big hug; ask how he feels when a scare is over.

cards.q: What does this story teach?
cards.note: Stay on the path and do not talk to strangers; Red's trouble began when she forgot both.

cards.q: In the story, who are 'strangers'?
cards.note: A stranger is anyone he does not know; it is a good moment to name his safe grown-ups.

cards.q: Which word is in the story?
cards.note: He reads the three words himself; only one of them is in the story.

decks.subject: storytime
decks.title: Anansi and the Pot of Wisdom
decks.about: A folk tale from Ghana about Anansi the spider, who tries to keep all the wisdom in the world in one pot at the top of a tree, until his little son shows him a better way to climb. Anansi stories are some of the best-loved folk tales of West Africa, and this one explains, the way folk tales do, why everyone has a little wisdom. It is a public-domain story retold here in first-grade words, five pages long.
decks.tip: Let him tuck a pillow under his shirt and crawl across the room, then try it on his back, and ask whose idea worked better.

book.author: a folk tale from Ghana (retold)
book.source: public domain, retold in first-grade words
book.blurb: A clever spider tries to keep all the wisdom for himself.

passage.text:
Long ago, there was a spider named Anansi.
Anansi wanted to be the smartest of all.
"I want all the wisdom in the world!" he said.
So he went all over the land.
He took every bit of wisdom he could find.
He put it all in one big pot.
***
"This wisdom is all for me," said Anansi.
"I will hide it at the top of a tree."
He tied the pot on his tummy.
Then he began to climb.
Bump, bump, bump!
The pot hit his tummy.
He slid back down.
***
Anansi tried again.
Bump, bump, bump!
He slid back down again.
He tried and tried.
Anansi got hot and grumpy.
His little son was watching.
"Father," said his son.
"Tie the pot on your back."
"Then you can climb up."
***
Anansi tied the pot on his back.
Up, up, up he went!
At the top, he stopped.
"My little son had a good idea," he said.
"I do not have all the wisdom after all!"
Anansi was so surprised that he let go.
The pot fell down, down, down.
Crash!
***
The pot broke into bits.
All the wisdom spilled out.
The wind blew it all over the world.
That is why we all have a little wisdom.
Nobody knows everything, and good ideas can come from anyone.

cards.q: Who wanted all the wisdom in the world?
cards.note: Anansi stories come from Ghana, in West Africa, and Anansi is often a clever trickster.

cards.q: Where did Anansi want to hide the pot?
cards.note: At the top of a tree, where nobody else could get it.

cards.q: What kept bumping Anansi's tummy?
cards.note: He tied the pot on his front, so it bumped him every time he tried to climb.

cards.q: Where did the little son say to tie the pot?
cards.note: With the pot on his back, Anansi could climb right up.

cards.q: What happened first in the story?
cards.note: He went all over the land and put every bit of wisdom in one big pot.

cards.q: What happened at the end of the story?
cards.note: The pot broke, and the wind blew the wisdom all over the world.

cards.q: How did Anansi feel when he saw his son was right?
cards.note: So surprised he let go of the pot; ask why a little son's idea surprised him so much.

cards.q: What does this story teach?
cards.note: Nobody knows everything, and good ideas can come from anyone, even the littlest one.

cards.q: In the story, what does 'wisdom' mean?
cards.note: Wisdom is knowing a lot and making good choices; Anansi wanted to be the smartest of all.

cards.q: Which word is in the story?
cards.note: He reads the three words himself; only one of them is in the story.

decks.subject: storytime
decks.title: Jack and the Beanstalk
decks.about: The English folk tale of the boy who trades his cow for five magic beans, climbs the beanstalk to a giant's castle and brings home the hen that lays golden eggs. First graders love the climb, the chant of fee, fi, fo, fum and chopping down the beanstalk, and the story is a good one for talking about brave choices and careful trades. In this softened telling nobody is hurt and the giant simply stays grumbling up in the clouds; it is a public-domain story retold in first-grade words, five pages long.
decks.tip: Ask: was one old cow for five beans a good trade, and how did it turn out in the end?

book.author: a folk tale from England (retold)
book.source: public domain, retold in first-grade words
book.blurb: Five magic beans, one tall beanstalk, and a grumpy giant.

passage.text:
Once there was a boy named Jack.
He lived with his mother.
They were very poor.
All they had was one old cow.
"Take the cow to market," said his mother.
"Sell her for some money."
On the way, Jack met a man.
"I will trade you for that cow," said the man.
"Five magic beans!"
So Jack made the trade.
***
"Beans?" said his mother.
"Oh, Jack! We needed that money."
She tossed the beans out the window.
In the night, the beans began to grow.
They grew and grew and grew.
In the morning, Jack saw a giant beanstalk.
It went up, up, up into the clouds!
Jack climbed it to the very top.
***
At the top was a huge castle.
Jack crept inside.
"Fee, fi, fo, fum!" boomed a giant.
"I smell a boy!"
He was big and grumpy.
Jack hid behind a big pot.
The giant sat down.
"Hen, lay!" he said.
A little hen laid a golden egg.
Jack knew that hen!
She was his family's hen.
The giant had taken her long ago.
***
Soon the giant fell asleep.
Jack tiptoed out.
He picked up the hen.
"Come home with me," he whispered.
Then he ran for the beanstalk.
"Cluck!" said the hen.
The giant woke up.
"Who took my hen?" he roared.
Jack climbed down as fast as he could.
The giant looked down.
The beanstalk was much too thin for him.
***
Jack got to the bottom.
"Mother! Get the axe!" he called.
Chop, chop, chop!
Down came the beanstalk.
Far up in the clouds, the giant grumbled.
"Humph!" he said.
He never came down.
Jack gave the hen to his mother.
"She lays golden eggs," he said.
Now they were never poor again.
Be brave, and think before you trade.

cards.q: What did Jack trade the cow for?
cards.note: His mother was upset, because they needed the money, and she tossed the beans out the window.

cards.q: What grew outside the window in the night?
cards.note: The beans grew and grew until the beanstalk reached up into the clouds.

cards.q: What did the little hen lay?
cards.note: Hen, lay, said the giant, and out came a golden egg.

cards.q: What did Jack take from the giant?
cards.note: The hen had been his family's hen all along, and the giant had taken her long ago.

cards.q: What happened first in the story?
cards.note: Everything starts with the trade on the way to market.

cards.q: What happened at the end of the story?
cards.note: Chop, chop, chop, and the giant stayed up in the clouds while Jack and his mother were never poor again.

cards.q: What was the giant like?
cards.note: He booms fee, fi, fo, fum, roars when his hen is gone, and grumbles when he cannot follow.

cards.q: What does this story teach?
cards.note: Be brave, and think before you trade; the last line says it.

cards.q: In the story, what does 'crept' mean?
cards.note: Jack crept into the castle so the giant would not hear him.

cards.q: Which word is in the story?
cards.note: He reads the three words himself; only one of them is in the story.

decks.subject: storytime
decks.title: Henny Penny
decks.about: The old English folk tale, also told as Chicken Little, about the hen who is bonked by an acorn, decides the sky is falling and sets off to tell the king with a line of friends behind her. The rhyming names and repeated lines make it a favorite for reading aloud, and it is a gentle way to talk about checking a scary story before you believe it. In this softened telling a wise owl stops everyone at the fox's den and shows them the acorn; it is a public-domain story retold in first-grade words, five pages long.
decks.tip: Ask: what should Henny Penny have done before she ran off to tell the king?

book.author: a folk tale from England (retold)
book.source: public domain, retold in first-grade words
book.blurb: One acorn, one worried hen, and a long line of friends.

passage.text:
One day Henny Penny was pecking in the yard.
Plop!
An acorn fell on her head.
"Oh, my!" said Henny Penny.
She was scared.
"The sky is falling!"
"I must go and tell the king."
On the way she met Cocky Locky.
"The sky is falling!" said Henny Penny.
"I am going to tell the king."
"I will come, too," said Cocky Locky.
***
Soon they met Ducky Lucky.
"The sky is falling!" said Henny Penny.
"We are going to tell the king."
"I will come, too," said Ducky Lucky.
Then they met Turkey Lurkey.
"Where are you going?" he asked.
"The sky is falling!" said Henny Penny.
"We are going to tell the king."
"I will come, too," said Turkey Lurkey.
Off they all went.
***
Then they met Foxy Loxy.
"Where are you going?" he asked.
"The sky is falling!" said Henny Penny.
"We are going to tell the king."
Foxy Loxy smiled a sly smile.
"I know a short way," he said.
"Come into my den."
"Oh, thank you," said Henny Penny.
And they all walked toward the den.
***
"Stop!" called a voice from a tree.
It was a wise old owl.
"Stay out of that den!"
"Henny Penny, did you look up?" asked the owl.
"No," said Henny Penny.
The owl held up a little brown acorn.
"This is an acorn," he said.
"Acorns fall from oak trees."
"One fell on your head."
"The sky is just fine."
***
Henny Penny looked up.
The sky was blue and still.
"It was only an acorn," she said.
Foxy Loxy gave a huff and ran off.
"Thank you, Owl," said Henny Penny.
Then they all went home for supper.
Henny Penny, Cocky Locky, Ducky Lucky, and Turkey Lurkey.
Nobody told the king.
Check before you believe a scary story.

cards.q: What fell on Henny Penny's head?
cards.note: Plop, one little brown acorn from the oak tree, and she never looked up to check.

cards.q: Who did Henny Penny want to tell?
cards.note: She was sure the sky was falling and that the king had to know.

cards.q: Where did Foxy Loxy want them to go?
cards.note: He smiled a sly smile and said it was a short way to the king.

cards.q: Who stopped them at the fox's den?
cards.note: The owl called stop from a tree and showed everyone what had really fallen.

cards.q: What happened first in the story?
cards.note: The whole story starts with one plop on Henny Penny's head.

cards.q: What happened at the end of the story?
cards.note: Nobody told the king, and they all went home for supper instead.

cards.q: How did Henny Penny feel when the acorn hit her head?
cards.note: She was so scared she did not stop to look at what had hit her.

cards.q: What does this story teach?
cards.note: Check before you believe a scary story; the last line says it.

cards.q: In the story, what does 'sly' mean?
cards.note: A sly fox is a tricky one, and his short way to the king was really a trick.

cards.q: Which word is in the story?
cards.note: He reads the three words himself; only one of them is in the story.

decks.subject: storytime
decks.title: The Bremen Town Musicians
decks.about: The Brothers Grimm's tale of a donkey, a dog, a cat and a rooster who are all too old to be wanted, so they set off together to be musicians in the town of Bremen. First graders love the growing chorus of hee-haw, woof, meow and cock-a-doodle-doo, the animal pile-up at the window and the robbers who run from a noise, and the ending says plainly that friends who work together are never too old to help. It is a public-domain story retold here in first-grade words, five pages long.
decks.tip: Say the four animal sounds together, louder each time, then ask why the robbers ran away.

book.author: the Brothers Grimm (retold)
book.source: public domain, retold in first-grade words
book.blurb: Four old friends, one big noise, and a snug new home.

passage.text:
Once there was an old donkey.
He was too old to carry sacks.
"No one needs me now," he said sadly.
"I will go to Bremen and be a musician."
Soon he met an old dog.
"I am too old to hunt," said the dog.
"Come with me!" said the donkey.
"We will be musicians in Bremen!"
Hee-haw! Woof!
***
Next they met an old cat.
"I am too old to catch mice," said the cat.
"Come with us!" said the donkey.
"We will be musicians in Bremen!"
Then they met an old rooster.
"No one wants me on the farm," said the rooster.
"Come with us!" said the cat.
"We will be musicians in Bremen!"
Hee-haw! Woof! Meow! Cock-a-doodle-doo!
***
Night came.
The four friends were tired and hungry.
Then they saw a light in the woods.
It was a little cottage.
They peeked in the window.
Three robbers sat at a big table.
They had bread and cheese and cake!
"I have a plan," said the donkey.
"Let's make some music."
***
The dog got on the donkey's back.
The cat got on the dog's back.
The rooster got on top of the cat.
Then they all sang at once.
Hee-haw! Woof! Meow! Cock-a-doodle-doo!
What a terrible noise!
The robbers jumped up.
"What is that?" they yelled.
They ran far, far away.
They never came back.
***
The four friends went inside.
They ate the bread and cheese and cake.
The cat slept by the warm fire.
The rooster slept up on a beam.
They never did get to Bremen.
But they did not mind.
They stayed in the snug cottage.
Friends who work together are never too old to help.

cards.q: What was the donkey too old to do?
cards.note: An old donkey cannot carry heavy sacks any more, so he sets off to make music instead.

cards.q: Where did the four friends want to go?
cards.note: Bremen is a town; the four friends head there to sing for their supper, though they never arrive.

cards.q: Who stood at the very top?
cards.note: Donkey, then dog, then cat, then rooster: the smallest climbs on top.

cards.q: What did the robbers do when they heard the noise?
cards.note: They never found out that the terrible noise was four old animals saying hello.

cards.q: What happened first in the story?
cards.note: Too old to carry sacks, the donkey leaves home to be a musician; everything else follows.

cards.q: What happened at the end of the story?
cards.note: They never reached Bremen and did not mind: they had a snug cottage and each other.

cards.q: How did the donkey feel at the start?
cards.note: Nobody needed him any more; ask what cheered him up again.

cards.q: What does this story teach?
cards.note: Alone, each friend was too old to be wanted; together they won a warm home.

cards.q: In the story, what is a 'musician'?
cards.note: A musician makes music by singing or playing; the friends plan to sing for their supper.

cards.q: Which word is in the story?
cards.note: He reads the three words himself; only one of them is in the story.

decks.subject: storytime
decks.title: The Frog Prince
decks.about: The Brothers Grimm's tale of a princess who promises a frog her friendship if he fetches her golden ball from the well, then has to be reminded by her father the king that a promise is a promise; in the morning the frog turns out to be a prince. First graders enjoy the splash, the knock at the door and the frog at the dinner table, and the story ends with its lesson said plainly: keep your promises. This gentle retelling, without the thrown frog of some versions, is a public-domain story in first-grade words, five pages long.
decks.tip: Ask what the princess promised the frog, and what the king said when she did not want to keep it.

book.author: the Brothers Grimm (retold)
book.source: public domain, retold in first-grade words
book.blurb: A golden ball, a deep well, and a promise to keep.

passage.text:
Once there was a princess.
She had a golden ball.
It was her best toy.
Every day she played by a deep well.
She tossed the ball up high.
One day she missed it.
Splash!
The ball fell into the well.
"Oh no!" cried the princess.
"My ball is gone!"
She sat by the well and cried.
***
"I can get it," said a voice.
It was a big green frog.
"But first you must promise," said the frog.
"Be my friend."
"Let me eat from your plate."
"Let me sleep on your pillow."
"Yes, yes, I promise!" said the princess.
The frog dove down and got the ball.
The princess grabbed it and ran home.
She forgot all about the frog.
***
That night, the princess sat down to eat.
Hop, hop, hop!
Something came up the steps.
Knock, knock!
"Princess! Princess! You made a promise!"
It was the frog.
The princess did not want to let him in.
"What is this?" asked the king.
She told him about the promise.
"A promise is a promise," said the king.
"Let him in."
***
So the frog sat at the table.
"Push your plate closer," said the frog.
He ate from her golden plate.
"Now take me to bed," said the frog.
He slept on her soft pillow.
The princess did not like it one bit.
But a promise is a promise.
So she kept it.
***
In the morning, the frog was gone.
A kind prince stood there instead.
"I was the frog," he said.
"Someone put a spell on me."
"You kept your promise."
"Now the spell is broken!"
The princess smiled.
From then on, they were the best of friends.
If you make a promise, keep it.

cards.q: What fell into the well?
cards.note: She tossed it up high every day, and one day she missed: splash.

cards.q: Who got the ball back for the princess?
cards.note: A big green frog in the well offered to dive for it, for a promise.

cards.q: Where did the frog sleep?
cards.note: First her plate, then her pillow: the two things the frog asked for.

cards.q: Who said, 'A promise is a promise'?
cards.note: Her father the king would not let her wriggle out of it.

cards.q: What happened first in the story?
cards.note: The golden ball splashes into the deep well; everything else follows from that.

cards.q: What happened at the end of the story?
cards.note: The frog was a prince under a spell, and her kept promise broke it.

cards.q: How did the princess feel when the ball fell in?
cards.note: She sat by the well and cried; ask how she felt when the frog offered to help.

cards.q: What does this story teach?
cards.note: She did not want to, but she kept her word, and that is what broke the spell.

cards.q: In the story, what is a 'well'?
cards.note: A well is a deep hole dug down to water; a dropped ball is very hard to get back.

cards.q: Which word is in the story?
cards.note: He reads the three words himself; only one of them is in the story.

decks.subject: storytime
decks.title: The Tale of Peter Rabbit
decks.about: Beatrix Potter's 1902 classic about the naughty bunny who sneaks into Mr. McGregor's garden, loses his shoes and his jacket, and gets home to bed with a cup of tea. This is a short retelling in first-grade words that keeps a few of Potter's own famous lines; the book itself is in the public domain, so he can meet the real one at the library afterwards. Five pages long.
decks.tip: Ask: what did Peter's mother tell him, and what did he do instead?

book.author: Beatrix Potter (retold)
book.source: public domain, retold in first-grade words
book.blurb: A naughty bunny in Mr. McGregor's garden.

passage.text:
Once upon a time there were four little rabbits.
Their names were Flopsy, Mopsy, Cotton-tail, and Peter.
They lived under a big fir tree.
"Now run along," said Mrs. Rabbit.
"But do not go into Mr. McGregor's garden."
"And don't get into mischief."
Flopsy, Mopsy, and Cotton-tail were good little bunnies.
They went to pick blackberries.
But Peter was very naughty.
He ran straight to Mr. McGregor's garden!
***
First he ate some lettuces.
Then he ate some beans.
Then he ate some radishes.
He felt rather sick.
So he went to look for some parsley.
At the end of the row was Mr. McGregor!
Mr. McGregor jumped up.
He ran after Peter, waving a rake.
"Stop, thief!" he called.
***
Peter was very scared.
He ran all over the garden.
He lost one shoe in the cabbages.
He lost the other in the potatoes.
Then he ran into a net!
The big buttons on his jacket got stuck.
He shed big tears.
Some sparrows flew to him.
"Try, try again!" they said.
***
Mr. McGregor came with a sieve.
He tried to pop it on Peter.
But Peter wriggled out just in time.
He left his jacket behind.
He ran into the tool shed.
He hid in a can of water!
Then Peter sneezed.
Mr. McGregor heard him.
He ran after Peter again.
Peter jumped out of a window.
Mr. McGregor got tired of running.
He went back to his work.
***
Peter ran and ran.
He did not stop till he got home.
He flopped down on the soft sand.
He was not very well that evening.
His mother put him to bed.
She made him a cup of tea.
But Flopsy, Mopsy, and Cotton-tail had bread and milk.
And blackberries for supper.

cards.q: Who was the naughty little rabbit?
cards.note: Four bunnies: Flopsy, Mopsy, Cotton-tail and Peter, and only one of them is naughty.

cards.q: Which place did Mrs. Rabbit say to stay out of?
cards.note: His mother said it plainly, and he went straight there anyway.

cards.q: What did Mr. McGregor do when he saw Peter?
cards.note: Stop, thief! A thief is someone who takes what is not theirs, like Peter and the lettuces.

cards.q: What did Peter lose in the garden?
cards.note: One shoe in the cabbages, one in the potatoes, and the jacket caught on the net.

cards.q: What happened first in the story?
cards.note: Mrs. Rabbit's warning comes first, which is what makes Peter naughty.

cards.q: What happened at the end of the story?
cards.note: Peter got tea in bed; the good bunnies got bread, milk and blackberries.

cards.q: How did Peter feel when he saw Mr. McGregor?
cards.note: So scared he ran the wrong way and lost both shoes.

cards.q: Where did the four little rabbits live?
cards.note: In the book they live in a sand bank under the roots of a very big fir tree.

cards.q: In the story, what does 'mischief' mean?
cards.note: Getting into mischief is doing naughty things; it is Potter's own word.

cards.q: Which word is in the story?
cards.note: He reads the three words himself; only one of them is in the story.

decks.subject: storytime
decks.title: The Ugly Duckling
decks.about: Hans Christian Andersen's 1843 tale of the big gray duckling the others say looks odd, who waits out a cold winter alone and finds in spring that he has grown into a swan. It gives first graders a gentle way to talk about teasing, being different and being kind, and the moment he sees himself in the water is a joy to read aloud. It is a public-domain story retold here in first-grade words, five pages long.
decks.tip: Ask: what could the other ducks have said to be kind to the gray duckling?

book.author: Hans Christian Andersen (retold)
book.source: public domain, retold in first-grade words
book.blurb: A duckling who looks odd grows up to be a swan.

passage.text:
A mother duck sat on her eggs.
Crack, crack, crack!
Out came her little ducklings.
They were small and yellow.
But one egg was very big.
It hatched last of all.
Out came a big gray duckling.
He did not look like the others.
His mother loved him just the same.
***
The ducklings went for a swim in the pond.
The big gray duckling swam the best of all.
But the other ducks said he looked odd.
That made him sad.
"Nobody wants to play with me," he said.
So he swam far away to find a new home.
***
Soon the leaves fell from the trees.
Then cold winter came.
Snow fell all around.
The duckling found a snug spot in the tall grass.
He waited for spring.
He dreamed of the warm sun.
***
At last, spring came.
The sun was warm again.
He saw three white swans on a big lake.
"They are so beautiful," he said.
He swam over to them.
Then he looked down into the water.
He saw a big white swan!
It was him!
He was a swan, too!
***
"Come and swim with us!" said the swans.
They swam all around him.
The young swan was so happy.
He had new friends at last.
Be kind, because everyone grows in their own way.

cards.q: Who sat on the eggs?
cards.note: She sat on them until they hatched, one by one, and the big egg hatched last.

cards.q: Where did the ducklings go for a swim?
cards.note: The gray duckling swam the best of all, even though the others said he looked odd.

cards.q: What came out of the very big egg?
cards.note: The other ducklings were small and yellow; this one was big and gray.

cards.q: What did the duckling see when he looked in the water?
cards.note: It was his own reflection: he had grown into a swan.

cards.q: What happened first in the story?
cards.note: Crack, crack, crack: the story starts with the eggs hatching.

cards.q: What happened at the end of the story?
cards.note: The swans asked him to swim with them, and he had new friends at last.

cards.q: How did the duckling feel when the ducks said he looked odd?
cards.note: The story says it plainly; ask what he could do for someone who felt that way.

cards.q: What does this story teach?
cards.note: Be kind, because everyone grows in their own way; the last line says it.

cards.q: In the story, what does 'hatched' mean?
cards.note: Baby birds hatch by cracking the shell open from the inside.

cards.q: Which word is in the story?
cards.note: He reads the three words himself; only one of them is in the story.

decks.subject: storytime
decks.title: The Princess and the Pea
decks.about: Hans Christian Andersen's 1835 tale of the soaking-wet girl who says she is a real princess, and the queen who tests her with one little pea under twenty mattresses. It is short, silly and easy to picture, with a funny ending, and a good story for talking about where and when a story happens. It is a public-domain story retold here in first-grade words, five pages long.
decks.tip: Ask: could you feel one little pea under twenty mattresses, and why did the queen think only a real princess could?

book.author: Hans Christian Andersen (retold)
book.source: public domain, retold in first-grade words
book.blurb: Twenty mattresses, one little pea, and one very real princess.

passage.text:
Once upon a time, there was a prince.
He lived in a castle with his mother, the queen.
He wanted to marry a real princess.
He looked all around the land.
He met lots of princesses.
But he could not tell if they were real.
So he went back home, feeling sad.
***
One night, there was a big storm.
The rain came down and the wind blew.
Knock, knock, knock!
A girl stood at the castle door.
She was very wet.
Water dripped from her hair.
Water ran out of her shoes!
"I am a real princess," she said.
"We will see about that," said the queen.
***
The queen went to get a bed ready.
She put one little green pea on the bed.
She did not tell the girl.
On top of the pea, she put a mattress.
Then another, and another, and another!
Soon there were twenty mattresses.
The bed was so tall!
The girl climbed a ladder to the top.
"Good night!" said the queen.
***
In the morning, the queen asked, "How did you sleep?"
"Oh, very badly!" said the girl.
"Something hard was in my bed."
"I tossed and turned all night."
"Now I am sore all over!"
The queen smiled a big smile.
Only a real princess could feel one little pea!
***
The prince was so happy.
He had found a real princess at last!
Soon they got married.
And the little green pea?
It went in a glass box for all to see.
After that, the princess slept on just one mattress.

cards.q: Who knocked at the castle door?
cards.note: Water ran out of her shoes, but she said she was a real princess.

cards.q: Where did the queen hide the pea?
cards.note: One little pea at the bottom, then twenty mattresses piled on top of it.

cards.q: What did the girl climb to get to the top?
cards.note: Twenty mattresses make a bed so tall you need a ladder to get in.
