cards.q: How did the queen know she was a real princess?
cards.note: Only a real princess, the queen thought, could feel one little pea through all those mattresses.

cards.q: What happened first in the story?
cards.note: The prince looked all around the land for a real princess before the stormy night.

cards.q: What happened at the end of the story?
cards.note: And the pea went in a glass box for all to see.

cards.q: How did the girl feel in the morning?
cards.note: She tossed and turned all night; ask him how one little pea could feel so big.

cards.q: When did the girl come to the castle?
cards.note: The setting is when and where a story happens: a castle, on a stormy night.

cards.q: In the story, what is a 'mattress'?
cards.note: A mattress is the thick, soft part of a bed that you sleep on.

cards.q: Which word is in the story?
cards.note: He reads the three words himself; only one of them is in the story.

decks.subject: storytime
decks.title: The Tale of Benjamin Bunny
decks.about: Beatrix Potter's 1904 sequel to Peter Rabbit: Peter's cousin Benjamin takes him back to Mr. McGregor's garden to get his jacket and shoes off the scarecrow, and old Mr. Benjamin Bunny shoos away the cat that keeps them stuck under a basket. This is a gentle retelling in first-grade words where nobody is hurt, and it keeps Potter's trit-trot of the pony; the book itself is in the public domain, so he can meet the real one at the library afterwards. Five pages long.
decks.tip: Ask: what did Benjamin put in the red hanky, and who was it for?

book.author: Beatrix Potter (retold)
book.source: public domain, retold in first-grade words
book.blurb: Peter and his cousin go back for his jacket and shoes.

passage.text:
One morning, a little rabbit sat on a grassy bank.
His name was Benjamin Bunny.
Trit-trot, trit-trot!
A pony and cart went down the road.
Mr. and Mrs. McGregor sat in the cart.
"They are going out for the day!" said Benjamin.
He hopped off to find his cousin Peter.
***
Peter sat all alone.
He had lost his jacket and shoes.
So he was wrapped up in a red hanky.
"Mr. McGregor put my things on his scarecrow," said Peter.
"Let's go get them back!" said Benjamin.
So they hopped to the garden wall.
They climbed down a pear tree into the garden.
***
There was the scarecrow!
It had on Peter's blue jacket and his shoes.
Peter put them on.
The shoes were full of rain.
Squish, squish!
Then Benjamin filled the red hanky with onions.
"A gift for your mother," he said.
Peter was worried.
He kept hearing noises.
***
The two bunnies came around a corner.
They stopped.
There sat a big cat!
They ran and hid under a big basket.
The cat came over and sat on top of it!
She sat there for five long hours.
Peter and Benjamin did not make a peep.
***
Then old Mr. Benjamin Bunny came along the wall.
He was Benjamin's father.
He saw the cat on the basket.
"Shoo, cat, shoo!" he said.
The cat ran far away.
He lifted the basket.
Out hopped Peter and Benjamin.
Then he took them home.
Peter gave the onions to his mother.
She was glad to have his jacket and shoes back.

cards.q: Who shooed the cat away?
cards.note: Benjamin's father came looking for his son and sent the cat running.

cards.q: What was the scarecrow wearing?
cards.note: Peter lost them in The Tale of Peter Rabbit, and Mr. McGregor dressed his scarecrow in them.

cards.q: What did Benjamin put in the red hanky?
cards.note: A gift for Peter's mother; a hanky is a small square of cloth, like a napkin.

cards.q: Where did the bunnies hide from the cat?
cards.note: Then the cat sat on top of the basket for five long hours.

cards.q: What happened first in the story?
cards.note: Trit-trot, trit-trot: with the McGregors gone for the day, the bunnies dare to visit the garden.

cards.q: What happened at the end of the story?
cards.note: Old Mr. Benjamin Bunny took them home, and Peter gave his mother the onions.

cards.q: How did Peter feel in the garden?
cards.note: He kept hearing noises; after his last visit to that garden, who could blame him?

cards.q: Where does most of this story happen?
cards.note: The setting is where a story happens; this is the same garden as in Peter Rabbit.

cards.q: In the story, what does a 'scarecrow' do?
cards.note: Scare plus crow: a pretend person in old clothes that keeps birds off the plants.

cards.q: Which word is in the story?
cards.note: He reads the three words himself; only one of them is in the story.

decks.subject: storytime
decks.title: The Little Engine That Could
decks.about: Watty Piper's 1930 picture book about a train full of toys that breaks down, the big engines that will not help, and the little blue engine who says she thinks she can and pulls the toys over the mountain. First graders love chanting the refrain, and the story gives them words for trying hard at something new. It is a public-domain story retold here in first-grade words, four pages long.
decks.tip: Chant I think I can, I think I can together while he pushes something heavy, like a box of books, across the room.

book.author: Watty Piper (retold)
book.source: public domain, retold in first-grade words
book.blurb: A little blue engine who thinks she can.

passage.text:
A little train was full of toys.
There were dolls and teddy bears.
There were toy trucks and red balls.
There were apples and oranges, too.
The toys were going to the good children.
The children lived on the other side of the mountain.
Then the train stopped.
Its engine would not go.
"Oh, no!" said the toys.
"How will we get over the mountain?"
***
A big shiny engine came by.
"Please pull us over the mountain," said the toys.
"I pull fancy trains," said the shiny engine.
"I will not pull toys."
And off it went.
Then a big strong engine came by.
"Please pull us over the mountain," said the toys.
"I pull heavy freight," said the strong engine.
"I will not pull toys."
And off it went.
The toys felt sad.
***
Then a little blue engine came by.
She was very small.
"Please pull us over the mountain," said the toys.
"I am not very big," she said.
"But the children need their toys."
"I think I can."
She hooked on to the little train.
Puff, puff! Chug, chug!
"I think I can. I think I can."
Up, up, up she went.
"I think I can. I think I can."
***
Slowly, slowly, she pulled the train up the mountain.
"I think I can. I think I can."
At last she got to the top!
"Hooray!" said the toys.
Then down the mountain she went.
"I thought I could. I thought I could."
The children got their toys.
They were so happy.
The little blue engine was happy, too.
Believe in yourself and try your best.

cards.q: What was the little train full of?
cards.note: Dolls, teddy bears, toy trucks, red balls, and apples and oranges too, all on their way to the children.

cards.q: Who were the toys going to?
cards.note: The good children lived on the other side of the mountain, which is why the train had to get over it.

cards.q: What did the big shiny engine pull?
cards.note: The shiny engine was too proud for toys, and the strong engine was too busy with its freight.

cards.q: What did the little blue engine say as she pulled?
cards.note: Say it with him, faster and faster, as the train climbs the mountain.

cards.q: What happened first in the story?
cards.note: The engine would not go, so the toys were stuck at the foot of the mountain.

cards.q: What happened at the end of the story?
cards.note: Down the other side of the mountain she went, saying I thought I could.

cards.q: How did the toys feel when the big engines left?
cards.note: Two big engines went off without them, so the toys felt sad until the little blue engine came.

cards.q: What does this story teach?
cards.note: Believe in yourself and try your best: the little engine was small, but she tried.

cards.q: In the story, what does 'freight' mean?
cards.note: Freight is the heavy load a train carries, like coal or boxes, and the strong engine pulled freight, not toys.

cards.q: Which word is in the story?
cards.note: He reads the three words himself; only one of them is in the story.

decks.subject: storytime
decks.title: Millions of Cats
decks.about: Wanda Gág's 1928 picture book about a lonely old man and woman, a hill covered with cats, and the one shy kitten who stays. First graders love the counting refrain of hundreds and thousands and millions of cats, and the ending is a kind one about being loved. In this softened telling the cats only quarrel and run off in a huff; it is a public-domain story retold in first-grade words, five pages long.
decks.tip: Ask: why did the shy kitten stay when all the other cats ran away?

book.author: Wanda Gág (retold)
book.source: public domain, retold in first-grade words
book.blurb: One old man, one hill, and millions of cats.

passage.text:
Once there was an old man and an old woman.
They lived in a neat little house.
They were happy.
But they were lonely.
"I wish we had a cat," said the old woman.
"I will find you one," said the old man.
So he set off over the hills.
***
At last he came to a hill.
The hill was covered with cats!
There were hundreds of cats.
There were thousands of cats.
There were millions of cats, all over the hill!
"Oh!" said the old man.
"Now I can pick the prettiest one."
He picked a white cat.
Then he saw a black cat.
He could not choose.
So he took them all.
***
The cats followed him home.
Hundreds of cats, thousands of cats, millions of cats!
The old woman came to the door.
"My dear!" she said.
"We cannot keep millions of cats."
"Let the cats pick," said the old man.
"Which cat is the prettiest?"
"I am!" said one cat.
"No, I am!" said another.
"I am the prettiest!" they all said.
***
The cats began to quarrel.
They hissed and fussed.
They stamped their paws.
Then, in a huff, they all ran away.
Hundreds and thousands and millions of cats, all gone!
The yard was quiet.
Only one little kitten was left.
She was thin and shy.
She had hidden in the tall grass.
"I did not think I was pretty," she said.
"So I did not quarrel."
***
The old man picked up the kitten.
The old woman gave her warm milk.
They loved her every day.
The kitten grew plump and happy.
Her fur shone like silk.
The old man smiled.
"She is the prettiest cat of all!"
"I think so, too," said the old woman.
A little love can make anyone shine.

cards.q: What did the old woman wish for?
cards.note: The old man and woman were happy but lonely, so she wished for a cat to keep them company.

cards.q: How many cats followed the old man home?
cards.note: Hundreds of cats, thousands of cats, millions of cats, all in a line behind him.

cards.q: What did the cats quarrel about?
cards.note: Every cat said I am the prettiest, and the fuss sent them all off in a huff.

cards.q: Which cat stayed with the old man and woman?
cards.note: She had hidden in the tall grass and did not quarrel, because she did not think she was pretty.

cards.q: What happened first in the story?
cards.note: The old woman's wish is what sends the old man off over the hills.

cards.q: What happened at the end of the story?
cards.note: Warm milk and love made the thin kitten plump, shiny and the prettiest cat of all.

cards.q: How did the old man and woman feel at the start?
cards.note: They were happy in their neat little house, but lonely, which is why they wanted a cat.

cards.q: What does this story teach?
cards.note: A little love can make anyone shine; the last line says it.

cards.q: In the story, what does 'quarrel' mean?
cards.note: To quarrel is to argue in an angry way, the way the cats did over who was prettiest.

cards.q: Which word is in the story?
cards.note: He reads the three words himself; only one of them is in the story.

decks.subject: storytime
decks.title: The Velveteen Rabbit
decks.about: Margery Williams's 1922 story of a toy rabbit who is loved by a boy until his fur is rubbed off, and who learns from the wise old Skin Horse that being loved is what makes a toy Real. It is a gentle story for talking about love, growing up and old favorite toys. This softened telling leaves out the illness and the bonfire: the boy simply grows up, and the nursery magic Fairy turns the old rabbit into a real one; it is a public-domain story retold in first-grade words, five pages long.
decks.tip: Ask: which toy at home is the most loved and most worn out, and is it Real?

book.author: Margery Williams (retold)
book.source: public domain, retold in first-grade words
book.blurb: A toy rabbit who is loved until he becomes Real.

passage.text:
Once there was a velveteen rabbit.
He was soft and brown.
He had pink ears and a white tail.
A boy got him as a present.
But the boy had fancy toys, too.
They had wheels and springs.
The rabbit sat in the toy box.
He felt plain and shy.
***
In the toy box lived the old Skin Horse.
"What is Real?" asked the rabbit.
"Real is not how you are made," said the Horse.
"A child loves you for a long, long time."
"Then you become Real."
"Does it hurt?" asked the rabbit.
"Sometimes," said the Horse.
"Your fur gets rubbed off."
"You get very shabby."
"But once you are Real, it does not matter."
***
One night the boy could not find his toy dog.
So Mother gave him the rabbit.
The boy hugged the rabbit all night.
After that, they were always together.
They played in the garden.
The boy took him to bed every night.
"He is not a toy," said the boy.
"He is Real!"
The rabbit was so happy.
***
Years went by.
The rabbit got old and shabby.
But the boy loved him, so he was Real.
Then the boy grew up.
He got new toys.
The old rabbit was put in a sack.
"Put him out in the garden," said Mother.
That night the rabbit sat all alone.
A tear rolled down his face.
***
Where the tear fell, a flower grew.
Out of the flower came a fairy.
"I am the nursery magic Fairy," she said.
"You were Real to the boy."
"Now you will be Real to everyone."
She kissed him on the nose.
His legs began to twitch.
He was a real rabbit at last!
He ran off with the wild rabbits.
Being loved is what makes you Real.

cards.q: Who said, 'Then you become Real'?
cards.note: The old Skin Horse had been loved for years, so he knew all about being Real.

cards.q: What did the boy take to bed every night?
cards.note: After the night he lost his toy dog, the boy and the rabbit were always together.

cards.q: What did the Skin Horse say happens to your fur?
cards.note: The Skin Horse said it would happen, and that once you are Real it does not matter.

cards.q: Where was the old rabbit put when the boy grew up?
cards.note: The boy got new toys, and the old rabbit went out to the garden in a sack.

cards.q: What happened first in the story?
cards.note: The story opens with the soft brown rabbit, brand new, before the fancy toys crowd him out.

cards.q: What happened at the end of the story?
cards.note: The Fairy kissed his nose, his legs began to twitch, and he ran off with the wild rabbits.

cards.q: How did the rabbit feel when the boy called him Real?
cards.note: He is not a toy, said the boy, he is Real, and that made the rabbit so happy.

cards.q: What does this story teach?
cards.note: Being loved is what makes you Real; the last line says it.

cards.q: In the story, what does 'shabby' mean?
cards.note: A shabby toy has been loved so much that its fur is rubbed thin and its seams are worn.

cards.q: Which word is in the story?
cards.note: He reads the three words himself; only one of them is in the story.

decks.subject: storytime
decks.title: Pooh Gets Stuck
decks.about: A. A. Milne's 1926 chapter in which Pooh visits Rabbit, eats far too much honey and gets wedged in Rabbit's front door, so his friends read to him for a week until he is thin enough to pull out with a pop. It is one of the funniest chapters in Winnie-the-Pooh and an easy one to act out, with a clear where and when to talk about. The 1926 book is in the public domain in the United States, and this is a retelling in first-grade words, five pages long.
decks.tip: Act it out: he is Pooh stuck in a doorway, you take his front paws and pull, and everyone shouts pop when he comes free.

book.author: A. A. Milne (retold)
book.source: public domain, retold in first-grade words
book.blurb: Too much honey, one tight front door, and a pop.

passage.text:
One day Pooh went for a walk.
He came to a hole in a sandy bank.
It was Rabbit's house.
"Is anybody home?" called Pooh.
"Come in," said Rabbit.
Pooh squeezed through the front door.
"Would you like a little something?" said Rabbit.
"Yes, please," said Pooh.
"Honey, if you have it."
***
Rabbit set out a big pot of honey.
Pooh ate it all up.
Then he ate another pot.
And another.
At last Pooh got up to go.
"Thank you, Rabbit," he said.
He started out the front door.
He pushed with his front paws.
He pushed with his back paws.
But he could not get out!
Pooh was stuck.
***
"Oh, help!" said Pooh.
"I am stuck."
"It is all that honey," said Rabbit.
"You ate too much, you silly old bear."
"We must wait for you to get thin."
"How long will that take?" asked Pooh.
"About a week," said Rabbit.
"A week!" said Pooh.
"But what about meals?"
"No meals," said Rabbit.
"That is how you get thin."
"Then will you read to me?" asked Pooh.
***
So Rabbit read to Pooh every day.
Pooh's front half was outside.
His back half was inside.
Rabbit hung his towels on Pooh's back legs.
Piglet came to visit.
Eeyore came to visit.
At the end of the week, Rabbit said, "Now!"
Piglet and Eeyore took hold of Pooh's paws.
Rabbit pushed from inside.
***
"Pull!" said Piglet.
"Pull!" said Eeyore.
"Push!" said Rabbit.
They pulled and pushed.
Then, pop!
Out popped Pooh, like a cork!
Piglet and Eeyore fell over in a heap.
"Thank you, my friends," said Pooh.
He went off into the wood, humming a hum.
And he did not eat so much honey after that.
Well, not for a day or two.

cards.q: Whose house did Pooh visit?
cards.note: Rabbit's house was a hole in a sandy bank, with a front door just big enough for a bear who has not had lunch.

cards.q: What did Pooh eat at Rabbit's house?
cards.note: A big pot, then another pot, then another, which is why he got stuck.

cards.q: Where did Pooh get stuck?
cards.note: His front half was outside and his back half was inside.

cards.q: Why did Pooh get stuck in the door?
cards.note: It is all that honey, said Rabbit, because Pooh was wider going out than he had been coming in.

cards.q: What happened first in the story?
cards.note: The story starts with Pooh walking through the wood to Rabbit's front door.

cards.q: What happened at the end of the story?
cards.note: Pop, out he came like a cork, and his friends fell over in a heap.

cards.q: What was Pooh like in the story?
cards.note: Rabbit calls him a silly old bear, and he ate pot after pot of honey.

cards.q: When did the friends pull Pooh out?
cards.note: Pooh had to go a whole week with no meals before he was thin enough to pull out.

cards.q: In the story, what does 'stuck' mean?
cards.note: Stuck means held so tight you cannot move, the way Pooh was wedged in the door.

cards.q: Which word is in the story?
cards.note: He reads the three words himself; only one of them is in the story.

decks.subject: storytime
decks.title: The Tale of Tom Kitten
decks.about: Beatrix Potter's 1907 tale of Tom Kitten and his sisters Mittens and Moppet, dressed in their best clothes for their mother's tea party and told to stay clean, who lose every button and stitch on the garden wall to three waddling Puddle-Ducks. First graders love the pop of the buttons, the pit-pat waddle-pat refrain and the thumping upstairs while the grown-ups sip their tea. It is a public-domain book retold here in first-grade words, five pages long; the real one with Potter's pictures is at the library.
decks.tip: Chant pit-pat, paddle-pat with him, then ask who ended up wearing the kittens' clothes.

book.author: Beatrix Potter (retold)
book.source: public domain, retold in first-grade words
book.blurb: Three kittens, their best clothes, and three cheeky ducks.

passage.text:
Once there were three little kittens.
Their names were Mittens, Tom Kitten, and Moppet.
Their mother was Mrs. Tabitha Twitchit.
One day, friends were coming for tea.
So she washed their faces.
She brushed their fur.
She put them in their best clothes.
Tom's suit had six shiny buttons.
"Now go out and play," she said.
"But keep your clothes clean!"
***
The kittens went out into the garden.
Moppet and Mittens tried to stay clean.
But they tripped on their long dresses.
Tom could not even hop.
His suit was too tight!
Then they climbed up the garden wall.
Pop! Pop! Pop!
Tom's buttons flew off one by one.
***
Just then, three ducks came waddling by.
Pit-pat, paddle-pat! Pit-pat, waddle-pat!
They were the Puddle-Ducks.
"Look at all the buttons!" said a duck.
Then Tom's hat fell off the wall.
His suit slid off, too.
The dresses slipped off next.
Soon all the clothes were in a heap.
The ducks picked them up.
And they put them on!
***
Off went the ducks in the fine clothes.
Pit-pat, paddle-pat! Pit-pat, waddle-pat!
Splash!
They jumped into the pond.
The clothes floated away.
The three kittens sat on the wall.
They had no clothes on at all!
Just then, Mrs. Tabitha Twitchit came out.
"Oh my!" she said.
"Look at you!"
"My friends are coming for tea!"
She was very upset.
***
She sent the kittens upstairs.
"Stay up there and be good," she said.
Then her friends came for tea.
They sat and sipped and talked.
But the kittens were not being good.
Thump! Bump! Thump!
They bounced on the beds.
What a noisy tea party!
And the Puddle-Ducks?
They are still looking for those clothes.

cards.q: Who was the kittens' mother?
cards.note: Tabitha Twitchit is the mother of Tom, Mittens and Moppet; the three ducks are the Puddle-Ducks.

cards.q: What did the mother tell the kittens to do?
cards.note: That is the one thing she asks, and it lasts about as long as a walk to the garden wall.

cards.q: What popped off Tom's suit?
cards.note: Pop, pop, pop: the suit was too tight, so the buttons flew off one by one.

cards.q: Who put on the kittens' clothes?
cards.note: The ducks picked up the heap of clothes, put them on and waddled off to the pond.

cards.q: What happened first in the story?
cards.note: Washed faces, brushed fur and best clothes come first; the garden wall undoes it all.

cards.q: What happened at the end of the story?
cards.note: The friends sipped tea downstairs while thump, bump, thump went the kittens upstairs.

cards.q: How did the kittens' mother feel when she saw them?
cards.note: Oh my, look at you: her friends were on the way and the kittens had nothing on.

cards.q: Where did the kittens go out to play?
cards.note: The setting is where a story happens: a house with a garden, a wall and a pond.

decks.subject: storytime
decks.title: The Emperor's New Clothes
decks.about: Hans Christian Andersen's tale of an emperor who pays two tricksters for magic clothes that only clever people can see, parades through town in his underthings because nobody wants to look foolish, and is finally set straight by a child who says what everyone can see. First graders find it very funny, and this telling keeps it kind: the emperor laughs at himself, and the ending says plainly that it is brave to say what is true. It is a public-domain story retold here in first-grade words, five pages long.
decks.tip: Ask why the grown-ups said the clothes were lovely, and why the child did not.

book.author: Hans Christian Andersen (retold)
book.source: public domain, retold in first-grade words
book.blurb: Magic clothes nobody can see, and a child who says so.

passage.text:
Once there was an emperor.
He loved new clothes more than anything.
He had a coat for every hour of the day.
One day, two tricksters came to town.
"We can weave the finest cloth," they said.
"It is magic cloth."
"Only clever people can see it."
"I must have it!" said the emperor.
He gave them a big bag of gold.
***
The tricksters sat at an empty loom.
They moved their hands back and forth.
But there was no cloth at all!
The emperor sent a wise old man to look.
The man saw nothing.
"Oh no!" he thought.
"Maybe I am not clever."
So he said, "What lovely cloth!"
Everyone else said the same.
Nobody wanted to look foolish.
***
At last the tricksters said, "It is done!"
They pretended to dress the emperor.
He had nothing on but his underthings!
He looked in the mirror.
"Oh my, they fit so well!" he said.
Nobody wanted to look foolish.
The tricksters took the gold and slipped away.
Then the emperor went out for a parade.
***
The people lined the streets.
"What a fine coat!" they said.
"What a fine hat!"
Nobody wanted to look foolish.
Then a little child looked up.
"But he has nothing on!" said the child.
Everyone got very quiet.
Then someone giggled.
Then everyone laughed and laughed.
***
The emperor looked down.
He saw his underthings.
He turned red.
"Oh my, I look silly!" he said.
Then he laughed too.
"Ho, ho! The child is right!"
"That child is brave."
"I am glad someone told the truth."
He went home and put on his old coat.
It is brave to say what is true.

cards.q: What did the emperor love more than anything?
cards.note: A coat for every hour of the day; that is why the magic cloth was so tempting.

cards.q: Who did the tricksters say could see the cloth?
cards.note: There was no cloth at all; saying only clever people could see it kept everyone quiet.

cards.q: What did the emperor give the tricksters?
cards.note: He paid a big bag of gold for cloth that did not exist.

cards.q: Who said, 'But he has nothing on!'?
cards.note: Everyone else was afraid of looking foolish; the child just said what was there.

cards.q: What happened first in the story?
cards.note: Two tricksters arrive with a promise of magic cloth; everything else follows from that.

cards.q: What happened at the end of the story?
cards.note: He turned red, laughed at himself, and went home for his old coat.

cards.q: How did the emperor feel when he looked down?
cards.note: He turned red and said so himself, then laughed: a good way to handle a mistake.

cards.q: What does this story teach?
cards.note: Everyone saw the truth, but only the child was brave enough to say it.

cards.q: In the story, what does 'clever' mean?
cards.note: Clever means smart, quick to understand; nobody wanted to seem the opposite.

cards.q: Which word is in the story?
cards.note: He reads the three words himself; only one of them is in the story.

cards.note: 4 walk, 7 ride the bus. 4 and 3 more makes 7.

cards.q: How many kids ride in a car or walk?
How many tulips?
Which flower has the fewest?
How many flowers in all?
How many more tulips than sunflowers?
Max counted cars with tally marks. How many cars?
cards.note: Two bundles of 5 and 1 more.

cards.q: Jo made a tally mark for each bird she saw. How many birds?
cards.note: Two bundles of 5 and 4 more.

cards.q: The class tallied the sunny days. How many sunny days?
cards.note: Three bundles of 5 and 3 more.

cards.q: How many groups of 5 are in these tally marks?
cards.note: Every fifth mark crosses the bundle. Count the bundles.

decks.subject: math
decks.title: Time to the Hour
decks.about: Reading and writing times like 3:00 on an analog clock and a digital clock, and knowing the short hand shows the hour while the long hand points to 12. NC asks for both kinds of clock.
decks.tip: Say "short hand first: what number is it pointing to?"

cards.q: What time is it?
What time is it?
What time is it?
What time is it?
What time is it?
What time is it?
What time is it?
What time is it?
What time is it?
What time is it?
What time does this clock show?
What time does this clock show?
It is 5:00. What number does the long hand point to?
It is 5:00. What number does the short hand point to?
How many minutes are in one hour?
At 8:00, what number does the long hand point to?
At 2:00, what number does the short hand point to?
It is 9:00. What time will it be one hour later?

decks.subject: math
decks.title: Half Past
decks.about: Times like 3:30, "half past 3": the long hand on the 6 and the short hand between two numbers. Half hours are the hardest part of first-grade time because the short hand has moved past the hour.
decks.tip: Ask "which two numbers is the short hand between? The smaller one is the hour."

cards.q: What time is it?
What time is it?
What time is it?
What time is it?
What time is it?
What time is it?
What time is it?
What time is it?
How many minutes past 2 is it?
It is half past what hour?
It is half past what hour?
How many minutes past 12 is it?
How do you write half past 4?
How do you write half past 9?
At 7:30, what number does the long hand point to?
At 7:30, the short hand is between which numbers?
How many minutes are in half an hour?
It is 5:30. What time will it be in half an hour?

decks.subject: math
decks.title: Match the Clocks
decks.about: Matching an analog clock to its digital time, a digital time to its words ("half past three"), and words back to digits, with hours and half hours mixed together. NC.1.MD.3 asks him to tell and write time to the hour and half hour on both kinds of clock.
decks.tip: Long hand first: on the 12 means o'clock, on the 6 means half past; then find the hour with the short hand.

cards.q: Which digital time matches this clock?
cards.note: Long hand on 6 means 30. Short hand is past 3.

cards.q: Which digital time matches this clock?
Which digital time matches this clock?
cards.note: The short hand is between 11 and 12, so the hour is still 11.

cards.q: Tap the time that matches.
Tap the time that matches.
Which digital time matches this clock?
cards.note: Both hands point straight up.

cards.q: Tap the time that matches.
Which digital time matches this clock?
Tap the time that matches.
cards.note: The short hand is between 1 and 2, so the hour is 1.

cards.q: Say it in words. What time is it?
cards.note: 3:30 is half past three: thirty minutes after 3.

cards.q: Say it in words. What time is it?
Say it in words. What time is it?
How do you say this time?
How do you say this time?
cards.note: 12:30 is half past twelve, not half past one.

cards.q: How do you say this time?
Which time is half past two?
Which time is six o'clock?
Which time is half past eleven?
The short hand points to 10 and the long hand points to 12. What time is it?
cards.note: Long hand on 12 means o'clock.

cards.q: The short hand is between 5 and 6 and the long hand is on 6. What time is it?
cards.note: Between 5 and 6 means the hour is 5; long hand on 6 means 30.

decks.subject: math
decks.title: Coins
decks.about: Naming the penny, nickel, dime and quarter and knowing each one's value in pennies (1, 5, 10, 25). NC first grade stops here: adding up a handful of coins is a second-grade skill, so this deck has no totals.
decks.tip: Point out that the dime is the smallest coin but worth more than the bigger nickel.

cards.q: What coin is this?
What coin is this?
What coin is this?
What coin is this?
How many pennies is a nickel worth?
How many pennies is a dime worth?
How many pennies is a quarter worth?
How many pennies is a penny worth?
Which coin is worth 10 pennies?
Which coin is worth 25 pennies?
Which coin is worth 5 pennies?
Which coin is worth the most?
Which coin is worth the least?
Which coin is bigger in size, the dime or the nickel?
Which coin is worth more, the dime or the nickel?

decks.subject: math
decks.title: Count the Coins
decks.about: Adding up a small handful of coins (totals to 50 cents) by starting with the biggest coin and counting on, plus choosing which two coins make a given amount. NC.1.MD.5 asks him to know each coin's value in pennies; counting a small group is the natural next step and is where second grade begins, so this deck stays small.
decks.tip: Start with the biggest coin and count on: "25, 35, 40" for a quarter, a dime and a nickel.

cards.q: How much money is this?
How much money is this?
How much money is this?
How many cents is this?
How many cents is this?
Count the coins. What is the total?
How much money is this?
Count the coins. What is the total?
How many cents is this?
How much money is this?
These coins are worth how many pennies?
Count the coins. What is the total?
Count the coins. What is the total?
How many cents is this?
cards.note: 6 coins, but 10 cents: 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10.

cards.q: These coins are worth how many pennies?
Count the coins. What is the total?
Which coins make 15¢?
cards.note: 10 and 5 is 15.

cards.q: Which coins make 6¢?
cards.note: 5 and 1 is 6.

cards.q: Which coins make 30¢?
cards.note: 25 and 5 is 30.

cards.q: Which coins make 20¢?
cards.note: 10 and 10 is 20.

decks.subject: math
decks.title: Flat Shapes
decks.about: Naming triangles, squares, rectangles, trapezoids, hexagons and circles in any colour, and counting their sides and corners. NC wants him to know that sides and corners define a shape, while colour and size do not.
decks.tip: Trace the edges with a finger and count sides out loud; colour never changes the name.

cards.q: What shape is this?
What shape is this?
What shape is this?
What shape is this?
What shape is this?
What shape is this?
What shape is this?
What shape is this?
What shape is this?
What shape is this?
How many sides does a triangle have?
How many corners does a triangle have?
How many sides does a square have?
How many sides does a rectangle have?
How many sides does a hexagon have?
How many corners does a hexagon have?
How many sides does a trapezoid have?
How many corners does a rectangle have?
What makes a triangle a triangle?
What makes a square a square?
Which shape has 4 sides?
Which shape has no corners?

decks.subject: math
decks.title: Sides and Corners
decks.about: Counting the sides and corners of a shape he is looking at (including the rhombus), picking a shape from its number of sides, and sorting what defines a shape (sides, corners) from what does not (color, size, which way it is turned). NC.1.G.1 calls these defining and non-defining attributes.
decks.tip: Touch each corner as you count, then each side; then ask "if I painted it red, would it still be a triangle?"

cards.q: How many sides does this shape have?
cards.note: This shape is a rhombus. All 4 sides are the same length.

cards.q: How many corners does this shape have?
Count the sides. How many?
How many corners does this shape have?
cards.note: A square has 4 square corners.

cards.q: Count the corners. How many?
Count the sides. How many?
Which shape has 3 sides?
Which shape has 6 sides?
Which shape has 4 equal sides and 4 square corners?
Which shape has the most corners?
Which has more sides, a hexagon or a triangle?
Which has more corners, a square or a triangle?
A shape has 4 sides and 4 corners. Which could it be?
cards.note: Squares, rectangles, trapezoids and rhombuses all have 4 sides and 4 corners.

cards.q: A triangle is still a triangle if you change its...
cards.sayQ: A triangle is still a triangle if you change its what?
cards.note: Color and size do not change a shape's name. Sides and corners do.

cards.q: A square is still a square if you change its...
cards.sayQ: A square is still a square if you change its what?

cards.q: Which change turns a shape into a different shape?
A big red triangle and a tiny blue triangle. What is the same about them?
Turn a square upside down. What shape is it now?
cards.note: Turning a shape does not change its name.

cards.q: What makes a hexagon a hexagon?
What is the name of this 4-sided shape?
cards.note: A rhombus has 4 sides that are all the same length.

decks.subject: math
decks.title: Solid Shapes
decks.about: The five solid shapes NC names: cube, rectangular prism, cone, sphere and cylinder, matched to everyday objects and their flat faces. Counting faces is expected; counting edges is not.
decks.tip: Hunt for the shapes at home: a ball, a can, a box, a party hat.

cards.q: What shape is this?
What shape is this?
What shape is this?
What shape is this?
What shape is this?
Which shape can roll?
Which shape is like a ball?
Which shape is like a can?
Which shape is like a party hat?
Which shape has 6 square faces?
How many flat faces does a cube have?
Which shape has a point on top and a round bottom?
Which shape is like a cereal box?
Which shape has no flat faces?

decks.subject: math
decks.title: Put Shapes Together
decks.about: Making new shapes from old ones (two squares make a rectangle, two trapezoids make a hexagon, a cube with a cone on top makes a tower) and naming the parts. NC lists this as its own standard.
decks.tip: Build it with pattern blocks or boxes first, then ask "what did we use?"

cards.q: Two squares side by side make what shape?
Two half-circles make what shape?
Two trapezoids can make what shape?
Six triangles can make what shape?
A house is a square with a triangle on top. What shape is the roof?
A bus is a rectangle with two circles under it. What shapes are the wheels?
Which two shapes make a square?
A tower is a cube with a cone on top. What is on top?
A can with a box on top: what shape is the can?
Two cubes stacked up make what shape?
A crayon is a cylinder with a cone on the end. What shape is the long part?
A half-circle sits on top of a rectangle. What is the top shape?

decks.subject: math
decks.title: Build with Solid Shapes
decks.about: Putting solid shapes together and taking them apart: a cylinder with a cone on top makes a rocket, cubes in a row make a rectangular prism, and each part keeps its own name. NC.1.G.2 covers building with cubes, rectangular prisms, cones and cylinders, and NC.1.G.1 adds the flat faces and whether a solid rolls, stacks or slides.
decks.tip: Build it from cans, boxes and a party hat, then ask "what shape is each piece?"

cards.q: A rocket is a cylinder with a cone on top. What shape is the bottom part?
Which two solids make a rocket shape?
Which pieces make a rectangular prism?
Put 3 cubes in a row. What shape do they make?
A drum is a cylinder. Stack 2 drums. What shape do they make?
A train car is a rectangular prism with 4 wheels. What solid shape is a wheel?
A party hat is a cone. Which flat shape is its bottom?
What shape are the two flat ends of a cylinder?
Which flat shape is a face of a rectangular prism?
How many flat faces does a cylinder have?
How many flat faces does a cone have?
How many flat faces does a rectangular prism have?
Which shape can roll and also stack?
Which shape slides on a flat face and stacks well?
You push a can on its side. What does it do?
Which shape is best for the bottom of a tall tower?
A tower has 4 cubes stacked up and a cone on top. How many solids were used?
Which solid rolls in a curve, like a party hat on its side?

decks.subject: math
decks.title: Halves and Fourths
decks.about: Cutting circles and rectangles into two or four equal parts, calling them halves and fourths, and seeing that more cuts make smaller pieces. NC uses "fourths", not "quarters", and no fraction symbols.
decks.tip: Fold a paper plate in half, then in half again, and count the equal pieces.

cards.q: How many equal parts?
What is each part called?
How many equal parts?
What is each part called?
What part is colored?
What part is colored?
All four fourths are colored. How much is colored?
How many halves make a whole?
How many fourths make a whole?
Which is bigger, half of a pizza or a fourth of the same pizza?
Cut a cookie into 2 equal parts. What is each part?
Cut a sandwich into 4 equal parts. What is each part?
You cut a cake into more equal pieces. What happens to the pieces?
Is this cut into halves or fourths?
Is this cut into halves or fourths?
Two friends share a pizza equally. How much does each get?

decks.subject: science
decks.title: Be a Scientist
decks.about: How a scientist works: observing with the five senses, the tools (hand lens, ruler, thermometer, balance scale, timer) and what each one shows, asking a question, trying it, writing down what you see, and staying safe with goggles and no tasting. Science practices are not a standard of their own in NC's 2023 Grade 1 science; this bridge deck sits under PS.1.1.2, the objective that has children carry out investigations, compare and collect data.
decks.tip: Hand him a hand lens and a ruler and let him be the scientist for one leaf: look, measure, say what he sees, then draw it.

cards.q: Which part of your body do you use to see the color of a rock?
cards.note: Looking closely at something is called observing.

cards.q: You hear a bird sing. Which sense are you using?
cards.note: Your ears are for hearing. Close your eyes and you can still observe with your ears.

cards.q: You sniff a flower. Which sense is that?
cards.note: Your nose is for smell. Smell can tell you a banana is ripe.

cards.q: You feel a rock and it is rough. Which sense tells you that?
cards.note: Your skin is for touch. Rough, smooth, warm and cold are things you feel.

cards.q: An apple is sweet. Which sense tells you that?
cards.note: Your tongue is for taste. In science, only taste food a grown-up says is safe.

cards.q: How many senses do you have?
cards.note: Sight, hearing, smell, touch and taste. One for each finger.

cards.q: What tool makes a tiny bug look bigger?
cards.note: A hand lens is a magnifying glass. It helps your eyes see small things.

cards.q: What tool do you use to measure how long a leaf is?
cards.note: A ruler measures length in inches or centimeters.

cards.q: What tool tells you how hot or cold the water is?
cards.note: Say ther-MOM-uh-ter. It measures temperature, how hot or cold something is.

cards.q: What tool tells you which rock is heavier?
cards.note: Put one rock on each side. The heavier side goes down.

cards.q: You want to know how long a toy car keeps rolling. What tool do you use?
cards.note: A timer measures time. Start it when the car starts and stop it when the car stops.

cards.q: A scientist wonders why the ice melted. What does the scientist do first?
cards.note: Science starts with a question, like why did the ice melt?

cards.q: You wonder if a toy boat floats. How do you find out?
cards.note: Scientists try things to find out. Trying it is called an investigation.

cards.q: You see the bean plant grow taller. What do you do so you remember?
cards.note: Scientists write or draw what they see. That is called recording.

cards.q: What do we call looking very closely at something?
cards.note: Say ob-ZER-ving. You can observe with all five senses, not just your eyes.

cards.q: What do you wear to keep your eyes safe in science?
cards.note: Goggles keep splashes and bits out of your eyes.

cards.q: You find a jar of strange powder in science class. What do you do?
cards.note: Never taste or eat something in science unless a grown-up says it is safe.

cards.q: You finish a science experiment with soil. What do you do with your hands?
cards.note: Clean hands after science keep germs and dirt off your snack.

decks.subject: science
decks.title: Push or Pull?
decks.about: Sorting everyday actions into pushes and pulls, the first idea in NC's Grade 1 forces standard (PS.1.1.1). Every force a first grader meets is one or the other.
decks.tip: Act each one out together: push the chair, pull the drawer, then ask which it was.

cards.q: You kick a ball. Is that a push or a pull?
cards.note: A push moves a thing away from you. A pull brings it toward you.

cards.q: You open a drawer. Push or pull?
cards.note: The drawer comes toward you, so it is a pull.

cards.q: You tug a rope in tug-of-war. Push or pull?
cards.note: The rope comes toward you, so it is a pull.

cards.q: You roll a shopping cart along in front of you. Push or pull?
cards.note: The cart moves away from you, so it is a push.

cards.q: You drag a sled behind you. Push or pull?
cards.note: The sled follows you, so it is a pull.

cards.q: You press a doorbell. Push or pull?
cards.note: Your finger pushes the button in.

cards.q: You zip up your coat. Push or pull?
cards.note: You pull the zipper tab up.

cards.q: You roll a bowling ball down the lane. Push or pull?
cards.note: Your hand pushes the ball away from you.

cards.q: You pick a flower off its stem. Push or pull?
cards.note: You pull the flower toward you, off the stem.

cards.q: A big dog drags you along by its leash. Push or pull?
cards.note: The dog pulls you toward it. Animals can push and pull too.

cards.q: You pedal a bike with your feet. Push or pull?
cards.note: Your feet push the pedals down.

cards.q: You shove a book away from you across the table. Push or pull?
cards.note: Away from you means a push.

cards.q: A magnet grabs a paper clip. Push or pull?
cards.note: The magnet pulls the clip to it without touching it first.

cards.q: You reel in a fish on a line. Push or pull?
cards.note: The line brings the fish toward you.

cards.q: You throw a ball. Push or pull?
cards.note: Your hand pushes the ball away.

cards.q: You hammer a nail. Push or pull?
cards.note: The hammer pushes the nail into the wood.

decks.subject: science
decks.title: Make It Move
decks.about: What a push or pull does to a thing: starts it, stops it, turns it, and how a harder or gentler force changes how fast and far it goes (PS.1.1.1, PS.1.1.2). Includes magnets pulling without touching.
decks.tip: Race a toy car with a soft push and a hard push and ask him to predict which goes farther before each try.

cards.q: A force is a push or a...
cards.note: Forces make things start, stop, speed up, slow down or turn.

cards.q: You push a ball that is sitting still. What happens?
You catch a rolling ball. What happens to it?
A ball comes to you. You hit it with a bat. What changes?
cards.note: A push can send a thing a new way.

cards.q: You push a toy car hard. How does it go?
You push the same toy car gently. How does it go?
Which kick sends a ball farther?
A ball sits still. Nobody pushes or pulls it. What does it do?
You pull a sled. Then you pull harder. What happens?
A rolling ball bumps into a block. What happens to the block?
cards.note: Things can push things, not just people.

cards.q: What can pull a paper clip without touching it?
Which one does a magnet pull?
cards.note: Magnets pull some metals, like iron and steel, not paper, wood or plastic.

cards.q: How does a magnet move a paper clip?
Same car, same floor, two pushes. One time it went farther. What was different?
You want to know which push makes the car go farther. What do you do?
cards.note: Scientists test to find out.

cards.q: A ball rolls slowly. You push it from behind. What happens?

decks.subject: science
decks.title: How Things Move
decks.about: The ways things move (straight, zigzag, round and round, back and forth, up and down, fast and slow), what changes that motion (a ramp, a wall, a harder push) and the position words that tell where a thing is (PS.1.1.1, PS.1.1.2). NC's forces objective has children describe motion and position before they explain it.
decks.tip: Roll a toy car down a book propped on a pillow, then on a taller stack, and ask him to say how it moved each time: straight, fast, slow, down.

cards.q: You roll a ball across a flat floor. How does it move?
cards.note: A rolling ball goes straight until something pushes it a new way.

cards.q: A rabbit runs this way, then that way, then this way again. How does it move?
cards.note: Zigzag means turning from side to side as you go.

cards.q: You ride a merry-go-round. How does it move?
cards.note: A spinning top and a bike wheel go round and round too.

cards.q: You sit on a swing. It goes out, then back, then out again. How does it move?
cards.note: A rocking chair and a seesaw go back and forth too.

cards.q: You bounce a ball. Which way does it go?
cards.note: Down to the floor, back up to your hand, again and again.

cards.q: A race car zooms past. Is it moving fast or slow?
cards.note: Fast and slow tell how quickly something moves.

cards.q: A snail creeps along a leaf. Is it moving fast or slow?
cards.note: Slow is still moving. Not moving at all is called still.

cards.q: You let go of a toy car at the top of a ramp. Which way does it roll?
cards.note: Things roll down a ramp on their own. You have to push to send one up.

cards.q: One ramp is tall and one is low. Which ramp makes the car roll faster?
cards.note: A taller, steeper ramp makes the car go faster and farther.

cards.q: A rolling ball hits a wall. What happens to the ball?
cards.note: The wall pushes back on the ball. Sometimes the ball bounces back a little.

cards.q: Your toy car stopped too soon. How do you make it roll farther next time?
cards.note: A bigger push makes a thing go faster and farther.

cards.q: A balloon floats up over your head. Where is the balloon?
cards.note: Above means higher than. Position words tell where a thing is.

cards.q: Your shoes are on the floor under your bed. Where are the shoes?
cards.note: Below means lower than. Under and beneath mean the same thing.

cards.q: Your cup is right next to your plate. Which word tells where the cup is?
cards.note: Beside means next to.

cards.q: You hide at the back of the couch where nobody can see you. Where are you?
cards.note: Behind means at the back of.

cards.q: A dog sits between you and the TV, so you cannot see the screen. Where is the dog?
cards.note: In front of is the opposite of behind.

cards.q: A ball is on the chair. You move it to the floor. What changed about the ball?
cards.note: Position means where a thing is. A push or a pull can change it.

decks.subject: science
decks.title: Day Sky, Night Sky
decks.about: What we see in the day sky and the night sky, and how the sun and moon seem to move across it (ESS.1.1.1). NC asks children to notice the apparent movement, not explain it.
decks.tip: Look out the same window in the morning and after dinner and talk about where the sun was each time.

cards.q: What do we see in the day sky that gives us light and heat?
What do we see in the night sky?
Can we ever see the moon in the daytime?
cards.note: Look for a pale moon on a bright day.

cards.q: When does the sun seem to come up?
When does the sun seem to go down?
In the morning the sun is low. By midday, where does the sun seem to be?
cards.note: Midday is the middle of the day. The sun seems highest then.

cards.q: Which one can hurt your eyes if you look right at it?
cards.note: Never look right at the sun.

cards.q: What kind of sky object is the sun?
cards.note: The sun is the star closest to us.

cards.q: Why do stars look so small?
cards.note: Stars are very big, but very far away.

cards.q: When can we see lots of stars?
From morning to evening, what does the sun seem to do?
cards.note: It only seems to move. We see this pattern every day.

cards.q: What shape does the sun look like in the sky?
What comes after night?
cards.note: Day and night repeat. That is a pattern.

cards.q: The sky is dark and you see the moon. Is it day or night?
On a clear day, what color is the sky?
cards.note: Clouds are part of the day sky too.

cards.q: Watch the moon all night. What does it seem to do?
cards.note: The moon and stars seem to move too, just like the sun.

decks.subject: science
decks.title: Weather Words
decks.about: The weather words a first grader hears every morning (sunny, cloudy, rainy, windy, snowy, foggy), reading hot and cold on a thermometer, what to wear and carry, puddles and where they go, and that weather can change in one day. Weather is a kindergarten standard in NC's 2023 science standards, so this is a bridge deck filed under ESS.1.1.1 (sun and sky patterns), the closest Grade 1 objective.
decks.tip: Make him the weather reporter at breakfast: he looks out the window, says the weather word and picks what to wear.

cards.q: The sky is clear and bright and the sun is out. What kind of day is it?
cards.note: A sunny day is a good day to look for your shadow.

cards.q: Gray clouds cover the whole sky. What kind of day is it?
cards.note: Clouds are made of tiny drops of water floating in the air.

cards.q: Drops of water fall from the clouds. What is the weather?
cards.note: Rain gives plants, animals and people the water they need.

cards.q: The trees bend and leaves fly around. What kind of day is it?
cards.note: Wind is moving air. You cannot see it, but you can feel it and see what it pushes.

cards.q: Soft white flakes fall and cover the ground. What is the weather?
cards.note: Snow is frozen water. It falls when the air is very cold.

cards.q: A low cloud sits on the ground and you can hardly see across the street. What is that?
cards.note: Fog is a cloud down at the ground. It often comes in the early morning.

cards.q: Where does rain fall from?
cards.note: When the drops in a cloud get big and heavy, they fall as rain.

cards.q: It rained all morning. What is left on the sidewalk?
cards.note: A puddle is rain water that has not soaked in or dried up yet.

cards.q: The sun comes out and the puddle gets smaller. Where did the water go?
cards.note: The sun's heat dries up puddles. We say the water evaporates.

cards.q: The red line in the thermometer is way up high. Is it hot or cold outside?
cards.note: A thermometer measures temperature. High line, hot day.

cards.q: The red line in the thermometer is very low. Is it hot or cold outside?
cards.note: Low line, cold day. Water outside can freeze into ice.

cards.q: It is raining. What do you carry to stay dry?
cards.note: A raincoat keeps you dry too.

cards.q: What do you wear on your feet to keep them dry in puddles?
cards.note: Rain boots keep your socks dry.

cards.q: It is hot and sunny. What do you wear to keep the bright sun out of your eyes?
cards.note: A sun hat helps too. Never look right at the sun.

cards.q: It is snowing. What do you put on your hands?
cards.note: Mittens keep your fingers warm together in one pocket.

cards.q: Which toy flies best on a windy day?
cards.note: The wind pushes on the kite and holds it up.

cards.q: What do we call what the sky and air are like today, like sunny or rainy?
cards.note: Weather can change from day to day. Seasons change slowly.

cards.q: It was sunny this morning. Now it is raining. Can weather change in one day?
cards.note: That is why we look out the window every morning.

decks.subject: science
decks.title: Sun and Shadows
decks.about: The sun's daily pattern (up in the east, high at midday, down in the west, light and heat) and the shadows it makes: long in the morning and evening, short at midday, always on the side away from the light (ESS.1.1.1). Shadows are not named in the Grade 1 standard; they are the easiest way for a child to see the sun's apparent movement, so this is a bridge inside ESS.1.1.1.
decks.tip: Trace his shadow with chalk after breakfast, at lunch and before dinner, then compare the three.

cards.q: In the morning, which part of the sky does the sun seem to come up in?
cards.note: We say the sun rises in the east.

cards.q: In the evening, which part of the sky does the sun seem to go down in?
cards.note: We say the sun sets in the west.

cards.q: Does the sun seem to come up in the same part of the sky every morning?
cards.note: Up in the east, down in the west, every single day. That is a pattern.

cards.q: A sidewalk has been in the sun all afternoon. How does it feel?
cards.note: The sun gives us heat as well as light.

cards.q: On a hot day, where is it cooler, in the sun or in the shade?
cards.note: Shade is the shadow of a tree or a building. Less of the sun's heat reaches there.

cards.q: What makes a shadow?
cards.note: Light cannot go through you, so a dark shape shows on the other side.

cards.q: The sun is in front of you. Where is your shadow?
cards.note: Your body blocks the sunlight, so the dark spot is behind you.

cards.q: Is a shadow on the side toward the light or on the side away from it?
cards.note: Try it with a flashlight and a toy.

cards.q: In the early morning the sun is low. Is your shadow long or short?
cards.note: When the sun is low, shadows stretch out long.

cards.q: At midday the sun is high in the sky. Is your shadow long or short?
cards.note: When the sun is high, your shadow is short and close to your feet.

cards.q: In the evening the sun is low again. What does your shadow do?
cards.note: Long in the morning, short at midday, long again in the evening.

cards.q: Your shadow points a different way in the afternoon than in the morning. What seemed to move?
cards.note: As the sun seems to cross the sky, shadows swing around and change length.

cards.q: There is no sunlight at night. What happens to your sun shadow?
cards.note: No light, no shadow. A lamp or a flashlight can still make one.

cards.q: You walk across a sunny yard. What does your shadow do?
cards.note: Your shadow stays joined to your feet wherever you go.

cards.q: A cloud drifts in front of the sun. What happens to your shadow?
cards.note: Less light means a fainter shadow. When the cloud moves on, it comes back.

cards.q: You want to know where the sun is. What is the safe way to find out?
cards.note: Never look right at the sun. Your shadow points away from it.

decks.subject: science
decks.title: The Moon Changes
decks.about: Noticing that the moon's look changes a little each day in a pattern that repeats about every four weeks (ESS.1.1.2). NC does not require phase names or the reason, only the pattern.
decks.tip: Keep a moon chart on the fridge: draw what the moon looks like a few nights a week and ask what he thinks comes next.

cards.q: How does the moon look from one night to the next?
How often does the moon's look change a little?
About how long until the moon looks the same again?
cards.note: That is about one month.

cards.q: What does the moon pattern do?
cards.note: A pattern is something that happens again and again.

cards.q: Look: 🌑 🌒 🌓. Which moon comes next?
cards.sayQ: Look at the moons. Which one comes next?
cards.sayA: the moon that is almost full

cards.q: Look: 🌒 🌓 🌔. Which moon comes next?
cards.sayQ: Look at the moons. Which one comes next?

cards.q: Look: 🌕 🌖 🌗. Which moon comes next?
cards.sayQ: Look at the moons. Which one comes next?

cards.q: Look: 🌔 🌕 🌖. Which moon comes next?
cards.sayQ: Look at the moons. Which one comes next?

cards.q: After a full moon, how much of the moon do we see each night?
Before a full moon, how much of the moon do we see each night?
How can you keep track of how the moon looks?
cards.note: Draw the moon a few nights each week.

cards.q: What helps you guess how the moon will look next week?
What lights up the moon?
cards.note: The moon is always round. We see more or less of the side the sun lights.

decks.subject: science
decks.title: Seasons
decks.about: The four seasons in order, what each looks like in North Carolina (fall leaves, cold winters with some snow, spring rain and flowers, hot summers), longer summer days and shorter winter days, and what people and animals do. Seasons are not named in NC's 2023 Grade 1 science standards; this is a bridge topic filed under ESS.1.1.1 (sun patterns), the closest objective.
decks.tip: Each month, ask him what season it is and for one clue from outside the window that proves it.

cards.q: How many seasons are there in a year?
cards.note: Fall, winter, spring, summer, then fall again.

cards.q: What season comes after fall?
cards.note: Fall leaves drop, then the cold of winter comes.

cards.q: What season comes after winter?
cards.note: After the cold, things warm up and flowers come back.

cards.q: What season comes after spring?
cards.note: Spring warms up into hot summer. School lets out.

cards.q: What season comes after summer?
cards.note: Fall is also called autumn.

cards.q: After summer comes fall again. What do the seasons do every year?
cards.note: The seasons go around in the same order every year. That is a pattern.

cards.q: In fall, many North Carolina leaves turn red, orange and yellow. Then what do they do?
cards.note: That is why we call this season fall.

cards.q: Which season is the coldest in North Carolina?
cards.note: Winter is December, January and February here.

cards.q: In North Carolina, when might you see snow?
cards.note: Some winters bring snow and some do not. The mountains get the most.

cards.q: In spring the days get warmer and it rains. What do plants start to do?
cards.note: Spring brings flowers, buds and new green leaves.

cards.q: Which season is the hottest in North Carolina?
cards.note: Summer here is hot and sticky. Many families cool off at a pool or the beach.

cards.q: In which season does the sun stay up the longest?
cards.note: In summer it is still light after supper. That is one of the sun's patterns.

cards.q: In winter, when does it get dark outside?
cards.note: Winter days are short. Summer days are long.

cards.q: What do you wear outside on a cold winter day?
cards.note: People change what they wear as the seasons change.

cards.q: In fall, what do many people rake up in their yards?
cards.note: Jumping in the leaf pile is the best part.

cards.q: Some birds fly to warmer places for the winter. When do they come back?
cards.note: Hummingbirds leave North Carolina in fall and come back in spring.

cards.q: A black bear rests through much of the cold winter. Where does it rest?
cards.note: North Carolina has black bears. In the cold mountains they rest in dens through winter.

decks.subject: science
decks.title: Rocks, Soil and Water
decks.about: The four Earth materials NC names (rocks, minerals, soil, water) and the properties children observe: color, size, shape, texture, solid or liquid, sink or float, magnetic, bendy (ESS.1.2.1). No mineral names are required.
decks.tip: Hand him three rocks and ask him to describe each one with a color word, a size word and a feel word.

cards.q: What are the four Earth materials?
cards.note: Earth materials come from the Earth. People do not make them.

cards.q: What are rocks made of?
cards.note: Rocks are made of minerals. Look closely and you can see little specks.

cards.q: Is a rock a solid or a liquid?
cards.note: A solid keeps its shape. A rock stays a rock in your hand or in a cup.

cards.q: Is water in a cup a solid or a liquid?
cards.note: A liquid flows. Water in a cup is a liquid.

cards.q: Which one takes the shape of its cup?
cards.note: A liquid takes the shape of what holds it. A solid does not.

cards.q: Which place has lots of water?
cards.note: Water is in oceans, rivers, lakes and ponds.

cards.q: Soil is the top layer of the ground where...
cards.note: Soil is the top layer of the ground where plants grow.

cards.q: Which rock is small enough to hold in your hand?
cards.note: A pebble is a small rock. A boulder is a very big rock.

cards.q: You drop a pebble in water. What happens?
cards.note: A pebble sinks. Sink or float is something we can test.

cards.q: A magnet pulls on some rocks. What property is that?
cards.note: Some rocks have iron in them. A magnet pulls on those rocks.

cards.q: Which Earth material can you squish and bend when it is wet?
cards.note: Wet clay bends. A rock does not. Bendy is a property too.

cards.q: Which Earth material can you pour?
cards.note: Water pours. It flows from one cup to another.

cards.q: Which word tells a rock's color?
cards.note: Rocks can be gray, brown, black, white or pink.

cards.q: Which word tells how a rock feels?
cards.note: How a rock feels is its texture. It can be rough or smooth.

cards.q: Which word tells a rock's size?
cards.note: Size words are big, small, tiny and huge.

cards.q: Which word tells a rock's shape?
cards.note: Shape words are round, flat, pointy and square.

decks.subject: science
decks.title: Dig Into Soil
decks.about: Comparing soils: sand, clay and humus, which holds water, which drains, and what good soil gives a plant (ESS.1.2.2). NC wants children to test local soil samples; these cards hold the ideas behind the test.
decks.tip: Fill two cups, one with sand and one with garden soil, pour in water and watch which one holds it longer.

cards.q: Soil from a beach and soil from a garden are...
cards.note: Soil is different in different places.

cards.q: Soil gives plants water and...
cards.note: Nutrients are things in soil that help plants grow.

cards.q: The word retain means to...
cards.note: Good soil retains water.

cards.q: Good soil helps plants...
cards.note: Plants grow best in soil that holds water and has nutrients.

cards.q: Which three things can be in soil?
cards.note: Soil can have sand, clay and humus in it.

cards.q: Which has bigger grains, sand or clay?
cards.note: Clay grains are too tiny to see one by one.

cards.q: Which one does water run through fastest, sand or clay?
cards.note: Big sand grains leave big gaps for water to run through.

cards.q: Which holds water longer, sand or clay?
cards.note: Clay retains water. Sand lets it drain away.

cards.q: What is the dark, crumbly part of soil made from rotted leaves?
cards.note: Rotted leaves and plants turn into humus.

cards.q: Which one feels gritty, like tiny rocks?
cards.note: Sand grains are tiny bits of rock.

cards.q: Which one feels sticky and smooth when it is wet?
cards.note: People shape wet clay into pots and bricks.

cards.q: How do you find out which soil holds the most water?
cards.note: Scientists test things to find out. They do not just guess.

cards.q: Same seeds, same water, same light, but not the same soil. One plant grew taller. What made the difference?
cards.note: A fair test changes only one thing.

cards.q: Where does soil come from?
cards.note: Soil is tiny bits of broken rock mixed with rotted plants.

decks.subject: science
decks.title: Gifts From Earth
decks.about: Natural resources and how people use them: trees, soil, water, clay, metal, oil, coal, plants and animals (ESS.1.3.1). Also that resources are not found everywhere.
decks.tip: At dinner, pick one thing on the table and trace it back: the glass came from sand, the fork from metal in the ground.

cards.q: Where does paper come from?
cards.note: Paper is made from wood. Wood comes from trees.

cards.q: What do we grow our food in?
cards.note: Soil gives plants water and nutrients.

cards.q: What are bricks and flower pots made from?
cards.note: Clay is soft, sticky earth. It gets hard when it is baked.

cards.q: Most cars burn gas. What is gas made from?
cards.note: Oil comes from deep in the ground.

cards.q: Where does our drinking water come from?
cards.note: Some drinking water also comes from wells deep in the ground.

cards.q: What are metal pots and pans made from?
cards.note: Metal is found inside rocks in the ground.

cards.q: Where do the fish we eat come from?
cards.note: Fish are a food that comes from water.

cards.q: Where do natural resources come from?
cards.note: A natural resource is something from Earth that people use.

cards.q: Where do wool, milk and eggs come from?
cards.note: Wool comes from sheep, milk from cows and eggs from hens.

cards.q: Where does the cotton in a shirt come from?
cards.note: Cotton grows in soft white puffs on a cotton plant.

cards.q: What do people melt to make glass?
cards.note: Sand gets so hot it melts. Then it cools into clear glass.

cards.q: People burn coal and oil. What does that make?
cards.note: Some power plants burn coal to make electricity for our homes.

cards.q: A desert has lots of sand. What does it have very little of?
cards.note: Natural resources are not found everywhere. A desert has very little water.

cards.q: What do people build with rocks and stone?
cards.note: Stone is strong. Stone walls can stand for hundreds of years.

cards.q: Where can the salt for our food come from?
cards.note: Salt also comes from salt rock in the ground.

decks.subject: science
decks.title: Protect Our Earth
decks.about: Ways people protect natural resources: recycle, reuse, reduce, compost, save water and power, replant trees, no litter (ESS.1.3.2). NC wants children to argue for these from evidence; the cards give them the facts to argue with.
decks.tip: Let him be the recycling boss for a week: he decides what goes in the bin and says why.

cards.q: You finish a box of cereal. What should you do with the empty box?
cards.note: Old boxes can be made into new paper.

cards.q: You have a bag from the store. How can you reuse it?
cards.note: Using a bag again means one less new bag.

cards.q: You want to reduce trash. What can you do?
cards.note: Less stuff used means less trash made.

cards.q: People cut down trees for wood. What should they do after?
cards.note: New trees grow up to take the place of the old ones.

cards.q: You leave a room. What do you do to save power?
cards.note: Lights that are off use no power.

cards.q: What can you make from food scraps and leaves?
cards.note: Compost turns scraps into rich soil.

cards.q: Which one goes in the recycling bin?
cards.note: Paper, plastic, metal and glass can be recycled.

cards.q: A hose is running and nobody is using it. What do you do?
cards.note: That is one way to conserve water.

cards.q: You brush your teeth. How do you save water?
cards.note: Turn the water on only to rinse.

cards.q: Why should we save water?
cards.note: If we waste it, we could run short.

cards.q: You have a candy wrapper outside. Where does it go?
cards.note: Trash in a can is not litter.

cards.q: What can litter in a pond hurt?
cards.note: A clean pond is a safe home for the animals in it.

cards.q: You draw on paper. How can you save trees?
cards.note: Using both sides of a sheet means fewer trees cut.

cards.q: What does riding a bike instead of a car save?
cards.note: A car burns fuel. A bike just needs your legs.

cards.q: What does a shorter shower save?
cards.note: Every minute in the shower uses more water.

decks.subject: science
decks.title: Force and Earth Words
decks.about: The science words from NC's forces, sky and Earth-materials standards, as 'what do we call' cards. These are the words the teacher uses, so hearing them often makes class easier.
decks.tip: After he taps the word, ask him to use it in a sentence about something in the room.

cards.q: What do we call a push or a pull?
cards.note: A kick is a push. Opening a drawer is a pull. Both are forces.

cards.q: What do we call it when something moves?
cards.note: A rolling car is in motion. A push or pull can start it, stop it or turn it.

cards.q: What do we call a thing that pulls some metals without touching them?
cards.note: A magnet can pull a paper clip without touching it. It pulls some metals, not all.

cards.q: What do we call a test to find an answer?
cards.note: Say in-ves-ti-GAY-shun. Pushing a toy car softly and then hard is an investigation.

cards.q: What do we call what we see and write down in a test?
cards.note: How far the car rolled each time is data.

cards.q: What do we call telling how two things are alike and different?
cards.note: We compare a soft push and a hard push to see what changed.

cards.q: What do we call something that happens again and again?
cards.note: Day, then night, then day again is a pattern.

cards.q: What do we call the star that gives us light and heat?
cards.note: The sun is a star. Never look right at it.

cards.q: What do we call a far-away ball of light in the night sky?
cards.note: Stars look tiny because they are so far away.

cards.q: What do we call a smart guess about what comes next?
cards.note: Say pre-DIK-shun. If you know the pattern, you can make a prediction.

cards.q: What do we call the bits that rocks are made of?
cards.note: Look closely at a rock. The little specks and sparkles are minerals.

cards.q: What do we call something that keeps its shape, like a rock?
cards.note: A rock stays a rock in a cup, in a box or in your hand.

cards.q: What do we call something that flows and takes the shape of its cup?
cards.note: Water in a cup is a liquid. Pour it in a bowl and it takes the shape of the bowl.

cards.q: What do we call how something feels?
cards.note: Rough, smooth, bumpy and soft are all textures.

cards.q: What do we call something you can observe about a thing, like its color?
cards.note: Color, size, shape and texture are properties of a rock.

cards.q: What do we call the top layer of ground where plants grow?
cards.note: Soil is not all the same. Some is sandy and some is sticky.

cards.q: What do we call the things in soil that help plants grow?
cards.note: Say NOO-tree-unts. Good soil gives plants water and nutrients.

cards.q: What do we call the dark part of soil made from rotted plants?
cards.note: Say HYOO-mus. Old leaves rot and turn into humus.

decks.subject: science
decks.title: What Living Things Need
decks.about: NC's list of basic needs: plants need water, air and light; animals need water, air and food; both need shelter and space (LS.1.1.1). Cards apply the list to real plants and animals.
decks.tip: Care for one houseplant together and name which need you are meeting each time: water, light, space.

cards.q: Plants need water, air and what else?
cards.note: A plant on a windowsill leans toward the light.

cards.q: Animals need water, air and what else?
cards.note: Food gives an animal energy to move and grow.

cards.q: Which one do plants need?
cards.note: Plants need air too, just like animals.

cards.q: What do plants and animals both need?
cards.note: Every living thing needs water. Plants take it in through their roots.

cards.q: What is a bird's shelter?
cards.note: A nest is a safe place for a bird and its eggs.

cards.q: Too many plants are in one pot. What do they need more of?
cards.note: Plants need room for their roots and leaves to grow.

cards.q: Animals eat plants or what else?
cards.note: Food is a need. Animals get it from plants or from other animals.

cards.q: Where do plants get their light from?
cards.note: Sunlight is the light plants use to grow.

cards.q: What does a rabbit eat?
cards.note: Rabbits eat grass, leaves and other plants.

cards.q: Where do a plant's roots get water?
cards.note: Roots take in water from the soil and send it up the stem.

cards.q: What happens to a plant with no water?
cards.note: A wilted plant droops. Watering it helps it stand up again.

cards.q: What do people need to breathe?
cards.note: People are animals too, so we need air, water and food.

cards.q: A dog has food, water and air. What else does it need?
cards.note: Shelter is a safe place to live, like a doghouse or a home.

cards.q: Which one does a seed need to sprout?
cards.note: A seed soaks up water, then a tiny root and shoot grow out.

cards.q: What is a fox's shelter?
cards.note: A den is a safe hole or cave. A burrow is a hole an animal digs to live in.

cards.q: A houseplant needs light. Where should it go?
cards.note: A window lets in sunlight for the plant.

decks.subject: science
decks.title: Living or Not Living?
decks.about: What every living thing does (grows, needs water, air and food or light, makes more of its kind, responds to the world) and sorting things that are living from things that only look alive or only move: a mushroom, an ant and a worm versus a cloud, a river, a ball and a toy robot (LS.1.1.1). Knowing what counts as living is the ground under NC's basic-needs objective.
decks.tip: Point at things on a walk and ask the four questions: does it grow, does it need water, can it have babies, does it react when you get close?

cards.q: A puppy gets bigger every month. What is the puppy doing?
cards.note: All living things grow.

cards.q: Which clue tells you a thing is living?
cards.note: Living things grow, need water, air and food or light, and make more of their kind.

cards.q: What needs water to stay alive?
cards.note: Every living thing needs water. A rock and a spoon do not.

cards.q: What needs to breathe air?
cards.note: Animals breathe air. Plants need air too, in their own way.

cards.q: What can have babies?
cards.note: Living things make more of their own kind. A cat has kittens.

cards.q: A sunflower makes seeds. What do the seeds grow into?
cards.note: Plants make more of their own kind with seeds.

cards.q: You gently touch it and it wiggles away. What is it?
cards.note: Living things respond to touch, light, heat and sound.

cards.q: A dog hears a loud noise and jumps. What is the dog doing?
cards.note: Living things respond to what is around them. A rock never jumps.

cards.q: Which one grows, so it must be living?
cards.note: A mushroom grows, so it is living, even though it is not a plant or an animal.

cards.q: Which one is alive?
cards.note: Even tiny ants grow, eat and make more ants.

cards.q: Which bear is living?
cards.note: A toy looks like an animal, but it never grows, eats or breathes.

cards.q: Which one is a living thing?
cards.note: People are living things, just like animals and plants.

cards.q: Look up at the sky. Which one up there is nonliving?
cards.sayQ: Look up at the sky. Which one up there is non-living?
cards.note: A cloud moves, but it does not grow, eat or have babies. The wind moves it.

cards.q: Which one is a nonliving thing?
cards.sayQ: Which one is a non-living thing?
cards.note: A ball only moves when something pushes or pulls it.

cards.q: What runs on batteries?
cards.note: A toy robot moves only with batteries. It never grows, so it is nonliving.

cards.q: A river moves fast and splashes. Why is it still nonliving?
cards.sayQ: A river moves fast and splashes. Why is it still non-living?
cards.note: Moving is not enough. Living things grow and need food or light.

cards.q: What makes a bike move?
cards.note: A bike only moves when someone pushes or pedals it. It is nonliving.

decks.subject: science
decks.title: Parts of a Plant
decks.about: The parts of a plant and the job each does: roots take in water and hold the plant, the stem carries water and holds it up, leaves use sunlight to make food, flowers make seeds and seeds grow into new plants, plus what a seed needs to sprout. Plant parts are not named in NC's 2023 Grade 1 standards; this bridge deck sits under LS.1.1.1 because each part meets one of the needs that objective lists (water, air, light).
decks.tip: Pull up a weed together, roots and all, and name each part from the bottom up.

cards.q: Which part of a plant grows down into the soil?
cards.note: Roots are under the ground, so you usually cannot see them.

cards.q: What do roots take in from the soil?
cards.note: Roots also take in nutrients from the soil.

cards.q: The wind blows hard, but the plant stays put. What holds it in the ground?
cards.note: Roots spread out in the soil like an anchor.

cards.q: What holds a flower up tall so it can reach the light?
cards.note: A sunflower stem can grow taller than a grown-up.

cards.q: Water travels from the roots up to the leaves. What does it travel through?
cards.note: A stem is like a straw for the plant.

cards.q: What do we call the thick, woody stem of a tree?
cards.note: A trunk holds up all the branches and carries water to every leaf.

cards.q: Which part uses sunlight to make food for the plant?
cards.note: Leaves use sunlight, air and water to make the plant's food.

cards.q: Where do most leaves grow, down in the soil or up in the light?
cards.note: Leaves need light, so they grow where the light is.

cards.q: Which part of a plant makes the seeds?
cards.note: After the petals drop, seeds grow where the flower was.

cards.q: What are the colorful parts of a flower called?
cards.note: Bright petals help bees and butterflies find the flower.

cards.q: A bee visits a flower. What is the bee looking for?
cards.note: The bee carries pollen from flower to flower. That helps flowers make seeds.

cards.q: An apple has seeds inside. What part of the plant is an apple?
cards.note: A fruit grows from a flower and holds the seeds.

cards.q: What grows out of a seed?
cards.note: A tiny seed can grow into a huge tree.

cards.q: A seed sprouts. What pokes out first and grows down?
cards.note: The root comes first. Then a shoot grows up toward the light.

cards.q: A seed needs water to sprout. What else does it need?
