cards.note: Most seeds also need air. They do not need light until they poke up.

cards.q: A carrot grows under the ground. Is it a root, a leaf or a flower?
cards.note: We eat roots like carrots, leaves like lettuce and seeds like peas.

cards.q: Lettuce is the flat green part of a plant. Is it a leaf, a root or a seed?
cards.note: Spinach and cabbage are leaves we eat too.

decks.subject: science
decks.title: Animal Groups
decks.about: Sorting animals into six groups by what covers their body, how many legs they have and where they start life: mammals (fur, milk), birds (feathers, eggs, two legs), fish (fins, gills), reptiles (dry scales), amphibians (frogs: water, then land) and insects (six legs). Animal groups are not named in NC's 2023 Grade 1 standards; this bridge deck sits under LS.1.1.2 because each group's body parts fit the place that meets its needs.
decks.tip: Play 'which group?' with the animals on a walk or in a picture book: fur or feathers, how many legs, wet skin or dry scales.

cards.q: A dog has fur and drank its mother's milk as a puppy. What group is a dog in?
cards.note: Mammals have fur or hair and feed their babies milk.

cards.q: You have hair and drank milk as a baby. Which animal group are people in?
cards.note: People are mammals, just like dogs, cats and cows.

cards.q: Which animal group has feathers?
cards.note: Only birds have feathers. Feathers keep them warm and help them fly.

cards.q: How many legs does a bird have?
cards.note: Two legs and two wings. A bird also has a beak instead of teeth.

cards.q: A hen lays eggs with hard shells. What group does a hen belong to?
cards.note: Baby birds hatch out of eggs. Most mammals are born, not hatched.

cards.q: Which animal group breathes with gills and swims with fins?
cards.note: Most fish are covered in slippery scales.

cards.q: A snake has dry, scaly skin. Is a snake a reptile, a bird or a fish?
cards.note: Reptiles have dry scales. Snakes, lizards, turtles and alligators are reptiles.

cards.q: A lizard with dry scales warms up on a sunny rock. What kind of animal is a lizard?
cards.note: Reptiles sit in the sun to warm their bodies.

cards.q: A frog starts life in the water and then lives on land. What group is a frog in?
cards.note: Say am-FIB-ee-uns. Amphibians have thin, damp skin with no scales. Toads and salamanders are amphibians too.

cards.q: A frog has wet skin. A lizard has dry scales. A dog has fur. Which one is the reptile?
cards.note: Wet skin means amphibian. Dry scales mean reptile.

cards.q: How many legs does an insect have?
cards.note: A spider has eight legs, so a spider is not an insect.

cards.q: A ladybug has six legs. Which group does a ladybug belong to?
cards.note: Insects have six legs and three body parts. Most have wings too.

cards.q: Which one is a bird?
cards.note: Feathers, a beak and two legs. An eagle is a bird.

cards.q: Which one is a fish?
cards.note: A shark has gills and fins, so it is a fish. A whale is not a fish.

cards.q: A whale breathes air and feeds its baby milk. Is a whale a mammal or a fish?
cards.note: A whale lives in the sea, but it comes up to breathe air through a blowhole.

cards.q: Which one is a reptile?
cards.note: An alligator has dry, scaly skin. Alligators live in the warm rivers near North Carolina's coast.

cards.q: Which one is an insect?
cards.note: Count the legs. A bee has six. A spider has eight and a worm has none.

cards.q: A penguin has feathers and lays eggs, but it swims instead of flying. What group is a penguin in?
cards.note: A penguin uses its wings to swim instead of fly. It is still a bird.

decks.subject: science
decks.title: Where Can It Live?
decks.about: Comparing places: a living thing can only live where its needs are met, so a whale cannot live in a lake and a pine tree cannot grow in a desert (LS.1.1.2). Also living versus nonliving.
decks.tip: Play 'could it live here?' on a walk: could a fish live in this tree? could a polar bear live in our yard? Ask why not.

cards.q: Where does a whale live?
cards.note: A lake is too small for a whale. It needs the big ocean.

cards.q: What kind of place does a polar bear need?
cards.note: A polar bear has thick fur and fat to stay warm on the ice and snow.

cards.q: A desert is too dry for which one?
cards.note: A pine tree needs more water than a desert has. A cactus and a lizard can live where it is dry.

cards.q: A land of ice and snow is too cold for which one?
cards.note: A snake needs warm sun to warm up its body.

cards.q: Where can a living thing live?
cards.note: Needs are water, air, food or light, shelter and space.

cards.q: Which one is living?
cards.note: Living things grow and need water, air and food or light.

cards.q: Which one is nonliving?
cards.sayQ: Which one is non-living?
cards.note: A rock does not grow and does not need water, air or food.

cards.q: Where does a fish live?
cards.note: Water gives a fish everything it needs.

cards.q: Where does a cactus grow?
cards.note: A cactus keeps water inside, so it can live where it is dry.

cards.q: Where does a camel live?
cards.note: A camel can go many days without a drink.

cards.q: A forest gives a squirrel nuts to eat and trees for what?
cards.note: A squirrel makes its nest high in a tree.

cards.q: Where does a fish get the air it needs?
cards.note: A fish's gills take what it needs from the water.

cards.q: Which animal can live where it is icy and cold?
cards.note: A penguin has thick feathers and fat to keep warm.

cards.q: What is missing for a plant in a dark cave?
cards.note: Plants need light to make their food.

cards.q: Where does an earthworm live?
cards.note: Soil is damp and dark, just what a worm needs.

decks.subject: science
decks.title: Growing and Changing
decks.about: Life cycles in order and 'what comes next': egg, caterpillar, chrysalis, butterfly; egg, tadpole, frog; seed, sprout, plant, flower; egg, chick, chicken; baby, child, grown-up, plus baby animal names and that young animals grow up to look like their parents. Life cycles are a Grade 2 topic in NC's 2023 science standards; this bridge deck sits under LS.1.1.1 because a living thing can only grow and change when its basic needs are met.
decks.tip: Say a life cycle out loud together and stop before the last step: egg, tadpole, then what? Let him finish it.

cards.q: A butterfly's life starts as a tiny egg on a leaf. What hatches out of the egg?
cards.note: The tiny caterpillar eats the leaf it hatched on.

cards.q: A caterpillar eats and grows. Then it makes a hard case around itself. What is the case called?
cards.note: Say KRIS-uh-lis. Inside it, the caterpillar changes into a butterfly. A moth spins a cocoon instead.

cards.q: Egg, caterpillar, chrysalis. What comes next?
cards.note: The butterfly comes out of the chrysalis with wet wings and lets them dry.

cards.q: Which comes first in a butterfly's life, the egg or the caterpillar?
cards.note: A grown butterfly lays eggs, and the cycle starts all over again.

cards.q: A frog lays its eggs in the water. What hatches out?
cards.note: A tadpole has a tail and breathes with gills, like a fish.

cards.q: Where does a tadpole live?
cards.note: A tadpole swims and eats in a pond until it grows legs.

cards.q: A tadpole grows legs and its tail gets shorter. What is it turning into?
cards.note: Back legs grow first, then front legs. Then the frog can hop onto land.

cards.q: A seed gets water and warmth. A tiny green shoot pops up. What do we call it?
cards.note: A sprout is a baby plant.

cards.q: Seed, sprout, plant. What comes next?
cards.note: The flower makes new seeds, and the cycle starts again.

cards.q: Seed, sprout, plant, flower, then seeds again. What do we call this?
cards.note: A life cycle goes round and round, like a circle.

cards.q: A hen sits on her eggs to keep them warm. What hatches out?
cards.note: The chick pecks a hole in the shell to get out.

cards.q: A fluffy yellow chick grows up. What does it become?
cards.note: A grown-up girl chicken is a hen. A grown-up boy chicken is a rooster.

cards.q: Which comes first, a baby or a child?
cards.note: Every grown-up was a baby once.

cards.q: Baby, child, then what?
cards.note: You are a child now. One day you will be a grown-up.

cards.q: What happens to your body as you grow up?
cards.note: Mark your height on a door frame and watch the marks climb.

cards.q: What do we call a baby cat?
cards.note: A baby cow is a calf and a baby sheep is a lamb.

cards.q: What do we call a baby dog?
cards.note: A puppy grows into a dog in about one year.

cards.q: A kitten grows up. What does it look like?
cards.note: Young animals grow up to look like their parents, but not exactly the same.

decks.subject: science
decks.title: Animal Homes
decks.about: Where animals live and the home or body part that makes the place fit: gills and fins for water, wings and nests in trees, dens, burrows, lodges, webs and hives, fur for the cold and wide feet for sand (LS.1.1.2). It goes one step past Where Can It Live by naming the part or the home that meets the need.
decks.tip: On a walk, spot an animal and ask two questions: where is its home, and what part of its body helps it live there?

cards.q: A fish has gills. What do gills help a fish do?
cards.note: Gills take the oxygen a fish needs out of the water. People cannot do that.

cards.q: What does a fish use to swim?
cards.note: The tail fin pushes the fish forward. The other fins help it steer and keep its balance.

cards.q: What part of a bird's body lets it fly?
cards.note: Wings and light bones help a bird fly up to its nest.

cards.q: What does a bird use to build its nest?
cards.note: Many birds build nests up in trees, out of reach.

cards.q: A beaver piles up sticks and mud in a pond to make its home. What is it called?
cards.note: Beavers live in North Carolina ponds and rivers too.

cards.q: What does a spider spin to catch its food?
cards.note: A web is sticky silk that comes out of the spider's body.

cards.q: Where do honeybees live and keep their honey?
cards.note: Thousands of bees can live in one hive.

cards.q: A chipmunk digs a hole in the ground to live in. What is the hole called?
cards.note: A burrow keeps a chipmunk safe and snug.

cards.q: Ants dig tunnels and rooms under the ground. What is their home called?
cards.note: The little mound on top is just the door. Most of the home is below.

cards.q: A black bear needs berries, nuts and a den. Which place has all three?
cards.note: North Carolina forests and mountains are home to black bears.

cards.q: A frog has smooth, wet skin and lays its eggs in water. Where does it live?
cards.note: A frog's skin must stay wet, so it stays close to water.

cards.q: A duck has webbed feet. What are they good for?
cards.note: Webbed feet work like little paddles.

cards.q: A polar bear has thick fur and a layer of fat. Why?
cards.note: Polar bears live in the far north where it is icy. White fur also hides them in the snow.

cards.q: A camel's feet are wide and flat. What does that help it do?
cards.note: Wide feet do not sink into the desert sand.

cards.q: What does a turtle carry on its back for shelter?
cards.note: Many turtles can pull their head and legs inside.

cards.q: An owl has very big eyes. When do they help it find food?
cards.note: Owls sleep in the day and hunt for mice at night.

cards.q: A mole has big, strong front paws. What are they for?
cards.note: A mole digs tunnels under the grass and lives there.

cards.q: A deer has long, thin legs. What are they good for?
cards.note: Fast legs help a deer get away from danger.

decks.subject: science
decks.title: Nature Words
decks.about: The words from NC's natural-resources and living-things standards: natural resource, recycle, reuse, reduce, conserve, compost, litter, basic needs, shelter, space, habitat, environment, ecosystem, living, nonliving. The last level on the science path.
decks.tip: Pick one word a day and hunt for an example of it around the house or yard.

cards.q: What do we call something from Earth that people use?
cards.note: Water, soil, trees and rocks are natural resources.

cards.q: What do we call soil that grows plants well?
cards.note: Say FER-tul. Fertile soil gives plants water and nutrients.

cards.q: What do we call turning used things into new things?
cards.note: Old cans can be made into new cans. Paper, plastic, metal and glass can be recycled.

cards.q: What do we call using something again?
cards.note: Using a bag again instead of taking a new one is reusing.

cards.q: What do we call using less of something?
cards.note: Turning off the lights when you leave a room reduces the power we use.

cards.q: What do we call saving something and not wasting it?
cards.note: Say kun-SERV. Turning off the water while you brush your teeth conserves water.

cards.q: What do we call food scraps and leaves rotting into soil?
cards.note: Rotted leaves turn into humus, the dark part of soil.

cards.q: What do we call trash dropped on the ground?
cards.note: Picking up litter helps keep land and water clean.

cards.q: What do we call the things a living thing must have to live?
cards.note: Plants need water, air and light. Animals need water, air and food.

cards.q: What do we call a safe place for an animal to live, like a nest or a den?
cards.note: A nest is a bird's shelter. Plants and animals both need shelter.

cards.q: What do we call the place where a plant or animal lives, like a pond or a forest?
cards.note: Say HAB-ih-tat. A pond, a forest and a desert are habitats.

cards.q: What do we call everything around a living thing?
cards.note: Say en-VY-run-ment. Air, water, soil and other living things are all part of it.

cards.q: What do we call living and nonliving things together in one place?
cards.note: Say EE-ko-sis-tum. A pond with frogs, plants, water and rocks is an ecosystem.

cards.q: What do we call something that grows and needs water, air and food or light?
cards.note: Plants and animals are living things.

cards.q: What do we call something that does not grow or need food, like a rock?
cards.note: Rocks, water and air are nonliving.

cards.q: What do we call room for a living thing to grow and move?
cards.note: Plants and animals both need space.

decks.subject: social
decks.title: Rules and Laws
decks.about: Why we have rules at home, at school and in the community, and that laws are rules everyone in a town, state or country must follow. NC 1.C&G.1.2: how people help make rules and laws.
decks.tip: Ask him to name one rule at home and say in his own words why it helps.

cards.q: Why do we have rules?
cards.a: to keep everyone safe and fair
cards.note: Rules help people stay safe and treat each other fairly.

cards.q: What do we call rules that everyone in a town, state or country must follow?
cards.note: A law is a rule for everyone, made by the government.

cards.q: Who helps make the rules for your classroom?
cards.note: Many classes talk together and agree on their rules.

cards.q: Who makes the rules at home?
cards.note: Families make rules so everyone at home stays safe and gets along.

cards.q: Every driver must stop at a red light. What do we call a rule like that?
cards.note: Traffic rules are laws. Every driver must follow them.

cards.q: Who must follow laws?
cards.note: Laws are for everyone, kids and grown-ups alike.

cards.q: Why do we wear a seat belt in the car?
cards.note: A seat belt holds you in your seat if the car stops fast.

cards.q: A fair rule is the same for which people?
cards.note: Fair means the rule is the same for every person.

cards.q: Why do we raise a hand before talking in class?
cards.note: Taking turns lets everyone be heard.

cards.q: Why do we walk, not run, in the hallway?
cards.note: Walking keeps everyone in the hallway safe.

cards.q: You break a rule and lose a turn. What is losing the turn called?
cards.note: A consequence is what happens after you break a rule.

cards.q: Why do kids need a grown-up with them at the pool?
cards.a: to stay safe in the water
cards.note: Pools have a rule that a grown-up watches kids in the water.

cards.q: Why is there a rule to wash hands before eating?
cards.note: Soap and water wash germs off your hands.

cards.q: Who must stop at a stop sign?
cards.note: Stopping at a stop sign is a law. Every driver must stop.

cards.q: Rules help us get along and stay what?
cards.note: Good rules keep people safe and help them get along.

cards.q: What do the rules of a game tell players?
cards.note: Game rules make sure every player plays the same way.

decks.subject: social
decks.title: Community Helpers
decks.about: What a community is and the people whose jobs keep it running: firefighters, mail carriers, farmers, doctors, teachers and more. NC 1.C&G.1.1: individuals and groups who shape communities.
decks.tip: On a drive, point at a truck or building and ask which helper works there.

cards.q: What do we call a place where people live, work and play together?
cards.note: Your town or neighborhood is a community.

cards.q: Who puts out fires?
cards.note: Firefighters spray water from big hoses on the fire truck.

cards.q: Who helps when you are lost and keeps the town safe?
cards.note: A police officer is a safe grown-up to ask for help.

cards.q: Who brings letters and packages to your home?
cards.note: Mail carriers bring mail to every house, rain or shine.

cards.q: Who grows the food we eat?
cards.note: Farmers grow fruits and vegetables and care for farm animals.

cards.q: Who helps you get better when you are sick?
cards.note: Doctors check your body and help you feel well.

cards.q: Who checks and cleans your teeth?
cards.note: Visit the dentist to keep your teeth strong and clean.

cards.q: Who helps you learn at school?
cards.note: Teachers help you read, write and count.

cards.q: Who helps you find books at the library?
cards.note: Librarians help you find and borrow books.

cards.q: Who drives kids safely to school?
cards.note: Bus drivers stop at each bus stop so kids can ride safely.

cards.q: Who takes away the trash each week?
cards.note: Trash collectors are also called sanitation workers.

cards.q: Who takes care of sick animals?
cards.note: Vet is short for veterinarian, a doctor for animals.

cards.q: Who builds houses and roads?
cards.note: Construction workers use tools and big machines to build.

cards.q: Who helps kids cross the street safely?
cards.note: A crossing guard holds up a sign so cars stop for you.

cards.q: Who bakes bread and cakes?
cards.note: Bakers get up early to make fresh bread.

cards.q: Who flies the airplane?
cards.note: Pilots sit at the front of the plane in the cockpit.

cards.q: Who fixes leaky pipes and sinks?
cards.note: Plumbers fix pipes so water runs in your home.

cards.q: Who cares for you at the hospital along with the doctor?
cards.note: Nurses check your temperature and help you feel better.

decks.subject: social
decks.title: Leaders and Voting
decks.about: Leaders as roles, from the teacher and principal up to the mayor, governor and president, who makes laws, and how people choose leaders by voting. NC 1.C&G.1.1 and 1.C&G.1.2.
decks.tip: Say a place (school, town, state, country) and let him name the leader; never use a current leader's name.

cards.q: What do we call a person who guides a group and helps make choices?
cards.note: A leader helps the group decide what to do.

cards.q: Who is the leader of your class?
cards.note: The teacher leads the class and helps everyone learn.

cards.q: Who leads the whole school?
cards.note: The principal is in charge of every class in the school.

cards.q: Who leads a town or city?
cards.note: The mayor works at town hall or city hall.

cards.q: Who leads our state, North Carolina?
cards.note: The governor works in Raleigh, the capital of North Carolina.

cards.q: Who leads our whole country, the United States?
cards.note: There is one president for the whole country.

cards.q: Where does the president live and work?
cards.note: The White House is in Washington, D.C., the capital of our country.

cards.q: Who makes the laws for the whole country?
cards.note: Congress is a big group of people chosen by voters.

cards.q: Who makes the laws for North Carolina?
cards.note: The General Assembly meets in Raleigh, our state capital.

cards.q: Who is in charge in a court of law?
cards.note: A judge listens to both sides and makes sure the court is fair.

cards.q: How do people choose their leaders?
cards.note: Each voter gets one vote.

cards.q: What do we call it when people vote to pick a leader?
cards.note: On election day, voters go to a voting place to vote.

cards.q: What do we call the paper or screen where you mark your vote?
cards.note: You mark your choice on the ballot, and your vote is kept private.

cards.q: Who can vote for the president in our country?
cards.note: Citizens who are 18 or older can vote.

cards.q: How can a class fairly pick which game to play?
cards.note: Voting is a fair way for a group to make a choice.

decks.subject: social
decks.title: Good Citizens
decks.about: Rights versus responsibilities, ways people make their community better (recycling, volunteering, picking up litter) and how to settle disagreements kindly. NC 1.C&G.1.3, 1.C&G.1.4 and 1.B.1.4.
decks.tip: When he says 'that's not fair', ask: is that a right or a responsibility, and what is a compromise?

cards.q: What do we call a member of a community or country?
cards.note: A citizen belongs to a community and helps take care of it.

cards.q: What do we call a freedom you are allowed to have?
cards.note: A right is something you are allowed to have, like being treated fairly.

cards.q: What do we call a job or duty you should do?
cards.note: A responsibility is something you should do, like cleaning up your toys.

cards.q: Is doing your homework a right or a responsibility?
cards.note: Homework is a job you should do. That makes it a responsibility.

cards.q: Is saying what you think a right or a responsibility?
cards.note: You are allowed to share your ideas. That makes it a right.

cards.q: Is following the rules a right or a responsibility?
cards.note: Following the rules is something you should do. That makes it a responsibility.

cards.q: Is being treated fairly a right or a responsibility?
cards.note: Everyone should be treated fairly. That is a right.

cards.q: Is taking care of your pet a right or a responsibility?
cards.note: A pet needs food, water and love. Caring for it is a responsibility.

cards.q: What do we call making old cans, paper and bottles into new things?
cards.note: Recycling means less trash and new things made from old ones.

cards.q: What do we call helping others without being paid?
cards.note: Volunteers help because they want to, not for money.

cards.q: What do we call a place where neighbors grow vegetables together?
cards.note: A community garden gives neighbors fresh food and a place to work together.

cards.q: You see litter at the park. What do you do?
cards.note: Pick it up and put it in the trash can. That keeps the park clean for everyone.

cards.q: What can you give to a food pantry to help hungry families?
cards.note: A food pantry gives food to families who need it.

cards.q: Two friends want the same ball. What can they do?
cards.note: Taking turns means both friends get to play.

cards.q: Each person gives up a little so everyone agrees. What is that called?
cards.note: In a compromise, nobody gets everything, but everyone gets something.

cards.q: What should you use to solve a problem with a friend?
cards.note: Kind words help friends fix a problem together.

cards.q: What do you do while a friend is talking?
cards.note: Listening shows your friend that you care about their idea.

cards.q: Classmates cannot agree. Who can help?
cards.note: A teacher can help everyone talk it out and find a fair way.

cards.q: What do we call working together nicely to finish a job?
cards.note: Cooperation means everyone does a part and the job gets done.

cards.q: You bumped a friend by accident. What do you say?
cards.note: Saying sorry helps a friend feel better.

decks.subject: social
decks.title: Solve It Together
decks.about: Working out everyday disagreements: fairness, asking for a turn, listening to both sides, calming down, compromise, making it right after sorry, when to get a grown-up, and how a class decides together by raising hands and voting. NC 1.B.1.4 (how disagreements are settled), 1.C&G.1.2 (how groups make rules and choices) and 1.C&G.1.3 (responsibilities of citizens).
decks.tip: Next time two kids want the same thing, ask him: what are two fair ways to solve it?

cards.q: Ten kids and ten cookies. Each kid gets one cookie. Is that fair or unfair?
cards.note: Fair means everyone is treated the same way.

cards.q: Max swings all of recess. Zoe waits and waits for a turn. Is that fair or unfair?
cards.note: A fair recess means Zoe gets to swing too.

cards.q: Leo wants the truck Mia is playing with. What can Leo do?
cards.note: Asking nicely works better than grabbing. Then wait for your turn.

cards.q: Two kids want the same blocks. They build one big tower together. What is that called?
cards.note: Sharing means using something together.

cards.q: Two kids both want the swing. How can they know when it is time to switch?
cards.note: A timer or counting to twenty makes turns fair.

cards.q: Two kids both want to go first. What is a quick, fair way to decide?
cards.note: Rock, paper, scissors gives both kids the same chance.

cards.q: Two friends have a problem. Who gets to tell their side of the story?
cards.note: Listen to both sides before deciding what is fair.

cards.q: How do you show a friend that you are listening?
cards.note: Eyes on the speaker and a quiet mouth show you care.

cards.q: You feel really mad at a friend. What should you do first?
cards.note: A deep breath helps your brain calm down so you can talk.

cards.q: Your friend took your pencil. What is a good thing to say?
cards.note: Say what you want in a calm, kind voice.

cards.q: Sam wants tag. Jo wants ball. They play tag first, then ball. What is that called?
cards.note: Each friend gives a little, and both get to play.

cards.q: Ella knocked down Ben's tower by accident. After she says sorry, what can she do?
cards.note: Saying sorry and helping fix it makes things right.

cards.q: A friend says sorry and really means it. What kind thing can you say back?
cards.note: Forgiving a friend helps you both feel better.

cards.q: A kid keeps pushing in line. You asked them to stop. What do you do next?
cards.note: If asking does not work, a grown-up can help.

cards.q: The whole class sits in a circle to talk about a problem. What is that called?
cards.note: In a class meeting, everyone gets a chance to talk.

cards.q: The teacher asks who wants to be line leader. How do kids show they want it?
cards.note: Raising a hand is a calm way to say 'pick me'.

cards.q: The class votes on a story. Eight kids pick the bear book. Five pick the fish book. Which wins?
cards.note: The choice with the most votes wins. Eight is more than five.

cards.q: In a class vote, how many votes does each kid get?
cards.note: One kid, one vote. That keeps it fair.

decks.subject: social
decks.title: Families and Cultures
decks.about: Families come in many shapes, and every family has a culture: the foods, music, languages, clothing and celebrations it shares, and learning about other families' traditions with respect. NC 1.B.1.1 (cultural practices and traditions) and 1.B.1.2 (how people of different cultures shape a community).
decks.tip: At dinner, name one food, song or word that comes from your family's culture and ask him to pick one from a friend's.

cards.q: The people who love you and take care of you at home are your...
cards.note: Families can be big or small. Every family is different.

cards.q: Leo lives with his grandma. Mia lives with her mom and dad. Who has a family?
cards.note: A family is the people who care for you, whoever they are.

cards.q: Ava has a stepdad and two stepbrothers. Those people are part of her...
cards.note: When grown-ups marry, their families join together.

cards.q: Your mom's mom or your dad's mom is your...
cards.note: Grandma, Nana and Abuela are all names for a grandmother.

cards.q: Your aunt's child or your uncle's child is your...
cards.note: Cousins are family too. Many cousins play together at family parties.

cards.q: The words a family uses to talk, like English or Spanish, are their...
cards.note: Thousands of languages are spoken around the world.

cards.q: Zoe speaks Spanish at home and English at school. How many languages does she speak?
cards.note: Knowing two languages is called being bilingual.

cards.q: Hola means hello in which language?
cards.note: Many families in North Carolina speak Spanish at home.

cards.q: Tacos, sushi and pizza each started in a different...
cards.note: Tacos come from Mexico, sushi from Japan and pizza from Italy.

cards.q: A kimono from Japan and a sari from India are special kinds of...
cards.note: Many families wear special clothes for holidays and celebrations.

cards.q: Which of these is part of a family's culture?
cards.note: Songs, dances and stories are passed down in families.

cards.q: The Mexican hat dance and Irish step dance are two kinds of...
cards.note: Many cultures have their own special dances.

cards.q: A new friend eats a food that is new to you. What is a kind thing to do?
cards.note: Asking kind questions is a great way to learn about a new culture.

cards.q: Ben's friend invites him to a Lunar New Year dinner. What can Ben learn there?
cards.note: Going to a friend's celebration is a fun way to learn about their culture.

cards.q: All families, big or small, give their kids what?
cards.note: Families look different, but they all take care of each other.

cards.q: How can you share your family's culture with your class?
cards.note: You could bring a food, teach a word or show a photo.

cards.q: A classmate's family celebrates a holiday that is new to you. What can you say?
cards.note: Everyone's traditions are special. Kind words show respect.

cards.q: Who has a culture?
cards.note: Your family's foods, words and celebrations are your culture.

decks.subject: social
decks.title: Maps and Globes
decks.about: Maps and globes, the map key and symbols, the compass rose and the four cardinal directions, continents and oceans. NC 1.G.1.2 (symbols on maps) and 1.G.1.1 (maps and globes).
decks.tip: Hold a map with north at the top and have him point north, south, east and west with his arm.

cards.q: What is a round model of the Earth called?
cards.note: A globe is round like the Earth. You can spin it.

cards.q: What is a flat drawing of a place seen from above called?
cards.note: A map shows a place the way a bird sees it from the sky.

cards.q: What is the box that explains what the symbols on a map mean?
cards.note: A map key is also called a legend.

cards.q: What do we call the small pictures on a map that stand for real things?
cards.note: A tiny school picture on a map means a real school is there.

cards.q: What on a map shows north, south, east and west?
cards.note: The compass rose has arrows for the four directions.

cards.q: Which direction is usually at the top of a map?
cards.note: Most maps put north at the top.

cards.q: Which direction is usually at the bottom of a map?
cards.note: When north is at the top, south is at the bottom.

cards.q: What is the opposite of east?
cards.note: East and west are opposites. On most maps, east is on the right and west is on the left.

cards.q: What is the opposite of north?
cards.note: North and south are opposites.

cards.q: Which way does the sun come up in the morning?
cards.note: The sun rises in the east.

cards.q: Which way does the sun go down in the evening?
cards.note: The sun sets in the west.

cards.q: What does blue on a map usually show?
cards.note: Blue on a map shows water. Green often shows land with plants.

cards.q: What would a map of your classroom, seen from above, show?
cards.note: A classroom map shows the room from above, like looking down from the ceiling.

cards.q: What tells you what a map is about?
cards.note: The title is the name at the top of the map.

cards.q: What are the very big pieces of land on a globe called?
cards.note: Continents are the biggest pieces of land on Earth.

cards.q: How many continents are on Earth?
cards.note: Earth has seven continents.

cards.q: What are the huge salty waters that cover most of the Earth called?
cards.note: Oceans are salty and cover most of the Earth.

decks.subject: social
decks.title: Follow the Map
decks.about: Using a map to get somewhere: north, south, east and west as ways to walk, the left and right sides of a map, between, next to and across from, reading the map key to know what a symbol stands for, and following a simple route. NC 1.G.1.2: symbols and locations on maps.
decks.tip: Draw a quick map of your street with north at the top and ask him which way he walks to a friend's house.

cards.q: The park is north of the school. You walk from the school to the park. Which way do you go?
cards.note: North of means toward the top of the map.

cards.q: The library is east of the park. You walk from the park to the library. Which direction?
cards.note: East is the side where the sun comes up.

cards.q: North is at the top of the map. Which side of the map is east?
cards.note: When north is up, east is on the right.

cards.q: With north at the top, where is west on the map?
cards.note: When north is up, west is on the left.

cards.q: You walk east to the store. Which way do you walk to get back home?
cards.note: To go back, you go the opposite way.

cards.q: You walked south to the pond. Which direction takes you back?
cards.note: North is the opposite of south.

cards.q: You stand facing north. Which hand points toward east?
cards.note: Face north and east is on your right, west on your left, just like a map with north at the top.

cards.q: The slide is between the swing and the sandbox. Which one is in the middle?
cards.note: Between means in the middle of two things.

cards.q: The bench is next to the tree. Is the bench close to the tree or far away?
cards.note: Next to means right beside something.

cards.q: The post office is across from the school. What is between them?
cards.note: Across from means on the other side of the street.

cards.q: The map key says a green tree means a park. You see a green tree on the map. What is there?
cards.note: The key tells you what each symbol stands for.

cards.q: The map key says a wavy blue line means a river. You see one on the map. What is there?
cards.note: Blue lines on a map are usually rivers or streams.

cards.q: The map key says a little airplane means an airport. You spot one. What is there?
cards.note: Always check the key before you guess what a symbol means.

cards.q: To get to school, Leo passes the park, then the library, then the school. What does he pass first?
cards.note: A route is the way you go from one place to another.

cards.q: Leo's route: walk south two blocks, then turn east. Which way does he walk first?
cards.note: Follow a route one step at a time.

cards.q: A big thing that is easy to spot, like a water tower, helps you find your way. It is a...
cards.note: A tall tower, a big statue or a bridge can be a landmark.

cards.q: North is at the top. On the map, the lake is above the farm. The lake is which way from the farm?
cards.note: Above on a map means north when north is at the top.

cards.q: The store is two blocks away. The zoo is twenty blocks away. Which one is closer?
cards.note: Fewer blocks means a shorter walk.

decks.subject: social
decks.title: Land and Water
decks.about: Naming landforms and bodies of water: mountain, hill, valley, island, lake, river, stream, pond, ocean, desert, forest, plain, beach and cave. NC 1.G.1.1: use maps and globes to identify landforms.
decks.tip: Ask him to find one landform in a picture book and name it.

cards.q: What do we call very high land with a peak at the top?
cards.note: A mountain is very high land. The top of a mountain is called the peak.

cards.q: What do we call high land that is smaller than a mountain?
cards.note: A hill is higher than the land around it but lower than a mountain. You can walk up a hill.

cards.q: What do we call the low land between mountains or hills?
cards.note: A valley is low land. Mountains or hills stand on each side of it.

cards.q: What do we call land with water all around it?
cards.note: An island has water on every side. You cross water to get there.

cards.q: What do we call water with land all around it?
cards.note: A lake is a big body of water with land on every side.

cards.q: What do we call a long body of water that flows toward the sea?
cards.note: A river moves. Its water flows downhill toward the sea.

cards.q: What do we call a small river that you can often step across?
cards.note: A stream is a small, narrow river. Streams flow into bigger rivers.

cards.q: What do we call a small body of still water, smaller than a lake?
cards.note: A pond is smaller than a lake. Frogs and ducks like ponds.

cards.q: What do we call the biggest and deepest body of salty water?
cards.note: Oceans cover most of the Earth. The Atlantic Ocean touches North Carolina.

cards.q: What do we call a very dry place that gets little rain?
cards.note: A desert is dry, not always hot. Some deserts are cold.

cards.q: What do we call a big area of land covered with many trees?
cards.note: A forest is full of trees. Many animals live in forests.

cards.q: What do we call flat land with few trees, often covered in grass?
cards.note: A plain is wide, flat land. Farmers often grow food on plains.

cards.q: What do we call the sandy or rocky land right next to the ocean?
cards.note: A beach is where the land meets the sea. The land along the ocean is also called the coast.

cards.q: Which is taller, a hill or a mountain?
cards.note: A mountain is much taller than a hill.

cards.q: Which is bigger, a lake or an ocean?
cards.note: An ocean is far bigger than any lake.

cards.q: Is ocean water salty or fresh?
cards.note: Ocean water is salty. It is not good to drink.

cards.q: Is river water salty or fresh?
cards.note: River water is fresh. Fresh water is not salty.

cards.q: What do we call a hole or tunnel that goes into rock or a hillside?
cards.note: A cave is a hollow space inside rock or a hill. Some caves are very big.

decks.subject: social
decks.title: City, Town or Farm
decks.about: Urban, suburban and rural places: tall buildings, buses and crowds in a city versus fields, barns and tractors on a farm, what you find in each and how people get around. NC 1.G.2.1 (how the land shapes where and how people live) and 1.G.2.2 (how people change the land with buildings, roads and farms).
decks.tip: On a drive, ask him: is this a city, a town or the country, and how can he tell?

cards.q: Skyscrapers, taxis and crowds of people. Which kind of place is this?
cards.note: Cities are crowded, so buildings grow up tall instead of out wide.

cards.q: Open fields, a barn and a tractor. Which kind of place is this?
cards.note: Farms need lots of open land for crops and animals.

cards.q: A busy city area with crowds and tall buildings is called...
cards.note: Urban means city. Urban areas have the most people.

cards.q: Land out in the country with farms and only a few houses is called...
cards.note: Rural means country. Farms and forests are in rural areas.

cards.q: A neighborhood of houses and yards just outside a city is called a...
cards.note: Suburban means in a suburb. Many families live in a suburb and drive into the city.

cards.q: What do we call a very, very tall building in a city?
cards.note: A skyscraper is so tall it seems to scrape the sky.

cards.q: In a city, many families live in one tall building. What is each home in it called?
cards.note: An apartment building has many homes stacked on top of each other.

cards.q: On a farm, what building keeps animals, hay and tools safe and dry?
cards.note: A barn is a big farm building. Horses, cows and hay stay inside.

cards.q: Where would you most likely see cows and chickens?
cards.note: Farm animals need open land, barns and fields of grass.

cards.q: On a farm in the country, are your neighbors close by or far apart?
cards.note: Farms are big, so the next house can be far down the road.

cards.q: Where would you hear the most car horns and buses?
cards.note: Cities are busy and noisy, with cars, buses and taxis everywhere.

cards.q: How do many people get around in a big city?
cards.note: Cities have buses, subways and taxis, so not everyone needs a car.

cards.q: What big machine do farmers drive to work in their fields?
cards.note: A tractor pulls plows and wagons across the fields.

cards.q: How do most families in a suburb get to the store?
cards.note: Suburbs are spread out, so most families drive.

cards.q: In a crowded city, where do kids go to play on grass?
cards.note: People build parks in cities so everyone has green space to play.

cards.q: Which is bigger: a town or a city?
cards.note: A town is smaller than a city, with fewer people and shorter buildings.

cards.q: Fruits, vegetables and milk come from which kind of place?
cards.note: Food is grown on farms, then trucks carry it to stores in towns and cities.

decks.subject: social
decks.title: People and Places
decks.about: How weather and land change what people wear, eat and build, and how people change the land with roads, bridges, dams and pollution. NC 1.G.2.1 and 1.G.2.2.
decks.tip: Look out the window and ask: what did people build here, and what did the weather make us wear today?

cards.q: What do you wear on a snowy day?
cards.note: Cold weather makes people put on warm clothes.

cards.q: What do you wear on a hot sunny day?
cards.note: Hot weather makes people wear light, cool clothes.

cards.q: What do you carry on a rainy day?
cards.note: An umbrella keeps the rain off your head.

cards.q: What can people who live by the ocean catch to eat?
cards.note: People who live near the water often fish for food.

cards.q: What do people often do on flat land with good soil?
cards.note: Flat land with good soil is just right for farms.

cards.q: What can people do near snowy mountains?
cards.note: Snowy hills are good for skiing and sledding.

cards.q: What do crops on a farm need from the clouds?
cards.note: Rain from the clouds gives plants the water they need to grow.

cards.q: What do people build so cars can cross a river?
cards.note: A bridge goes over the water so cars can get across.

cards.q: What do we call a big spinning storm from the ocean that brings wind and rain to the coast?
cards.note: Families get ready and stay inside until the storm passes.

cards.q: In a dry desert, what do people need to bring with them?
cards.note: A desert gets very little rain, so people carry water with them.

cards.q: What do we call making the air, land or water dirty?
cards.note: Pollution is dirt and smoke that people put into nature.

cards.q: What do we call a big wall built to hold back river water?
cards.note: A dam holds back a river and makes a lake behind it.

cards.q: What do people build to drive on across the land?
cards.note: People build roads so cars and trucks can travel from place to place.

cards.q: When people cut down a forest to build houses, what happens to the land?
cards.note: People change the land when they build on it.

cards.q: What can people plant to clean the air and give shade?
cards.note: Trees clean the air, give shade and make homes for animals.

cards.q: What can smoke from cars and factories do to the air?
cards.note: Smoke is one kind of air pollution.

decks.subject: social
decks.title: Needs and Wants
decks.about: Needs (food, water, shelter, clothing) versus wants, scarcity, and making a choice when there is not enough. NC 1.E.1.1: scarcity and limited resources.
decks.tip: At the store, let him sort three items into need or want and say why.

cards.q: What do we call something you must have to live?
cards.note: A need is something your body must have, like food and water.

cards.q: What do we call something nice to have that you can live without?
cards.note: Wants are fun to have. We just do not need them to live.

cards.q: Which group is all needs?
cards.note: Clothing is a need too. It keeps your body warm and dry.

cards.q: Is water a need or a want?
cards.note: Every person must drink water to live.

cards.q: Is a toy a need or a want?
cards.note: Toys are fun, but you can live without them.

cards.q: Is a safe home a need or a want?
cards.note: A safe home is shelter. Shelter is a need.

cards.q: Is candy a need or a want?
cards.note: Candy is a treat. Your body does not need it to live.

cards.q: Is a warm coat in winter a need or a want?
cards.note: Clothing keeps your body warm and safe, so it is a need.

cards.q: Is a video game a need or a want?
cards.note: A video game is fun, but no one needs it to live.

cards.q: Is healthy food a need or a want?
cards.note: Your body needs healthy food to grow and have energy.

cards.q: Is a new bike a need or a want?
cards.note: A new bike is nice to have, but it is not needed to live.

cards.q: Is air to breathe a need or a want?
cards.note: Every person must breathe air to live.

cards.q: What does shelter mean?
cards.note: A house, an apartment or a tent can all be shelter.

cards.q: What do we call it when there is not enough of something for everyone?
cards.note: Scarcity means there is not enough to go around.

cards.q: When you cannot have everything, what do you make?
cards.note: Making a choice means picking one thing and letting the other go.

cards.q: There is one cookie and two kids want it. Is the cookie scarce or plentiful?
cards.note: Scarce means there is not enough for everyone who wants it.

cards.q: You have money for one toy but want two. What do you do?
cards.note: When money is limited, you pick the one you want most.

decks.subject: social
decks.title: Goods, Services, Money
decks.about: Goods versus services, buyers and sellers, money, prices, jobs and saving, and simple supply-and-demand stories. NC 1.E.1.4 (trade), 1.E.1.2 and 1.E.1.3 (supply and demand).
decks.tip: Name something you bought today and ask: was that a good or a service, and who was the seller?

cards.q: What do we call things people make or grow that you can touch and buy?
cards.note: Apples, shoes and toys are goods. You can hold them in your hands.

cards.q: What do we call work that people do to help others?
cards.note: A haircut, a bus ride and a checkup are services. You cannot hold a service.

cards.q: Is an apple a good or a service?
cards.note: An apple is a good. A farmer grew it and you can hold it.

cards.q: Is a haircut a good or a service?
cards.note: A haircut is work someone does for you, so it is a service.

cards.q: Are shoes a good or a service?
cards.note: Shoes are goods. People made them and you can touch them.

cards.q: Is a bus ride a good or a service?
cards.note: The driver does the work of taking you somewhere, so a ride is a service.

cards.q: Is a doctor checkup a good or a service?
cards.note: The doctor does work to help you stay well, so a checkup is a service.

cards.q: What do we call giving something to get something else?
cards.note: When you give one thing and get another thing back, that is a trade.

cards.q: Why do countries trade with each other?
cards.a: to get things they do not have
cards.note: One country may grow bananas and another may make cars. They trade so both can have bananas and cars.

cards.q: What do we call someone who buys things?
cards.note: When you pay for a snack at the store, you are the buyer.

cards.q: What do we call someone who sells things?
cards.note: The store worker who takes your money is the seller.

cards.q: What do we use to pay for goods and services?
cards.note: Coins and paper bills are money. These coins are a quarter, a dime, a nickel and a penny.

cards.q: What do we call the amount something costs?
cards.note: The price tag tells how much money you need to buy something.

cards.q: What do we call work you do to earn money?
cards.note: Grown-ups go to a job and get paid money for their work.

cards.q: What do we call keeping some money to use later?
cards.note: Putting coins in a piggy bank for later is saving.

cards.q: What is a safe place that keeps people's money?
cards.note: A bank keeps money safe until people need it.

cards.q: On a hot day, do more or fewer people want ice cream?
cards.note: When more people want something, that is more demand.

cards.q: The store is out of your favorite cereal. What can you do?
wrong: wait in the store all night
cards.note: When a store runs out of something, people pick something else.

cards.q: The farm has too many pumpkins to sell. Does the price go up or down?
cards.note: A big supply makes the price lower, so more people will buy.

cards.q: Everyone wants the same new toy. Is it easy or hard to find in stores?
cards.note: When many people want the same thing, stores can run out fast.

decks.subject: social
decks.title: Earn, Save, Spend
decks.about: Where money comes from and where it goes: earning by working, spending, saving for a goal, keeping money safe in a piggy bank or a bank, choosing when you cannot buy both, and a simple budget. NC 1.E.1.1 (scarcity and choice), 1.E.1.2 and 1.E.1.3 (money, prices and how they change choices).
decks.tip: Give him three jars labeled spend, save and give and let him sort his next few coins.

cards.q: Dad gets paid for fixing cars at his job. What is getting money for work called?
cards.note: People earn money by working.

cards.q: Zoe walks the neighbor's dog and gets two dollars. How did Zoe get the money?
cards.note: Kids can earn money by doing jobs too.

cards.q: Using your money to buy something is called...
cards.note: Once money is spent, it is gone.

cards.q: Ben wants a toy robot that costs ten dollars. He has two dollars. What can he do?
cards.note: Saving a little at a time adds up.

cards.q: Where can a kid keep coins safe at home?
cards.note: A piggy bank or a jar keeps your coins in one safe spot.

cards.q: Mia saves one dollar every week. After two weeks, how much has she saved?
cards.note: Saving a little each week makes the pile grow.

cards.q: Who works at a bank and helps people put money in or take it out?
cards.note: Money in a bank is still yours. You can take it out later.

cards.q: Sam has three dollars. A ball costs three dollars. A book costs three dollars. How many can he buy?
cards.note: There is only enough money for one, so Sam must choose.

cards.q: Ava can buy a ball or a book, but only one. She picks the ball. What does she give up?
cards.note: Every choice means letting something else go.

cards.q: A plan for how to spend and save your money is called a...
cards.note: A budget helps money last until the next payday.

cards.q: Leo's budget says save half and spend half. He gets ten dollars. How much does he save?
cards.note: Half of ten is five.

cards.q: Kim saved for a long time and bought her bike with her own money. How might she feel?
cards.note: Reaching a saving goal feels great.

cards.q: Money a family gives a kid each week, often for doing chores, is called an...
cards.note: Families decide if and how a kid gets an allowance.

cards.q: Giving some of your money to help people in need is called...
cards.note: Donating money helps groups that feed or care for people.

cards.q: You get money for your birthday. What are three things you can do with it?
cards.note: Many families use three jars: spend, save and give.

cards.q: A red ball costs two dollars. A blue ball costs five dollars. Which costs less?
cards.note: Comparing prices helps you make a smart choice.

cards.q: The store puts toys on sale, so the prices go down. Will more or fewer people buy them?
cards.note: Lower prices make more people want to buy.

decks.subject: social
decks.title: Makers and Buyers
decks.about: Producers make or grow things and consumers buy and use them, how bread, milk, eggs, wool and wood get from the farm or factory to the store, and trading. NC 1.E.1.4: why people trade goods and services.
decks.tip: At the store, pick up one food and ask him who made or grew it and how it got here.

cards.q: A person who makes or grows things to sell is called a...
cards.note: Farmers, bakers and builders are producers.

cards.q: A person who buys and uses things is called a...
cards.note: When you eat the bread you bought, you are a consumer.

cards.q: A baker makes bread to sell. Is the baker a producer or a consumer?
cards.note: The baker made the bread, so the baker is the producer.

cards.q: You buy a snack and eat it. Are you a producer or a consumer?
cards.note: You bought it and used it, so you are the consumer.

cards.q: Mr. Lee sells corn at his farm stand. Then he buys shoes at a store. When he buys shoes, what is he?
cards.note: People can be producers and consumers at different times.

cards.q: A farm where rows of apple trees grow is called an...
cards.note: Many North Carolina orchards are in the mountains.

cards.q: Bread is made from flour. Flour is made from a plant. Which plant?
cards.note: Farmers grow wheat, a mill grinds it into flour, and a baker bakes the bread.

cards.q: The milk at the store comes from which farm animal?
cards.note: Dairy farmers milk cows, and a truck takes the milk to be bottled.

cards.q: The eggs at the store come from which farm animal?
cards.note: A hen is a grown-up female chicken.

cards.q: Warm sweaters are often made from wool. Which animal gives us wool?
cards.note: Wool is cut off the sheep, spun into yarn and knit into clothes.

cards.q: Many houses are built with wood. Where does wood come from?
cards.note: Loggers cut the trees, a sawmill cuts boards, and builders build the house.

cards.q: Carrots grow on a farm. A truck carries them away. Where do they go so people can buy them?
cards.note: Farm, truck, store, then your kitchen.

cards.q: Who moves goods from the farm or factory to the store?
cards.note: Trucks, trains and ships carry goods from place to place.

cards.q: A big building where workers make lots of the same thing, like shoes, is a...
cards.note: Factories use machines to make many things fast.

cards.q: Where do farmers sell fruits and vegetables straight to the people who eat them?
cards.note: At a farmers market, the producer and the consumer meet face to face.

cards.q: Ava gives Ben a sticker. Ben gives Ava a marble. What did Ava and Ben do?
cards.note: A trade can happen with things instead of money.

cards.q: A farmer has lots of eggs and needs bread. A baker has bread and needs eggs. What can they do?
cards.note: Trading helps both people get what they need.

cards.q: When you pay money for a toy, what are you trading for the toy?
cards.note: Buying is a trade: money for a good or a service.

decks.subject: social
decks.title: Long Ago and Today
decks.about: Past, present and future, timelines, how everyday life changed from long ago to today, and a few people whose achievements changed how we live. NC 1.H.1.1.
decks.tip: Ask a grandparent to tell him one thing that was different when they were six.

cards.q: What do we call the time that has already happened?
cards.note: Yesterday is in the past.

cards.q: What do we call the time that is happening right now?
cards.note: Today is the present.

cards.q: What do we call the time that has not happened yet?
cards.note: Tomorrow is in the future.

cards.q: Which comes first: yesterday, today or tomorrow?
cards.note: Yesterday, then today, then tomorrow.

cards.q: What do we call a line that shows events in the order they happened?
cards.note: A timeline puts the oldest event first and the newest event last.

cards.q: On a timeline, where is the oldest event?
cards.note: A timeline goes from long ago at the start to now at the end.

cards.q: On a timeline, where is the newest event?
cards.note: The newest event is the one closest to now, so it goes last.

cards.q: Long ago, people rode horses to travel. What do most people travel in today?
cards.note: Cars go much faster than horses.

cards.q: Long ago, people used candles for light at night. What do we use today?
cards.note: Electric lights turn on with a switch.

cards.q: Long ago, people washed clothes by hand. What do many people use today?
cards.note: A washing machine washes many clothes at once.

cards.q: Long ago, kids wrote on small slates. What do kids write on today?
cards.note: A slate was a small board, like a tiny chalkboard.

cards.q: Long ago, people kept food cold with big blocks of ice. What do we use today?
cards.note: A refrigerator keeps food cold all day and all night.

cards.q: Long ago, a letter took many days to arrive. How long does a phone call take to reach someone today?
cards.note: A phone call reaches someone far away right away.

cards.q: Your grandparents are grown-ups now. What were they long ago?
cards.note: Everyone grows and changes over time. Old photos show it.

cards.q: Who flew the first airplane?
cards.note: The Wright brothers flew at Kitty Hawk, North Carolina, in 1903.

cards.q: Who invented the telephone?
cards.note: Before the telephone, people far apart sent letters to talk.

cards.q: Who was the first president of the United States?
cards.note: George Washington was the very first president of our country.

cards.q: Long ago, which president helped end slavery?
cards.note: Abraham Lincoln was president long ago. He helped make slavery against the law so people could be free.

cards.q: Who gave a famous speech about his dream that all people be treated fairly?
cards.note: His famous speech is called I Have a Dream.

decks.subject: social
decks.title: Timelines
decks.about: Putting events in order with first, next and last, reading a short timeline told in words, baby to child to grown-up, yesterday, today and tomorrow, and past, present and future. NC 1.H.1.1: how people and communities change over time.
decks.tip: Tell him three things you did today out of order and let him put them in order.

cards.q: Mia was born, then she started school, then she got a dog. What happened first?
cards.note: First is the thing that happened before all the others.

cards.q: Leo got a puppy, then the puppy grew big, then it learned to sit. What happened last?
cards.note: Last is the thing that happened after all the others.

cards.q: First you put on socks. Last you tie your shoes. What comes in the middle?
cards.note: Next tells what comes in the middle.

cards.q: In the morning, what do you do first: wake up or eat breakfast?
cards.note: You have to wake up before you can eat.

cards.q: Put these in order: grown-up, baby, child. Which comes first?
cards.note: Everyone starts out as a baby.

cards.q: A baby grows into a child. What does a child grow into?
cards.note: Baby, child, grown-up. That is the order of a life.

cards.q: Grandma was a baby long before Mom was a baby. Who is older?
cards.note: The person born first is the oldest.

cards.q: Today is Tuesday. What day was yesterday?
cards.note: Yesterday is the day right before today.

cards.q: Today is Friday. What day is tomorrow?
cards.note: Tomorrow is the day right after today.

cards.q: Ben lost a tooth last week. Is that in the past, the present or the future?
cards.note: Last week already happened, so it is in the past.

cards.q: Zoe will visit the zoo next month. Is that in the past, the present or the future?
cards.note: Next month has not happened yet, so it is in the future.

cards.q: Right now you are tapping on this card. Is that the past, the present or the future?
cards.note: Right now is always the present.

cards.q: A timeline shows: born, first steps, first day of school. What is at the end?
cards.note: The newest thing goes at the end of a timeline.

cards.q: Lunch comes after morning work and before recess. What comes right after lunch?
cards.note: Before and after tell you the order of the day.

cards.q: Spring, summer, fall, winter. Which season comes right after summer?
cards.note: The seasons go around in the same order every year.

cards.q: Which happened longer ago: when Grandpa was a boy, or last summer?
cards.note: Grandpa was a boy many, many years ago.

cards.q: January is the first month of the year. Which month comes right after it?
cards.note: January, February, March. The months always go in the same order.

decks.subject: social
decks.title: Getting Around, Then and Now
decks.about: How getting around and sending messages changed over time: horse and wagon to car, letter to phone and video call, candle to light bulb, washboard to washing machine, and which came first. NC 1.H.1.1: how people's inventions and achievements changed life in communities over time.
decks.tip: Ask him which came first, then ask what people did before that invention.

cards.q: Which came first: the horse and wagon or the car?
cards.note: Long before cars, horses pulled wagons down dirt roads.

cards.q: Which came first: the candle or the light bulb?
cards.note: People lit candles at night for hundreds of years before light bulbs.

cards.q: Which came first: the washboard or the washing machine?
cards.note: People rubbed wet clothes up and down a bumpy washboard to get them clean.

cards.q: Which came first: a letter in the mail or a video call?
cards.note: People mailed letters long before phones or computers were invented.

cards.q: Which came first: the bicycle or the car?
cards.note: The first bicycles came before the first cars.

cards.q: Which is older: the radio or the television?
cards.note: Families sat around the radio to hear stories before there was TV.

cards.q: Which is older: the telephone or the computer?
cards.note: The telephone was invented long before the first computers.

cards.q: Horse and wagon, train, car, airplane. Which one came last?
cards.note: The first airplane flew in 1903, after trains and the first cars.

cards.q: Long ago, before engines, what pushed big ships across the ocean?
cards.note: Big sails caught the wind and pushed the ship along.

cards.q: Long ago, roads were bumpy dirt. What are most roads made of today?
cards.note: Pavement is the hard, smooth surface cars drive on.

cards.q: With no cars or buses long ago, how did most people make short trips?
cards.note: People walked, or rode a horse if they had one.

cards.q: Which is faster for a long trip: a horse and wagon or a car?
cards.note: A trip that took days by wagon takes hours by car.

cards.q: Today, how can you see Grandma's face and talk to her when she lives far away?
cards.note: A video call lets you see someone's face while you talk.

cards.q: Which gets a message to a friend faster: a letter or a phone call?
cards.note: A phone call gets there in seconds. A letter takes days.

cards.q: Long ago people used wagons. Today we use cars. What do both of them do?
cards.note: The tools change, but people still need to get from place to place.

cards.q: Long ago, before mail trucks, what did mail riders ride to carry letters?
cards.note: Riders on fast horses carried mail bags from town to town.

cards.q: People once typed letters on a typewriter. What do many people type on today?
cards.note: A typewriter printed each letter on paper as you pressed the keys.

decks.subject: social
decks.title: Holidays and Traditions
decks.about: What holidays, traditions and culture are, which national and cultural holidays we celebrate and why, and the arts and stories different cultures share. NC 1.B.1.1, 1.B.1.2 and 1.B.1.3.
decks.tip: Before a holiday, ask him what it celebrates and name one family tradition you have for it.

cards.q: A special day that people celebrate is a...
cards.note: Independence Day and Thanksgiving are holidays.

cards.q: Something a family does the same way every year is a...
cards.note: Eating the same special meal every year is a tradition.

cards.q: The food, clothes, music and celebrations of a group of people are their...
cards.note: Every family has a culture, and families share it with each other.

cards.q: Which holiday on July 4 has fireworks and celebrates the birthday of the USA?
cards.note: The USA began on July 4, 1776. Many people call it the Fourth of July.

cards.q: Which November holiday is for giving thanks with a big meal?
cards.note: Thanksgiving is on the fourth Thursday in November.

cards.q: Which holiday on January 1 celebrates a brand new year?
cards.note: The night before, people count down to midnight.

cards.q: On which February holiday do people give cards and hearts to people they love?
cards.note: Valentine's Day is February 14.

cards.q: Which April holiday reminds us to take care of our planet?
cards.note: Earth Day is April 22. Many people plant trees or pick up litter.

cards.q: Which January holiday remembers a leader who worked for fairness for all people?
cards.note: Dr. King gave speeches so that all people would be treated fairly.

cards.q: On which November holiday do we thank people who served in the military?
cards.note: Veterans Day is November 11. A veteran is a person who served in the military.

cards.q: Which June 19 holiday celebrates freedom and the end of slavery?
cards.note: The name Juneteenth mixes the words June and nineteenth.

cards.q: Which May 5 celebration honors Mexican culture?
cards.note: Cinco de Mayo means the fifth of May in Spanish. People enjoy music, food and dancing.

cards.q: Which holiday do many families celebrate with lion dances and red envelopes?
cards.note: Lunar New Year comes in January or February. Red is a lucky color.

cards.q: Each October a big fair with rides and farm animals comes to Raleigh. It is the...
cards.note: The NC State Fair happens every October in Raleigh, our state capital.

cards.q: Blowing out candles on a cake is a tradition for a...
cards.note: A birthday celebrates the day you were born.

cards.q: An old story told again and again, passed down from long ago, is a...
cards.note: Many folktales have talking animals. The Little Red Hen is one.

cards.q: Folding paper into animals and shapes, a tradition from Japan, is...
cards.note: Origami cranes and frogs are folded from one square of paper.

cards.q: A blanket sewn from many pieces of cloth is a...
cards.note: Many quilts are sewn by hand and passed down in families.

cards.q: People in a community can come from many different...
cards.note: Neighbors may speak different languages and eat different foods.

cards.q: How should we treat people whose traditions are different from ours?
cards.note: We can ask kind questions to learn about new traditions.

decks.subject: social
decks.title: People We Remember
decks.about: Why we have Martin Luther King Jr. Day, Presidents' Day, Veterans Day, Memorial Day and Labor Day, and the people behind them: Dr. King's work for fairness, George Washington and Abraham Lincoln, and the workers and service members we thank. NC 1.H.1.1 (people whose achievements changed communities) and 1.B.1.1 (holidays and traditions).
decks.tip: When a holiday closes school, ask him who or what it remembers and one thing that person did for others.

cards.q: Martin Luther King Jr. worked so that all people would be treated how?
cards.sayQ: Martin Luther King Junior worked so that all people would be treated how?
cards.note: Dr. King wanted every person treated fairly, no matter the color of their skin.

cards.q: How did Dr. King try to change unfair rules?
cards.note: He used words, not fists. Many people marched with him.

cards.q: Dr. King dreamed that children of every skin color could do what together?
cards.note: He hoped kids of all colors would be friends and go to school together.

cards.q: On Martin Luther King Jr. Day, many people help neighbors and clean up parks. It is a day of...
cards.sayQ: On Martin Luther King Junior Day, many people help neighbors and clean up parks. It is a day of...
cards.note: Service means helping others. It is a way to honor Dr. King.

cards.q: Presidents' Day comes in which month?
cards.note: Presidents' Day is the third Monday in February.

cards.q: Presidents' Day honors George Washington and which other famous president?
cards.note: Both presidents were born in February. Dr. King was not a president. He has his own day in January.

cards.q: Long before he was president, George Washington led which group?
cards.note: He led the army that helped America become its own country.

cards.q: George Washington is called the Father of our...
cards.note: People call him that because he helped start the United States.

cards.q: Whose face is on the one-dollar bill?
cards.note: Look at a one-dollar bill and you will see George Washington.

cards.q: Which coin has George Washington on it?
cards.note: A quarter is worth 25 cents. George Washington is on the front.

cards.q: Which coin has Abraham Lincoln on it?
cards.note: A penny is worth 1 cent. Abraham Lincoln is on the front.

cards.q: Abraham Lincoln always tried to tell the truth. What nickname did people give him?
cards.note: Abe is short for Abraham.

cards.q: Abraham Lincoln grew up in a small log cabin and loved to read. What did he grow up to be?
cards.note: He read every book he could borrow, by the light of the fire.

cards.q: Abraham Lincoln worked so that people who were enslaved could be...
cards.note: Free means you can choose where to live and where to work.

cards.q: A veteran is a person who did what?
cards.note: Veterans were soldiers, sailors, pilots or marines.

cards.q: On Veterans Day, what can you say to a veteran?
cards.note: Veterans Day is November 11. Saying thank you shows we remember their service.

cards.q: Memorial Day, at the end of May, remembers soldiers who did what for our country?
cards.note: People put out flowers and flags to remember them.

cards.q: Labor Day, in September, is a holiday that honors which people?
cards.note: Labor means work. Labor Day thanks everyone who works hard at a job.

decks.subject: social
decks.title: History Detectives
decks.about: Asking questions, telling facts from opinions, who made a book, and primary versus secondary sources (diaries, old photos, artifacts, museums). NC inquiry I.1.1, I.1.6, I.1.7 and 1.H.1.2.
decks.tip: At dinner, take turns saying one fact and one opinion about the meal.

cards.q: What do we ask when we want to learn something?
cards.note: Good detectives ask who, what, when, where and why.

cards.q: What do we call something that is true and you can check?
cards.note: You can check a fact by counting or looking.

cards.q: What do we call what someone thinks or feels about something?
cards.note: People can have different opinions, and that is okay.

cards.q: 'Pizza is the best food.' Is that a fact or an opinion?
cards.note: It is an opinion because someone else might like tacos best.

cards.q: 'A week has seven days.' Is that a fact or an opinion?
cards.note: It is a fact because you can count the days on a calendar.

cards.q: 'Dogs are the best pets.' Is that a fact or an opinion?
cards.note: It is an opinion because someone else might think cats are the best pets.

cards.q: 'A cat has four legs.' Is that a fact or an opinion?
cards.note: It is a fact because you can count the legs on a cat.

cards.q: Who writes the words in a book?
cards.note: The author's name is usually on the front of the book.

cards.q: Who draws the pictures in a book?
cards.note: Sometimes one person is both the author and the illustrator.

cards.q: When we look at an old book or photo, we ask who made it, when, where, and what else?
cards.note: Who, when, where and why help us understand a source, like a book, a photo or a diary.

cards.q: What do we call something made by a person who was there, like a diary or an old photo?
cards.note: A primary source comes straight from someone who was there.

cards.q: What do we call something made later by someone who was not there, like a textbook?
cards.note: A secondary source tells about the past by using other sources.

cards.q: Is an old diary a primary source or a secondary source?
cards.note: The person who wrote the diary was there, so it is a primary source.

cards.q: Is an encyclopedia a primary source or a secondary source?
cards.note: An encyclopedia is a big book of facts written later by people who were not there.

cards.q: Is a photo taken long ago a primary source or a secondary source?
cards.note: The person who took the photo was there, so it is a primary source.

cards.q: What do we call an old object from the past, like a tool or a toy?
cards.note: Artifacts help us learn how people lived long ago.

cards.q: What do we call a place that keeps and shows old things from the past?
cards.note: Museums keep artifacts, old photos and art safe so everyone can see them.

cards.q: Two friends tell about the same party. What can we say about their two stories?
cards.note: Each person sees and remembers things in their own way, so detectives look at more than one source.

decks.subject: social
decks.title: Where I Live
decks.about: The nesting of neighborhood, town, state (North Carolina), country (USA), continent (North America) and planet, plus North Carolina's own geography: Raleigh, the Atlantic coast in the east, mountains in the west, Mount Mitchell and Kitty Hawk. NC 1.G.1.1.
decks.tip: Say 'I live in a town, in a state, in a country' and let him fill in each name.

cards.q: What do we call a group of homes close together where people live?
cards.note: A neighborhood is the homes and streets near where you live.

cards.q: What do we call the people who live near you?
cards.note: Neighbors live in the homes near yours.

cards.q: What do we call a big place with many tall buildings and more people than a town?
cards.note: A city is bigger than a town. Raleigh and Charlotte are cities in North Carolina.

cards.q: What state do we live in?
cards.note: North Carolina is our state. Its state tree is the pine.

cards.q: What country do we live in?
cards.note: The United States is our country. The bald eagle is its national bird.

cards.q: What continent do we live on?
cards.note: North America is one of Earth's seven continents.

cards.q: What planet do we live on?
cards.note: Earth is the planet we all live on. Most of it is covered by water.

cards.q: Which is bigger, a state or a country?
cards.note: A country is made of many states. The United States has 50 states.

cards.q: Which is smaller, a town or a state?
cards.note: Many towns fit inside one state.

cards.q: What is the capital city of North Carolina, where the governor works?
cards.note: Raleigh is the capital. Charlotte is the biggest city in North Carolina, but it is not the capital.

cards.q: Which ocean is at North Carolina's beaches?
cards.note: The Atlantic Ocean is on the east side of North Carolina.

cards.q: Where in North Carolina are the tall mountains?
cards.note: The mountains are in the west, far from the beach.

cards.q: Where in North Carolina are the beaches?
cards.note: The beaches are in the east, next to the Atlantic Ocean.

cards.q: What is the tallest mountain in North Carolina?
cards.note: Mount Mitchell is the tallest mountain east of the Mississippi River.

cards.q: Where in North Carolina did the first airplane fly?
cards.note: The Wright brothers flew the first airplane near Kitty Hawk in 1903.

cards.q: Which state is right above North Carolina, to the north?
cards.note: Virginia is North Carolina's neighbor to the north.

cards.q: Which state is right below North Carolina and shares part of its name?
cards.note: South Carolina is our neighbor to the south.

decks.subject: social
decks.title: North Carolina Places
decks.about: North Carolina's three regions (mountains in the west, piedmont in the middle, coastal plain in the east), the Outer Banks, the Appalachian and Blue Ridge Mountains, Charlotte as the biggest city, and the four neighbor states. NC 1.G.1.1: use maps to identify places and landforms.
decks.tip: Open a North Carolina map and have him point to the mountains, the piedmont and the coast, then to where you live.

cards.q: North Carolina is split into three big land areas. What are those areas called?
cards.note: The three regions are the mountains, the piedmont and the coastal plain.

cards.q: Which North Carolina region has the tallest land?
cards.note: The mountain region is in the west.

cards.q: The middle region of North Carolina, with rolling hills, is called the...
cards.note: Most people in North Carolina live in the piedmont.

cards.q: The flat region of North Carolina next to the ocean is called the...
cards.note: The coastal plain is in the east, by the Atlantic Ocean.

cards.q: The word piedmont means foot of the...
cards.note: The piedmont sits at the foot of the mountains.

cards.q: From the piedmont, which direction do you drive to reach the ocean?
cards.note: The beach is east. The sun comes up over the ocean there.

cards.q: From the piedmont, which direction do you drive to reach the mountains?
cards.note: The mountains are west. The sun sets behind them.

cards.q: Raleigh, the state capital, is in which region of North Carolina?
cards.note: Raleigh and Charlotte are both in the piedmont.

cards.q: What is the biggest city in North Carolina?
cards.note: Charlotte has the most people. Raleigh is the capital.

cards.q: The long, thin islands along North Carolina's coast are called the...
cards.note: The Outer Banks have beaches, wild horses and the Kitty Hawk flight spot.

cards.q: On the Outer Banks, what tall tower with a bright light helps ships stay safe?
cards.note: The Cape Hatteras Lighthouse is on the Outer Banks. It has black and white stripes.

cards.q: North Carolina's mountains are part of a long mountain chain called the...
cards.note: The Appalachian Mountains run through many states.

cards.q: Some North Carolina mountains look blue from far away. They are called the...
cards.note: A soft blue haze hangs over the Blue Ridge Mountains.

cards.q: Which is bigger: North Carolina or the United States?
cards.note: North Carolina is one of the 50 states inside the United States.

cards.q: Which state is to the west of North Carolina, past the mountains?
cards.note: Tennessee is on the other side of the mountains.

cards.q: North Carolina touches four states: Virginia, South Carolina, Tennessee and...
cards.note: Georgia touches the bottom left corner of North Carolina.

cards.q: How many states touch North Carolina?
cards.note: Virginia, South Carolina, Georgia and Tennessee.

cards.q: The coastal plain has flat land and good soil. What do many people there do?
cards.note: Sweet potatoes and many other crops grow on the coastal plain.

decks.subject: social
decks.title: NC and USA Symbols
decks.about: North Carolina's state symbols (cardinal, dogwood, pine, the N and C flag, Tar Heel State, gray squirrel and more) and the main United States symbols (50 stars, 13 stripes, bald eagle, Washington D.C.). Not named in any NC K-2 objective; tagged to 1.B.1.1 as local traditions and enrichment most NC first-grade classes include.
decks.tip: Spot a cardinal, a pine or a dogwood outside and ask what it is the state symbol of.

cards.q: What is North Carolina's state bird?
cards.note: The male cardinal is bright red. Cardinals stay in North Carolina all year.

cards.q: What is North Carolina's state flower?
cards.note: The dogwood tree blooms in spring with white or pink flowers.

cards.q: What is North Carolina's state tree?
cards.note: Pine trees stay green all year long.

cards.q: Which two big gold letters are on the North Carolina flag?
