cards.note: N and C stand for North Carolina. The gold letters sit on each side of a white star on the blue part of the flag.

cards.q: What are North Carolina's two state colors?
cards.note: You can see both state colors on the North Carolina flag.

cards.q: What is North Carolina's nickname?
cards.note: People from North Carolina are called Tar Heels. North Carolina is also called the Old North State.

cards.q: What is North Carolina's state mammal?
cards.note: A mammal is an animal with fur or hair. Gray squirrels live in parks and yards all over North Carolina.

cards.q: What is North Carolina's state insect?
cards.note: Honeybees make honey and help flowers and crops grow.

cards.q: What is North Carolina's state reptile?
cards.note: A reptile has scales. The eastern box turtle can close its shell up tight like a box.

cards.q: What is North Carolina's state dog?
cards.note: The Plott Hound was first raised in the mountains of North Carolina.

cards.q: What is North Carolina's state vegetable?
cards.note: North Carolina grows more sweet potatoes than any other state.

cards.q: What is North Carolina's state drink?
cards.note: Milk helps build strong bones and teeth.

cards.q: What is North Carolina's state red berry?
cards.note: Strawberries are picked in North Carolina in the spring.

cards.q: North Carolina has two state berries. One is the strawberry. What is the other one?
cards.note: Blueberries are picked in North Carolina in the summer.

cards.q: How many stars are on the United States flag?
cards.note: There is one star for each of the 50 states.

cards.q: How many stripes are on the United States flag?
cards.note: There is one stripe for each of the first 13 states.

cards.q: What colors are on the United States flag?
cards.note: The stripes are red and white. The stars are white on the blue part in the corner.

cards.q: What is the national bird of the United States?
cards.note: A bald eagle is not really bald. It has white feathers on its head.

cards.q: What is the capital of the United States?
cards.note: Raleigh is the capital of North Carolina. Washington, D.C. is the capital of the whole country.

cards.q: What is the big green statue holding a torch in New York Harbor?
cards.note: The Statue of Liberty was a gift to the United States from France.

decks.subject: health
decks.title: My Feelings
decks.about: Naming feelings (happy, sad, angry, scared, tired, proud), seeing that people can feel differently about the same thing, and using calm words, I-messages and slow breaths. This is the first unit of NC Grade 1 mental and emotional health (1.MEH.1) and the start of the school year.
decks.tip: Ask him to make the face for each feeling before he taps the answer.

cards.q: A friend shares a toy with you. How do you feel?
cards.note: Sharing can make both of you feel happy.

cards.q: Your ice cream falls on the ground. How might you feel?
cards.note: It is okay to feel sad. Feelings come and go.

cards.q: Someone grabs your crayon without asking. How might you feel?
cards.note: It is okay to feel angry. Use words to say so.

cards.q: A big dog barks very loudly. How might you feel?
cards.note: It is okay to feel scared. Tell a grown-up.

cards.q: It is late and you keep yawning. How do you feel?
cards.note: Tired is a feeling too. Sleep helps your body.

cards.q: You learn to tie your shoes all by yourself. How do you feel?
cards.note: Proud means you feel good about what you did.

cards.q: You see a friend with tears and a frown. How do they feel?
cards.note: Tears and a frown often mean sad. You can ask, are you okay?

cards.q: You are angry. What is a good way to show it?
cards.note: Try saying, I feel angry, and then say why.

cards.q: You want a turn on the swing. What do you say?
cards.note: Asking nicely helps you get a turn.

cards.q: Someone says, I feel sad when you leave me out. What kind of message is this?
cards.note: An I-message says how you feel and why.

cards.q: What kind of voice helps you share your feelings?
cards.note: A calm voice helps people listen to you.

cards.q: Can two kids feel differently about the same thing?
cards.note: One kid may love thunder. Another may not. Both are okay.

cards.q: You feel very angry. What can help your body calm down?
cards.note: Breathe in slowly. Breathe out slowly. Try it three times.

cards.q: You feel sad or worried. What can you do?
cards.note: Grown-ups can help with big feelings.

decks.subject: health
decks.title: Calm-Down Tools
decks.about: Naming a big feeling first, then picking a tool to settle the body: belly breaths, counting to ten, squeeze and relax, a quiet break, drawing it out, a hug, and talking once calm. NC 1.MEH.1.1 and 1.MEH.1.3 (healthy ways to express feelings and cope); builds on My Feelings.
decks.tip: Practice one tool while he is already calm, like smell the flower and blow out the candle, so it is ready when a big feeling comes.

cards.q: A big feeling comes. What is a good first step?
cards.note: Say it out loud: I feel angry. I feel worried. Naming a feeling helps it shrink.

cards.q: Which words name a feeling?
cards.note: Frustrated means something is hard and you want to give up. Everyone feels it sometimes.

cards.q: You take a belly breath. What moves in and out?
cards.note: Put a hand on your belly. Breathe in through your nose and feel it fill up like a balloon.

cards.q: Smell the flower, then blow out the candle. What are you practicing?
cards.note: Breathe in slowly through your nose, then out slowly through your mouth. Do it three times.

cards.q: You feel angry. You count slowly. What number do you count up to?
cards.note: Counting slowly to ten gives your body time to cool down.

cards.q: Squeeze your fists tight like a lemon. Then what?
cards.note: Squeeze for a few seconds, then let your hands go soft. Feel the difference.

cards.q: You feel upset. Where can you go to calm down?
cards.note: Many classrooms have a calm corner. At home it can be your bed or a soft chair.

cards.q: What can you say to ask for a calm-down break?
cards.note: Asking for a break is a strong, smart thing to do.

cards.q: Which one is a calm-down tool?
cards.note: Draw how the feeling looks. Big, scribbly and red is fine.

cards.q: You feel mad and wiggly. What can help your body?
cards.note: Moving your body uses up the mad energy.

cards.q: You ask your grown-up for a hug. How can a hug help you feel?
cards.note: It is okay to ask for a hug. It is also okay to say no thanks to one.

cards.q: Is it okay to cry when you feel sad?
cards.note: Crying is one way the body lets a feeling out. Big kids and grown-ups cry too.

cards.q: Does everyone have big feelings sometimes?
cards.note: Big feelings are normal. What matters is what you do with them.

cards.q: Feelings come and go, like what in the sky?
cards.note: A big feeling floats by like a cloud. It will pass.

cards.q: You tried a belly breath and still feel angry. What can you do?
cards.note: Count to ten, squeeze and relax, or take a break. You have lots of tools.

cards.q: You feel calm again. What can you do about the problem now?
cards.note: Calm first, then talk. Try an I-message: I feel sad when...

decks.subject: health
decks.title: Good Friends
decks.about: Kind words, taking turns, personal space and asking before a hug, saying no and walking away, everyone is special, and knowing that bullying is never the target's fault. NC 1.ICHR.1 (healthy relationships) plus following directions and cooperating from PE (PE.1.PR.4.1).
decks.tip: Act out one card together, for example asking before a hug or saying no and walking away.

cards.q: What are please and thank you?
cards.note: Kind words help people feel good.

cards.q: Your friend drops all their crayons. What do you do?
cards.note: A good friend helps.

cards.q: Two friends want the same ball. What can they do?
cards.note: Taking turns means you both get to play.

cards.q: What do we call the space around your body?
cards.note: Everyone likes some room around them.

cards.q: Before you hug a friend, what should you do?
cards.note: Ask first. It is okay if a friend says no thanks.

cards.q: A friend says, please stop tickling me. What do you do?
cards.note: When someone says stop, we stop.

cards.q: Someone is mean to you again and again on purpose. What is that called?
cards.note: If this happens, tell a trusted adult. They can help.

cards.q: A kid is being bullied. Is it that kid's fault?
cards.note: Being bullied is never your fault. Tell a trusted adult.

cards.q: Someone asks you to do something unsafe. What do you say?
cards.note: You can say no in a strong, clear voice.

cards.q: After you say no, what can you do next?
cards.note: Say no, walk away, and tell a trusted adult.

cards.q: Sam draws well. Mia runs fast. Who is special?
cards.note: Everyone has something special about them.

cards.q: Your teacher gives directions. What do you do?
cards.note: Listening to directions keeps games fair and safe.

cards.q: What do we call working together and taking turns?
cards.note: Cooperation means we work as a team.

cards.q: A new kid is alone at recess. What can you do?
cards.note: Asking someone to play is a kind thing to do.

decks.subject: health
decks.title: Kind Words
decks.about: Telling kind words from unkind ones, please, thank you and sorry, what teasing is and telling a trusted adult, and being an upstander who invites others in. NC 1.ICHR.1.2 (everyone is special), 1.ICHR.1.3 and 1.ICHR.1.4 (tell a trusted adult; bullying is never the target's fault) plus 1.MEH.1.1 (good ways to ask for what you need); builds on Good Friends.
decks.tip: Catch him using a kind word today and tell him which one it was.

cards.q: Which one is a kind thing to say?
cards.note: Kind words make a friend feel welcome.

cards.q: A kid says, you are too slow to play. Are those kind words or unkind words?
cards.note: Unkind words can hurt as much as a bump. We do not use them.

cards.q: Your friend gives you a sticker. What do you say?
cards.note: Thank you tells a friend you noticed their kindness.

cards.q: You want to use the scissors. What word do you add when you ask?
cards.note: May I use the scissors, please? Please turns a want into a kind ask.

cards.q: You bump into a friend by accident. What do you say?
cards.note: Say sorry, then ask, are you okay?

cards.q: A friend says sorry for knocking over your tower. What can you say?
wrong: I am not talking to you
cards.note: Everyone makes mistakes. Letting it go feels good for both of you.

cards.q: Someone makes fun of your shoes to make you feel bad. What is that called?
cards.note: Teasing that keeps happening on purpose is bullying. Tell a trusted adult.

cards.q: Someone keeps teasing you and it does not stop. Who do you tell?
cards.note: A teacher, a parent or a counselor can help it stop. It is not your fault.

cards.q: You see a kid being teased. You ask them to come play with you. What are you?
cards.note: An upstander stands up for others. A bystander just stands and watches.

cards.q: A kid asks, can I play too? What do you say?
cards.note: There is always room for one more.

cards.q: Which words help a friend who is sad?
cards.note: Then listen. You do not have to fix it.

cards.q: Your friend likes bugs and you like trucks. Can you still be friends?
cards.note: Friends can like different things. That makes playing more fun.

cards.q: You tell a grown-up so someone stays safe. What is that called?
cards.note: Tattling tries to get someone in trouble. Telling keeps someone safe. Telling is always okay.

cards.q: You win the game. What do you say to the other player?
cards.note: Kind winners say good game. Kind losers say it too.

cards.q: How do kind words make a friend feel?
cards.note: Your words can make someone's whole day better.

cards.q: A new kid sits alone at lunch. What kind thing can you do?
cards.note: Including others is one of the kindest things you can do.

cards.q: Which is a kind thing to do with your words?
cards.note: Go, you can do it! is a gift you can give any time.

decks.subject: health
decks.title: Good Manners
decks.about: Excuse me, waiting for a turn to talk, listening with eyes and a quiet mouth, napkin on the lap, chewing with a closed mouth, asking to be excused, giving people room, holding the door, greeting people, a library voice, and making things right after sorry. NC 1.ICHR.1.1 (respect personal space and boundaries) and 1.MEH.1.1 (good ways to ask for what you need) plus PE.1.PR.4.1 (listen and follow directions); builds on Good Friends and Kind Words with new situations.
decks.tip: Pick one manner for the week, like napkin on lap or excuse me, and cheer every time he remembers it on his own.

cards.q: You burp at the table. What do you say?
cards.note: Everyone burps sometimes. A quick excuse me is all it takes.

cards.q: Two kids are standing in your way in the hall. What do you say to get by?
cards.note: Say excuse me, then wait a moment for them to make room.

cards.q: Two grown-ups are talking. You want to tell them about your day. What do you do?
cards.note: Put a hand gently on your grown-up's arm and wait. If it really cannot wait, say excuse me.

cards.q: Your teacher is talking to the class. Where do your eyes go?
cards.note: Listening with your eyes shows the teacher you are ready to learn.

cards.q: A friend is telling you a story. What does a good listener do?
cards.note: Eyes on the talker, mouth quiet, body still. That is whole-body listening.

cards.q: Where does your napkin go while you eat?
cards.note: Use it to wipe your mouth and fingers, then put it back on your lap.

cards.q: Your mouth is full of food. When is it polite to talk?
cards.note: Chew, swallow, then talk. No one wants to see your food.

cards.q: How do you chew your food at the table?
cards.note: Small bites make it easier to chew with your mouth closed.

cards.q: The peas are across the table. What is the polite thing to say?
cards.note: Asking someone to pass a dish keeps elbows out of the food.

cards.q: You are done eating. What do you ask before you leave the table?
cards.note: Ask, wait for a yes, then carry your plate to the sink.

cards.q: A friend takes a step back while you talk. What does that tell you?
cards.note: About an arm's length apart is a good talking distance.

cards.q: You open a door and someone is right behind you. What can you do?
cards.note: Hold it until they have it. When they say thanks, say you are welcome.

cards.q: Someone is ahead of you in line. What do you do?
cards.note: Hands to yourself, feet still, and your turn will come.

cards.q: You open a gift and it is a toy you already have. What do you say?
cards.note: Someone picked it just for you. Thank them for thinking of you.

cards.q: A neighbor says, good morning! What do you say back?
cards.note: Look at the person and use a clear voice. A wave works too.

cards.q: What kind of voice do you use in the library?
cards.note: An inside voice is for inside. Save the big voice for the playground.

cards.q: You spill juice on a friend's drawing. After you say sorry, what can you do?
cards.note: Sorry plus helping makes it right.

cards.q: You want some milk. What is the polite way to ask?
cards.note: May I have milk, please? Please and thank you turn a grab into a kind ask.

decks.subject: health
decks.title: Ask for Help
decks.about: Who his trusted adults are at home, at school and in the community, telling them when something feels unsafe or a secret feels bad, and trying another way when a problem is hard. NC 1.MEH.2 (more than one way to solve a problem, who can help) and 1.ICHR.1.3 and 1.ICHR.1.6.
decks.tip: After the deck, have him name his own three trusted adults out loud: one at home, one at school, one in town.

cards.q: What do you call a grown-up you know well who keeps you safe?
cards.note: A trusted adult is a grown-up you know well, like a parent or a teacher.

cards.q: Who is a trusted adult at home?
cards.note: A guardian is the grown-up who takes care of you at home.

cards.q: Who is a trusted adult at school?
wrong: a visitor you do not know
cards.note: The principal and the school nurse are trusted adults too.

cards.q: Who is a trusted adult in your community?
wrong: a person you do not know
cards.note: Nurses and librarians are community helpers too.

cards.q: You feel unsafe or scared. What do you do?
cards.note: Telling a trusted adult is always the right thing to do.

cards.q: Someone asks you to keep a secret that makes you feel bad. What do you do?
cards.note: A secret that feels bad is never one to keep.

cards.q: You tell a grown-up, but they are busy. What do you do next?
cards.note: Keep asking until a grown-up listens.

cards.q: Your block tower keeps falling. What can you do?
cards.note: Make the bottom wider or stack more slowly. There is more than one way to build it.

cards.q: One way to fix a problem did not work. What now?
cards.note: There is more than one way to solve a problem. Think of a new idea, or ask for help.

cards.q: You cannot open your juice box. Who can help?
cards.note: It is okay to ask for help with small things too.

cards.q: You have a problem at school. Who can help?
cards.note: A counselor is a grown-up at school who helps with feelings and problems.

cards.q: Are mistakes part of learning?
cards.note: Everyone makes mistakes. Keep trying.

cards.q: If you practice a lot, what will your skills be?
cards.note: The more you practice, the better you get.

decks.subject: health
decks.title: Safe Outside
decks.about: Crossing streets, seatbelts and the back seat, helmets, water and boats, the playground, and what to do if he gets lost, all taught as calm habits rather than warnings. NC 1.PCH.2.1 (situations that cause injury) plus safe play with little reminding from PE (PE.1.PR.4.3).
decks.tip: On your next walk, let him be the one who says stop, look and listen at the curb.

cards.q: Before you cross a street, what do you do?
cards.note: Stop at the curb. Look. Listen for cars. Then cross.

cards.q: Which way do you look before crossing?
cards.note: Look left, then right, then left again before you step off the curb.

cards.q: Where is the safe place to cross a street?
wrong: in the middle of the road
cards.note: Crosswalks are where drivers know to look for people walking.

cards.q: What do you buckle every time you ride in a car?
cards.note: Buckle up before the car moves, every single ride.

cards.q: Where do kids your age sit in a car?
cards.note: In North Carolina, kids under 8 years old and under 80 pounds ride in a car seat or booster seat.

cards.q: What keeps your head safe when you ride a bike or scooter?
cards.note: North Carolina law says kids under 16 wear a bike helmet.

cards.q: Where is it safe to swim?
wrong: where no one can see you
cards.note: A grown-up watches the water the whole time you swim.

cards.q: What do you wear on a boat?
cards.note: A life jacket goes on before you get in the boat and stays on.

cards.q: How do you move when you are next to the pool?
cards.note: The ground by a pool is wet, so we walk.

cards.q: You get lost in a store. What do you do?
cards.a: stay where you are and ask a worker
cards.note: Stay put. Look for a worker with a name tag.

cards.q: Who is a safe person to ask for help if you are lost?
cards.a: a store worker with a name tag
wrong: someone who says come with me
cards.note: Workers with name tags and police officers are good helpers.

cards.q: A grown-up you do not know asks you to go with them. What do you do?
cards.a: say no and find your grown-up
cards.note: You always check with your own grown-up first. That is the rule.

cards.q: What should you know by heart in case you get lost?
cards.note: Practice your full name and a grown-up's phone number.

cards.q: How do you go down a slide?
cards.note: Sit down, feet first, one at a time.

cards.q: Before you throw a ball in PE, what do you check?
cards.sayQ: Before you throw a ball in gym class, what do you check?
cards.a: that no one is in the way
wrong: that you throw as hard as you can
cards.note: Look first, then throw to a friend who is ready to catch.

cards.q: A classmate falls down. What do you do?
cards.note: Getting a grown-up is the kind and safe thing to do.

decks.subject: health
decks.title: Safety Signs and Safe Adults
decks.about: Reading the signs that keep him safe (stop sign, walk and wait lights, exit, wet floor, do not enter, poison, railroad crossing), which grown-ups are safe helpers, staying put when lost, checking first before going anywhere with anyone, and learning a grown-up's phone number. NC 1.PCH.2.1 (situations that can cause injury) with 1.ICHR.1.3, 1.ICHR.1.5 and 1.ICHR.1.6 (tell a trusted adult, say no, trusted adults in the community); builds on Safe Outside.
decks.tip: Point out signs on your next drive and let him read each one aloud before you say what it means.

cards.q: Which sign is red with eight sides?
cards.note: A shape with eight sides is an octagon. Only the stop sign has that shape.

cards.q: What does a stop sign tell every car and bike to do?
cards.note: Drivers stop, look both ways, then go. You stop at it on your bike too.

cards.q: The crossing light shows a walking person. What does it mean?
cards.note: Still look left, right and left before you step off the curb.

cards.q: The crossing light shows a red hand. Do you cross or wait?
cards.note: Wait on the curb until the walking person comes back.

cards.q: A bottle has a skull and crossbones on it. What is inside?
cards.note: You may see it on cleaners or garden sprays. Leave it alone and tell a grown-up.

cards.q: A sign says EXIT in red or green letters. What does it show?
cards.note: Exit signs glow so you can find the way out even in the dark.

cards.q: A yellow sign on the floor shows a person slipping. How do you move past it?
cards.note: A wet floor sign means the floor is slippery. Walk slowly around it.

cards.q: A sign says DO NOT ENTER. What do you do?
cards.note: A red circle with a white bar means do not go in.

cards.q: A sign with a big X says RAILROAD CROSSING. What is ahead?
cards.note: Stop, look and listen for a train. Cross tracks only with a grown-up.

cards.q: Who helps kids cross the street near school?
cards.note: The crossing guard holds up a stop sign so cars wait for you.

cards.q: You feel sick at school. Which safe adult helps you?
wrong: a person you do not know
cards.note: Your teacher can send you to the nurse.

cards.q: Which grown-ups wear a uniform and help keep people safe?
cards.note: A badge and a uniform show they are on duty to help.

cards.q: You get lost at a park. What do you do first?
cards.note: Stay put and call your grown-up's name in a big voice. They will come looking for you.

cards.q: You are lost and there is no worker around. Who is a safe grown-up to ask?
wrong: someone who wants you to go with them
cards.note: A mom or dad with children is a good helper when there is no worker or police officer.

cards.q: Someone you do not know offers candy and says, come see my puppy. What do you do?
cards.a: say no and stay with your grown-up
cards.note: Grown-ups ask other grown-ups for help, not kids. You may say no to any grown-up you do not know.

cards.q: Before you go anywhere with anyone, what is the rule?
cards.note: Check first, every time, even with people you know.

cards.q: What should you learn by heart so a helper can call home?
cards.note: Practice it like a song until you know it cold.

cards.q: Who may you tell your address to?
cards.a: a safe adult who is helping you
cards.note: A police officer, a teacher or a store worker helping you find your grown-up may need your address.

decks.subject: health
decks.title: Sun and Water Safety
decks.about: Sunscreen and putting more on, hats and sunglasses, shade and water on hot days, what to do if he feels too hot, never swimming alone, a grown-up water watcher, life jackets before the boat, staying out of water with no grown-up around, and checking how deep before jumping in. NC 1.PCH.2.1 (situations that can cause injury) with 1.PCH.1.4 (dress for the weather) and 1.NPA.1.1 (reasons to drink water); builds on Safe Outside for summer.
decks.tip: Make him the sunscreen helper: he squeezes the dot and names the spots we always forget, like ears and the back of the neck.

cards.q: Sunscreen keeps your skin safe from what?
cards.note: A sunburn is red, hot and sore. Sunscreen blocks the sun's rays so skin does not burn.

cards.q: When do you put sunscreen on?
cards.note: Put it on about 15 minutes before you go out so it has time to soak in.

cards.q: You have been swimming for a long time. What do you do with sunscreen?
cards.note: Water and sweat wash sunscreen away. Put more on every two hours and after swimming.

cards.q: What keeps the sun off your face, ears and neck?
cards.note: A wide brim shades the spots sunscreen misses.

cards.q: What protects your eyes from bright sun?
cards.note: Even on a cloudy day, the sun's rays can reach your eyes.

cards.q: It is very hot at the park. Where is a cool place to take a break?
cards.note: Under a tree, a tent or an umbrella. Shade can feel many degrees cooler.

cards.q: When is the sun the strongest?
cards.note: From late morning to late afternoon, look for shade and keep the hat on.

cards.q: You are playing hard on a hot day. When should you drink water?
cards.note: By the time you feel thirsty, your body already needs water. Sip before you get thirsty.

cards.q: You feel dizzy and much too hot while playing outside. What do you do?
cards.note: Stop, get to shade, sip water and tell a grown-up. Dizzy, sick or a headache in the heat means your body needs to cool down.

cards.q: You got too hot. What helps your body cool down?
cards.note: A cool wet cloth on your neck helps too.

cards.q: You are a good swimmer. Is it okay to swim all by yourself?
cards.note: Even great swimmers only swim when a grown-up is watching. That is the rule for everyone.

cards.q: A grown-up is the water watcher. What do they keep their eyes on?
cards.note: The water watcher does not read, text or chat. Eyes on the water the whole time.

cards.q: When do you put on your life jacket for a boat ride?
cards.note: It goes on at the dock and stays buckled until you are back on land.

cards.q: Which one is made to keep you safe in the water?
cards.note: Floaties and pool toys are for fun. Only a life jacket is made to keep you afloat.

cards.q: Before you jump into water, what does a grown-up check first?
cards.note: Jumping into shallow water can hurt your head. Feet first, and only where a grown-up says it is okay.

cards.q: Who sits in the tall chair and watches the swimmers at a pool or beach?
cards.note: The lifeguard's whistle means stop and listen. Your own grown-up still watches you too.

cards.q: The pool gate is shut. Do you open it by yourself?
cards.note: A pool fence and gate keep kids out until a grown-up is ready to watch.

cards.q: You find a pond or pool and no grown-up is around. What do you do?
cards.note: Water is only for when a grown-up is watching. Go find one first.

decks.subject: health
decks.title: Fire Safety and 9-1-1
decks.sayTitle: Fire Safety and nine one one
decks.about: Hot things that burn, matches are for grown-ups, what the smoke alarm means, get out and stay out, stop-drop-roll, and calling 9-1-1 for real emergencies only. NC 1.PCH.2.2 to 1.PCH.2.4; schools teach this around Fire Prevention Week in October.
decks.tip: Pick a family meeting spot outside and practice stop, drop and roll on the carpet so it feels like a game.

cards.q: Which of these can burn you?
cards.note: Stoves, ovens, irons and hot pans get very hot. Stay back from them.

cards.q: Who may use matches and lighters?
cards.note: Only grown-ups. If you find matches or a lighter, leave them alone and tell a grown-up.

cards.q: Where do you stay when someone is cooking?
wrong: right next to the hot pan
cards.note: Stay three big steps away from the stove.

cards.q: What beeps loudly to warn you about smoke?
cards.note: A smoke alarm is loud so it can wake you up.

cards.q: You hear the smoke alarm. What do you do?
cards.note: Get outside first. Do not stop for toys.

cards.q: If you see smoke, how do you move?
cards.note: Smoke rises. Clean air is near the floor.

cards.q: Once you are outside, do you go back in?
cards.note: Get out and stay out. Firefighters go in, not kids.

cards.q: Where does your family meet after getting out?
cards.note: Pick a spot outside, like the mailbox or a big tree.

cards.q: If your clothes ever catch fire, what do you do?
cards.note: Stop where you are. Drop to the ground. Roll over and over.

cards.q: In stop, drop and roll, why do you roll?
cards.note: Rolling on the ground puts the flames out.

cards.q: When you stop, drop and roll, what do you cover?
cards.note: Cover your face with your hands while you roll.

cards.q: What number do you call in an emergency?
cards.note: Say it like this: nine, one, one. A grown-up can help you call.

cards.q: Which one is an emergency?
cards.note: An emergency means someone needs help right away.

cards.q: Is it okay to call 9-1-1 for fun?
cards.sayQ: Is it okay to call nine one one for fun?
cards.note: The helpers must stay free for people who really need them.

cards.q: What do you tell the 9-1-1 helper?
cards.sayQ: What do you tell the nine one one helper?
cards.a: your name, address and what is wrong
wrong: a funny joke and a song
cards.note: The helper needs to know where to send help.

cards.q: After you tell 9-1-1 what is wrong, what do you do?
cards.sayQ: After you tell nine one one what is wrong, what do you do?
cards.note: Stay on until the 9-1-1 helper says it is okay to hang up.

cards.q: A firefighter in a big mask comes to help. What do you do?
cards.note: Firefighters look big and loud in their gear, but they are helpers.

decks.subject: health
decks.title: Medicine Safety
decks.about: Medicine is not candy, only a trusted adult gives it, too much can hurt, cleaning products are for grown-ups, and tell a grown-up if you find pills or an unmarked bottle. NC 1.ANCOD.1, which in Grade 1 is household product and medicine safety, not drugs.
decks.tip: Show him where medicines live in your home and that the cabinet stays closed and up high.

cards.q: Some pills look like candy. Are they candy?
cards.note: Medicine is never candy, even when it looks like it.

cards.q: Who should give you medicine?
Is it safe to take a friend's medicine?
Can too much medicine hurt you?
Who decides how much medicine you get?
You find pills on the floor. What do you do?
You find a bottle with no label. Should you drink it?
Where do medicines belong?
Who are cleaning sprays for?
Should you smell or taste cleaning products?
Before you touch a spray bottle at home, what do you do?
You see a baby reaching for a pill. What do you do?
Someone swallowed something that is not food. What does a grown-up do?
cards.note: Grown-ups can call Poison Help at 1-800-222-1222 or 9-1-1.

decks.subject: health
decks.title: Germs and Handwashing
decks.about: How germs get in and around (hands, coughs, sneezes, shared cups, doorknobs) and the habits that stop them: soap for the length of the ABC song, scrubbing between fingers, drying, tissues in the trash, your own cup, and resting at home when sick. NC 1.PCH.1.1 (how germs cause illness and spread) and 1.PCH.1.2 (ways to stop them); builds on Healthy Habits for cold season.
decks.tip: Rub a little lotion and glitter on his hands, then see how much soap and scrubbing it takes to get it all off; that is how germs hide.

cards.q: What song can you sing while you scrub your hands?
cards.note: The ABC song takes about 20 seconds. Happy Birthday two times works too.

cards.q: Where should you scrub when you wash your hands?
cards.note: Backs of hands, between fingers and under nails. Germs hide there.

cards.q: After you rinse, what do you do with your hands?
cards.a: dry them with a clean towel
cards.note: Wet hands pick up germs more easily, so dry them well.

cards.q: You just used the bathroom. What do you do next?
cards.note: Every time, even if you only went a little.

cards.q: You come inside after playing in the dirt. What do you do before snack?
cards.note: Also wash after petting an animal and after blowing your nose.

cards.q: You sneeze into a tissue. Where does the tissue go?
cards.note: Trash the tissue, then wash your hands.

cards.q: Why is your elbow a better place to cough than your hands?
cards.note: Germs on your hands get on everything you touch. Your elbow stays out of the way.

cards.q: Your friend wants a sip from your cup. What is a smart idea?
cards.note: Cups, spoons and straws carry germs from mouth to mouth.

cards.q: Which is a kind way to say hello without spreading germs?
cards.note: A wave, a smile or an elbow bump all work.

cards.q: Germs are too tiny to see. What tool do scientists use to see them?
cards.note: A microscope makes tiny things look big.

cards.q: Why do you stay home when you are sick?
cards.a: to rest and not share germs
cards.note: Rest helps your body fight the germs. Staying home keeps them away from your friends.

cards.q: Who gives you a checkup and a shot that helps your body fight germs?
cards.note: A shot is called a vaccine. It teaches your body to beat a germ before it makes you sick.

cards.q: Which one spreads germs?
cards.a: touching your nose, then a toy
cards.note: Germs from your nose ride on your fingers to the toy, then to a friend.

cards.q: Your hands look clean. Can they still have germs on them?
cards.note: Germs are too small to see, so wash even when hands look clean.

cards.q: Sleep and healthy food help your body do what?
cards.note: A rested, well-fed body has a strong germ-fighting team inside.

cards.q: Where do germs hide at home that many hands touch?
cards.note: Remote controls, faucets and tablets too. Grown-ups wipe them clean.

cards.q: Germs get into your body through which places?
cards.note: Try not to touch your face with unwashed hands.

decks.subject: health
decks.title: Healthy Teeth
decks.about: Brushing for two minutes morning and bedtime with a pea of toothpaste, spitting it out, flossing, brushing the tongue, dentist checkups, wiggly teeth, cavities and sugar, tooth-friendly snacks and water, and a mouthguard for sports. NC 1.PCH.1.3 (baby teeth give way to permanent teeth; dental care); builds on Healthy Habits for Dental Health Month in February.
decks.tip: Set a two-minute timer or play one song tonight and brush along with him.

cards.q: How long do you brush your teeth each time?
cards.note: Play one song. Brush until it ends.

cards.q: When do you brush your teeth?
cards.note: Two times a day, two minutes each time.

cards.q: How much toothpaste goes on your brush?
cards.note: A dot the size of a pea is plenty for kids. A grown-up can squeeze it.

cards.q: After you brush, do you swallow the toothpaste or spit it out?
cards.note: Spit, then rinse your brush. Toothpaste is for teeth, not tummies.

cards.q: What cleans between your teeth where a brush cannot reach?
cards.note: Floss once a day. A grown-up can help until your hands get the hang of it.

cards.q: Which part of your mouth should you brush too, for fresh breath?
cards.note: Germs sit on your tongue. A gentle brush sweeps them off.

cards.q: How often do you visit the dentist for a checkup?
cards.note: Many kids go every six months. The dentist counts, cleans and checks your teeth.

cards.q: What does the dentist use to see the backs of your teeth?
cards.note: The little mirror on a stick lets the dentist see every side.

cards.q: Your tooth is wiggly. What do you do?
cards.note: Tell a grown-up. It will come out on its own when it is ready.

cards.q: Baby teeth fall out and grown-up teeth grow in. How many grown-up teeth will you have?
cards.note: Most grown-ups have 32 teeth, counting the four wisdom teeth that come last.

cards.q: What is a cavity?
cards.note: Germs in your mouth turn sugar into acid that makes little holes. Brushing stops them.

cards.q: What do the germs on your teeth love to eat?
cards.note: That is why sticky, sweet treats are sometimes foods.

cards.q: Which snack is good for your teeth?
cards.note: Cheese, apples, carrots and milk all help teeth. Crunchy veggies scrub them too.

cards.q: Which drink is best for your teeth?
cards.note: Water washes away sugar and has no sugar of its own.

cards.q: You ate a sweet treat. What helps your teeth right after?
cards.note: Swish some water around, then brush at bedtime.

cards.q: What protects your teeth when you play sports?
cards.note: A mouthguard is a soft shield you wear over your teeth.

cards.q: How often do you get a new toothbrush?
cards.note: Sooner if the bristles look bent and frayed.

cards.q: Should you share your toothbrush?
cards.note: A toothbrush carries your germs. Everyone gets their own.

decks.subject: health
decks.title: Food Safety and Allergies
decks.about: Washing hands and fruit, keeping cold food cold, tossing food that fell on the floor or smells bad, mold, what a food allergy is and the signs (itchy mouth, swollen lips) that mean get a grown-up fast, keeping your lunch to yourself, only eating what a grown-up says is safe, and hot ovens, hot soup and raw dough. NC 1.PCH.1.1 and 1.PCH.1.2 (germs cause illness and how to stop them) with 1.NPA.1.2 (foods and why we eat them) and 1.PCH.2.2 (burn hazards); builds on Germs and Handwashing.
decks.tip: Let him be the fruit washer before snack and the lunchbox ice-pack checker before school.

cards.q: What do you do to an apple before you eat it?
cards.note: Rub it under running water, even if you plan to peel it.

cards.q: Why do we wash fruit before eating it?
cards.note: Fruit travels a long way from the farm. Lots of hands touch it before yours.

cards.q: You are helping make sandwiches. What do you wash first?
cards.note: Soap and water for 20 seconds before you touch any food.

cards.q: You pour a glass of milk. Where does the milk carton go next?
cards.note: Milk, meat, eggs and yogurt stay cold so germs cannot grow in them.

cards.q: What keeps the yogurt in your lunchbox cold until lunchtime?
cards.note: Cold food stays safe for a few hours with an ice pack. Pack it right next to the yogurt.

cards.q: Your cracker falls on the floor. What do you do with it?
wrong: put it back in the box
cards.note: Floors have germs even when they look clean. Get a fresh cracker.

cards.q: The milk smells sour and yucky. What do you do?
cards.note: A bad smell is your nose warning you. Food that smells off goes out.

cards.q: Bread has green fuzzy spots on it. What is that?
cards.note: Mold means the bread is too old to eat. Show a grown-up and toss it.

cards.q: Some kids get very sick if they eat peanuts. What is that called?
cards.note: Peanuts, milk, eggs and tree nuts are common allergies. Those kids stay safe by staying away from that food.

cards.q: After eating, a friend's lips swell and their mouth itches. What do you do?
cards.note: Swelling, itching, hives or trouble breathing after food means a grown-up is needed right away.

cards.q: Your friend has a milk allergy. Should you share your yogurt?
cards.note: Even a tiny bite can make a kid with an allergy very sick. Keep your lunch yours.

cards.q: Why does a school have a nut-free table?
cards.note: Kids with nut allergies sit where no nuts are near. It keeps lunch safe for everyone.

cards.q: You try a new food and your mouth feels itchy or tingly. What should you do?
cards.note: An itchy mouth or a tummy ache after a new food is worth telling about. A grown-up can check.

cards.q: You find berries growing on a bush outside. Do you eat them?
wrong: yes, if a bird eats them
cards.note: Some wild berries and mushrooms are poison. Only eat what a grown-up says is safe.

cards.q: A kid at the park offers you a snack from their bag. What is the safe thing to do?
cards.note: Your grown-up knows what is safe for you to eat.

cards.q: Cookies are baking in the oven. Who opens the oven door?
cards.note: The oven, the door and the pan are all very hot. Stay back until a grown-up says it has cooled.

cards.q: Your soup is steaming hot. What do you do?
cards.note: Steam means hot. Little sips from the edge of the spoon once it cools.

cards.q: The cookie dough has raw egg in it. When is it safe to eat?
cards.note: Raw egg and raw flour can carry germs. Baking kills them.

decks.subject: health
decks.title: Healthy Habits
decks.about: Germs and handwashing, coughing into the elbow, staying home when sick, baby teeth and brushing, enough sleep, and dressing for the weather. NC 1.PCH.1 (behaviors that promote health); handwashing comes up in cold season and dental health in February.
decks.tip: Sing the ABC song together while he scrubs his hands tonight; that is about 20 seconds.

cards.q: Tiny living things that can make you sick are called what?
cards.note: Germs are so small you need a microscope to see them.

cards.q: Can you see germs with your eyes?
cards.note: Germs can be on your hands even when your hands look clean.

cards.q: How do germs move from one person to another?
cards.note: Germs ride on tiny drops from a cough or a sneeze, and on hands.

cards.q: What is the best way to get germs off your hands?
cards.note: Soap lifts the germs off and the water washes them away.

cards.q: How long do you scrub your hands with soap?
cards.note: Sing the ABC song while you scrub.

cards.q: When should you wash your hands?
cards.note: Wash before you eat and after you use the bathroom.

cards.q: Where do you cough or sneeze?
cards.note: Your elbow does not touch doors, toys or friends, so germs stay put.

cards.q: You have a fever. Where should you stay?
cards.note: Resting at home helps you get better and keeps germs away from friends.

cards.q: Your first set of teeth are called what?
cards.note: Baby teeth start to fall out around age six.

cards.q: A baby tooth falls out. What grows in its place?
cards.note: Grown-up teeth are also called permanent teeth.

cards.q: How many baby teeth do most kids have?
cards.note: Count them in rows of five.

cards.q: How many times a day do you brush your teeth?
cards.note: Brush in the morning and before bed, for two minutes each time.

cards.q: Who checks and fixes teeth?
cards.note: The dentist counts your teeth and cleans them.

cards.q: Your tooth hurts. What do you do?
cards.note: A grown-up can take you to the dentist to make it better.

cards.q: How many hours of sleep does a first grader need?
cards.note: Doctors say kids 6 to 12 need 9 to 12 hours each night.

cards.q: It is snowing. What do you wear?
cards.note: Warm clothes keep your body heat in on a cold day.

cards.q: It is raining. What keeps you dry?
cards.note: Rain boots keep your feet dry too.

cards.q: It is hot and sunny. What do you wear?
cards.note: Sunscreen and a hat protect your skin from the sun.

decks.subject: health
decks.title: Sleep and Screens
decks.about: Why sleep matters (growing, remembering, feeling good), who needs more of it, a bedtime routine, screens off and out of the bedroom at night, eye breaks, and choosing play time over screen time. Sleep and screens are a bridge topic: NC puts them under 1.PCH.1 (behaviors that promote health) and 1.NPA.2.2 (fun activities in and out of school), plus PE.1.HF.3.3 (join in actively).
decks.tip: Draw his bedtime routine as four pictures on a card by his bed and let him check them off.

cards.q: What does your body do while you sleep?
cards.note: Your body does a lot of its growing while you sleep.

cards.q: Sleep helps your brain do what with the things you learned today?
cards.note: While you sleep, your brain files away what you learned.

cards.q: You did not get enough sleep. How might you feel?
cards.note: Not enough sleep makes it hard to listen, learn and be kind.

cards.q: Who needs more sleep each night, a first grader or a grown-up?
cards.note: Kids 6 to 12 need 9 to 12 hours. Most grown-ups need 7 or more.

cards.q: What do you call the same steps you do every night before bed?
cards.note: Bath, teeth, pajamas, story, lights out. Same order every night.

cards.q: Which one belongs in a good bedtime routine?
cards.note: Calm, quiet things tell your body it is almost time to sleep.

cards.q: What should be turned off before bedtime?
cards.note: Turn screens off at least an hour before bed.

cards.q: Does screen light before bed make it easier or harder to fall asleep?
cards.note: Bright screen light tells your brain it is still daytime.

cards.q: Where should a tablet or phone sleep at night?
cards.note: Screens charge in the kitchen or living room. Bedrooms are for sleeping.

cards.q: What kind of room helps you fall asleep?
cards.note: A night light is fine if it is dim.

cards.q: Which is a calm thing to do right before sleep?
cards.note: A story with a grown-up is a perfect last step.

cards.q: You look at a screen for a long time. What do your eyes need?
cards.note: Blink, look out a window, and rest your eyes.

cards.q: After 20 minutes on a screen, look far away for how long?
cards.note: The 20-20-20 rule: every 20 minutes, look 20 feet away for 20 seconds.

cards.q: Which one makes your muscles stronger?
cards.note: Screens are fun, but your body grows strong by moving.

cards.q: Who decides how long you may use a screen?
cards.note: Screen rules keep time for play, sleep and family.

cards.q: Your screen time is over. What do you do?
cards.a: turn it off and go play
cards.note: Turning it off the first time you are asked shows you are growing up.

cards.q: Why do you have a bedtime?
cards.note: A set bedtime helps you fall asleep faster and wake up ready.

cards.q: It is time to move in PE class. What do you do?
cards.sayQ: It is time to move in gym class. What do you do?
cards.a: join in and try your best
cards.note: Joining in is how you get stronger and have more fun.

decks.subject: health
decks.title: Healthy Foods
decks.about: Why we drink water, the five food groups and why we eat from all of them, half a plate of fruits and vegetables, healthy snacks, and where foods come from (plant or animal, grown on farms). NC 1.NPA.1; nutrition units usually run in late winter and spring.
decks.tip: At dinner, ask him which food group each thing on his plate belongs to.

cards.q: What does your body need to drink every day?
cards.note: Water is the best drink for your body.

cards.q: When your body needs water, how do you feel?
cards.note: Feeling thirsty means your body needs more water. Take a drink!

cards.q: Why do we need to drink water?
cards.a: to keep our body working well
cards.note: Drink extra water when you are hot and sweaty.

cards.q: How many food groups are there?
cards.note: The five groups are fruits, vegetables, grains, protein and dairy.

cards.q: Which food group are apples and bananas in?
cards.note: Berries, oranges and grapes are fruits too.

cards.q: Which food group are carrots and broccoli in?
cards.note: Peas, peppers and spinach are vegetables too.

cards.q: Which food group are bread and rice in?
cards.note: Grains come from plants like wheat, rice and oats.

cards.q: Which food group are milk, cheese and yogurt in?
cards.note: Dairy foods are made from milk.

cards.q: Which food group are chicken, eggs and fish in?
cards.note: Protein foods help build strong muscles.

cards.q: What should fill half of your plate?
cards.note: Make half your plate fruits and vegetables at each meal.

cards.q: Which one is a healthy snack?
cards.note: Fruit, veggies and yogurt make good snacks too.

cards.q: Why do we eat foods from all five groups?
cards.a: to help our body grow strong
cards.note: Each food group gives your body something it needs.

cards.q: Where does milk come from?
cards.note: Farmers milk cows. Goats give milk too.

cards.q: Where do eggs come from?
cards.note: A hen is a girl chicken. Hens lay eggs.

cards.q: Where do apples grow?
cards.note: Apple trees grow on farms called orchards.

cards.q: Where do carrots grow?
cards.note: The orange part of a carrot is its root. Roots grow down in the dirt.

cards.q: Where is most of our food grown?
cards.note: Farmers grow plants and raise animals for our food.

cards.q: Does cheese come from a plant or an animal?
cards.note: Cheese is made from milk, and milk comes from animals.

decks.subject: health
decks.title: Food Groups
decks.about: Sorting everyday foods into the five food groups (fruits, vegetables, grains, protein, dairy), what fills each half of the plate, water or milk with meals, a rainbow of colors, and why breakfast matters. NC 1.NPA.1.2 (a variety of foods and why to eat them) and 1.NPA.1.1 (reasons to drink water); builds on Healthy Foods and is all about sorting.
decks.tip: At the grocery store, hand him one food at a time and let him call out its group before it goes in the cart.

cards.q: Which food group is corn in?
cards.note: Corn, potatoes and peas are starchy vegetables.

cards.q: Oatmeal is made from oats. Where does it belong?
cards.note: Oats, wheat, rice and corn flour are all grains.

cards.q: You drink a glass of milk at lunch. What group did you just eat from?
cards.note: Dairy foods give your bones calcium.

cards.q: Which food group is peanut butter in?
cards.note: Nuts, seeds, eggs, fish and meat are all protein foods.

cards.q: Where do grapes and watermelon belong?
cards.note: Fruits are sweet because they have natural sugar.

cards.q: Which one is a vegetable?
cards.note: Spinach, lettuce and kale are leafy green vegetables.

cards.q: Which one is a grain?
cards.note: Tortillas are made from corn or wheat flour.

cards.q: Which one is a fruit?
cards.note: Pears grow on trees, like apples.

cards.q: Turkey goes in the same group as chicken. What group is that?
cards.note: Turkey, chicken, beef and fish are protein foods.

cards.q: You pick a cup of yogurt. Which group did you pick from?
cards.note: Yogurt is made from milk, so it is dairy.

cards.q: Sort a sweet potato. It goes with the...?
cards.note: The sweet potato is North Carolina's state vegetable.

cards.q: Popcorn. Which group does it go in?
cards.note: Popcorn is a whole grain. Plain popcorn is a healthy snack.

cards.q: Fruits and vegetables fill half your plate. What fills the other half?
cards.note: Add a cup of milk or yogurt on the side and you have all five groups.

cards.q: Which drink goes best with your meal?
cards.note: Sugary drinks have lots of sugar and not much your body needs.

cards.q: Which breakfast gives you energy for school?
cards.note: Grains plus a fruit is a great start.

cards.q: Why do we eat breakfast?
cards.note: Breakfast means break the fast. Your body has not eaten all night.

cards.q: Eating a rainbow means eating fruits and veggies of many...?
cards.note: Red, orange, green, purple. Each color helps your body a different way.

cards.q: A sandwich has bread, turkey, cheese and lettuce. How many food groups is that?
cards.note: Bread is grains, turkey is protein, cheese is dairy, lettuce is vegetables.

decks.subject: health
decks.title: Move Your Body
decks.about: Why moving is good for the body and how it feels, the PE words for hopping, skipping, sliding, galloping, dribbling and striking, and the movement ideas of pathways, levels, the beat and using the teacher's tip. NC 1.NPA.2 and the Grade 1 PE standards; a vocabulary deck, the real practice happens in PE and at the park.
decks.tip: Call out hop, skip, slide and gallop and let him do each one across the room before he answers.

cards.q: Which one is a physical activity that is good for your body?
cards.note: Physical activity means moving your body.

cards.q: What happens to your muscles and bones when you move a lot?
cards.note: Running, jumping and climbing all help you grow strong.

cards.q: How do you often feel after playing outside?
cards.note: Moving your body can put you in a good mood.

cards.q: Which is a fun way to move at recess?
cards.note: Recess is a great time to run and play.

cards.q: Which is a fun way to move at home?
cards.note: You can move at home too. Put on a song and dance.

cards.q: What pumps blood all around your body?
cards.note: Your heart is a muscle. Running and jumping make your heart strong.

cards.q: You stretch and touch your toes. What does this help your body become?
cards.note: Flexible means your body can bend and stretch.

cards.q: What do we call jumping on one foot and landing on that same foot?
cards.note: A hop takes off on one foot and lands on that same foot.

cards.q: You go step-hop, step-hop, step-hop. What is this called?
cards.note: A skip is a step and a hop on one foot, then a step and a hop on the other.

cards.q: You move sideways. Step, feet together, step. What is this called?
cards.note: To slide, step to the side, bring your other foot to meet it, and step again.

cards.q: One foot leads and the other foot chases it, like a horse. What is this called?
cards.note: In a gallop the same foot stays in front the whole time.

cards.q: What do we call bouncing a ball with one hand over and over?
cards.note: Push the ball down with your fingertips so it bounces back up to you.

cards.q: What do we call hitting a ball with a bat?
cards.note: You can strike a ball with a bat, a paddle or your hand.

cards.q: When you catch a ball, what do you watch?
cards.note: Watch the ball all the way into your hands.

cards.q: Straight, curved and zigzag are three kinds of what?
cards.note: A pathway is the line you make as you move. A zigzag goes sharp one way, then the other.

cards.q: Low, medium and high are three kinds of what?
cards.note: Low is down near the floor. High is up by your head or higher.

cards.q: You clap and march along with the music. What are you moving to?
cards.note: The beat is the steady pulse in music that you can clap to.

cards.q: Your teacher says, bend your knees when you land. What do you do?
cards.note: A tip from your teacher is called feedback. Using it helps you get better.

decks.subject: health
decks.title: Heart, Lungs and Bones
decks.about: The heartbeat he can feel, the heart in the chest beating faster when he runs, lungs filling with air and why he breathes hard after a race, blood carrying food and air, the skeleton, skull and ribs, calcium from milk, muscles moving the body and growing stronger with use, endurance, and rest after hard play. NC 1.NPA.2.1 (activities good for the body) and PE.1.HF.3.1 and PE.1.HF.3.2 (fitness parts and the benefits of activity) with 1.NPA.1.2 (why we eat certain foods); builds on Move Your Body.
decks.tip: Have him feel his heartbeat sitting still, then do 20 jumping jacks and feel it again.

cards.q: Put your hand on your chest. What is the thump, thump you feel?
cards.note: Your heart beats all day and all night, even while you sleep.

cards.q: Where in your body is your heart?
cards.note: It sits in the middle of your chest, a little to the left, and is about the size of your fist.

cards.q: You run fast across the yard. What does your heart do?
cards.note: A faster heartbeat sends more blood to your busy muscles.

cards.q: What carries food and air to every part of your body?
cards.note: The heart pumps blood through tiny tubes called blood vessels.

cards.q: What do your lungs do?
cards.note: Lungs pull air in and push it out, many times every minute.

cards.q: Take a big breath in. What fills up with air?
cards.note: Lungs stretch like two balloons when you breathe in.

cards.q: How many lungs do you have?
cards.note: One on the left and one on the right, inside your chest.

cards.q: Which parts of your body let air in?
cards.note: Air goes in your nose or mouth, down a tube called the windpipe, and into your lungs.

cards.q: After a race you breathe hard and fast. Why?
cards.note: Working muscles need extra air, so your lungs work harder too.

cards.q: What holds your body up and gives it its shape?
cards.note: Without bones you would be floppy like a jellyfish.

cards.q: All the bones in your body together are called your...?
cards.note: A grown-up has 206 bones. Kids have even more, and some join together as you grow.

cards.q: Which bone is a hard helmet for your brain?
cards.note: The skull keeps your brain safe. A bike helmet protects the skull.

cards.q: Which bones make a cage around your heart and lungs?
cards.note: Feel the ribs on the sides of your chest. You have twelve pairs.

cards.q: What in milk, cheese and yogurt helps bones grow strong?
cards.note: Bones keep growing until you are grown. Calcium helps make them hard and strong.

cards.q: What do your muscles do?
cards.note: Muscles pull on bones to bend your arm, kick a ball or smile.

cards.q: How do muscles get stronger?
cards.note: Climbing, carrying and pushing make muscles grow. Use them and they get stronger.

cards.q: You can run and play a long time without getting tired. Your heart and lungs have what?
cards.note: Endurance means keeping going. Running, biking and swimming build it.

cards.q: After hard play, what does your body need?
cards.note: Rest and sleep are when muscles and bones do their growing.

decks.subject: health
decks.title: Hop, Skip and Jump
decks.about: The PE words for hopping, skipping, sliding, galloping, leaping, dribbling, striking and kicking, and the movement ideas of pathways, levels, speed, general space, the beat and using the teacher's tip. NC Grade 1 PE motor skills and movement concepts (PE.1.MS.1, PE.1.MC.2); a vocabulary deck, the real practice happens in PE and at the park.
decks.tip: Call out hop, skip, slide and gallop and let him do each one across the room before he answers.

cards.q: Stand on one foot and bounce up and down on that foot. What move is that?
cards.note: A hop takes off on one foot and lands on that same foot.

cards.q: You bounce along with a step and a hop, switching feet each time. What move is that?
cards.note: A skip is a step and a hop on one foot, then a step and a hop on the other.

cards.q: To move sideways across the gym, step out and bring your feet together. What move is that?
cards.note: To slide, step to the side, bring your other foot to meet it, and step again.

cards.q: Which move is like a horse running, with the same foot always in front?
cards.note: In a gallop the same foot stays in front the whole time.

cards.q: What do we call jumping off one foot and landing on the other foot?
cards.note: A leap takes off on one foot and lands on the other foot.

cards.q: A basketball player pushes the ball down so it bounces back up, again and again. What is that called?
cards.note: Push the ball down with your fingertips so it bounces back up to you.

cards.q: In baseball or tennis, you swing and hit the ball. What is that called?
cards.note: You can strike a ball with a bat, a paddle or your hand.

cards.q: Which part of your body do you kick a ball with?
cards.note: Plant one foot next to the ball and kick with the other foot.

cards.q: A friend tosses you a ball. To catch it, what do you keep your eyes on?
cards.note: Watch the ball all the way into your hands.

cards.q: When you throw a ball, which way do you step?
cards.note: Step with the foot opposite your throwing hand, toward where you want the ball to go.

cards.q: You can move along a straight line, a curvy line or a zigzag. These lines are called what?
cards.note: A pathway is the line you make as you move. A zigzag goes sharp one way, then the other.

cards.q: You can crawl down low, walk at medium height or stretch up high. Those are three what?
cards.note: Low is down near the floor. High is up by your head or higher.

cards.q: You can tiptoe slowly or run fast. Slow and fast are two kinds of what?
cards.note: Speed is how fast or how slow you move.

cards.q: What do we call all the room you can move in during PE?
cards.sayQ: What do we call all the room you can move in during P E class?
cards.note: Personal space is just the bubble around you. General space is the whole room.

cards.q: What do we call moving the same way the hands on a clock turn?
cards.note: Clock hands go to the right across the top. The other way is counterclockwise.

cards.q: The drum goes boom, boom, boom and you stomp with every boom. What are you stomping to?
cards.note: The beat is the steady pulse in music that you can clap to.

cards.q: Your coach says, step toward your target when you throw. What do you do with that tip?
cards.note: A tip from your teacher is called feedback. Using it helps you get better.

decks.subject: tech
decks.title: What Is a Computer?
decks.about: What a computer is: a machine that follows the instructions people give it, the kinds he sees every day (laptop, desktop, tablet, phone, game console, smartwatch, even a tiny board computer), the small computers hiding inside a calculator and a traffic light, and why a block or a book is not one. NC K2-CS-01 (choosing devices for a task) and K2-CS-02 (naming computer parts). Read it together: the tablet reads every card aloud, and you add the stories from your own house.
decks.tip: Walk through the house together and point: computer or not a computer? Ask him how he can tell.

cards.q: A computer is a machine. What does it do?
cards.note: A computer is a machine that follows the instructions people give it, step by step.

cards.q: A computer that folds shut and sits on your lap. What is it called?
cards.note: A laptop is a computer you can carry. The screen folds down over the keys like a book closing.

cards.q: A big computer that stays on a desk with its own screen. What is it called?
cards.note: A desktop computer stays in one place. Its screen, keyboard and mouse are separate parts.

cards.q: A flat computer you hold in your hands and tap with a finger. What is it?
cards.note: A tablet is a computer. The whole front is a touch screen, so you tap instead of typing.

cards.q: A small computer that fits in a pocket and makes calls. Which kind is that?
cards.note: A phone is a tiny computer. It can call, take photos, play music and play games.

cards.q: What do you call the computer box that plays games on the TV?
cards.note: A game console is a computer made just for games. The TV is its screen and the controller is how you talk to it.

cards.q: A tiny computer you wear on your wrist. What do people call it?
cards.note: A smartwatch tells the time and counts your steps. It is a computer small enough to wear.

cards.q: Some computers are little boards as small as a cracker. What do you plug in to use one?
cards.note: A little board computer works like a big one. Plug in a screen and a keyboard and it is ready to go.

cards.q: Which one is a computer?
cards.note: A block and a ball cannot follow instructions. A tablet can, so it is a computer.

cards.q: What is inside a paper book?
cards.note: A paper book is not a computer. It has no chip and needs no electricity, just your eyes.

cards.q: What is hiding inside a calculator?
cards.note: A calculator has a tiny computer chip inside. The chip does the math and shows the answer.

cards.q: What tells a traffic light when to turn red or green?
cards.note: A tiny computer inside the traffic light counts the seconds and changes the light.

cards.q: What does every computer need to turn on?
cards.note: Electricity comes from a plug in the wall or from a battery. No power, no computer.

cards.q: Who makes computers?
cards.note: People design computers and build them in factories. Computers do not grow on their own.

cards.q: Who tells a computer what to do?
cards.note: A computer waits for a person to tap, type or program it. Then it does exactly that.

cards.q: A computer adds a hundred numbers in a blink. What is a computer very good at?
cards.note: Computers are super fast at math and at finding things. That is why people use them.

cards.q: Who has feelings and ideas of their own, you or a computer?
cards.note: A computer has no feelings and no ideas of its own. It only follows instructions. Your ideas are yours.

cards.q: What do we call the steps a person gives a computer to follow?
cards.note: Instructions tell a computer what to do, step by step. A list of them is called a program.

decks.subject: tech
decks.title: Parts of a Computer
decks.about: The parts of a computer and the job each one does: the screen, keyboard, mouse and trackpad, touch screen, speaker, microphone, camera, headphones, battery and charger, the processor chip that works like a brain, the memory that keeps things, the printer and the cable. NC K2-CS-02 (describe what common hardware does, using the right words). Read it together with his tablet in front of you so he can touch each part as it comes up.
decks.tip: Put his tablet in front of him and have him touch each part as the card names it: screen, camera, speaker, charger.

cards.q: Which part of a computer shows the pictures and words?
cards.note: The screen is also called a monitor. Everything the computer shows you appears there.

cards.q: You want to type your name. Which part do you use?
cards.note: A keyboard has a key for every letter and number. Press a key and that letter appears on the screen.

cards.q: You slide it on the desk and the pointer on the screen moves. What is it?
cards.note: A computer mouse has a tail-like cord or no cord at all. Slide it and the arrow on the screen slides too.

cards.q: On a laptop, what is the flat square you rub with a finger to move the pointer?
cards.note: A trackpad does the mouse's job on a laptop. Slide one finger to move and tap to click.

cards.q: On a tablet you tap the screen itself to make things happen. What kind of screen is that?
cards.note: A touch screen feels your finger. It shows pictures and takes your taps, both at once.

cards.q: Which part plays the music and sounds you hear?
cards.note: The speaker turns the computer's sound into sound for your ears. Turn it down when others are near.

cards.q: You talk to the tablet and it hears you. What catches your voice?
cards.note: A microphone catches your voice and sends it into the computer. It is tiny, often just a little hole.

cards.q: Which part lets the tablet take a photo or see your face?
cards.note: The camera is the little round eye on the front or back. It sees, but it does not hear.

cards.q: What do you wear on your ears so only you hear the sound?
cards.note: Headphones are little speakers for your ears. Keep the sound low so your ears stay healthy.

cards.q: A tablet works with no cord plugged in. What is storing the power inside?
cards.note: The battery holds electricity. When it runs low, the tablet needs its charger.

cards.q: The battery is almost empty. What does a grown-up plug in to fill it up?
cards.note: The charger fills the battery back up with electricity from the wall. A grown-up does the plugging in.

cards.q: Deep inside is a chip that works like a brain. What is its name?
cards.note: People call the processor the computer's brain. It follows the instructions, millions of steps every second.

cards.q: You save a drawing and it is still there tomorrow. What keeps it safe inside?
cards.note: Saved things live in the computer's storage. Many people call it the memory. It holds your pictures, games and words so they are there next time.

cards.q: Which machine puts your words and pictures onto paper?
cards.note: A printer puts ink onto paper in tiny dots. Out comes your drawing on a real page.

cards.q: What carries electricity from the wall to the computer?
cards.note: Cables carry electricity and information. Only a grown-up should plug things into the wall.

cards.q: What is another name for the computer screen?
cards.note: Monitor is a grown-up word for screen. Say mon-ih-ter.

cards.q: What is the little arrow on the screen that the mouse moves around?
cards.note: The pointer, also called the cursor, points at things. Move it onto a picture and click to pick it.

decks.subject: tech
decks.title: In and Out
decks.about: Input and output: input is what we tell the computer (a tap, a key, a click, our voice, a photo) and output is what it gives back (a picture on the screen, a sound, a printed page, a buzz), then sorting real examples, with the touch screen as the part that does both. NC K2-CS-02 (what each part of a computer does). Read it together and act it out: point in at the tablet for input, then out at yourselves for output.
decks.tip: Play the in-and-out game: you name a thing (a tap, a beep, a photo) and he points IN at the tablet or OUT at himself.

cards.q: When you tap, type or talk to a computer, what do we call that?
cards.note: Input goes IN. It is anything you tell the computer: a tap, a key press, your voice.

cards.q: The computer shows a picture or plays a sound. What do we call what comes out?
cards.note: Output comes OUT. It is what the computer shows you or does for you.

cards.q: Which one is input?
cards.note: Typing puts letters into the computer. In means input.

cards.q: Which one is output?
cards.note: The picture comes out of the computer for you to see. Out means output.

cards.q: You tap the screen to open a game. Your tap is an example of what?
cards.note: Your tap tells the computer what you want. Anything you tell it is input.

cards.q: The tablet buzzes in your hand. The buzz is an example of what?
cards.note: A buzz, or vibration, is the computer doing something for you. That makes it output.

cards.q: You say, play my song, and the song starts. Which part of that is input?
cards.note: Your voice goes in through the microphone. The song that comes out is the output.

cards.q: You take a photo with the tablet. The light coming into the camera is what?
cards.note: The camera takes in light from the world. That is input the computer turns into a picture.

cards.q: The printer gives you a page with your drawing on it. Which word fits?
cards.note: A printed page comes out of the computer. Out means output.

cards.q: Which part gives output you can hear?
cards.note: The speaker sends sound out. Sound you hear is output.

cards.q: You click the mouse on a picture. Does the click go into or out of the computer?
cards.note: A click goes into the computer, so it is input. The computer answers with output on the screen.

cards.q: The screen shows you a cat video. The screen is giving you what?
cards.note: Everything you see on the screen is output from the computer.

cards.q: A touch screen feels your tap and shows the pictures. Which is it?
cards.note: A touch screen takes your tap in and sends pictures out. It is input and output in one part.

cards.q: Which part takes in your voice as input?
cards.note: The microphone hears you. Hearing is taking in, so it is an input part.

cards.q: Here are three things. Which one goes into the computer?
cards.note: Talking, tapping, typing and clicking all go in. They are input.

cards.q: Here are three things. Which one comes out of the computer?
cards.note: Songs, pictures, printed pages and buzzes all come out. They are output.

decks.subject: tech
decks.title: Apps and Programs
decks.about: Apps and programs: software is instructions that do a job, icons are the little pictures you tap, the home screen, opening and closing, picking the right app for the task (draw, read, snap a photo, play music, find the way, add numbers), apps are made by people, some cost money so ask first, and an update makes an app newer. NC K2-CS-03 (operate software to do tasks), K2-IC-02 (choose software that fits the need) and K2-CS-01 (choose the right device). Read it together with his home screen open so he can point at each icon.
decks.tip: Open his home screen and let him say what each icon's app is for before he taps it.

cards.q: What is an app?
cards.note: An app is a set of instructions for the computer. Each app does one job, like drawing or reading.

cards.q: Apps and programs have a grown-up name. What is it?
cards.note: Software is the instructions. Hardware is the parts you can touch, like the screen and the keys.

cards.q: The little pictures on the home screen that you tap to open apps are called what?
cards.note: Each icon is a tiny picture for one app. Tap it once and the app opens.

cards.q: Where do you see all the icons lined up?
cards.note: The home screen is where the tablet starts. Press the home button or swipe up from the bottom to get back to it.

cards.q: You want to start an app. What do you do to its icon?
cards.note: One gentle tap on the icon opens the app. No need to press hard.

cards.q: You are finished with an app. What do you do to leave it?
cards.note: Go back to the home screen to leave the app. Closing apps you are done with keeps the tablet tidy.

cards.q: You want to draw a picture. Which app do you open?
cards.note: Pick the app made for the job. A drawing app has brushes and colors.

cards.q: You want to read a story on the tablet. Which app fits?
cards.note: A reading app shows books. Some can read the story aloud with you.

cards.q: You want to take a photo of your dog. What app do you need?
cards.note: The camera app turns on the camera. Tap the big round button to snap the photo.

cards.q: You want to hear a song. Which app plays it?
cards.note: A music app plays songs. Use headphones if someone nearby is reading.

cards.q: You are in the car and need to find the way to Grandma's house. Which app helps?
cards.note: A maps app shows where you are and the road to take, like a paper map that talks.

cards.q: You need to add 5 plus 3. What is the best app to pick?
cards.note: Different jobs need different apps. Think: what is this job? Then pick the app made for it.

cards.q: Who makes apps?
cards.note: People called programmers write the instructions for every app. Someone made your favorite game.

cards.q: An app says it costs money to get. What do you do first?
cards.note: Some apps cost real money. A grown-up decides and types the password, not you.

cards.q: The tablet says an app has an update. What does an update do?
cards.note: An update is the people who made the app sending fixes and new things. A grown-up taps update.

cards.q: What is another word for an app?
cards.note: Program and app mean the same thing: instructions that tell the computer what to do.

cards.q: Your favorite game on the tablet is a kind of what?
cards.note: Games are apps too. Someone wrote the instructions for every jump and every level.

cards.q: A game pops up and asks you to buy more coins. What do you do?
cards.note: Pop-ups that want money are a grown-up's job. Stop, and show the screen to your grown-up.

decks.subject: tech
decks.title: Computers Around Us
decks.about: Computers hidden all around us (the car, the microwave, the washing machine, traffic lights, the cash register, the library checkout, the thermostat), the workers who use them (doctor, pilot, teacher, farmer, builder, store worker), how life changed from letters, paper maps, film and heavy books to messages, map apps, phone cameras and search, and the idea that computers help but people decide. NC K2-IC-01 (how people lived and worked before and after new technology) and K2-CS-01 (choosing devices for a task). Read it together and spot the hidden computers on your next errand.
decks.tip: On your next errand, count the hidden computers together: the car, the traffic light, the cash register.

cards.q: A car has a small computer inside. What is one job it does?
cards.note: The car's computer checks the engine and lights up the dashboard. The driver still steers.

cards.q: You press the buttons on the microwave and it starts. What counts the seconds?
cards.note: A microwave has a small computer chip. It counts the time and turns the heat off.

cards.q: The washing machine fills, spins and stops all by itself. What tells it the steps?
cards.note: The machine follows a program: fill, wash, rinse, spin. A chip inside runs the steps.

cards.q: Traffic lights on a busy street change together. What keeps them in step?
cards.note: Computers time the lights so cars on one street stop while the others go.

cards.q: At the store, a machine beeps at each thing and adds up the price. What is it?
cards.note: The cash register is a computer. It reads the bar code and adds up the prices.

cards.q: At the library you scan your card and your book. What remembers you have the book?
cards.note: The library's computer keeps a list of who has each book and when it comes back.

cards.q: A little box on the wall keeps the house warm or cool. What is it called?
cards.note: Many thermostats have a small computer. It reads the temperature and turns the heat or air on and off.

cards.q: A doctor looks at a picture of your bones on a screen. What helped make the picture?
cards.note: Doctors use computers to take X-ray pictures and to keep notes about how you are growing.

cards.q: Which worker uses computers to fly a big airplane?
cards.note: The plane's computers show the pilot how high and how fast they are going.

cards.q: Your teacher shows a video on the big board at school. What is the board?
cards.note: Teachers use computers to show lessons, play songs and take attendance.

cards.q: Which worker can use a computer to check if the fields need water?
cards.note: Farmers use computers in tractors and to check the weather and the soil.

cards.q: Before a builder builds a house, what shows the plan on a screen?
cards.note: Builders draw house plans on computers and measure with laser tools.

cards.q: A store worker needs to know how many apples are left. What helps count them?
cards.note: Store computers count what sells so the worker knows what to order.

cards.q: Long ago, people wrote letters on paper and waited days. What do many people send now?
cards.note: A message on a phone or tablet arrives in seconds. A paper letter takes days.

cards.q: Long ago, drivers unfolded big paper maps. What do many drivers use now?
cards.note: A maps app finds the way and talks. Paper maps still work with no battery.

cards.q: Old cameras used film that had to be sent away. What do phone cameras show you?
cards.note: Film cameras made you wait days. A phone camera shows the photo in a blink.

cards.q: Long ago, you looked up facts in big heavy books. What do many people use now?
cards.note: Searching finds facts in seconds. Books are still great, and some things online are not true, so ask a grown-up.

cards.q: Computers help people do jobs faster. Who decides what to do with the help?
cards.note: A computer gives the doctor a picture, but the doctor decides how to help you.

decks.subject: tech
decks.title: Point, Click, Drag
decks.about: Getting around a screen: the pointer follows the mouse or a finger on the trackpad, a click chooses and a double-click opens, a tap is a click on a touch screen, drag means press, hold and move, plus scrolling and the mouse wheel, spreading and pinching to zoom, swiping, a long press and the right mouse button for more choices, the back arrow, and which action fits which job. NC K2-CS-03 (operate software to perform tasks) and K2-CS-02 (hardware parts and what they do). Read it together with a mouse or his tablet in reach so he can try each move as it comes up.
decks.tip: Say the action and let him do it on the real tablet or mouse: tap, drag, swipe, pinch, long press, back.

cards.q: You slide the mouse to the right. Which way does the pointer on the screen go?
cards.note: The pointer copies the mouse. Slide right and it goes right, slide up and it goes up.

cards.q: You slide one finger up the trackpad on a laptop. Which way does the pointer move?
cards.note: A trackpad is a mouse you rub. One finger slides the pointer, and a tap on the pad is a click.

cards.q: You press the mouse button once and let go. What is that called?
cards.note: A click is one quick press. Put the pointer on a thing and click to choose it.

cards.q: You click two times very fast on a folder. What happens to the folder?
