cards.note: Two fast clicks open a folder or a file on a computer with a mouse. On a tablet, one tap opens.

cards.q: On a tablet there is no mouse. What is the same as a click?
cards.note: One gentle tap with a finger does what a click does: it chooses or opens.

cards.q: You press on a picture, hold, and move it across the screen. What is that called?
cards.note: Drag means press, hold and move, then let go. It carries things to a new spot.

cards.q: You drag a picture to a new spot. How do you put it down there?
cards.note: Lift your finger or let go of the button. The picture stays where you dropped it.

cards.q: You want to draw a line in a drawing app. Which action do you use?
cards.note: Press where the line starts and drag to where it ends. The line follows your finger.

cards.q: The page is too long to see all at once. How do you see the rest?
cards.note: Scroll means slide the page up or down. On a tablet slide one finger, and on a computer roll the wheel.

cards.q: What does the little wheel on top of a mouse do?
cards.note: Roll the wheel toward you and the page slides down. Roll it away and the page slides up.

cards.q: You put two fingers on a photo and spread them apart. What happens to the photo?
cards.note: Spreading two fingers zooms in. The photo grows so you can see the little things.

cards.q: You pinch two fingers together on a big photo. What happens to the photo?
cards.note: Pinching zooms out. The photo shrinks back so you can see all of it.

cards.q: You slide your finger fast across the screen to see the next photo. What is that called?
cards.note: A swipe is a quick slide. Swipe left or right for the next picture or page.

cards.q: You hold your finger on an icon and little choices pop up. What did you do?
cards.note: A long press is a tap that stays. It shows extra choices, like move or delete.

cards.q: A mouse has two buttons. What does the right button do?
cards.note: The left button clicks and chooses. The right button opens a little list of extra choices.

cards.q: You opened the wrong page. Which arrow takes you back to the page before?
cards.note: The back arrow points left. It takes you to the page you were on before.

cards.q: You want to move a photo into a folder. Which action do you use?
cards.note: Drag carries things. Press on the photo, hold, slide it onto the folder, let go.

cards.q: You want to see the next page of a story on a tablet. Which action do you use?
cards.note: Swipe from right to left like turning a page. Swipe back to go to the page before.

decks.subject: tech
decks.title: On, Off and Logging In
decks.about: Turning a device on and off and logging in: the power button, starting up, holding the button to shut down, a quick press for sleep (dark screen, still on), waking it, the charging light, what logging in means, a grown-up's face or finger unlock, the lock screen, logging out so nobody else can use your account, a kid account versus a grown-up account, shut down versus sleep, and checking your work is saved before the lid closes. NC K2-IC-04 (responsible login and logoff procedures on all devices) and K2-CS-03 (operate software). Read it together and let him do the real log in and log out on his own account.
decks.tip: Make it his routine: he presses the button, logs in to his kid account, and logs out himself when he is done.

cards.q: The tablet is all the way off. Which button turns it on?
cards.note: The power button is usually on the top or the side. One press and the screen lights up.

cards.q: You press the power button and the tablet takes a little while to start. What is it doing?
cards.note: Grown-ups say it is booting up. The computer is waking every part up, so give it a moment.

cards.q: You want to turn the tablet all the way off. What do you do to the power button?
cards.note: A quick press only puts it to sleep, but holding the button down turns it all the way off. Ask a grown-up to show you.

cards.q: Turning a computer all the way off has a name. What is it called?
cards.note: Shutting down closes everything and turns the power off. Shut down before a long trip or when a grown-up says so.

cards.q: You press the power button quickly and the screen goes dark. Is the tablet off or asleep?
cards.note: A quick press is sleep. The screen is dark, but the tablet is still on, resting and ready.

cards.q: A tablet goes to sleep when nobody uses it for a while. Why does it sleep?
cards.note: Sleep saves battery while the tablet waits for you. Press once and it wakes up right where you were.

cards.q: The screen went dark by itself while you were reading. How do you wake it up?
cards.note: One press on the power button or a tap on the screen wakes a sleeping tablet. No shaking needed.

cards.q: You shut down the laptop. What happens to the apps you had open?
cards.note: Shut down closes all the apps, but sleep keeps them open. Save your work before you shut down.

cards.q: A grown-up plugs in the charger and a tiny light comes on. What does the light mean?
cards.note: The little light says charging. When the battery is full, the light may change color or turn off.

cards.q: Logging in means telling the computer something. What do you tell it?
cards.note: Logging in tells the computer who you are, with your name and password, so it shows your things.

cards.q: A grown-up unlocks the phone with a look or a touch. What is the phone checking?
cards.note: Some phones check a face or a fingerprint instead of a typed password. It is still a kind of password.

cards.q: Before you log in, you see a screen with a big clock on it. What is it called?
cards.note: The lock screen shows the time but keeps your things locked until the right person logs in.

cards.q: You log out when you are done. Who can use your account then?
cards.note: Nobody. Logging out closes your account so the next person cannot see or change your things.

cards.q: The tablet has a grown-up account and a kid account. Which one is yours?
cards.note: A kid account is set up just for you. The grown-up account is for grown-up jobs, so leave it alone.

cards.q: What does a kid account show you?
cards.note: A kid account shows the games and apps your grown-ups picked for you and hides the rest.

cards.q: A grown-up's account is open on the screen. What do you do?
cards.note: Someone else's account is theirs. Ask first, and never tap around in a grown-up's work.

cards.q: You are about to close the laptop lid. What do you check first?
cards.note: Check that your drawing or story is saved. Then close the lid and the laptop goes to sleep.

cards.q: You close the laptop lid. What does the laptop do?
cards.note: Closing the lid puts a laptop to sleep. Open it and press a key or the button to wake it.

decks.subject: tech
decks.title: Keys and Letters
decks.about: Finding his way around a real keyboard: the space bar, enter, backspace, shift and caps lock, the arrow keys, why the letters are not in ABC order (the top row starts Q W E), where the numbers sit, capital letters on the keys but small letters on the screen, where thumbs and pointer fingers rest, and typing his name one key at a time. NC K2-CS-03 (operate software to perform tasks) and K2-CS-02 (hardware parts and what they do). Read it together at a keyboard so he can press each key as it comes up.
decks.tip: Sit him at a real keyboard and let him type his name one key at a time, with shift for the first letter.

cards.q: Which key is the long one at the bottom of the keyboard?
cards.note: The space bar is the longest key. Press it with your thumb to leave a space between words.

cards.q: What does the space bar put between two words?
cards.note: cat dog needs a space in the middle. Without it you get catdog.

cards.q: Which key starts a new line of writing?
cards.note: Enter is also called return. On many keyboards it has a bent arrow on it.

cards.q: You typed the wrong letter. Which key erases the letter before the blinking line?
cards.note: Backspace erases backwards, one letter each press. On some keyboards it is called delete.

cards.q: You want a capital B. What do you hold down while you press B?
cards.note: Hold shift with one hand and tap the letter with the other. Let go and the letters are small again.

cards.q: What do the four arrow keys do?
cards.note: Up, down, left, right. The arrows move your blinking line, the cursor, without erasing anything.

cards.q: Which three letters start the top letter row on a keyboard?
cards.note: Keyboard letters are not in ABC order. Look for the Q at the top left to find your way.

cards.q: Are the letters on a keyboard in ABC order or mixed up?
cards.note: The letters sit in a special order called QWERTY, named for the first six keys in the top row.

cards.q: Where are the number keys on a keyboard?
cards.note: The numbers run in a row above the letters. Some big keyboards have a number pad on the right too.

cards.q: The keys show capital letters. What kind of letters show up on the screen when you type?
cards.note: Keys show capitals so they are easy to read. You get small letters unless you hold shift.

cards.q: Which fingers rest on the space bar?
cards.note: Thumbs tap the space bar. The other fingers reach for the letters.

cards.q: On the F and J keys you can feel tiny bumps. Which fingers go there?
cards.note: Feel the bumps on F and J. Your pointer fingers rest there so your hands know where they are.

cards.q: You want to type your name. How do you do it?
cards.note: Find each letter and press it once. Hold shift for the capital letter at the start.

cards.q: You want a whole word in CAPITAL letters. What locks the capitals on?
cards.sayQ: You want a whole word in capital letters. What locks the capitals on?
cards.note: Caps lock keeps every letter capital until you press it again. A little light may show it is on.

cards.q: You hold a key down too long and get aaaaa. How many times should you press a key for one letter?
cards.sayQ: You hold a key down too long and the same letter comes out again and again. How many times should you press a key for one letter?
cards.note: Press and let go. Holding a key down makes the letter repeat and repeat.

cards.q: Which hands do good typists use?
cards.note: Left hand on the left side, right hand on the right. Each hand takes care of its own keys.

cards.q: You typed a word in the search box. Which key tells the computer go?
cards.note: Enter means go. It sends your words off, or starts a new line when you are writing.

decks.subject: tech
decks.title: Save, Find, Delete
decks.about: Where work goes on a computer: saving, files and folders, naming a drawing so you can find it, searching, copying, opening and changing a file, deleting to the trash and asking before the trash is emptied, undo, the cloud as a far-away copy, and the word data. NC K2-DA-01 (store, copy, search, retrieve, modify and delete information) and K2-DA-02 (information stored on a device is data). Read it together: every question and choice is read aloud.
decks.tip: Next time he draws on the tablet, let him pick a name for the file and find it again tomorrow by searching for that name.

cards.q: You drew a picture on the tablet and want to see it tomorrow. What do you do?
cards.note: Saving keeps your work so it is there later. Nothing saved means nothing to find tomorrow.

cards.q: You close a drawing app without saving. What might happen to your drawing?
cards.note: Save before you close. Some apps save for you, but checking is a good habit.

cards.q: What do we call a saved picture or story on a computer?
cards.note: Each saved thing is one file. Pictures, stories and songs are all files.

cards.q: You have ten drawings of dinosaurs. What can hold them all together?
cards.note: A folder is like a paper folder at school. It keeps files that go together in one place.

cards.q: A folder is named Dinosaurs. What goes inside it?
cards.note: The folder name tells you what is inside. Good names make things easy to find.

cards.q: You draw a red truck. What is a good name to save it with?
cards.note: Name a file for what it is. Later you can find red truck fast.

cards.q: You cannot find your drawing called red truck. What can you type in the search box?
cards.note: Searching looks through every file for the name you typed. That is why good names matter.

cards.q: You tap a saved story and it shows up on the screen. What did you just do?
cards.note: Opening a file brings your saved work back so you can see it or change it.

cards.q: You open your story, add a new page, and save again. What did you do to the file?
cards.note: You can open a saved file, change it, and save it again. The new version is kept.

cards.q: You copy your drawing. How many drawings do you have now?
cards.note: Copy makes a second one that looks just the same. The first one stays where it was.

cards.q: You copy a photo into a new folder. What happens to the first photo?
cards.note: Copying never takes the first one away. Now there is one in each place.

cards.q: You delete a drawing you do not want. Where does it go first?
cards.note: Deleting moves a file to the trash. It is not gone for good yet.

cards.q: Oops, you deleted the wrong drawing. Where can you look for it?
cards.note: Open the trash and put the file back. A grown-up can show you how.

cards.q: Emptying the trash makes files go away for good. What do you do before you empty it?
cards.note: Once the trash is emptied, the files cannot come back. Check with a grown-up first.

cards.q: You made a slip and scribbled on your drawing. Which button fixes the last thing you did?
cards.note: Undo takes back your last step. Many apps show it as a curved arrow.

cards.q: Some tablets keep a copy of your photos in the cloud. What is the cloud?
wrong: a rain cloud in the sky
cards.note: The cloud is another computer far away that keeps a copy. If the tablet breaks, the copy is still safe.

cards.q: What is the word for all the information a computer keeps?
cards.note: Data is any information a computer keeps. Photos, stories, game scores: every file is data.

decks.subject: tech
decks.title: Taking Care of Devices
decks.about: Looking after a tablet or computer: clean dry hands, no food or drinks nearby, two hands to carry it, a case, charging, gentle taps, eye breaks, a kind headphone volume, asking before downloads or purchases, what to try when it freezes, and naming simple problems (no sound, black screen, no internet) so a grown-up can fix them. NC K2-CS-04 (describe basic hardware and software problems) and K2-IC-04 (responsible logoff). Read it together: the tablet reads every question and choice aloud.
decks.tip: When something goes wrong on the tablet, ask him to say what is wrong in words before you fix it: no sound, black screen or no internet.

cards.q: Your hands are sticky from a snack. What do you do before you touch the tablet?
cards.note: Clean, dry hands keep the screen clear and working. Sticky fingers leave smudges that are hard to clean off.

cards.q: Where should your juice go while you use the tablet?
cards.note: One spill can break a tablet for good. Drinks and snacks stay far away from it.

cards.q: How do you carry a tablet from one room to another?
cards.note: Two hands and a slow walk. A dropped tablet can crack.

cards.q: You want to watch a video. What do you do before you press play?
cards.note: Walking while looking at a screen means you cannot see steps, doors or toys on the floor. Sit first.

cards.q: What is the soft or hard cover around a tablet for?
cards.note: A case is like a helmet for the tablet. It softens bumps and drops.

cards.q: The battery picture is red and almost empty. What does the tablet need?
cards.note: Ask a grown-up to plug in the charger, then let the tablet fill up.

cards.q: How do you touch the screen when you tap a button?
cards.note: The screen feels even a soft tap. Hard pokes can crack it.

cards.q: You have looked at the screen for a long time. What is a good break for your eyes?
cards.note: Look out a window at something far away for a little while. Your eyes get to rest.

cards.q: A game says, get this new app! What do you do first?
cards.note: Some apps cost money or are not for kids. A grown-up checks first.

cards.q: A game asks you to buy more coins with real money. Who decides?
cards.note: Buying in a game uses real money. Always ask first. It is okay to say no to the game.

cards.q: You put on headphones. How loud should the sound be?
wrong: loud enough for the whole house
cards.note: If someone next to you can hear your headphones, it is too loud. Loud sound can hurt your ears.

cards.q: The game is frozen and stuck on the screen. What is a good first thing to try?
cards.note: Closing the app and opening it again fixes many stuck screens. If that does not work, a grown-up can help.

cards.q: You closed the app, but the tablet is still stuck. Who can help restart it?
cards.note: Restarting means turning it all the way off and on again. Many problems go away after a restart.

cards.q: The video plays but you hear nothing. What should you check first?
cards.note: Saying what is wrong helps fix it. No sound? Check the volume buttons and the mute switch.

cards.q: You press the button and the screen stays black. What is probably the problem?
cards.note: A black screen often means the battery is empty. Plug it in and wait a few minutes.

cards.q: The drawing app works, but websites will not open. What is probably off?
cards.note: No internet? Look for the Wi-Fi picture at the top of the screen. A grown-up can turn it back on.

cards.q: You are done with the tablet. What do you do before you put it away?
cards.note: Locking or logging out keeps your things safe until next time. Then put it back in its spot.

decks.subject: tech
decks.title: When It Doesn't Work
decks.about: What to do when a device stops working, in order: stay calm, say what is wrong in the right words (frozen, crashed, no Wi-Fi, won't charge), check the easy things (volume, headphones, cable, battery), close the app and open it again, restart with a grown-up, then ask for help, plus the spinning wheel that means wait, trying one fix at a time, a warm tablet that needs a rest, a crash that is not your fault, and never shaking or hitting it. NC K2-CS-04 (describe basic hardware and software problems with accurate terminology) and K2-CS-02 (hardware parts). Read it together; it goes deeper than the three fix-it cards in Taking Care of Devices.
decks.tip: Next time something freezes, let him lead: stay calm, say the problem in words, check the easy things, close and reopen, then come get you.

cards.q: The game stops working. What is the very first thing to do?
cards.note: Machines break sometimes, so take a breath. A calm head finds the fix faster.

cards.q: Which words help a grown-up fix the problem the fastest?
cards.note: Use the real words: frozen, no sound, no Wi-Fi, won't charge. Then a grown-up knows where to look.

cards.q: You tap and tap but the screen does not change. What is the word for this?
cards.note: Frozen means the app does not answer your taps. Wait a little, then close it.

cards.q: A little wheel spins round and round on the screen. What should you do?
cards.note: The spinning wheel means the tablet is busy working. Tapping more only gives it more to do, so wait.

cards.q: Before you ask for help, which easy things do you check?
cards.note: Easy things first: is the volume up, is the charger plugged in, is the battery empty? Look, but let a grown-up touch the plug.

cards.q: The volume is up but there is still no sound. What might be plugged in?
cards.note: Headphones plugged in send all the sound to the headphones. Unplug them and the speaker works again.

cards.q: The Wi-Fi picture at the top of the screen has no bars. What does that mean?
cards.note: The Wi-Fi picture shows little curved bars, and no bars means no Wi-Fi. A grown-up can turn it back on.

cards.q: The charger is plugged in but the battery is not filling up. What might be loose?
cards.note: A charger cable can wiggle loose at either end. A grown-up pushes both ends in, because only grown-ups touch the outlet.

cards.q: You closed the frozen app. What do you try next?
cards.note: Close it, wait a moment, open it again. That fixes many stuck apps.

cards.q: The screen is so dim you can hardly see it. What do you turn up?
cards.note: Brightness is how much the screen glows, and you can slide it up a little. Bright sun also makes a screen look dim, so move into the shade.

cards.q: Turning it off and on again fixes many problems. Why does it work?
cards.note: Everything stops and starts over clean, like a good night of sleep. The stuck part gets unstuck.

cards.q: The tablet is stuck. Does shaking or hitting it help?
cards.note: Shaking and hitting can break the tablet for good. Gentle hands fix things.

cards.q: You tried the easy things and it still does not work. What now?
cards.note: Asking for help is a smart step, not giving up. Tell the grown-up what you already tried.

cards.q: An app closes all by itself in the middle of a game. What do grown-ups call that?
cards.note: A crash is when an app stops and closes on its own. Open it again, and if it keeps crashing, tell a grown-up.

cards.q: An app crashed while you were playing. Is it your fault?
cards.note: Apps crash because of bugs in their instructions, not because of you. Just open it again.

cards.q: You are trying to fix a problem. How many fixes do you try at a time?
cards.note: Try one fix, then test. If you change ten things at once, you cannot tell which one helped.

cards.q: The tablet feels very warm. What does it need?
cards.note: A hot tablet needs a rest with the screen off, out of the sun and off the blanket. Never a bath.

cards.q: A grown-up asks what you were doing when it stopped. Why do they ask?
cards.note: What you were doing is a clue. It helps the grown-up find the bug, like a detective.

decks.subject: tech
decks.title: What Is the Internet?
decks.about: What the internet is: many computers joined to share information, Wi-Fi through the air and long cables under the ground and sea, websites, how a message or video is chopped into small numbered pieces and put back together like a puzzle, searching, checking facts with a grown-up, video calls, and what still works when the Wi-Fi is off. NC K2-NI-01 (information broken into pieces and reassembled), K2-CS-02 (what the router and Wi-Fi do) and K2-CS-04 (naming a slow or missing connection). Read it together: the tablet reads every question and choice aloud.
decks.tip: Cut a drawing into four numbered pieces, carry them across the room one at a time, and put them back together: that is how a photo travels.

cards.q: What is the internet?
cards.note: The internet is many, many computers all over the world, joined up so they can share information.

cards.q: Computers on the internet are joined up. What do they share with each other?
cards.note: Pictures, messages, videos and games travel from computer to computer.

cards.q: Your tablet has no wires. How does the internet reach it?
cards.note: Wi-Fi sends invisible signals through the air, like a radio. A box at home called a router sends them out.

cards.q: How does the internet travel between faraway cities and across the ocean?
cards.note: Long cables run under the ground and along the bottom of the sea, joining countries together.

cards.q: What do we call a page you can visit on the internet?
cards.note: A website is a page of words, pictures and videos that lives on a computer somewhere, and you can look at it.

cards.q: You send Grandma a video. Does it travel in one big piece or in many small pieces?
cards.note: A computer chops the video into tiny pieces called packets. Small pieces travel faster and easier.

cards.q: The small pieces of a message arrive at Grandma's tablet. What happens next?
cards.note: Each piece has a number, like puzzle pieces, so the tablet knows how to put them in order.

cards.q: A photo is cut into pieces to travel. How does the other computer know the right order?
cards.note: Like numbered puzzle pieces: one, two, three. Put them in order and the picture is whole again.

cards.q: One piece of the video gets lost on the way. What does the tablet do?
cards.note: If a puzzle piece is missing, the tablet asks the other computer to send that piece again.

cards.q: You want to see pictures of real frogs. What helps you find them on the internet?
cards.note: Type what you want, and the search looks through millions of websites for you. Search with a grown-up.

cards.q: A website says dogs can fly. Is it true just because it is on the internet?
cards.note: Anyone can put things on the internet, even things that are wrong. A grown-up helps you check.

cards.q: Is the internet a person who talks to you, or lots of machines sharing information?
cards.note: When a game or video app talks, it is a program written by people, not a friend who knows you.

cards.q: Grandma lives far away. How can you see her face and talk to her today?
cards.note: A video call sends your picture and voice over the internet, chopped into pieces and put back together, fast.

cards.q: The Wi-Fi is off. Can you still draw in your drawing app?
cards.note: Drawing, saved games and photos live on the tablet, so they work without the internet.

cards.q: The tablet has no internet. Will a website open?
cards.note: Websites live on other computers, so they need the internet to reach you. A grown-up can turn the Wi-Fi back on.

cards.q: A video keeps stopping and spinning. What is probably the problem?
cards.note: The spinning circle means the pieces are arriving slowly. Saying the internet is slow helps a grown-up fix it.

cards.q: What is the box at home that sends the Wi-Fi out?
cards.note: The router is plugged into the wall and sends Wi-Fi through the house. If it is off, there is no internet.

decks.subject: tech
decks.title: Passwords and Private Info
decks.about: Passwords as secret keys shared only with parents, why long passwords are strong, what counts as private information (full name, address, phone number, school, passwords, photos of your home) and keeping it out of games and websites, asking before signing up, logging out, and the digital footprint. NC K2-NI-02 (passwords and strong passwords), K2-NI-03 (digital footprint and protecting personal information) and K2-IC-04 (responsible login and logoff). Read it together and keep the tone calm: he is never in trouble for asking.
decks.tip: Make up a silly strong password together, like purple frog jumps 9, and talk about why it beats 1234.

cards.q: What is a password like?
cards.note: A password unlocks your account, like a key unlocks a door. Only you and your parents hold it.

cards.q: Who are the only people you share your password with?
cards.note: Your parents keep your password safe with you. Nobody else needs it, not even friends.

cards.q: A friend asks for your password. What do you do?
cards.note: You can say, sorry, passwords are private. Then tell your grown-up that a friend asked.

cards.q: Which password is the hardest for someone to guess?
cards.note: Long passwords made of a few words and a number are hard to guess. Short ones like 1 2 3 4 are easy.

cards.q: Is your own name a good password?
cards.note: Everyone knows your name, so it is easy to guess. Pick words nobody would think of.

cards.q: Why do we use a strong password?
cards.note: A strong password stops other people from getting into your account and your things.

cards.q: Your full name, address and phone number are what kind of information?
cards.note: Private information is about you and your family. It stays with you and your grown-ups.

cards.q: A game asks, what is your name and your school? What do you do?
cards.note: Games and websites do not need to know who you are or where you go to school. Stop and get a grown-up.

cards.q: A website wants your home address to send you a free prize. What do you do?
cards.note: Free prizes online are often tricks to get your private information. Grown-ups know what to do.

cards.q: Is a photo of your house with the house number private information?
cards.note: A photo can show where you live. Ask a grown-up before any photo goes online.

cards.q: A new app says, sign up here! Who do you ask before you make an account?
cards.note: Signing up means giving the app information about you. A grown-up decides if the app is okay.

cards.q: You finish playing on a shared computer. What do you do before you walk away?
cards.note: Logging out closes your account so the next person cannot see your things. Log in again next time.

cards.q: What do you type to get into your own account?
cards.note: Logging in with your password tells the computer it is really you.

cards.q: Things you post or type online can stay there for a long time. What is that called?
cards.note: Like footprints in wet sand, what you do online leaves marks that can stay. Think before you post.

cards.q: A video you post online can be seen by how many people?
cards.note: Once something is online, many people may see it and copy it. That is part of your digital footprint.

cards.q: Where is a safe place to keep passwords?
wrong: on a sign in the yard
cards.note: Your parents can write passwords down in a safe place at home. Never in a game or a message.

cards.q: Which of these is private information?
cards.note: Favorite colors and animals are fine to share. Phone numbers, addresses and passwords are private.

decks.subject: tech
decks.title: Sending a Message
decks.about: How a message gets from you to Grandma: the address says where it goes, the send button, the message travels in small pieces that are put back together before she sees it and a photo needs more pieces than words (K2-NI-01), it waits in the inbox to be read later while a video call is live, replies, read marks, emoji for feelings and voice messages. Only message people your family knows, a grown-up helps you send, read it again because you cannot take it back, wait kindly for a reply (K2-IC-03), and keep photos of yourself, your school and your address out of messages to people you have never met (K2-NI-03). Read it together, then send one real message to a family member.
decks.tip: Help him send one real message to a grandparent: pick the address, type, read it again, send, then watch for the reply.

cards.q: You type Grandma's email address on a message. What does the address tell the tablet?
cards.note: An address says where the message goes, like the address on a letter. Each person has their own.

cards.q: You spell Grandma's address wrong. Does the message reach her?
cards.note: A wrong address sends it to the wrong place, or nowhere. A grown-up checks the address with you.

cards.q: Your message is all typed. Which button makes it go?
cards.note: Send is the button that lets the message go. Before send, you can still fix it.

cards.q: Why does a photo travel in many small pieces instead of one big piece?
cards.note: Small pieces slip through the wires and Wi-Fi more easily, and if one gets lost only that piece is sent again. Grandma's tablet puts them back together.

cards.q: You send a few words and a photo. Which one is cut into more pieces?
cards.note: A photo is much more data than a few words, so it needs many more pieces and takes a bit longer.

cards.q: Where does a new message wait until you open it?
cards.note: New messages wait in the inbox, like letters in a mailbox, until the person opens them.

cards.q: You send a message. Does Grandma have to read it right away?
cards.note: A message waits for her. She reads it when she has time and writes back later.

cards.q: In a video call, you talk and Grandma answers. When does she hear you?
cards.note: A video call is live. You see and hear each other at the same time, like being in the same room.

cards.q: Who is it okay to send messages to?
cards.note: Message only people your family knows: grandparents, cousins, friends your grown-ups know.

cards.q: You want to send a message. Who helps you?
cards.note: A grown-up helps you pick the address, type and send. Messaging is a together job.

cards.q: You tap send. Can you grab the message back?
cards.note: Once it is sent, the other person can see it right away. That is why you think before you send.

cards.q: Before you tap send, what is a smart thing to do?
cards.note: Read it again and ask: is it kind, is it right, is it going to the right person? Then send.

cards.q: You add a smiley face to your message. What does it show Grandma?
cards.note: An emoji shows a feeling that words alone might not. A smiley says I am happy.

cards.q: Grandma writes back to your message. What is her message called?
cards.note: When someone writes back, that is a reply. Replies go back and forth like a talk.

cards.q: A small word under your message says seen. What does that mean?
cards.note: Seen means the person opened your message. Seen or read marks can take a while to show.

cards.q: A game friend you have never met asks for a photo of you. What do you do?
cards.note: Photos of you are private, so never send one to someone you have not met. Stop and show a grown-up what they asked.

cards.q: You hold a button and talk, then let go. What did you send?
cards.note: A voice message records your voice and sends it. The other person taps play to hear you.

cards.q: Your cousin has not written back yet. What do you do?
cards.note: People are busy. Wait kindly, and do not send the same message again and again.

decks.subject: tech
decks.title: Kind and Safe Online
decks.about: Being kind and staying safe online: kind words and the would-I-say-it-to-their-face test, what to do when someone is unkind or a stranger messages, prize pop-ups, stopping and telling when something feels yucky, taking turns and sharing in games, giving credit for a friend's drawing or idea, asking before sharing a photo, screen-time balance and pause-and-think. NC K2-IC-03 (work respectfully and responsibly with others online), K2-AP-06 (give attribution) and K2-NI-03 (your digital footprint). Read it together: the tablet reads every question and choice aloud.
decks.tip: Before he taps anything new, say the two words with him: pause and think.

cards.q: Before you type a message to a friend, what kind of words do you use?
cards.note: Typed words can hurt too. Use words that would make your friend smile.

cards.q: Here is a test for a message: would you say it to the person's face? If no, what do you do?
cards.note: If you would not say it face to face, it does not belong in a message either.

cards.q: Someone online says something mean to you. What do you do first?
cards.note: You do not have to answer mean words. A grown-up can help, and it is never your fault.

cards.q: You see a kid being mean to your friend in a game. What can you do?
cards.note: Do not type back at the mean kid. A grown-up can stop it, and your friend will feel better.

cards.q: A message pops up from someone you do not know. What do you do?
cards.note: You do not have to answer anyone you do not know. Your grown-up decides if it is safe.

cards.q: A pop-up says, you won a prize! Tap here! Should you tap it?
cards.note: Pop-ups that promise prizes are tricks. Show a grown-up and they will close it.

cards.q: Something on the screen makes you feel yucky or scared. What is the smart move?
cards.note: Turn the screen over and get a grown-up. You are never in trouble for telling.

cards.q: You and a friend both want to play the same tablet game. What is a fair way?
cards.note: Taking turns online works just like at the playground. A timer helps.

cards.q: Two of you are building in a game together. How do you work well as a team?
cards.note: Teams online share the work and listen to each other's ideas.

cards.q: You use your friend's drawing in your project. What do you say?
cards.note: Giving credit means saying who made it. It is honest and makes your friend proud.

cards.q: You build a tower from a plan you saw in a video. What do you tell people?
cards.note: Programmers give credit too. When you use someone's idea, say where it came from.

cards.q: You took a funny photo of your friend. What do you do before you share it?
cards.note: A photo belongs to the person in it. Ask your friend, and ask a grown-up, before it goes anywhere.

cards.q: You have played on the tablet for a while. What is a good thing to do next?
cards.note: Screens are fun, but bodies need running, jumping and fresh air too. That is balance.

cards.q: Before you tap a new button or link, what two words do you remember?
cards.note: Pause and think: is this safe? Is this kind? If you are not sure, ask.

cards.q: Your friend types, my tower fell down, I am sad. What is a kind thing to type back?
cards.note: Kind words help a friend feel better online too.

cards.q: Who makes the rules about which games and videos are okay for you?
cards.note: Grown-ups pick what is right for your age. If you are not sure, ask.

decks.subject: tech
decks.title: Steps in Order
decks.about: An algorithm is a list of steps in order, like brushing teeth or making a sandwich, and a computer follows its steps exactly, so the order matters (K2-AP-01, K2-AP-04). The cards ask what comes first, next and last, and how to break a big job into small steps. Read it together: the word algorithm is new, but the idea is one he already lives every morning.
decks.tip: Say the steps of something you are doing right now, like making lunch, and ask him what would go wrong if two of them swapped places.

cards.q: A list of steps you follow in order has a special name. What is it?
cards.note: Algorithm is a big word for a list of steps in order. Say it: AL-go-rith-um.

cards.q: A cookie recipe lists the steps in order. So a recipe is a kind of what?
cards.note: A recipe is an algorithm for food: step one, step two, step three, cookies!

cards.q: You brush your teeth. What comes first?
cards.note: First the toothpaste goes on. Then you brush. Then you spit and rinse.

cards.q: You brush your teeth. What comes last?
cards.note: Last means the very end. The brush goes back in its cup when everything else is done.

cards.q: You make a jelly sandwich. What is the first step?
cards.note: You cannot spread jelly on bread you have not taken out yet. First things first.

cards.q: You spread jelly on the bread. What comes next?
cards.note: Next means the step right after this one.

cards.q: You are getting dressed. What do you put on right before your shoes?
cards.note: Socks first, then shoes. If a robot did shoes first, the socks would not fit!

cards.q: A robot's steps say: put on shoes, then put on socks. What happens?
cards.note: A computer does exactly what the steps say, even when it looks silly. The order matters.

cards.q: Your steps say spread the jelly, but you forgot to say open the jar. What does a computer do?
cards.note: A computer only does what the steps say. People fill in missing steps; computers cannot.

cards.q: You plant a seed. What is the first step?
cards.note: Hole, seed, cover, water, wait, flower. Each step gets the next one ready.

cards.q: You plant a seed. Which step comes last?
cards.note: Some steps are fast and some, like waiting, take days and days.

cards.q: You close the toy box lid, then try to put the toy in. What is wrong?
cards.note: Toy in first, then lid. When steps come out of order, the job goes wrong.

cards.q: Cleaning your room is a big job. What makes a big job easier?
cards.note: Big job, small steps: books on the shelf, toys in the box, clothes in the basket. One at a time.

cards.q: Which is a small step of cleaning your room?
cards.note: A small step is one thing you can finish. Then you start the next one.

cards.q: Wake up, eat breakfast, go to school. Which comes next after wake up?
cards.note: Next is the step right after. Last is the very end.

cards.q: Wake up, eat breakfast, go to school. Which step is last?
cards.note: First, next, last. School is the end of this list.

cards.q: You wash your hands. What comes first?
cards.note: Water on, wet hands, soap, scrub, rinse, water off, dry. Seven little steps!

cards.q: You tell a robot: walk 3 steps, then turn. What does the robot do?
cards.note: Robots and computers do exactly what the steps say, no more and no less.

decks.subject: tech
decks.title: Patterns and Loops
decks.about: A pattern repeats, and a loop tells a computer to do the same steps again instead of writing them over and over (K2-AP-03). The cards find what comes next, count how many times a part repeats, and spot loops in real life, like brushing every tooth and the days of the week. Read it together and say each pattern out loud; hearing the rhythm is half the fun.
decks.tip: Clap a pattern like clap, clap, stomp, and ask him to say the repeating part before he joins in.

cards.q: Doing the same steps again and again has a name. What is it called?
cards.note: Loop is the word for repeating steps. Brushing each tooth and a clock going round are loops too.

cards.q: 🔴 🔵 🔴 🔵 🔴 What comes next?
cards.sayQ: A pattern: red, blue, red, blue, red. What comes next?
cards.note: The pattern is red, blue, over and over. After red comes blue.

cards.q: ⭐ 🌙 ⭐ 🌙 ⭐ 🌙 What comes next?
cards.sayQ: A pattern: star, moon, star, moon, star, moon. What comes next?
cards.note: Star, moon, star, moon. The pattern starts again with a star.

cards.q: 🍎 🍎 🍌 🍎 🍎 🍌 🍎 🍎 What comes next?
cards.sayQ: A pattern: apple, apple, banana, apple, apple, banana, apple, apple. What comes next?
cards.note: The repeating part is apple, apple, banana. Two apples are done, so a banana is next.

cards.q: 🔴 🔵 ⭐ 🔴 🔵 ⭐ 🔴 What comes next?
cards.sayQ: A pattern: red, blue, star, red, blue, star, red. What comes next?
cards.note: Three things repeat: red, blue, star. After red comes blue.

cards.q: Clap, clap, stomp. Clap, clap, stomp. Clap, clap... What comes next?
cards.note: Clap, clap, stomp is the part that repeats. Say it with your body!

cards.q: 🐶 🐱 🐶 🐱 🐶 🐱 Which part repeats?
cards.sayQ: A pattern: dog, cat, dog, cat, dog, cat. Which part repeats?
cards.note: Find the smallest piece that comes back again and again. Here it is dog, cat.

cards.q: 🔴 🔵 🔴 🔵 🔴 🔵 How many times does red, blue repeat?
cards.sayQ: A pattern: red, blue, red, blue, red, blue. How many times does red, blue repeat?
cards.note: Red, blue is one time. Count the pairs: one, two, three.

cards.q: Which is the short way to say clap, clap, clap, clap, clap?
cards.note: A loop says the step once and how many times. Clap 5 times, done!

cards.q: You want a robot to hop 3 times. Which is the short way to tell it?
cards.note: A loop is shorter to say and shorter to write. That is why programs use them.

cards.q: A robot is told: jump 4 times. How many jumps does it do?
cards.note: The loop runs the step jump four times, then stops.

cards.q: You brush each tooth the same way, tooth after tooth. What is that like?
cards.note: Brush, move over, brush, move over: the same steps again and again is a loop.

cards.q: The clock hand goes all the way round. What does it do next?
cards.note: Round and round, then again. The clock is a loop that never ends.

cards.q: The days of the week go round and round. What day comes after Sunday?
cards.note: After the last day, the week starts again. The days of the week are a loop.

cards.q: Which one is a pattern?
cards.note: A pattern has a part that repeats. Red, blue, red, blue repeats red, blue.

cards.q: ⚽ 🏀 ⚽ 🏀 What are the next two?
cards.sayQ: A pattern: soccer ball, basketball, soccer ball, basketball. What are the next two?
cards.note: Keep the same order: soccer ball first, then basketball.

cards.q: A loop says: stir 10 times. When does the stirring stop?
cards.note: A loop runs its steps the number of times you say, then stops.

decks.subject: tech
decks.title: Find the Bug
decks.about: A bug is a mistake in the steps, and debugging means finding it and fixing it, then trying again (K2-AP-07, K2-AP-08). The cards show a robot that put socks on after shoes, a square drawn with three sides and a pattern with one wrong spot, and ask which step to fix. Read it together and keep it light: everyone makes bugs, and computers never get mad about them.
decks.tip: When something he builds or draws goes wrong, say 'I think there is a bug, let's find it' instead of 'that's wrong', then check one step at a time together.

cards.q: A mistake in the steps has a funny name. What is it called?
cards.note: A bug is a mistake in the steps. Long ago, people even found a real moth stuck inside a big computer!

cards.q: Finding a bug and fixing it has a name too. What is it?
cards.note: De-bugging means taking the bug out. Find it, fix it, try again.

cards.q: A robot put on shoes, then socks. Which step should come first?
cards.note: The bug is the order. Fix: socks first, then shoes, then try again.

cards.q: A drawing program drew a square with 3 sides. What is the fix?
cards.note: A square has 4 sides. The steps said 3, so change the number to 4 and run it again.

cards.q: The steps say: draw a side, turn, draw a side, turn, draw a side. What is missing?
cards.note: Check one step at a time and count. Three sides drawn, one still missing.

cards.q: You found the bug and fixed it. What do you do next?
cards.note: Fix, then test. Trying again shows if the fix worked.

cards.q: You made a bug. What does the computer do?
cards.note: A computer never gets mad. It just waits for you to find and fix the bug.

cards.q: Everyone who writes steps makes bugs sometimes. Is a bug a bad thing or a normal thing?
cards.note: Bugs happen to everyone, even grown-ups who make games. Finding one is part of the job.

cards.q: Your steps went wrong somewhere. What is the best way to find the bug?
cards.note: Go step by step: did step 1 work? Did step 2? The bug is hiding in one of them.

cards.q: 🔴 🔵 🔴 🔴 🔴 🔵 This pattern has a bug. Which spot is wrong?
cards.sayQ: A pattern: red, blue, red, red, red, blue. This pattern has a bug. Which spot is wrong?
cards.note: Red, blue, red, blue is the pattern. The fourth spot should be blue, not red.

cards.q: 🔴 🔵 🔴 🔴 🔴 🔵 What should the fourth spot be?
cards.sayQ: A pattern: red, blue, red, red, red, blue. What should the fourth spot be?
cards.note: After red comes blue. Swap the fourth spot to blue and the pattern is fixed.

cards.q: ⭐ 🌙 ⭐ 🌙 🌙 🌙 Which spot is the bug?
cards.sayQ: A pattern: star, moon, star, moon, moon, moon. Which spot is the bug?
cards.note: Star, moon, star, moon... the fifth spot should be a star.

cards.q: Your block tower falls. The steps said: big block on top. Which step is the bug?
cards.note: Big blocks go on the bottom. Move the big block down and build again.

cards.q: Steps for cereal: get a bowl, pour milk, eat. What step is missing?
cards.note: A missing step is a bug too. You cannot eat cereal that is not in the bowl!

cards.q: A bug in a game makes your car drive backwards. What do the game makers do?
cards.note: Even grown-ups who make games have bugs. They debug, test, and share the fix.

cards.q: You fixed a bug. A friend asks how you did it. What is a good answer?
cards.note: Telling how you found and fixed a bug helps you and your friend next time.

cards.q: You tried a fix and it is still broken. What now?
cards.note: Sometimes there is more than one bug. Keep checking, one step at a time.

decks.subject: tech
decks.title: If This, Then That
decks.about: If this, then that: if it is raining, then take an umbrella; if the light is red, then stop. A plan says what should happen and what comes next, with a goal at the end (K2-AP-05). If-then rules are a bridge topic, since conditionals are taught from Grade 3 on, but a six-year-old already uses them all day, so read it together and let him make up his own rules.
decks.tip: Play if-then at the door: 'If it is raining, then...' and let him finish the rule before you both check the window.

cards.q: If it is raining, then take an umbrella. It is raining. What do you do?
cards.note: A rule has two parts: if this happens, then do that. Rain is the if, umbrella is the then.

cards.q: If it is sunny, then wear a hat. If it is raining, then take an umbrella. It is sunny. What do you do?
cards.note: Two rules. Only the one whose if part is true gets to happen.

cards.q: If the light is red, then stop. The light is red. What do you do?
cards.note: Red is the if. Stop is the then. Cars follow this rule all day.

cards.q: If the light is green, then go. The light turns green. What happens?
cards.note: When the if part comes true, the then part happens.

cards.q: In a game: if you tap the star, then it sparkles. You tap the star. What happens?
cards.note: Games are full of if-then rules. Your tap is the if, the sparkle is the then.

cards.q: In a game: if you tap the star, then it sparkles. You tap the moon. What does the star do?
cards.note: You did not tap the star, so the if part did not happen. No sparkle.

cards.q: If the battery is low, then charge it. The tablet says the battery is low. What do you do?
cards.a: ask a grown-up to charge it
cards.note: The tablet checks its own battery with an if-then rule. Ask a grown-up to plug the charger in.

cards.q: A robot bumps into a wall. Its rule: if you bump, then turn around. What does it do?
cards.note: Robots use if-then rules to decide what to do next.

cards.q: Rule: if it is dark, then turn on the light. It is dark. What happens?
cards.note: Is it dark? is a yes-or-no question. A computer can check it and then act.

cards.q: A computer can check a yes-or-no question. Which one is a yes-or-no question?
cards.note: Yes-or-no questions are easy for computers to check. Then they follow the rule.

cards.q: Before you build, you say what you want to make and what should happen. What is that called?
cards.note: A plan says the goal and what should happen. Programmers plan before they code.

cards.q: Your plan says: the robot should reach the door. What is that part of the plan?
cards.note: The goal is what you want to happen at the end.

cards.q: Rule: if the bell rings, then line up. The bell rings. What comes next?
cards.note: The ring is the if. Lining up is the then. School has lots of if-then rules.

cards.q: Rule: if it is cold, then wear a coat. It is a hot day. What do you wear?
cards.note: The if part did not happen, so the then part does not happen either.

cards.q: You want the light to come on when you clap. Which rule do you write?
cards.note: Put what you check after if, and what should happen after then.

cards.q: If it is a school day, then pack your bag. If it is Saturday, then play. It is Saturday. What do you do?
cards.note: Check each rule. Saturday is not a school day, so only the play rule happens.

cards.q: Rule: if the dog's bowl is empty, then fill it. The bowl is empty. What happens now?
cards.note: Empty bowl is the if, fill it is the then. You just ran an if-then rule!

decks.subject: tech
decks.title: Sorting and Searching
decks.about: Sorting means putting things in order, by size, by color or in ABC order, and searching means finding one thing fast, the way a computer finds a photo by its name or its tag (K2-DA-01); sorting things into piles is also one more way to show the same data (K2-DA-03). The cards ask which word or number comes first, why a sorted toy box beats a jumbled one, how a library keeps its books, and what typing a word in the search box brings back. Read it together: ABC order is new this year, so keep an alphabet strip nearby.
decks.tip: Dump a handful of crayons on the table and sort them two ways, by color and then by length, and time how fast he finds the blue one each time.

cards.q: Putting things in order, like smallest to biggest, has a name. What is it called?
cards.note: Sorting means putting things in order: by size, by color, or in ABC order.

cards.q: Looking for one special thing, like your red sock in a big pile, is called what?
cards.note: Searching means looking for one thing. A computer searches by the name you type.

cards.q: You sort three toy cars from smallest to biggest. Which car goes first?
cards.note: Smallest to biggest means the tiny one leads the line and the big one comes last.

cards.q: You sort your blocks by color. Where does a red block go?
cards.note: Sorting by color puts things that match together. Every red thing goes in the red group.

cards.q: Three words: apple, banana, cat. Which word comes first in ABC order?
cards.note: ABC order follows the alphabet. A comes before B and C, so apple is first.

cards.q: Put these in ABC order: dog, bird, fish. Which word comes first?
cards.note: Look at the first letters: b, d, f. B comes first in the alphabet, so bird is first.

cards.q: Put these in ABC order: dog, bird, fish. Which word comes last?
cards.note: B, then D, then F. F is the farthest along the alphabet, so fish goes last.

cards.q: A computer sorts the pet names Zip, Fluffy and Rover into ABC order. Which name is first?
cards.note: A computer sorts names by their first letter, just like you: F, then R, then Z.

cards.q: Library books sit on shelves by first letter. The C shelf comes right after which shelf?
cards.note: Shelves follow the alphabet too. A, then B, then C, all the way to Z.

cards.q: A library has thousands of books. How does it keep them so you can find one fast?
cards.note: Sorted shelves let you walk right to the book. A big pile would take all day.

cards.q: One toy box is sorted: cars here, blocks there. One is a jumble. Which box is faster to search?
cards.note: Sorting first makes searching fast. That is why computers sort their lists.

cards.q: You type cat in the photo search box. Which pictures show up?
cards.note: Search finds the pictures whose name or tag matches the word you typed.

cards.q: A word you add to a photo, like beach or birthday, has a name. What is it?
cards.note: A tag is a label. One photo can have many tags: beach, summer, Grandma.

cards.q: You tagged every beach photo with the word beach. How do you find them all later?
cards.note: Tags make searching easy. Type the tag and every photo with it shows up.

cards.q: Sort the numbers 9, 4 and 6 from smallest to biggest. Which comes first?
cards.note: Smallest first. 4 is smaller than 6 and 9, so it leads the line.

cards.q: Sort the numbers 3, 8 and 1 from smallest to biggest. Which comes last?
cards.note: Biggest goes last. 1, then 3, then 8.

cards.q: You sort your crayons by color, then sort the same crayons by length. Did the crayons change?
cards.note: Same crayons, two ways to sort them. The data stays the same and only the order changes.

cards.q: You sort crayons into color piles. The red pile is the tallest. Which color do you have most of?
cards.note: Sorting into piles shows your data a new way. The tallest pile is the color you have most of.

decks.subject: tech
decks.title: Data and Pictures
decks.about: Data is the information a computer keeps: numbers, words, pictures and sounds (K2-DA-02). The cards zoom into a picture to find its tiny dots, show the same counts as a tally chart and as a picture graph (K2-DA-03), predict from a graph (K2-DA-04), and use numbers and symbols to stand for things, like 1 for on and A for 1 (K2-AP-02, K2-NI-01). Read it together and point at the graph while he counts.
decks.tip: Ask everyone at dinner their favorite fruit, make tally marks on paper, then draw the same answers as a picture graph and show him they match.

cards.q: Numbers, words, pictures and sounds a computer keeps all have one name. What is it?
cards.note: Data is information a computer keeps. Your photos and your game scores are data.

cards.q: You take a photo on the tablet and it saves it. What is the photo now?
cards.note: Pictures, songs and words all become data inside a computer.

cards.q: You zoom way in on a picture. What do you see?
cards.note: A picture is made of tiny dots called pixels. Zoom in and they look like little squares.

cards.q: The tiny dots that make up a picture have a name. What is it?
cards.note: Pixel is short for picture element. Millions of them make one photo.

cards.q: Which one is data a tablet can keep?
cards.note: Sounds are data too. The tablet keeps a song as a long list of numbers.

cards.q: You want to know the class's favorite pet. How do you collect the data?
cards.note: Collecting data means asking or counting. Each answer is one piece of data.

cards.q: Each tally mark is one kid who likes dogs. How many kids like dogs?
cards.note: Tally marks count in bundles of five: four lines and one across. Five and two more is seven.

cards.q: Each tally mark is one kid who likes cats. How many kids like cats?
cards.note: Four lines, no bundle yet. One more would make five and close the bundle.

cards.q: Look at the picture graph. How many kids like cats?
cards.sayQ: Look at the picture graph. Each picture is one kid. How many kids like cats?
cards.note: Count the cat row. A picture graph shows data with one picture for each one.

cards.q: 7 kids like dogs. You can show it with tally marks or with 7 dog pictures. What is the same?
cards.note: Same data, two ways to show it. A tally chart and a picture graph tell the same story.

cards.q: Look at the graph of snack picks. Which snack should we buy more of?
cards.sayQ: Look at the picture graph of snack picks. Each picture is one kid. Which snack should we buy more of?
cards.note: The longest row shows what most kids want. Using data to guess well is called a prediction.

cards.q: Look at the snack graph. Which snack will the fewest kids take?
cards.sayQ: Look at the picture graph of snack picks. Each picture is one kid. Which snack will the fewest kids take?
cards.note: The shortest row is the one fewest kids picked. You can predict it will be left over.

cards.q: Inside a computer, 1 can mean on and 0 can mean off. The light is on. Which number?
cards.note: Computers use just 1 and 0 to stand for things: on and off, yes and no.

cards.q: Under a photo, a little heart picture means something. What does it mean?
cards.note: A symbol is a little picture that stands for an idea. Heart means like.

cards.q: In a code, A is 1, B is 2, C is 3. What number is C?
cards.note: Numbers can stand for letters. Computers keep words as numbers like this.

cards.q: In the code A is 1, B is 2, C is 3, what letter is 2?
cards.note: Read the code backwards: 2 stands for B. You could send a secret number message!

cards.q: A big picture is sent in little pieces, then put back together. What is it like?
cards.note: Computers send big things in small pieces and put them back together, like a jigsaw puzzle.

cards.q: A long message is cut into small pieces to send. What happens to the pieces at the other end?
cards.note: Each piece has a number so they go back in the right order.

decks.subject: tech
decks.title: Making Things on a Computer
decks.about: A computer is for making things, not just watching them: a drawing, a typed story, a photo, a recording, a slideshow, using the brush, eraser, fill and undo tools of a drawing app, then saving each creation as its own file and sharing it with family with a grown-up's help (K2-CS-03, K2-DA-01). Giving credit means saying who made a picture or song you used, why that is honest, and putting your own name on what you made yourself (K2-AP-06). Read it together, ideally with a drawing app open so he can try each tool as it comes up.
decks.tip: Open a drawing app together, let him try the brush, eraser, fill and undo, then save it with a name he picks and send it to a relative.

cards.q: A computer is for making things too. Which one can you make on a tablet?
cards.note: You can make drawings, stories, photos, songs and slideshows on a computer.

cards.q: You type a story about a dragon on the tablet. What did you make?
cards.note: Typing words into a writing app makes a story. You are the author!

cards.q: You press the red button and sing into the tablet. What did you make?
cards.note: A recording keeps your voice or song so you can play it again.

cards.q: You point the tablet at your dog and tap the round button. What did you make?
cards.note: The camera turns what it sees into a picture file. You made it by choosing what to snap.

cards.q: You put five photos in a row to show one after another. What is it called?
cards.note: A slideshow shows pictures one at a time. Add words and music to tell a story.

cards.q: In a drawing app, which tool makes a line follow your finger?
cards.note: The brush paints lines. Pick a color and a size, then drag your finger.

cards.q: You drew one line in the wrong spot. Which tool rubs it out?
cards.note: The eraser takes away only where you rub. The rest of the drawing stays.

cards.q: You want the whole sky blue with one tap. Which tool fills a big space fast?
cards.note: The fill tool pours one color into a whole space. One tap and the sky is blue.

cards.q: You tap undo three times. How many of your last lines go away?
cards.note: Each undo takes back one step. Three taps, three steps back.

cards.q: You made a song recording and a drawing. How many files did you make?
cards.note: Each thing you make is saved as its own file: a song file and a picture file.

cards.q: You open your saved drawing and add a sun. What do you do so the sun stays?
cards.note: Saving again keeps the new version. The sun is still there tomorrow.

cards.q: You want Grandma to see your drawing. What is a good way to share it?
cards.note: Sharing what you made with family is great. A grown-up picks the safe way to send it.

cards.q: Saying who made a picture or song you used has a name. What is it?
cards.note: Giving credit is honest. Programmers and artists do it every day.

cards.q: You put a picture from a website in your slideshow. What do you add under it?
cards.note: Write the maker's name under the picture. That is giving credit.

cards.q: Why do we say who made a picture or song we used?
cards.note: The maker worked hard on it, so saying their name is honest and fair. It also lets people find more of their work.

cards.q: You drew the picture all by yourself. Whose name goes under it?
cards.note: You made it, so the credit is yours. Sign your drawings like a real artist.

cards.q: A watcher only watches videos. A maker makes things. Which one are you when you draw on the tablet?
cards.note: Making beats only watching. Your ideas go into the computer and come out as something new.

cards.q: Who can make a drawing, a story or a song on a computer?
cards.note: Kids make real things on computers. You already did: the first drawing you saved.

decks.subject: tech
decks.title: Plan It Out
decks.about: Before building a program, a game or a drawing, programmers make a plan: a goal, the steps, and what they expect at the end, sometimes as a storyboard of little pictures (K2-AP-05). The cards find the goal of a plan, spot a missing step, predict the result, check the result against the plan, and then change the plan and say what changed and why, which is the iterative process in K2-AP-08. Read it together and plan something real afterwards, like a block tower or a paper airplane.
decks.tip: Before his next block tower, ask him to say the goal, the steps, and what it will look like, then check the finished tower against the plan.

cards.q: You want to make a game on the tablet. Which comes first, planning it or building it?
cards.note: Plan first, build second. A plan says the goal, the steps and what should happen.

cards.q: A plan has a goal, the steps, and the ending you expect. Which part is the list of things to do?
cards.note: The goal is what you want and the steps are how. The ending is what you expect to see.

cards.q: Plan: get flour, mix, bake, frost. What is the goal of this plan?
cards.note: The goal is the thing you want at the end. Every step points at it.

cards.q: Plan: get a pot, add dirt, drop in a seed, water it. What is the goal?
cards.note: Read the steps and ask: what are they all for? That is the goal.

cards.q: Plan: draw a house, color it, add a sun. What do you expect to see at the end?
cards.note: Saying what you expect before you start is part of the plan.

cards.q: Your plan says: the robot rolls to the door, then beeps. What do you expect at the end?
cards.note: Predict first, then run it. If the robot beeps at the door, the plan worked.

cards.q: Before making a video, you draw little pictures of each part in order. What is that called?
cards.note: A storyboard is a plan made of pictures. Movie makers use them too.

cards.q: Your storyboard shows: puppet waves, puppet sings, puppet bows. Which part do you film first?
cards.note: A storyboard goes in order, left to right. The first picture is the first thing you film.

cards.q: Plan: open the drawing app, pick blue, save the drawing. Which step is missing?
cards.note: You cannot save a drawing you never drew. Check a plan for missing steps.

cards.q: Your plan said a red house. Your drawing shows a blue house. What do you do next?
cards.note: Checking the result against the plan shows you what to fix.

cards.q: You compare your drawing with your plan and they match. What does that mean?
cards.note: A match means your plan worked. Now you can share it or make the next plan.

cards.q: Your paper airplane plan made a plane that fell straight down. What do you do to the plan?
cards.note: Changing a plan that is not working is smart. Programmers do it all the time.

cards.q: You changed your plan and now the plane flies. A friend asks how. What do you tell your friend?
cards.note: Say what you changed and why: I made the wings wider because it fell fast.

cards.q: You made the wings wider because the plane fell fast. Which part is the why?
cards.note: The why is the reason for the change. Saying it helps you remember what works.

cards.q: Plan, build, test, fix, and go round again. What is this round-and-round way of working called?
cards.note: Iteration means going round again, a little better each time. Say it: it-er-AY-shun.

cards.q: Which one of these is a plan?
cards.note: A plan is steps that lead to a goal, with a guess about what happens at the end.

cards.q: Your guess about what will happen at the end of your plan has a name. What is it?
cards.note: A prediction is a careful guess. Make one, then test to see if it comes true.

decks.subject: tech
decks.title: When This Happens: Events
decks.about: An event is something that happens and starts a program: a tap plays a sound, a shake changes the picture, the alarm time makes the alarm ring (K2-AP-05, K2-AP-01). The cards ask what started it, what happened because of it, how a program waits for an event, and how two different events make two different things happen. Events are a bridge topic, taught from Grade 3 on, so read it together and point out the real-life events all day: the doorbell rings, you open the door.
decks.tip: Play what started it: every time something beeps, rings or lights up today, ask him to name the event and then the action.

cards.q: Something that happens and starts a program, like a tap on a button, has a name. What is it?
cards.note: An event is a happening the program waits for: a tap, a shake, a clap, a time.

cards.q: When the button is tapped, the sound plays. What is the event?
cards.note: The event is the thing that happens first and starts everything else.

cards.q: When the button is tapped, the sound plays. What happens because of the event?
cards.note: Event first, then the action. The tap starts it, the sound is what happens.

cards.q: When you shake the tablet, the picture changes. What started the change?
cards.note: A tablet can feel a shake. The shake is the event that starts the change.

cards.q: When the alarm time comes, the alarm rings. What is the event here?
cards.note: Time can be an event too. The clock reaching seven is what starts the ring.

cards.q: When you clap, the robot turns. What is the event?
cards.note: The robot's microphone hears the clap. That sound is the event.

cards.q: The doorbell rings and you open the door. Which part is the event?
cards.note: Life is full of events. The ring happens, then you act.

cards.q: The phone rings and Grandma answers it. What happens because of the ring?
cards.note: The ring is the event. Answering is the action it starts.

cards.q: A program has one button. Nobody has tapped it yet. What is the program doing?
cards.note: A program can wait and wait. The moment the event happens, it acts.

cards.q: Tap the drum: boom. Tap the bell: ding. You tap the bell. What do you hear?
cards.note: Two events, two actions. Each tap starts its own sound.

cards.q: Tap the drum: boom. Tap the bell: ding. You tap the drum. What happens?
cards.note: The drum tap is a different event, so a different sound plays.

cards.q: In a game, which event would make the character jump?
cards.note: Match the event to the action. A tap on the jump button makes a jump.

cards.q: A night light turns on when the room gets dark. What starts the light?
cards.note: Getting dark is the event. Turning on is the action.

cards.q: Brushing your teeth is a list of steps. A tap that starts a game is what?
cards.note: Steps are what to do. An event is what starts it.

cards.q: You want the picture to change when the tablet is shaken. Which event do you pick?
cards.note: Pick the event, then the action: when shake, change the picture.

cards.q: You tilt the tablet and the ball rolls. What started the roll?
cards.note: A tablet can feel a tilt. The tilt is the event that starts the rolling.

cards.q: A game waits for a tap, a shake and a swipe. How many different events is that?
cards.note: Tap, shake, swipe: three events. Each one can start its own action.

cards.q: The microwave beeps and you take out the popcorn. What was the event?
cards.note: The beep happens, then you act. The beep is the event.

decks.subject: tech
decks.title: On and Off: Computer Codes
decks.about: Deep inside, a computer keeps everything with tiny switches that are only on or off, written as 1 and 0: a row of lights spells a code, a yes-or-no answer is one bit, numbers can spell a word, three numbers can mix a color, and a little picture like an envelope stands for an idea (K2-AP-02, K2-NI-01). Binary is a bridge topic, taught from Grade 3 on, so the cards stay with lights, codes and colors he can see and count. Read it together with a flashlight in hand: on, off, on.
decks.tip: Use a flashlight to send on, off, on across the room, then let him send a code back and tell you its 1s and 0s.

cards.q: Inside a computer, words, pictures and songs are all kept as which two numbers?
cards.note: Everything in a computer is long rows of 1s and 0s. 1 is on, 0 is off.

cards.q: Writing everything with only 1 and 0 has a grown-up name. What is it?
cards.note: Binary means made of two, and you say it BY-nah-ree. You will learn more about it in a few years.

cards.q: A computer is full of tiny switches. Each switch can be only two ways. Which two?
cards.note: On is 1 and off is 0. Millions of tiny switches make everything the computer does.

cards.q: 💡 ⚫ 💡 The lights are on, off, on. 1 means on. Which code is it?
cards.sayQ: Three lights: on, off, on. One means on and zero means off. Which code is it?
cards.note: Read the lights left to right: on is 1, off is 0. One, zero, one.

cards.q: The code is 0 1 1 and 1 means on. Which lights are on?
cards.sayQ: The code is zero, one, one, and one means on. Which lights are on?
cards.note: Zero is off, so the first light is dark. The two 1s at the end are on.

cards.q: A yes-or-no answer fits in a single 1 or 0. That tiny piece has a name. What is it?
cards.sayQ: A yes-or-no answer fits in a single one or zero. That tiny piece has a name. What is it?
cards.note: A bit is the smallest piece of computer data: one 1 or one 0, one yes or one no.

cards.q: One light can be on or off. How many different things can it show?
cards.note: On means one thing, off means another. One light, two choices.

cards.q: Two lights can be on on, on off, off on, or off off. How many different codes is that?
cards.sayQ: Two lights can be: on and on, on and off, off and on, or off and off. How many different codes is that?
cards.note: Count them: on on, on off, off on, off off. Two lights make four codes.

cards.q: Three friends each want their own light code. One light makes only 2 codes. How many lights do you need?
cards.note: Two lights make 4 codes, and 3 friends need only 3. One light makes just 2, so it is one short.

cards.q: A is 1, B is 2, C is 3, D is 4. Which word do the numbers 3 1 2 spell?
cards.sayQ: The letter A is one, B is two, C is three, D is four. Which word do the numbers three, one, two spell?
cards.note: 3 is C, 1 is A, 2 is B. Numbers can spell words: that is how a computer keeps them.

cards.q: A is 1, B is 2, C is 3, D is 4. Which word do the numbers 4 1 4 spell?
cards.sayQ: The letter A is one, B is two, C is three, D is four. Which word do the numbers four, one, four spell?
cards.note: 4 is D, 1 is A, 4 is D again. Dad!

cards.q: A is 1, B is 2, C is 3, D is 4. Which numbers spell the word bad?
cards.sayQ: The letter A is one, B is two, C is three, D is four. Which numbers spell the word bad?
cards.note: B is 2, A is 1, D is 4. Now you can write a secret number message.

cards.q: A screen dot mixes red, green and blue light. Its numbers are red 9, green 0, blue 0. What color is it?
cards.note: Only the red light is on, so the dot looks red. Three numbers make every color.

cards.q: A dot's red number tells how much red light it makes. Which is brighter, red 2 or red 9?
cards.note: Bigger number, brighter light. Zero means that light is off.

cards.q: A dot's numbers are red 0, green 0, blue 0. All three lights are off. What color is the dot?
cards.note: No light at all looks black. Turn all three lights up high and the dot looks white.

cards.q: A row of a picture is 1 1 1 0. Here 1 means a black square. How many black squares?
cards.sayQ: A row of a picture is one, one, one, zero. Here one means a black square. How many black squares?
cards.note: Count the 1s: three black squares and one white one. Every pixel is a number.

cards.q: A row of a picture is 0 0 1 0. Here 1 means black. Which square is black?
cards.sayQ: A row of a picture is zero, zero, one, zero. Here one means black. Which square is black?
cards.note: Read left to right: white, white, black, white. The 1 sits in the third spot.

cards.q: A tiny envelope picture on the screen is a symbol. What does it stand for?
cards.note: A symbol stands for something else. An envelope means message, a red light means stop, and 1 means on.

decks.subject: tech
decks.title: Electricity and Batteries
decks.about: Electricity is the energy that makes things light up, move and make sound; it comes from the wall outlet (sent from a power plant far away) or from a battery that stores it, and a charger fills the tablet's battery back up (K2-CS-02, the parts that make a device work). Electricity is a bridge topic, since NC science teaches it in Grade 4, so this level stays simple and calm: what needs power, plus and minus ends, solar panels, and the safety rules. Read it together, and say the safety rules in your own words too.
decks.tip: Walk around the house and sort things together: this needs electricity, this does not, and only grown-ups plug things in.

cards.q: Lights, fans and tablets all need a kind of energy to work. What is it?
cards.note: Electricity is energy that makes things light up, move or make sound.

cards.q: Electricity flows into a lamp. What does the lamp do?
cards.note: Light, sound and movement: electricity can make all three.

cards.q: Electricity flows into a fan. What does the fan do?
cards.note: A motor inside the fan turns electricity into spinning.

cards.q: The lamp plugs into the wall. Where does that electricity come from?
cards.note: Wires carry electricity from a power plant along tall poles and into the walls of your house.

cards.q: A flashlight has no cord. Where does it get electricity?
cards.note: A battery stores electricity so a thing can work with no cord.

cards.q: Which one needs electricity to work?
cards.note: A tablet, a lamp and a fridge need electricity. A book and a ball do not.

cards.q: Which one works with no electricity at all?
cards.note: Lots of fun things need no power: balls, books, crayons, blocks.

cards.q: The tablet battery is empty. What fills it up again?
cards.note: The charger pours electricity from the wall into the battery. A grown-up plugs it in.

cards.q: The battery is all the way empty. What does the tablet do?
cards.note: No electricity, no tablet. Charge it and it wakes up again.

cards.q: A battery has two ends with marks on them. What are the marks?
cards.note: Look for the + and − marks. The battery only works when each end goes the right way.

cards.q: A battery goes into a toy backwards. What happens?
cards.note: Match plus to plus and minus to minus. A backwards battery gives no power.

cards.q: What may go into a wall outlet?
cards.note: Never put fingers or anything else in an outlet. Only a plug goes in, and only a grown-up puts it there.

cards.q: Who plugs things into the wall?
cards.note: Plugs are a grown-up job. Ask, and a grown-up will plug the charger in for you.

cards.q: Water and electricity must stay far apart. Where do you keep the tablet?
cards.note: Keep drinks, sinks, tubs and pools away from anything that plugs in.

cards.q: Your hands are wet from the sink. What do you do before touching the tablet?
cards.note: Dry hands first. Water and electricity do not mix.

cards.q: You find a tiny round battery on the floor. What do you do?
cards.note: Batteries are not toys and never go in your mouth. Small ones are extra dangerous, so hand it to a grown-up right away.

cards.q: A solar panel sits in the sun. What does it make?
cards.note: Solar panels turn sunlight into electricity. Some calculators and houses use them.

cards.q: What does a battery do?
cards.note: A battery is like a little tank full of electricity, ready for when you need it.

decks.subject: tech
decks.title: Circuits and Switches
decks.about: A circuit is a loop that electricity travels around: a battery, two wires and a bulb make one, and the light comes on only when the loop is closed (K2-CS-02). A switch opens and closes the loop, and a gap or loose wire is a bug you fix by checking the connections (K2-CS-04). Circuits are a bridge topic from Grade 4 science, so read it together; a flashlight is a circuit in a tube you can open up and look at.
decks.tip: Open a flashlight together, take the battery out and put it back, and say the loop out loud: battery, wire, bulb, wire, back to the battery.

cards.q: Electricity travels around a loop to light a bulb. What is the loop called?
cards.note: A circuit is a loop for electricity: out of the battery, through the bulb, and back again.

cards.q: A battery, two wires and a bulb are joined in a loop. What happens to the bulb?
cards.note: Battery, wire, bulb, wire, back to the battery. The loop is closed, so the bulb lights.

cards.q: The light comes on only when the loop is what?
cards.note: Closed means no gaps. Electricity can go all the way round.

cards.q: One wire comes loose. There is a gap in the loop. What does the bulb do?
cards.note: A gap means the electricity cannot get round. No loop, no light.

cards.q: What opens and closes the loop so you can turn the light on and off?
cards.note: A switch is a tiny gate in the loop. Closed: light on. Open: light off.

cards.q: You flip the switch and the light goes off. What did the switch do to the loop?
cards.note: Off means the switch opened a gap. On means it closed the gap.

cards.q: You flip the switch and the light comes on. What did the switch do to the loop?
