cards.note: Closed loop, light on. Open loop, light off.

cards.q: Your bulb stays dark. What do you check first?
cards.note: A loose wire is a bug in the circuit. Check each connection, one at a time, like debugging.

cards.q: You find the loose wire and hook it back on. What happens?
cards.note: Fix the gap, close the loop, and the light comes back. That is debugging a circuit.

cards.q: Wires are made of metal inside. Why?
cards.note: Metal lets electricity flow. We say metal is a conductor.

cards.q: Wires have a plastic cover. What is it for?
cards.note: Plastic does not let electricity through, so the cover keeps it inside the wire and off your hands.

cards.q: The light switch on your wall does what to a circuit?
cards.note: Flip up: the loop closes and the ceiling light comes on. Flip down: a gap opens, light off.

cards.q: You take the bulb out and put a buzzer in the loop. What happens when the loop closes?
cards.note: A buzzer, a tiny motor or a bulb can all sit in the loop. Each turns electricity into something: sound, spin or light.

cards.q: You put a small motor in the circuit. What does it do when the loop closes?
cards.note: A motor turns electricity into spinning. Fans and toy cars have motors inside.

cards.q: A flashlight is a circuit in a tube. What are the parts inside?
cards.note: Push the switch: the loop closes, and electricity goes from the battery to the bulb.

cards.q: Which of these lets electricity through?
cards.note: Metal conducts. Plastic and rubber do not, which is why they cover wires and plugs.

cards.q: Which one is for grown-ups only?
cards.note: A little battery circuit is a safe thing to learn with a grown-up. Wall outlets carry much more electricity and are only for grown-ups.

cards.q: The circuit is battery, wire, bulb, wire. Where does the electricity start?
cards.note: The battery is the push. Electricity leaves one end, goes round the loop and comes back to the other end.

decks.subject: tech
decks.title: Lights, Buzzers and Motors
decks.about: The outputs electricity can drive: a tiny light (LED) glows, a buzzer makes a sound, a motor spins fan blades or toy car wheels, a tiny motor makes a tablet buzz, and a screen is many tiny lights; a sensor is an input, each output has its own switch, more electricity means brighter or faster up to a point, and a motor empties a battery faster than a tiny light. Electricity is a bridge topic (NC science teaches it in Grade 4), tagged to K2-CS-02 (what hardware parts do), and it follows Circuits and Switches (the loop) and In and Out (computer parts) without repeating them. Read it together with a flashlight, a battery toy and a fan in reach.
decks.tip: Hunt for outputs around the house: point at each thing and ask, does it make light, sound or movement?

cards.q: A light, a buzzer and a motor each do something when electricity flows in. What do we call them?
cards.note: Light, sound and movement are outputs, the things electricity comes out as. A sensor or a button is an input.

cards.q: A light sensor notices the dark and a lamp turns on. Which part is the output?
cards.note: The sensor notices, so it is the input. The lamp does something you can see, so it is the output.

cards.q: The tiny glowing light on a charger or a toy has a three-letter name. What is it?
cards.note: L E D is a tiny light that glows with very little electricity. Count the LEDs on your charger and toys.

cards.q: A doorbell needs to make a sound when you press it. Which part does the job?
cards.note: A buzzer turns electricity into sound. Press the button and it buzzes or rings.

cards.q: A night-light needs a soft glow all night. Which part does the job?
cards.note: A tiny light gives a soft glow and uses very little electricity, so it can stay on all night.

cards.q: A fan needs to spin its blades. Which part does the job?
cards.note: A motor turns electricity into spinning. Fans, toy cars and blenders all have one.

cards.q: A motor gets electricity. Which kind of output does it make?
cards.note: A motor turns electricity into movement: spinning wheels, fan blades, a wiggling toothbrush. A tiny light makes light and a buzzer makes sound.

cards.q: A clock must make a loud sound to wake you up. Which part do you pick?
cards.note: A buzzer makes the loud sound. A tiny light could not wake you, and a motor would just spin.

cards.q: You press the doorbell button and the buzzer sounds. What kind of part is the button?
cards.note: The button is a switch. It is the input that closes the loop, and the buzzer is the output.

cards.q: The tablet buzzes in your pocket. What tiny part is spinning inside to make the buzz?
cards.note: A tiny motor with a lopsided weight spins fast, and that makes the buzz you feel. It is called a vibration motor.

cards.q: A screen lights up with a picture. What makes the glow?
cards.note: A screen is made of many, many tiny lights that change color. Together they make the picture.

cards.q: A tiny light gets a little more electricity. What happens?
cards.note: More electricity, brighter light, up to a point. Every light has a limit.

cards.q: A grown-up puts a second battery in a toy car. What does the motor do?
cards.note: Two batteries push harder, so the motor spins faster. Only use as many as the toy is made for.

cards.q: A tiny light gets way too much electricity. What can happen?
cards.note: Too much electricity and a light burns out. Toys are made to give each part just the right amount.

cards.q: A toy has a light and a buzzer, each with its own switch. You flip only the light switch. What turns on?
cards.note: Each output can have its own switch. Flip one switch, and only that part gets electricity.

cards.q: A toy runs on one small battery. Which part empties the battery the fastest?
cards.note: A motor pulls a lot of electricity to spin, but a tiny light only sips. Motor toys need new batteries sooner.

cards.q: Why can a tiny light glow all night on one small battery?
cards.note: A tiny light uses very little electricity, so one small battery lasts a long, long time.

cards.q: An electric toothbrush wiggles back and forth. What is inside making it move?
cards.note: A small motor spins inside the handle and makes the brush wiggle. Motors are everywhere!

decks.subject: tech
decks.title: Robots and Sensors
decks.about: Robots as machines that follow a program written by people, sensors as their way of noticing (camera eyes, microphone ears, touch and light sensors), robot vacuums, factory arms, delivery robots and toy robots programmed with arrows, steps in order, bugs, why robots are good at repeating a job, how they do not feel or decide like people, smart speakers and their wake word, and how life changed before and after these machines. NC K2-CS-02 (hardware parts and what they do), K2-AP-01 (daily processes as algorithms) and K2-IC-01 (life before and after new technology). Read it together: the tablet reads every question and choice aloud.
decks.tip: Be the robot: let him give you three steps in order (stand up, turn, clap) and follow them exactly, even if the order is funny.

cards.q: What is a robot?
cards.note: A robot is a machine that follows a program, a list of steps written by people.

cards.q: A robot follows a program. Who writes the program?
cards.note: Robots do what they are told. People think of the steps and type them in.

cards.q: What does a robot use to notice the world around it?
cards.note: A sensor is a part that senses something, like light, sound or a bump, and tells the program.

cards.q: A robot's camera works like which part of your body?
cards.note: A camera lets the robot see shapes and colors, just like eyes.

cards.q: A robot's microphone works like which part of your body?
cards.note: A microphone hears sounds. A smart speaker uses one to hear your voice.

cards.q: A robot vacuum bumps into a wall and turns. Which sensor felt the wall?
cards.note: A bumper or touch sensor feels a bump, like your hand feeling a wall in the dark.

cards.q: The room gets dark and a robot stops. Which sensor noticed the dark?
cards.note: A light sensor measures how bright it is. Night lights that turn on by themselves use one too.

cards.q: Before robot vacuums, how did people clean the floor?
cards.note: New machines change how people live. A robot vacuum cleans while people do other things.

cards.q: In a factory, a robot arm puts the same part on every car. Why is a robot good at this job?
cards.note: Robots are great at doing the same job again and again, exactly the same way.

cards.q: A small robot rolls down the sidewalk with a pizza inside. What is it?
cards.note: Delivery robots use cameras and sensors to find the way and to stop for people.

cards.q: A toy robot moves when you press arrow buttons: forward, forward, turn. What did you make?
cards.note: A list of steps the robot follows is a program. You are the programmer!

cards.q: You tell a robot: get a bowl, pour cereal, pour milk. What is this list of steps called?
cards.note: An algorithm is a list of steps in order. People follow them too, like a recipe.

cards.q: A robot pours the milk before the bowl is there. What was wrong?
cards.note: Robots follow steps exactly in order. Put the bowl first, then pour.

cards.q: A robot turns left when it should turn right. What does its program have?
cards.note: A bug is a mistake in a program. Finding and fixing it is called debugging.

cards.q: Can a robot feel happy or sad like you do?
cards.note: A robot may show a smiley face, but it does not feel. It only follows its program.

cards.q: In a video, a robot seems to choose a toy. Who really chose it?
cards.note: A robot does not decide like a person. It follows the choices people wrote into the program.

cards.q: A smart speaker sits quietly until you say its special word. What is that word called?
cards.note: The speaker's microphone listens for its wake word, then it listens to your question.

cards.q: Before robot arms, who put the parts on cars in a factory?
cards.note: People did the heavy, repeated work by hand. Now robots help, and people fix and program the robots.

decks.subject: body
decks.title: Head to Toe
decks.about: Naming the parts of the body from head to toe and where each one is: head, neck, shoulder, elbow, wrist, hands and fingers, chest, tummy, back, hip, knee, ankle, heel, feet and toes, plus higher and lower, left and right, and how many fingers and toes. Body-part names are not a Grade 1 objective of their own in NC's Healthful Living standards, so this is a bridge topic tagged to the closest codes, 1.PCH.1.4 (dressing the right parts for the weather) and 1.PCH.2.1 (keeping those parts safe from injury). Read it together and let him touch each part as the card names it.
decks.tip: Play Simon Says with the parts in this deck: Simon says touch your wrist, your heel, your left shoulder.

cards.q: Which part of your body is at the very top?
cards.note: Your head holds your brain, eyes, ears, nose and mouth. Hats go here.

cards.q: What holds your head up and lets it turn from side to side?
cards.note: Your neck joins your head to your body. Nod yes and shake no to feel it work.

cards.q: Where does your arm join your body, up at the top?
cards.note: Shrug and your shoulders go up. A backpack rests on them.

cards.q: What bends in the middle of your arm?
cards.note: Bend your elbow to bring your hand up to your mouth. Cough into it, too.

cards.q: What bends between your hand and your arm?
cards.note: A watch sits on your wrist. Wave and feel it bend.

cards.q: Count the fingers and thumbs on two hands. How many do most people have?
cards.note: Five on each hand. Two hands make ten, so you can count to ten on them.

cards.q: What is the front of your body between your neck and your tummy?
cards.note: Your heart and lungs are inside your chest. Feel it rise when you breathe in.

cards.q: What is the soft front part of your body, under your chest?
cards.note: Grown-ups also say belly. Your stomach, where food goes, is inside it.

cards.q: You lie down on it. It runs behind you from your shoulders to your hips. What is it?
cards.note: Your backbone runs down the middle of your back. Sit up tall to keep it happy.

cards.q: Where does your leg join your body?
cards.note: Put your hands on your hips. Each leg swings from a hip.

cards.q: What bends in the middle of your leg?
cards.note: Knees bend when you sit, run and jump. Knee pads keep them safe when you skate.

cards.q: What joins your foot to your leg?
cards.note: Your sock folds over your ankle. Circle your foot to feel it move.

cards.q: What is the back part of your foot called, under your ankle?
cards.note: Your heel touches the ground first when you walk. Shoes have a heel too.

cards.q: How many toes do most people have on one foot?
cards.note: Five toes on each foot. The big toe helps you balance.

cards.q: You stand up straight. Which part of your body is lowest, touching the floor?
cards.note: Head at the top, feet at the bottom. That is head to toe.

cards.q: Which is higher up on your body, your shoulder or your knee?
cards.note: Shoulders are up near your head. Knees are down near the floor.

cards.q: You put a hand on your heart. Your heart is a little to which side?
cards.note: Your heart sits in the middle of your chest, tipped a little to the left.

cards.q: Hold your hands up, backs toward your face. Which hand's thumb and pointer make a letter L?
cards.note: L is for left. The right hand makes a backwards L.

decks.subject: body
decks.title: The Five Senses
decks.about: The five senses and the body part for each: eyes see, ears hear, nose smells, tongue tastes and skin feels; which sense tells him the soup is hot, the music is loud, the honey is sweet or the cookies smell good; how senses keep him safe (smelling smoke, hearing a car, reading a stop sign, spitting out something strange that is not food); senses working as a team; and the kind truth that people who cannot see or hear use their other senses and tools like a white cane, hearing aids, braille and sign language, and how he can help a friend who cannot hear well. The five senses are a classic early-grades science topic that NC's 2023 Grade 1 science standards do not name, so this is a bridge topic tagged to 1.PCH.2.1 and 1.PCH.2.2 (noticing danger such as smoke), 1.ICHR.1.2 (what makes each person special) and Science PS.1.1.2 (observing and comparing with the senses). Read it together: every question and choice is read aloud.
decks.tip: Play a guessing game with his eyes closed: a spoon, a sock, a lemon. Which sense told him what it was?

cards.q: Which body part do you taste with?
cards.note: Tiny taste buds all over your tongue sort out sweet, salty, sour and bitter. Lick a lemon and the sour ones get busy.

cards.q: The music is very loud. Which body part tells you that?
cards.note: Ears catch sounds. Very loud sounds can hurt them, so turn the music down.

cards.q: Which body part do you smell with?
cards.note: Air carries tiny bits of smell into your nose when you breathe in.

cards.q: A big red sign says STOP. Which sense reads it for you?
cards.note: Sight means seeing. Your eyes read signs, lights and faces so you know what to do.

cards.q: One sense works all over your body, in your skin. Which sense is it?
cards.note: Skin feels soft and rough, hot and cold, tickles and hugs.

cards.q: You hold an ice cube and it feels cold. Which body part felt that?
cards.note: Your skin feels hot and cold so you can pull away from things that could hurt you.

cards.q: Cookies are baking and the house smells yummy. Which sense is that?
cards.note: Smells float through the air into your nose, even from another room.

cards.q: Honey is sweet and a pickle is sour. Which sense tells them apart?
cards.note: Sweet and sour are two of the four tastes your tongue knows. Smell helps too, so food tastes dull when your nose is stuffy.

cards.q: You take a tiny sip and the soup is too hot. Which parts felt the heat?
cards.note: Lips and tongue feel hot and cold just like skin does. Blow on hot food and wait.

cards.q: Your friend cannot hear well. How can you help them understand you?
cards.note: Seeing your face and lips helps a lot. Speak clearly, and never shout.

cards.q: You smell smoke in the house. What should you do?
cards.note: Your nose can warn you before your eyes see fire. Smelling smoke means get a grown-up right away.

cards.q: You hear a car coming before you step into the street. Which sense kept you safe?
cards.note: Stop, look and listen. Your ears can hear a car even when it is around the corner.

cards.q: A person who cannot see well may carry a long white cane. What is the cane for?
cards.note: The cane taps the ground to find steps and curbs before the feet get there. A guide dog can help too.

cards.q: Some people's ears hear sounds very softly. What makes sounds louder for them?
cards.note: A hearing aid is a tiny speaker that sits in or behind the ear.

cards.q: A person who cannot see can read a book with bumpy dots. What do they read with?
cards.note: The dots are called braille, and fingertips feel each letter. Touch does the job that eyes usually do.

cards.q: Some people who cannot hear talk with their hands. What is that called?
cards.note: Sign language uses hand shapes and faces to say words. You can learn some too.

cards.q: You see a dog's tail wag and hear it bark. How many senses are you using?
cards.note: Sight and hearing. Your senses work as a team, and your brain puts the messages together.

cards.q: You put something strange in your mouth and it tastes nasty. What do you do?
cards.note: A nasty taste from something that is not food can be your body's warning. Spit it out and tell a grown-up what it was.

decks.subject: body
decks.title: Skin, Hair and Nails
decks.about: What skin does (covers and protects, sweats to cool him, heals a scrape under a scab, grows with him), keeping it clean, melanin and freckles and why every skin color is good, goosebumps, hair that keeps the head warm and grows back after a cut, eyebrows, and nails that protect fingertips and need trimming. Hygiene sits under NC 1.PCH.1.1 and 1.PCH.1.2 (how germs spread and how to stop them) and skin colors under 1.ICHR.1.2 (what makes each person special); how skin, hair and nails work is a bridge topic. Read it together: every question and choice is read aloud.
decks.tip: Look at the back of his hand with a magnifier: pores, tiny hairs and the lines on his knuckles.

cards.q: What covers your whole body on the outside?
cards.note: Skin is your biggest organ. It keeps dirt and germs out and keeps your insides in.

cards.q: Your skin makes sweat when you are hot. What is sweat for?
cards.note: Sweat dries off your skin and carries the heat away. Every skin color sweats the same way.

cards.q: Sweat comes out through tiny holes in your skin. What are the holes called?
cards.note: Pores are too small to see without a magnifier. You have millions of them.

cards.q: A scab is a hard crust of dried blood over a scrape. What is its job?
cards.note: The scab is a lid. Under it, your skin is quietly building a brand-new layer.

cards.q: What is growing under a scab while it is on your knee?
cards.note: When the new skin is ready, the scab falls off by itself. Leave it alone until then.

cards.q: You take a bath or shower. What does the soap wash off your skin?
cards.note: Clean skin stays healthy. Wash well under your arms, behind your ears and between your toes.

cards.q: What gives skin its color?
cards.note: Say MEL-uh-nin. More melanin makes darker skin and less makes lighter skin; every color is good, and every color needs sunscreen outside.

cards.q: Some people have little brown dots on their nose and cheeks. What are they?
cards.note: Freckles are tiny spots with extra melanin. Many people get more of them in summer.

cards.q: You feel chilly and tiny bumps pop up on your arms. What are they?
cards.note: A tiny muscle pulls each hair up straight. It happens when you are cold or get a surprise.

cards.q: What grows on top of your head and helps keep it warm?
cards.note: Hair also shades your head from the sun. A hat helps on cold days and sunny days.

cards.q: You get a haircut. What happens to your hair after that?
cards.note: Hair grows about half an inch every month. That is why haircuts keep coming.

cards.q: Does it hurt when hair is cut?
cards.note: The part of your hair you can see is not alive, so it has no feeling. Only pulling hurts.

cards.q: Eyebrows are hair too. What do eyebrows do for you?
cards.note: Eyebrows steer sweat and rain off to the side. Eyelashes catch dust before it reaches your eye.

cards.q: What are the hard covers on the tips of your fingers?
cards.note: Nails are made of the same tough stuff as hair. Toenails protect your toes the same way.

cards.q: Why do you have fingernails?
cards.note: Nails also help you pick up tiny things like a bead or the edge of a sticker.

cards.q: Nails keep growing. What should a grown-up do when yours get long?
cards.note: Short, clean nails hold fewer germs. Trimming does not hurt, just like a haircut.

cards.q: You grow bigger every year. What does your skin do?
cards.note: Skin is stretchy and makes new skin all the time. Old bits flake off so tiny you never see them.

decks.subject: body
decks.title: Joints That Bend
decks.about: What a joint is (where two bones meet), the hinge joints at knee and elbow that bend one way like a door, the ball-in-a-cup shoulder and hip that swing in circles, the wrist, ankle, neck and finger joints, the slippery cartilage on bone ends, muscles that pull to bend a joint, which joint works when he kicks, throws or nods, and pads that protect joints. How joints are built is a bridge topic; the moving part is NC PE.1.MS.1.1 and PE.1.MS.1.2 (running, kicking, throwing), PE.1.HF.3.1 (flexibility) and 1.PCH.2.1 (avoiding injury). Read it together and let him bend each joint as it comes up.
decks.tip: Ask him to walk across the room without bending his knees, then with. Which joints did he miss?

cards.q: Your knee and your elbow are joints. What meets at a joint?
cards.note: A joint is the meeting place of two bones. A grown-up has 206 bones, so there are lots of joints to bend.

cards.q: Your knee bends one way and straightens back, like a door swinging. What kind of joint is that?
cards.note: A door hinge opens and shuts one way. So does your knee.

cards.q: Which joint in your arm bends like a door hinge?
cards.note: Bend your elbow and your hand comes up to your face. Straighten it and your arm is long again.

cards.q: Your shoulder lets your arm swing all the way around in a circle. What is it shaped like?
cards.note: The round top of your arm bone sits in a cup on your shoulder. It can roll in any direction.

cards.q: Which joint lets your whole leg swing in a big circle, up at the top of your leg?
cards.note: Your hip is a ball-in-a-cup joint too. Swing your leg forward, sideways and back.

cards.q: You swing your lower leg to kick a ball. Which joint bends?
cards.note: Your hip swings the leg and your knee snaps it straight. Both joints help you kick.

cards.q: You throw a ball far. Which joint swings your whole arm around?
cards.note: A big throw uses the shoulder, then the elbow, then the wrist, all in a row.

cards.q: You nod your head yes. Which part has the joints that move?
cards.note: Small joints in your neck let your head nod yes, shake no and tilt sideways.

cards.q: You wave hello and your hand flaps up and down. Which joint bends?
cards.note: Your wrist bends up and down and tilts side to side. It has lots of little bones inside.

cards.q: You stand on tiptoe to reach a shelf. Which joint bends to lift your heel?
cards.note: Your ankle moves your foot up and down like a hinge. Circle your foot to feel it.

cards.q: How many joints are in one of your fingers?
cards.note: Look at the knuckle, the middle and the tip. Your thumb has two.

cards.q: Which is the biggest joint in your body?
cards.note: The knee joins your thigh bone and your shin bone and carries you all day.

cards.q: Can your knee bend backward the way it bends forward?
cards.note: A hinge only goes one way, and that keeps your knee safe. Never force a joint the wrong way.

cards.q: The ends of bones in a joint are covered with smooth, slippery stuff. What is it called?
cards.note: Say KAR-tih-lij. It lets bones glide instead of grind, and your ears and the tip of your nose are cartilage too.

cards.q: What pulls on your bones to make a joint bend?
cards.note: Muscles only pull, they never push. One muscle bends your elbow and another pulls it straight.

cards.q: Which three moves happen at your joints?
cards.note: Every move you make happens at a joint. Stiff legs with no knees could not run.

cards.q: Knee pads and elbow pads protect which parts when you skate or ride a scooter?
cards.note: A helmet protects the skull. Pads protect the joints that hit the ground first in a fall.

decks.subject: body
decks.title: Bones and the Skeleton
decks.about: Goes deeper than Heart, Lungs and Bones: how many bones a grown-up has (206) and why a baby has more, the backbone that bends because it is a stack, the long leg bones, kneecap and jaw, 27 bones in one hand and 12 pairs of ribs, bones that are alive and make new blood in their marrow, how a cast lets a broken bone mend, the X-ray, sunshine and vitamin D, and two fun facts (the smallest bone is in the ear, the funny bone is a nerve). Inside-the-body anatomy is a bridge topic beyond NC Grade 1; the closest codes are 1.NPA.1.2 (foods and why we eat them), 1.NPA.2.1 and PE.1.HF.3.2 (activity that builds a strong body). Read it together: the tablet reads every card aloud while he feels each bone on himself.
decks.tip: Have him feel his own backbone, kneecap and jaw as each card comes up, and bend his elbow to find the joint.

cards.q: How many bones does a grown-up have?
cards.note: Two hundred six bones, from the big thigh bone to the tiny bones inside your ears.

cards.q: A baby is born with about 300 bones, but a grown-up has 206. Where did the extra bones go?
cards.note: Many baby bones are soft and in pieces. As you grow, the pieces harden and join into one bigger bone.

cards.q: Feel the bumpy row of bones down the middle of your back. What is it called?
cards.note: The backbone is also called the spine. It holds you up straight and protects the nerves inside it.

cards.q: Your backbone is a stack of many small bones instead of one long bone. Why is that good?
cards.note: One stiff bone could not curl. A stack of little bones bends forward, back and side to side.

cards.q: The longest and strongest bone in your body is in your...?
cards.note: It is the thigh bone, from your hip to your knee. Your arms and legs are full of long, strong bones.

cards.q: Are your bones dry sticks, or are they alive and growing?
cards.note: Bones are living parts of you, with blood flowing to them. They grow longer and thicker until you are grown.

cards.q: Deep inside your big bones is a soft, jelly-like part. What does it make?
cards.note: That soft part is called bone marrow. It makes new blood cells every second of the day.

cards.q: A bone breaks. What does the doctor put on it while it heals?
cards.note: A cast holds the bone still so the two ends can grow back together. Most casts come off in a few weeks.

cards.q: Wiggle your fingers. About how many small bones are in just one hand?
cards.note: Twenty seven bones in each hand, with long thin ones in your fingers. That is why hands can do so much.

cards.q: The round bone in front of your knee is your...?
cards.note: The kneecap is a little shield for your knee joint. Knee pads cover it when you skate or ride.

cards.q: Which bone moves up and down when you chew and talk?
cards.note: The lower jaw is the only big bone in your head that moves. Your teeth sit in your jaws.

cards.q: Playing outside in the sun helps your skin make vitamin D. What does vitamin D help you build?
cards.note: Vitamin D helps bones soak up calcium from milk and food. Eggs, fish and milk have vitamin D too.

cards.q: The smallest bone in your body is inside your...?
cards.note: It is called the stirrup and is about the size of a grain of rice. It helps you hear.

cards.q: You bump your elbow and it tingles. People call that the funny bone. What is it really?
cards.note: A nerve runs right past your elbow bone. Bump it and the nerve sends a buzzy, tingly message.

cards.q: What kind of picture lets a doctor see the bones inside you?
cards.note: An X-ray camera takes a picture right through your skin. Bones show up white.

cards.q: Feel the ribs on the sides of your chest. How many pairs of ribs do you have?
cards.note: Twelve pairs, twenty four ribs in all. They join the backbone behind and the breastbone in front.

decks.subject: body
decks.title: Muscles
decks.about: How muscles move you: they pull on bones through tendons, work in pairs so an arm can bend and straighten, and come in two kinds, the ones you steer (arms, legs, jaw, tongue, smile) and the ones that run on their own (heart, stomach); also how many you have (about 600), what they need (protein, rest, stretching), why you shiver and which muscle is the biggest. Inside-the-body anatomy is a bridge topic beyond NC Grade 1; the nearest codes are PE.1.HF.3.1 and PE.1.HF.3.2 (muscle strength and the benefits of activity) and 1.NPA.1.2 and 1.NPA.2.1 (foods and activity that build a strong body). Read it together: the tablet reads every card aloud while he bends his arm, makes a muscle and feels his jaw.
decks.tip: Have him bend his arm and feel the biceps bunch up, then straighten it and feel the back of his arm tighten instead.

cards.q: Muscles move your bones. Do they push the bones or pull them?
cards.note: A muscle can only pull. It gets shorter and tugs on the bone it is tied to.

cards.q: What tough cord ties a muscle to a bone?
cards.note: Feel the tight cord above your heel. That is the Achilles tendon, the biggest one you have.

cards.q: Bend your arm. The front muscle pulls. What does its partner on the back of your arm do?
cards.note: Muscles work in pairs. To straighten your arm, the back muscle pulls and the front one relaxes.

cards.q: Make a muscle! The bump on the front of your upper arm is called your...?
cards.note: Say BY-seps. It bends your elbow, and the triceps on the back of your arm straightens it again.

cards.q: About how many muscles do you have?
cards.note: More than 600 muscles, big and small. Your face alone has more than 40.

cards.q: Which muscle squeezes all day and all night and never takes a rest?
cards.note: The heart is a muscle that squeezes more than once every second, even while you sleep.

cards.q: Which muscle works on its own, without you telling it to?
cards.note: Stomach and heart muscles run on their own, even in your sleep. Arm and leg muscles wait for your orders.

cards.q: You smile at a friend. What is pulling the corners of your mouth up?
cards.note: Little muscles in your cheeks lift your smile. A frown uses a different set.

cards.q: Stick out your tongue and wiggle it. What is your tongue made of?
cards.note: The tongue is a bundle of muscles with no bone inside. It pushes food to your teeth and shapes your words.

cards.q: Eggs, beans, fish and meat have a muscle-building part in them. What is it called?
cards.note: Say PRO-teen. Muscles use protein as building blocks to mend and grow, and milk, nuts and yogurt have it too.

cards.q: The day after a big hike, your legs feel a little sore. What does that soreness mean?
cards.note: Hard work makes tiny changes in muscles. Rest and sleep mend them, and they come back stronger.

cards.q: Why do you stretch before you run and play?
cards.note: Stretching warms muscles up so they bend easily and do not get hurt.

cards.q: You are cold and you start to shiver. What is shivering?
cards.note: Working muscles make heat, so shivering warms you up. Put on a coat and they can stop.

cards.q: The biggest muscle in your body is the one you...?
cards.note: The big muscle in your bottom helps you stand up, climb stairs and jump.

cards.q: Chew a crunchy carrot and touch your cheeks. Which muscles are squeezing?
cards.note: Jaw muscles are some of the strongest for their size. They bite through apples and carrots.

cards.q: You stand still in line. Are your muscles resting or working?
cards.note: Lots of small muscles hold you up even when you stand still. Lie down and they finally get a rest.

decks.subject: body
decks.title: Heart and Blood
decks.about: Deeper than Heart, Lungs and Bones: the heart as a fist-sized pump with four rooms behind the breastbone, blood vessels and the veins he can see, blood carrying oxygen from the lungs and taking carbon dioxide back, the pulse at his wrist, a heartbeat that is slowest in sleep, blood that is red and mostly water, how blood thickens to stop a cut bleeding and what to do for a small cut, and what the heart loves. Inside-the-body anatomy is a bridge topic beyond NC Grade 1; the nearest codes are PE.1.HF.3.1 and PE.1.HF.3.2 (the heart and lungs in fitness) and 1.NPA.1.1 and 1.NPA.2.1 (water and activity). Read it together: the tablet reads every card aloud while he finds his own pulse.
decks.tip: Help him press two fingers on the inside of his wrist and count beats for ten seconds, then jump for a minute and count again.

cards.q: Squeeze your fist, open it, squeeze again. Your heart works like that. What is it squeezing out?
cards.note: Each squeeze pushes blood out into your body. Each time it opens, it fills up again.

cards.q: Make a fist. Which part inside you is about that same size?
cards.note: Your heart grows as your fist grows. A grown-up's heart is about the size of a grown-up's fist.

cards.q: Your heart sits in the middle of your chest, tipped a little left. Which hard bone is right in front of it?
cards.note: Put a hand flat on the middle of your chest to feel the breastbone. It and the ribs make a strong cage around the heart.

cards.q: Blood travels around your body inside tiny tubes. What are the tubes called?
cards.note: The biggest vessels are as wide as a finger. The tiniest are thinner than a hair.

cards.q: Some people can see blue or green lines under the skin on their wrist. What are they?
cards.note: Veins carry blood back to the heart. The blood inside is red; a vein only looks blue or green through your skin, and on some skin it does not show at all.

cards.q: Blood picks something up in your lungs and delivers it to every part of you. What is it?
cards.note: Oxygen is a gas in the air. Every part of your body needs it to work.

cards.q: Blood also carries away a used-up gas your body wants to get rid of. Where does it drop it off?
cards.note: The gas is carbon dioxide. You breathe it out, and the blood heads back for more oxygen.

cards.q: When does your heart beat the slowest?
cards.note: A sleeping body needs the least blood, so the heart takes it easy. It still never stops.

cards.q: Press two fingers on the inside of your wrist. What is the little beat you feel?
cards.note: Each pulse is a push of blood from one heartbeat. You can feel it on the side of your neck too.

cards.q: Why does the doctor listen to your chest with a stethoscope?
cards.note: Say STETH-uh-scope. The doctor listens to the lub-dub of your heart and the whoosh of your lungs.

cards.q: A small cut bleeds, then the bleeding stops all by itself. How does blood do that?
cards.note: Tiny bits in your blood stick together and make a plug. The plug dries into a scab while new skin grows under it.

cards.q: You get a small cut on your finger. What should you do?
cards.note: Rinse with clean water, pat dry, put on a bandage and tell a grown-up.

cards.q: What color is your blood?
cards.note: Blood is always red, bright red when it is full of oxygen and darker red when it is not.

cards.q: Blood is mostly made of something you drink every day. What is it?
cards.note: More than half of your blood is water. Drinking water keeps blood flowing smoothly.

cards.q: Your heart has little rooms inside, with doors that open and shut. How many rooms?
cards.note: Two rooms on top fill up with blood, two on the bottom pump it out. The lub-dub sound is the little doors snapping shut.

cards.q: Which three things keep your heart strong and happy?
cards.note: Running, biking and swimming make the heart muscle stronger. Water and good food keep the blood healthy.

decks.subject: body
decks.title: Lungs and Breathing
decks.about: Deeper than Heart, Lungs and Bones: what the lungs take from the air (oxygen) and what you breathe out (carbon dioxide), the nose that cleans and warms air, the windpipe, the millions of tiny air sacs, the diaphragm muscle that pulls air in, hiccups, yawns, candles, breath clouds on cold days, why the left lung is smaller, and why clean air matters. Inside-the-body anatomy is a bridge topic beyond NC Grade 1; the nearest codes are PE.1.HF.3.1 and PE.1.HF.3.2 (heart and lungs in fitness), 1.NPA.2.1 (activity) and Science LS.1.1.1 (living things need air). Read it together: the tablet reads every card aloud while he puts a hand on his belly and breathes.
decks.tip: Have him lie on his back with a stuffed animal on his belly and watch it ride up and down as he breathes.

cards.q: What do your lungs take out of the air you breathe in?
cards.note: Oxygen is a gas in the air that every part of your body needs. Your blood carries it from the lungs.

cards.q: Which used-up gas do you breathe out to get rid of it?
cards.note: Say CAR-bon dye-OX-ide. Trees take it in and give back oxygen, so trees and people help each other.

cards.q: Why is it good to breathe in through your nose?
cards.note: Tiny hairs and sticky stuff inside your nose catch dust. The nose also warms the air before it reaches your lungs.

cards.q: You are running hard. Which lets in more air quickly, your nose or your mouth?
cards.note: The mouth is a bigger opening, so it helps when your body needs lots of air fast.

cards.q: Air goes down a tube from your throat to your lungs. What is the tube called?
cards.note: Feel the ridges on the front of your neck. Those are stiff rings that keep the windpipe open.

cards.q: Inside your lungs, air fills millions of tiny sacs like little...?
cards.note: Oxygen passes from the tiny sacs into your blood. They are called alveoli.

cards.q: A big flat muscle under your lungs pulls down to suck air in. What is it called?
cards.note: Say DY-uh-fram. When it pulls down your lungs get bigger and air rushes in; when it relaxes, air flows out.

cards.q: Hic! What is happening when you get the hiccups?
cards.note: The diaphragm gives a sudden jerk and your throat snaps shut: hic! Hiccups usually stop on their own.

cards.q: You run and your breathing speeds up. Who needs all that extra oxygen?
cards.note: Busy muscles burn energy and need more oxygen. Lungs and heart both speed up to deliver it.

cards.q: Sitting still, about how many breaths do you take in one minute?
cards.note: Kids breathe about 20 to 30 times a minute at rest, faster than grown-ups. Running can double it.

cards.q: Blowing out candles, blowing bubbles and whistling all use what?
cards.note: Your belly and chest muscles squeeze the lungs and push the air out in a stream.

cards.q: You open wide and yawn. What does a yawn pull in?
cards.note: Nobody knows for sure why we yawn. Being sleepy or bored, or seeing a friend yawn, can start one.

cards.q: Which air is best for your lungs?
cards.note: Smoke from cigarettes and fires harms lungs. Step away from smoke and let a grown-up know.

cards.q: Your left lung is a little smaller than your right lung. Why?
cards.note: The heart tips to the left, so the left lung has a dent to make space for it.

cards.q: On a cold day you can see your breath. What is that little cloud?
cards.note: Your breath is warm and wet. Cold air turns the wetness into tiny drops, like a small cloud.

cards.q: You fall asleep. What do your lungs do all night?
cards.note: Your brain keeps your lungs breathing slow and steady, so you never have to remember to breathe.

decks.subject: body
decks.title: Brain and Nerves
decks.about: The brain as the boss of thinking, feeling, remembering and moving, nerves that carry messages like tiny wires, the spinal cord inside the backbone, the super-fast reflex, how practice builds new brain connections, a brain that keeps working through sleep and dreams, why it is wrinkly, and what protects it: a cushion of liquid inside the skull and a helmet on wheels. Inside-the-body anatomy is a bridge topic beyond NC Grade 1; the nearest codes are 1.PCH.2.1 (avoiding injury, the helmet), 1.MEH.1.2 (feelings start in the brain) and 1.MEH.2.1 (trying again when something is hard: the practice and try-again cards). Read it together: the tablet reads every card aloud while he tries the hot-pan reflex story and the left-brain, right-hand trick.
decks.tip: Ask him to wiggle one toe and talk through the trip: brain, down the backbone, along a nerve, to the toe muscle.

cards.q: Which part of your body is the boss that tells all the other parts what to do?
cards.note: The brain runs thinking, feeling, remembering and moving. It even keeps you breathing.

cards.q: Messages race between your brain and the rest of you along tiny wires. What are they called?
cards.note: Nerves reach every part of you, from your scalp to your toes.

cards.q: A thick bundle of nerves runs down inside your backbone. What is it called?
cards.note: The backbone protects the spinal cord the way the skull protects the brain. Messages run up and down it.

cards.q: Something soft and fluffy brushes your hand. Where does that touch message travel to?
cards.note: Skin nerves send the message up the spinal cord, and the brain decides: soft! Then it may tell your hand to pet it again.

cards.q: You touch a hot pan and your hand jerks away before you even think. What is that called?
cards.note: A reflex is a super-fast shortcut. The spinal cord answers before the brain even hears about it.

cards.q: How fast do nerves carry their messages?
cards.note: Some nerve messages travel more than 200 miles an hour, faster than a race car.

cards.q: A balloon pops and you jump. What does your brain tell your heart to do?
cards.note: Feelings start in the brain, and a quick heartbeat gets you ready to move. Slow breaths tell the brain all is well.

cards.q: You practice tying your shoes. What is your brain building each time?
cards.note: Practice makes brain paths stronger, like a trail you walk every day. Mistakes help build them too.

cards.q: You get a puzzle wrong, then try again. What is your brain doing?
cards.note: Trying again is how the brain learns. Every try makes the path a little clearer.

cards.q: Late at night you are fast asleep. What is your brain doing?
cards.note: At night the brain sorts the day, keeps you breathing and makes dreams.

cards.q: The pictures and stories you see while you sleep are called...?
cards.note: Dreams are your brain playing while you rest. You dream most in the hours near morning.

cards.q: You tumble off your bike and your helmet bumps the ground. What did the helmet do for your brain?
cards.note: The skull is hard, but a hard fall can still shake the brain, so the helmet squashes a little and takes the bump instead. After a big bump a grown-up should check the helmet.

cards.q: The outside of your brain is wrinkly, with lots of folds. Why?
cards.note: The folds pack a big thinking surface into a small skull, like crumpling a big sheet of paper into a ball.

cards.q: Your brain is made of billions of tiny...?
cards.note: They are called neurons, and each one can talk to thousands of others. That is how you think.

cards.q: Your brain has a left half and a right half. The left half controls which hand?
cards.note: The wires cross over. The left half of your brain runs the right side of your body, and the right half runs the left.

cards.q: Inside your skull, your brain floats in a little clear liquid. What is the liquid for?
cards.note: The liquid works like a cushion, so a bump on the head does not shake the brain hard. A helmet adds even more cushion.

decks.subject: body
decks.title: Food's Journey
decks.about: Follows a bite of food from the mouth, where teeth chew and saliva softens it, down the food tube to the stomach that mixes it into a thick soup, through the long small intestine that passes the good parts into the blood, to the large intestine that takes back water, and out as poop a day or two later; also tummy rumbles, the liver, fiber and water. Digestion is a bridge topic beyond NC Grade 1; the nearest codes are 1.NPA.1.1 (why drink water), 1.NPA.1.2 (foods and why we eat them) and Science LS.1.1.1 (living things need food). Read it together: the tablet reads every card aloud, so you can trace the trip on his tummy as you go.
decks.tip: At a meal, have him chew one bite slowly and count the chews, then follow the swallow with a finger down to his stomach.

cards.q: A bite of apple starts a long trip through your body. Where does the trip begin?
cards.note: The trip runs from your mouth all the way through you. These cards follow the bite step by step.

cards.q: What do your teeth do to a crunchy bite of apple?
cards.note: Front teeth bite, back teeth grind. Small bits are easier for the rest of your body to handle.

cards.q: The watery spit in your mouth has a science name. What is it?
cards.note: Say suh-LIE-vuh. It makes food soft and slippery and starts breaking it down, and just thinking about lemons makes it flow!

cards.q: Why is it smart to chew your food well before you swallow?
cards.note: Small, soft bits are easier for the stomach to mix. Chewing slowly also lets you taste more.

cards.q: You swallow. Which tube carries the food from your mouth down to your stomach?
cards.note: Its grown-up name is the esophagus, say ee-SOF-uh-gus. Its muscles squeeze food down, so you could even swallow upside down.

cards.q: The food tube ends in a stretchy bag that mixes food with juices. What is the bag?
cards.note: The stomach is a muscle bag. It churns and squeezes food with juices for a few hours.

cards.q: After the stomach mixes and squeezes, what does the food look like?
cards.note: The stomach turns even a crunchy carrot into a thick, mushy soup, ready for the next stop.

cards.q: Your tummy rumbles and growls. What is making that sound?
cards.note: Squeezing muscles push air and juice around. It is loudest when the stomach is empty, so it often means lunch time.

cards.q: After the stomach, food moves into a long, curly tube. What is it called?
cards.note: Say in-TES-tin. It is small around but very long, three or four times as long as you are tall, folded up neatly inside you.

cards.q: The small intestine takes the good parts out of food. Where do those good parts go next?
cards.note: Energy and building blocks pass through the intestine wall into the blood, which delivers them everywhere.

cards.q: Which big organ beside your stomach makes a juice that helps break down fats?
cards.note: The liver also cleans your blood and stores energy. The pancreas nearby makes more digesting juices.

cards.q: The last stop is the large intestine. What does it take back from what is left?
cards.note: The large intestine is wider but shorter. It soaks up water so your body can use it again.

cards.q: What is left leaves your body when you use the toilet. What is it called?
cards.note: Poop is the part of food your body could not use, and everyone makes it. Wash your hands after.

cards.q: About how long does food's whole trip through your body take?
cards.note: A day or two, sometimes three. The stomach part alone takes a few hours.

cards.q: Fruits, vegetables and whole grains have fiber. What does fiber do inside you?
cards.note: Fiber is the part of plants you cannot digest. It sweeps through the intestines and keeps things moving along.

cards.q: Which drink helps your stomach and intestines do their job?
cards.note: Water helps break food down and keeps everything moving. Drink some with every meal.

decks.subject: body
decks.title: Eyes and Ears
decks.about: How seeing and hearing work, not which sense is which: the pupil that lets light in and grows in the dark, the lens that focuses, the brain that makes the picture, two eyes for judging distance, eyelids, lashes, tears and glasses; then the outer ear that catches sound, the eardrum that vibrates, the three tiny bones, the snail-shaped inner ear, two ears for finding where a sound comes from, earwax, balance, and keeping loud sounds down. Inside-the-body anatomy is a bridge topic beyond NC Grade 1; the nearest codes are 1.PCH.2.1 (avoiding injury: loud sounds, poking ears) and 1.ICHR.1.2 (what makes each person special: glasses, and eyes and ears that work differently). Read it together: the tablet reads every card aloud while he watches his pupils change in a mirror.
decks.tip: Dim the lights and watch his pupils grow in a mirror, then flick the light on and watch them shrink.

cards.q: Look in a mirror. What is the black circle in the middle of your eye?
cards.note: The pupil is really a hole. Light goes through it into your eye.

cards.q: You walk into a dark room. What does your pupil do?
cards.note: A bigger pupil lets in more light so you can see in the dark. In bright sun it shrinks to a dot.

cards.q: Behind the pupil is a clear lens. What does it do with the light?
cards.note: The lens bends light to make a sharp picture at the back of your eye, like a camera.

cards.q: The back of your eye catches the light. Who turns it into the picture you see?
cards.note: The eye sends a message along a nerve. The brain makes the picture, even flipping it right side up.

cards.q: Why is seeing with two eyes better than with one?
cards.note: Each eye sees a slightly different view, and the brain uses both to judge distance. Try catching a ball with one eye shut!

cards.q: What closes over your eyes when you blink or sleep?
cards.note: Blinking spreads tears over your eyes to keep them wet and clean, about 15 times every minute.

cards.q: What are the tiny hairs along the edge of your eyelids for?
cards.note: Eyelashes catch dust and tell your eyelid to blink when something comes too close.

cards.q: You cry a little and your nose gets runny too. Where do the extra teardrops go?
cards.note: A tiny tube in the corner of each eye drains tears into the nose. That is why crying makes your nose run.

cards.q: Glasses help blurry eyes see sharp. How do they do it?
cards.note: Glasses bend light a little before it reaches the eye, so the picture lands sharp. Many kids and grown-ups wear them.

cards.q: The part of your ear you can see is shaped like a cup. What is it for?
cards.note: Cup your hands behind your ears and listen. Bigger cups catch more sound.

cards.q: Sound goes into your ear and hits a thin skin stretched tight like a drum. What is it?
cards.note: Sound makes the eardrum shake, or vibrate, like a drum top when you tap it.

cards.q: Behind the eardrum sit three tiny bones. What do they do with the shaking?
cards.note: They are the smallest bones you have, called the hammer, anvil and stirrup.

cards.q: Deep in your ear is a part curled like a snail shell. What does it do?
cards.note: It is called the cochlea, say KOK-lee-uh. Tiny hairs inside it send sound messages along a nerve to the brain.

cards.q: Two ears are better than one for knowing...?
cards.note: A sound reaches one ear a tiny bit sooner and louder. The brain uses that to point you the right way.

cards.q: A sound is so loud it hurts your ears. What should you do?
cards.note: Very loud sounds can hurt the tiny hairs inside the ear, and they do not grow back. Keep headphones low.

cards.q: The sticky yellow stuff inside your ear is earwax. What is it for?
cards.note: Earwax protects the ear and slowly moves out on its own. Never poke anything inside your ear.

cards.q: You spin around and feel dizzy. Which part of you helps keep your balance?
cards.note: Tiny loops of liquid in the inner ear tell the brain which way is up. Spinning sloshes them, so you feel dizzy for a moment.

decks.subject: body
decks.title: Growing Up
decks.about: How a first grader grows: feet, legs and arms getting longer, height measured at a yearly checkup and the growth chart, why a baby tooth wiggles and when the first one usually falls out, learning new skills by practice, what the body needs to grow (sleep, food, play), babies to kids to teens to grown-ups, and the kind truths that everyone grows at their own speed and nobody can rush it. NC 1.PCH.1.3 (baby teeth give way to permanent teeth), 1.ICHR.1.2 (what makes each person special), 1.NPA.2.1 (activities good for the body) and Science LS.1.1.1 (what living things need to grow); the checkup and growth-stage cards are a bridge topic. Read it together: every question and choice is read aloud.
decks.tip: Find his baby pictures and a shoe he has outgrown. Ask what has changed and what he can do now that he could not do then.

cards.q: Last year's shoes feel tight on your feet. What happened?
cards.note: Growing feet need a bigger size about once a year. A shoe store can measure them.

cards.q: Your pants that fit last winter are too short now. Which part of you grew?
cards.note: Legs do a lot of the growing at your age. That is why pants get short before they get tight.

cards.q: At a checkup, the doctor stands you against a measuring stick. What is being measured?
cards.note: Height is how tall you are. Most first graders grow about two inches in a year.

cards.q: Your coat sleeves stop above your wrists this winter. Which part of you grew?
cards.note: Arms and legs do most of the growing at your age. Grown-ups buy coats a little big so you can grow into them.

cards.q: The doctor draws a dot on a chart at every checkup. What does the chart show?
cards.note: A growth chart connects the dots from baby to now. Doctors like to see a steady climb.

cards.q: How often do healthy kids go to the doctor for a checkup?
cards.note: A well visit checks your growing, your eyes and ears, and your shots, even when you feel fine.

cards.q: A baby tooth gets wiggly. What is pushing up under it?
cards.note: The new tooth melts away the baby tooth's root, so the baby tooth comes loose and falls out.

cards.q: About how old are most kids when the first baby tooth falls out?
cards.note: Some start at five, some at seven. Both are normal.

cards.q: Which teeth do you keep for your whole life?
cards.note: Grown-up teeth are also called permanent teeth. Brush them well, they have to last.

cards.q: Babies learn to move in an order. Which usually comes first, crawling or walking?
cards.note: Most babies crawl first. Some scoot on their bottoms and go straight to walking.

cards.q: When you were a baby, riding a bike was too hard. How did you learn new things like that?
cards.note: Growing up means learning: walking, talking, reading, tying shoes. Practice does it.

cards.q: Which three things does your body need most to grow well?
cards.note: Sleep is when a lot of growing happens, food is the building material, and play makes bones and muscles strong.

cards.q: Some kids grow fast and some grow slowly. Is that okay?
cards.note: Bodies grow on their own schedules. Short, tall, early, late, all of it is normal.

cards.q: Baby, kid, then what comes next, before grown-up?
cards.note: Teenagers are 13 to 19. Teens grow fast and need lots of sleep too.

cards.q: Can you make yourself grow faster by trying really hard?
cards.note: Growing happens a little every day. Good food, sleep and play are all you can do.

cards.q: When do people stop growing taller?
cards.note: Most people reach their full height near the end of the teen years. Then you are done growing up, but never done learning.

decks.subject: body
decks.title: Body Fighters
decks.about: The body's side of germs: skin as the first wall, the white blood cells in his blood that hunt and gobble germs, why a fever makes him hot and tired, sneezes, coughs and mucus as germ-pushers, why a scrape turns red and why a scab should be left alone, what a vaccine teaches the fighters, how rest and clean hands help, that some germs are friendly, and the feeling-better day when the fighters have won. NC 1.PCH.1.1 and 1.PCH.1.2 (how germs cause illness and ways to stop them); how the body fights germs is a bridge topic told calmly. Read it together: every question and choice is read aloud, and it pairs with Germs and Handwashing in Healthy Me.
decks.tip: Next time he has a scrape, look at it together each day: the red edge, the scab, then the new pink skin.

cards.q: What is the body's first wall that keeps most germs out?
cards.note: Germs cannot get through healthy skin. A scrape is a gap in the wall, so wash it and cover it.

cards.q: Tiny fighters in your blood that hunt down germs are called what?
cards.note: White blood cells are too small to see. They zoom through your blood looking for germs.

cards.q: How do white blood cells get to a germ anywhere in your body?
cards.note: Blood goes everywhere, so the fighters do too.

cards.q: A white blood cell finds a germ. What does it do?
cards.note: Some white blood cells swallow germs whole. Others make special stickers that tag germs for the team.

cards.q: You have a fever and feel hot. What is your body doing?
cards.note: A warmer body makes it harder for germs to grow and helps the fighters work. Rest and water help it along.

cards.q: What does a grown-up use to check if you have a fever?
cards.note: A thermometer shows how warm your body is. A grown-up decides if you need the doctor.

cards.q: Why do you feel so tired when you are sick?
cards.note: Your body saves its energy for the fight. Resting is helping.

cards.q: Why does your body make you sneeze?
cards.note: A sneeze blasts dust and germs out of your nose. Catch it in your elbow so they do not fly to a friend.

cards.q: A cough pushes germs and gunk out of which parts?
cards.note: Coughing clears the tubes you breathe through. Cover it with your elbow.

cards.q: Sticky stuff inside your nose traps dust and germs. What is it called?
cards.note: Say MYOO-kus; you might call it snot. It is a germ trap, so blow it into a tissue and wash your hands.

cards.q: A scrape turns red and warm around the edges. What is happening?
cards.note: Extra blood brings white blood cells to clean out germs. A little red and puffy means the team is working; if it gets redder or hurts more, show a grown-up.

cards.q: Should you pick at a scab?
cards.note: Picking opens the door for germs and slows the new skin. It falls off when it is ready.

cards.q: What does a vaccine teach your body?
cards.note: A vaccine shows your fighters a harmless piece or a weak copy of a germ. They learn it and remember it, so if the real germ comes they beat it fast.

cards.q: You have a cold. What helps your body fighters most?
cards.note: Sleep, water and good food give the fighters what they need. The grumpy feeling passes.

cards.q: Clean hands mean fewer germs get in. Who gets an easier job?
cards.note: Washing hands is like keeping the front door shut. Fewer germs in, fewer fights.

cards.q: Are all germs bad?
cards.note: Friendly germs in your tummy help you digest food. Yogurt has friendly ones too.

cards.q: After a few sick days you feel well again. What did your body fighters do?
cards.note: The fighters won, and they remember that germ. Feeling better is your body's hard work paying off.

decks.subject: body
decks.title: Rest, Move, Grow
decks.about: What happens inside when he runs (muscles make heat, cheeks flush to let it out, sweat is mostly water so he drinks), warming up, gentle stretching, a stitch and a cool-down, why the heart slows at rest, where energy comes from, why muscles repair and grow during sleep, about an hour of active play a day, the calm feeling after playing outside, and balancing active time with quiet time (a movement break when he is wiggly, a run after a long sit). NC 1.NPA.2.1 (activities good for the body), 1.NPA.1.1 (reasons to drink water), PE.1.HF.3.1 and PE.1.HF.3.2 (flexibility and the benefits of activity) and PE.1.PR.4.2 (good feelings from activity); builds on Move Your Body and Heart, Lungs and Bones in Healthy Me. Read it together: every question and choice is read aloud.
decks.tip: After he runs around the yard, ask him to report: warm muscles, pink cheeks, sweat, fast heart. Then watch it all calm down together.

cards.q: After running, your muscles feel warm. Why?
cards.note: Muscles make heat when they work, like an engine. That is why you warm up fast when you move.

cards.q: Your cheeks feel hot after you run hard. What is your body doing?
cards.note: Blood rushes to the skin to let heat escape, so cheeks feel warm and may look pinker or darker. That is normal and healthy after play.

cards.q: Sweat is mostly made of what?
cards.note: Sweating uses up your body's water, so drink some when you play hard.

cards.q: Before a race you jog slowly and swing your arms. What is that called?
cards.note: A warm-up wakes muscles up gently so they are ready to go fast.

cards.q: How should you stretch your muscles?
cards.note: Hold a gentle stretch and breathe. Stretching should feel good, never painful.

cards.q: You get a sharp little pain in your side while running. What do you do?
cards.note: That pain is called a stitch. Slow down, take deep breaths and it fades away.

cards.q: After a race you walk slowly instead of stopping still. What is that called?
cards.note: A cool-down lets your heart slow down gently and keeps your legs from feeling stiff later.

cards.q: You sit down to read after running. Why does your heart slow down?
cards.note: Resting muscles need less oxygen, so the heart can take it easy. Fast when you play and slow when you rest are both part of a healthy day.

cards.q: Where does the energy to run and play come from?
cards.note: Food is fuel. Breakfast fills the tank for a busy day.

cards.q: You sat and drew pictures all afternoon. What does your body want next?
cards.note: Quiet time is good. After a long sit, your legs and lungs are ready for a run around the yard.

cards.q: You played hard today. When do your tired muscles get fixed up and grow?
cards.note: Your body does its repair work at night. A special growing signal is strongest while you sleep.

cards.q: After a big day of playing outside you feel sleepy early. Why?
cards.note: A tired body after play is a good tired. Sleep refills your energy for tomorrow.

cards.q: How much running, jumping and active play do kids need each day?
cards.note: Sixty minutes a day, and it can come in little pieces: recess, a bike ride, a dance in the kitchen.

cards.q: Playing outside helps your mind feel what?
cards.note: Moving your body helps worries shrink and helps you focus afterward.

cards.q: Which day has a good balance for your body?
cards.note: Active time makes you strong, and quiet time lets your body and brain rest. You need both.

cards.q: Playing outside in the daytime helps you do what at night?
cards.note: Daylight and exercise set your body clock, so you fall asleep faster at bedtime.

cards.q: You feel wiggly and cannot sit still in class. What helps?
cards.note: A quick stretch, a walk or ten jumping jacks wakes up your brain so you can sit and listen again.

decks.subject: body
decks.title: Food Is Fuel
decks.about: Why we eat: food is the body's fuel for running, thinking and growing, different foods do different jobs (go foods for energy, builder foods, protecting foods), the hungry and full signals, why breakfast wakes up the brain, fuel being used even in sleep, water as part of the fuel, and where food's energy first came from (the sun). NC 1.NPA.1.2 (foods and why we eat them) and 1.NPA.1.1 (reasons to drink water); the first level of Healthy Eating. Read it together: the tablet reads every card aloud, and you add what was on his plate today.
decks.tip: Before a meal, ask him how his fuel tank feels: empty, half full or full. Ask again at the end.

cards.q: A car needs gas to go. What does your body need to go?
cards.note: Food is your body's fuel. It gives you the energy to run, think and grow.

cards.q: Food is like fuel. What does fuel do for a car or a body?
cards.note: Fuel is what makes something go. Gas for the car, food for you.

cards.q: Food does three big jobs. It gives you energy, helps you think, and helps you...?
cards.note: Every day your body builds new bone, skin and muscle. Food brings the building blocks.

cards.q: Bread, rice and pasta are go foods. What do go foods give you?
cards.note: Go foods are grains: bread, rice, oats, pasta and tortillas. They are the quickest way to fill your energy tank.

cards.q: Protein foods like eggs and beans are the builders. What do they build?
cards.note: Builder foods are protein: eggs, beans, fish, chicken, nuts and tofu. They build and fix your body.

cards.q: Grains give energy and protein builds. What job do fruits and vegetables do?
cards.note: Fruits and vegetables carry vitamins that protect your eyes, your skin and your germ fighters.

cards.q: Your tummy rumbles and feels empty. What is your body saying?
cards.note: A rumbling, empty tummy is your hunger signal. It means it is time to eat.

cards.q: You are eating dinner and your tummy starts to feel full. What do you do?
cards.note: Full means the tank is topped up. You can stop, even if some food is left on the plate.

cards.q: Who knows best if you are hungry or full?
cards.note: Listen to your body. Eat when it says hungry and stop when it says full.

cards.q: You slept all night with no food. What does breakfast do for your brain?
cards.note: Breakfast gives your brain fresh fuel to think, listen and learn at school.

cards.q: You skip lunch. By the afternoon, how might you feel?
cards.note: An empty tank makes it hard to think and play nicely. Meals keep your energy steady.

cards.q: Plants make their food from sunlight, and we eat plants. So where did food's energy first come from?
cards.note: Plants catch sunlight to make their food. We eat plants, or animals that ate plants, so the energy in your lunch started as sunshine.

cards.q: Your brain works best when you drink enough...?
cards.note: Water is part of your fuel too. Every part of you, even your thinking, needs it.

cards.q: You sleep all night long. Does your body use fuel while you sleep?
cards.note: Even asleep, your heart beats, you breathe and you grow, and all of that uses fuel. That is why you wake up ready for breakfast.

cards.q: Your tummy is like a fuel tank. It empties as you play. When does it fill back up?
cards.note: Playing, thinking and growing all use fuel. Meals and snacks fill the tank again.

cards.q: Reading and math make your brain work hard. What does your brain run on?
cards.note: Your brain uses lots of energy, even when you sit still. That is one more reason to eat breakfast.

cards.q: Who needs fuel from food every single day?
cards.note: Kids, grown-ups and grandparents all need food every day. Growing kids use lots of fuel.

decks.subject: body
decks.title: Fruits and Vegetables
decks.about: Eating a rainbow and what each color does (red for the heart, orange for the eyes, green for bones, blue and purple for the brain, white for the germ fighters), vitamins and apple-skin fiber, why fresh, frozen, canned and dried all count and raw or cooked both count, fruit for something sweet, telling a fruit from a vegetable (with the tomato as the tricky one in a note), where strawberries grow, seeds, cutting grapes small for little kids, and the five-a-day idea. NC 1.NPA.1.2 (a variety of foods and why we eat them) and 1.NPA.1.3 (where foods come from); goes deeper than the Food Groups sorting level in Healthy Me. Read it together and hunt for each color in the fridge.
decks.tip: At the store, let him pick one fruit or vegetable of a color you did not eat this week.

cards.q: Why do we eat fruits and vegetables of every color?
cards.note: Red, orange, green, purple and white foods each carry different helpers for your body.

cards.q: Red foods like strawberries and tomatoes help which part of you stay strong?
cards.note: Red fruits and vegetables carry helpers that are good for your heart and blood.

cards.q: Orange foods like carrots and sweet potatoes help keep which part of you healthy?
cards.note: Your body turns the orange color helper into vitamin A, which your eyes need to stay healthy. Carrots do not give you super night vision, though.

cards.q: Green foods like broccoli and spinach help build strong...?
cards.note: Green vegetables carry calcium and vitamin K, two helpers that make bones hard and strong.

cards.q: Blue and purple foods like grapes and plums help which thinking part of you?
cards.note: Blueberries, grapes, plums and eggplant carry helpers that are good for your brain and memory.

cards.q: White foods like bananas, cauliflower and onions help your body do what?
cards.note: White counts as a rainbow color too. Garlic, onions, mushrooms and bananas help your germ fighters.

cards.q: Fruits and vegetables are full of tiny helpers for your eyes, skin and germ fighters. What are they?
cards.note: Vitamins are too small to see. Your body cannot make most of them, so you eat them.

cards.q: Carrots can be raw and crunchy or cooked and soft. Which way counts as a vegetable?
cards.note: Raw, cooked, frozen or canned, a vegetable is a vegetable. Cooking changes the texture, and some kids like one way better than the other.

cards.q: A raisin is a dried fruit. What was it before it dried out?
cards.note: Raisins are grapes dried in the sun. Dried fruit counts as fruit too, so raisins in your lunchbox are a fruit.

cards.q: Fresh, frozen or canned. Which fruits and vegetables count?
cards.note: Frozen peas and canned peaches count just like fresh ones. Pick canned fruit packed in juice or water.

cards.q: You want something sweet after dinner. Which sweet food is an everyday food?
cards.note: Fruit is nature's dessert. Its sugar comes with vitamins, fiber and water.

cards.q: Fruits grow from a flower and hold seeds inside. Which one is a fruit?
cards.note: A peach grows from a blossom and has a pit, a big seed, inside, while carrots and potatoes grow under the ground. Tricky one: a tomato has seeds too, so scientists call it a fruit, but at mealtime it counts as a vegetable.

cards.q: Carrots are roots and lettuce is leaves. What do we call plant roots, stems and leaves we eat?
cards.note: Broccoli is a flower bud, celery is a stem, spinach is leaves. All vegetables.

cards.q: Apples grow high on trees. Where do strawberries grow?
cards.note: Strawberries grow on small plants close to the ground. In North Carolina you can pick them at a farm in spring.

cards.q: Whole grapes are round and can get stuck in a little kid's throat. What does a grown-up do first?
cards.note: Round, slippery foods like whole grapes, cherry tomatoes and hot dog pieces get cut small for little kids. Sit down and chew well too.

cards.q: About how many handfuls of fruits and vegetables should you eat each day?
cards.note: Five a day: a fruit or veggie at every meal and every snack adds up fast.

cards.q: Which fruit can you eat with the skin on for extra fiber?
cards.note: Apple, pear and potato skins have lots of fiber. Wash well and crunch away.

cards.q: What is inside most fruits that can grow into a new plant?
cards.note: Apple seeds, peach pits and watermelon seeds can all grow into new plants. Fruit comes from plants.

decks.subject: body
decks.title: Grains, Protein, Dairy
decks.about: What the other three food groups do for the body: grains from grass plants give lasting energy, whole grains keep the whole seed, and rice, tortillas, naan and noodles are everyday grains around the world; protein builds and fixes muscles and skin (eggs, beans, fish, nuts and tofu, with beans counting twice and plant protein for families who eat no meat); and dairy brings calcium and vitamin D for bones and teeth, with fortified soy milk for kids who cannot drink cow's milk. NC 1.NPA.1.2 (foods and why we eat them) and 1.NPA.1.3 (plant or animal source). Read it together; sorting foods into groups was the Food Groups level, this one is about the jobs.
decks.tip: At dinner, point to one food and ask: is this a go food, a builder or a bone helper?

cards.q: Bread, tortillas, rice and oats all come from which kind of plant?
cards.note: Wheat, rice, oats and corn are all grasses. Their seeds are the grains we grind into flour or cook whole.

cards.q: Oatmeal, brown rice and whole wheat bread keep the whole grain seed. What are they called?
cards.note: Whole grains keep the whole seed, so they have more fiber and helpers. Try to make about half of your grains whole grains.

cards.q: Whole grain bread and rice are usually which color?
cards.note: Brown rice, brown bread, oats. A grown-up can check the label for the word whole.

cards.q: Oatmeal for breakfast is a whole grain. How long does its energy last?
cards.note: Whole grains let out their energy slowly, so you stay full and ready to learn until lunch.

cards.q: Pasta, bread and crackers are made from grains ground into a powder. What is the powder called?
cards.note: Flour is ground-up grain. Whole wheat flour keeps the whole seed.

cards.q: You scrape your knee. Which food job helps your body build new skin?
cards.note: Protein builds new skin, muscle, hair and blood. Eggs, beans, fish, meat, nuts and tofu are protein foods.

cards.q: Some families eat no meat at all. What can they eat to get plenty of protein?
cards.note: Beans, lentils, peas, tofu and nuts are plant protein foods. Vegetarians build strong muscles with them every day.

cards.q: Beans are special. They count as protein and also as which other group?
cards.note: Beans, peas and lentils are in two groups at once. They build like protein and have fiber like vegetables.

cards.q: Fish is a protein food with a special helper for which thinking part of you?
cards.note: Fish like salmon have omega-3, a helper that growing brains need. Fish is a builder food too.

cards.q: Peanut butter, nuts, beans and tofu are protein foods. Where do they come from?
cards.note: Protein does not only come from animals; plants give protein too. Check with a grown-up before sharing nuts, since some kids are allergic.

cards.q: Chicken, fish, beef and eggs are protein foods. Where do they come from?
cards.note: Farmers raise chickens and cows. Fish come from rivers, lakes and the sea.

cards.q: Milk, yogurt and cheese give you calcium. Which two hard parts does calcium make strong?
cards.note: Calcium is the hard stuff in bones and teeth. Kids need lots because bones are still growing.

cards.q: Milk has a sunshine vitamin added that helps calcium work. What is it called?
cards.note: Vitamin D helps your body use calcium. Sunshine on your skin makes some, and milk has it added.

cards.q: Some kids cannot drink cow's milk. What can they drink to get calcium instead?
cards.note: Fortified means calcium and vitamins are added. Some families use oat or almond milk with calcium added; a grown-up checks the label.

cards.q: Yogurt has friendly tiny helpers that live in your tummy. What do they help?
cards.note: Yogurt is milk with friendly bacteria added that help your tummy break food down. Pick plain or low-sugar yogurt and add fruit.

cards.q: Rice, tortillas, naan and noodles are everyday foods around the world. Which group are they all in?
cards.note: Every country has its own grain food. Rice in China, tortillas in Mexico, naan in India, pasta in Italy, injera in Ethiopia.

cards.q: Which food group is the main energy giver for running and playing?
cards.note: Grains are the go foods. Bread, rice, pasta, oats and tortillas fill your energy tank.

decks.subject: body
decks.title: Drinks and Water
decks.about: Water is the best drink because the body is mostly water and it has no sugar, juice as a sometimes drink and the whole orange over orange juice, soda and sports drinks as sometimes drinks and energy drinks as not for kids, the signs of needing water (dark yellow pee, dry mouth, headache), a water bottle at school, the water in watermelon and soup, plain sparkling water counting as water, warm milk or soy milk in winter, water in winter too, and never sipping from a stream or puddle. NC 1.NPA.1.1 (reasons to drink water), 1.NPA.1.2 (choosing drinks) and 1.PCH.1.1 (germs in untreated water can make you sick). Read it together with a glass of water on the table.
decks.tip: Make him the pee checker: pale yellow means good, dark yellow means go get a drink.

cards.q: Your body is made of lots of water. How much of you is water?
cards.note: More than half of your body is water. It is in your blood, your muscles, even your brain.

cards.q: Why is water the best drink of all?
cards.note: Water has zero sugar and is exactly what your body is thirsty for. Milk is a great drink too.

cards.q: On a hike you see a clear, cold stream. Is it safe to drink from it?
cards.note: Stream, pond and puddle water can carry germs you cannot see, even when it looks clean. Tap water and bottled water have been cleaned, so drink those.

cards.q: Energy drinks are made for grown-ups and have lots of caffeine. Are they for kids?
cards.note: Caffeine can make a kid's heart race and keep you awake. Doctors say energy drinks are never for children; water does the job.

cards.q: Juice has lots of sugar. Is juice an everyday drink or a sometimes drink?
cards.note: Juice has the fruit's sugar without the fiber, so it is a sometimes drink. Whole fruit is the everyday pick, and water is the everyday drink.

cards.q: Which has more fiber, an orange or orange juice?
cards.note: Juice is fruit with the fiber squeezed out. Eat the whole fruit most of the time.

cards.q: What does soda have a whole lot of?
cards.note: A can of soda has about ten spoons of sugar. That is why soda is a sometimes drink.

cards.q: Sports drinks are made for long, hard races. What do kids need at a soccer game?
cards.note: Sports drinks have sugar and salt for long, hard races. For games and playing, water does the job.

cards.q: Your pee is dark yellow. What is your body asking for?
cards.note: Pale yellow pee means you are drinking enough. Dark yellow means drink up.

cards.q: Your mouth feels dry and sticky and your head hurts a little. What might help?
cards.note: A dry mouth, a headache or feeling tired can all mean your body needs water.

cards.q: What do you bring to school so you can sip water all day?
cards.note: Fill it in the morning and refill it at the fountain. Sip at snack, lunch and after recess.

cards.q: Which food is mostly water?
cards.note: Watermelon, cucumbers, oranges and soup are full of water. Food gives you some water too.

cards.q: In winter it is cold and you hardly sweat. Do you still need water?
cards.note: You lose water by breathing and peeing all year. Dry winter air makes you thirsty too.

cards.q: It is cold outside. Which warm drink is an everyday choice?
cards.note: Warm milk, or warm soy milk if you cannot drink cow's milk, warm water with lemon and a bowl of soup all count. Hot cocoa is a sometimes drink.

cards.q: Plain sparkling water is bubbly but has no sugar. Which is it more like, water or soda?
cards.note: The bubbles are just a gas, so with no sugar added, sparkling water counts as water. Soda is sugar plus bubbles.

cards.q: You wake up in the morning. Your body had no water all night. What is a good first drink?
cards.note: You lose water while you sleep, even just by breathing. A morning drink of water wakes your body up.
