cards.q: Plain water feels boring today. What can you add for taste with no sugar?
cards.note: Add lemon, orange, cucumber or berries to water for a little taste with no added sugar.

decks.subject: body
decks.title: Everyday and Sometimes Foods
decks.about: Everyday foods and sometimes foods: no food is bad, but candy, chips, cookies, cake and fries are for once in a while, what makes a food a sometimes food (lots of added sugar or salt), candy's quick energy that fades, a treat at a party is fine and a treat at a friend's house gets a thank you, a crunchy everyday snack, the label that shows added sugar, why salty snacks make you thirsty, one treat not changing the rest of the day, and where sugar comes from. NC 1.NPA.1.2 (foods and why we eat them) and 1.NPA.1.3 (where foods come from). Read it together with no food called bad and no talk about size or weight, just everyday and sometimes.
decks.tip: When he asks for a treat, answer with the words: is that an everyday food or a sometimes food?

cards.q: Foods you can eat every day, like fruit, rice and bread, are called...?
cards.note: Everyday foods give your body what it needs. Most of what you eat should be everyday foods.

cards.q: Candy, chips, cookies and cake are small treats for once in a while. What do we call them?
cards.note: Sometimes foods taste great but give your body little of what it needs to grow. They are for once in a while, not every day.

cards.q: Cake is a sometimes food. Can you ever have cake?
cards.note: No food is off limits; sometimes foods are just not for every day. Enjoy a slice at a party!

cards.q: It is a birthday party and there is cake. What do you do?
cards.note: A treat at a party is part of the fun. Enjoy it, then back to everyday foods tomorrow.

cards.q: Candy gives you a quick bit of energy. Does that energy last a long time?
cards.note: Candy's energy comes and goes quickly. Whole grains, fruit and protein foods give energy that lasts all morning.

cards.q: Candy, soda and chips are sometimes foods because they have lots of added...?
cards.note: Lots of added sugar or salt is what makes a food a sometimes food. Everyday foods bring vitamins, fiber and protein instead.

cards.q: At a friend's house, their grown-up gives you a cookie at snack time. What do you say?
cards.note: Every family has its own treats. A grown-up offers, you say thank you and enjoy it; nobody needs a lecture about food.

cards.q: Which snack is crunchy and an everyday food?
cards.note: Carrots crunch like chips and carry vitamins. Dip them in hummus or yogurt.

cards.q: Many boxed foods have sugar added. Where can a grown-up read what is inside?
cards.note: The ingredient list shows what is inside. Sugar hides under names like syrup too.

cards.q: Chips and pretzels are salty. What do salty snacks make you feel?
cards.note: Salt makes you thirsty. Have a glass of water with salty snacks.

cards.q: You had cake at a party today. What do you eat at dinner tonight?
cards.note: One treat does not change the rest of the day. Dinner is dinner: everyday foods, like always.

cards.q: How often do we eat a sometimes food?
cards.note: Not every day. A sometimes food is a treat, not a habit.

cards.q: Sugar is made from the sweet juice of a tall grass plant. What is the plant called?
cards.note: Sugar comes from sugar cane, a tall grass, and from sugar beets, a root. Honey is made by bees, and fruit has its own sugar.

cards.q: Fries are a sometimes food. What could you have most days instead?
cards.note: A baked potato or corn on the cob is a vegetable. Fries now and then are fine too.

cards.q: Which one is a sometimes food?
cards.note: Doughnuts are sweet and fried. A yummy treat for once in a while.

cards.q: Which one is an everyday food?
cards.note: Toast is grains. Top it with mashed banana, or peanut butter if nuts are safe for you, for a tasty start.

decks.subject: body
decks.title: Meals and Snacks
decks.about: Three meals with snacks in between, a snack with two food groups, the balanced plate (half fruits and vegetables, a quarter grains, a quarter protein, dairy on the side), spotting what a plate is missing, a three-group breakfast, eating together, the serving spoon for shared bowls, sitting while eating, eating slowly, thanking the cook, and kid-sized kitchen jobs. NC 1.NPA.1.2 (foods and why we eat them), 1.PCH.1.2 (keeping germs out of shared food) and 1.PCH.2.1 (spotting what can cause injury, like running with food). Read it together and let him be the plate checker at dinner.
decks.tip: Hand him the job of plate checker: is half the plate fruits and veggies? What is missing?

cards.q: How many meals do most kids eat each day?
cards.note: Breakfast, lunch and dinner, plus one or two small snacks in between.

cards.q: Breakfast, lunch and dinner are the meals. What small bites come in between?
cards.note: A snack in the afternoon, maybe one in the morning. Snacks are little bites that keep you going until the next meal.

cards.q: A good snack is like a tiny meal. Which snack has two food groups?
cards.note: Carrots are vegetables and hummus is made from chickpeas, a protein food. Apple and cheese or crackers and beans work the same way.

cards.q: Half the plate is fruits and vegetables. Grains fill one quarter. Which group fills the last quarter?
cards.note: The plate picture: half fruits and vegetables, a quarter grains, a quarter protein, and a cup of dairy on the side.

cards.q: On a balanced plate, what goes in the cup on the side?
cards.note: Dairy sits beside the plate. Milk, yogurt or fortified soy milk all work.

cards.q: Your plate has rice and chicken. What could you add to fill half the plate?
cards.note: Rice is grains and chicken is protein. Add broccoli or a salad and some fruit, and the plate is balanced.

cards.q: Your lunch is a cheese sandwich and milk. What is missing?
cards.note: Bread is grains, cheese and milk are dairy. Add an apple or carrot sticks.

cards.q: Yogurt, berries and granola for breakfast. How many food groups is that?
cards.note: Yogurt is dairy, berries are fruit, granola is grains. Three groups before school!

cards.q: Why is it nice to eat dinner together as a family?
cards.note: Family meals are for talking about your day. Kids who eat with family often try more foods.

cards.q: Everyone shares one big bowl of rice. Which spoon do you use to take some?
cards.note: A serving spoon keeps everyone's germs out of the shared bowl. Your own spoon goes in your own mouth only.

cards.q: Why do we sit down while we eat?
cards.note: Running or lying down with food in your mouth can make you choke. Sit, chew, swallow, then play.

cards.q: Your tummy takes a while to tell your brain it is full. So how should you eat?
cards.note: It takes about twenty minutes for the full signal to reach your brain. Eating slowly gives it time to arrive.

cards.q: Someone cooked dinner for you. What is a kind thing to say?
cards.note: Cooking takes work. A thank you makes the cook smile, even on nights you are not sure about the food.

cards.q: You want to help make dinner. Which job is a good one for a kid?
cards.note: Kids can wash veggies, tear lettuce, stir cold things and set the table. Hot and sharp jobs are for grown-ups.

cards.q: Before dinner, what can you set out for everyone at the table?
cards.note: Setting the table is a real help. One plate, one cup, and a fork or chopsticks for each person.

cards.q: A meal with food from many groups is called a...?
cards.note: Balanced means a bit of everything: fruits, vegetables, grains, protein and dairy.

cards.q: You eat a snack right before dinner. How does your tummy feel when dinner comes?
cards.note: Snack time works best a few hours before a meal, so your tummy is ready for dinner.

decks.subject: body
decks.title: Taste and Trying New Foods
decks.about: How tasting works (the tongue and its taste buds, sweet, salty, sour, bitter and savory, and the nose doing half the job), textures, trying a new food ten or more times with one polite bite, foods from different families and countries, being kind about what others eat, and dips and growing a vegetable to make trying fun. NC 1.NPA.1.2 (exploring a variety of foods) with 1.NPA.1.3 (where foods come from) and 1.ICHR.1.2 (respecting the ways families and friends are different, including what they eat); the senses part is a bridge topic. Read it together, and bring a lemon slice and a pretzel to taste as you go.
decks.tip: Serve one new food next to two favorites and ask only for one polite bite; no pressure after that.

cards.q: Stick out your tongue and look in a mirror. What are the tiny bumps all over it for?
cards.note: The bumps have a big name, papillae. Hiding inside them are your taste buds.

cards.q: Sweet, salty, sour, bitter, and one more. The fifth taste, in soup broth and cheese, is called...?
cards.note: Savory is also called umami, and you taste it in broth, tomatoes, mushrooms and cheese. Spicy is not a taste at all; it is your tongue feeling heat.

cards.q: Sweet, salty, sour and bitter are four kinds of...?
cards.note: Your taste buds sort every bite into these tastes and send the news to your brain. Most foods are a mix of more than one.

cards.q: You lick a lemon and your face scrunches up. Which taste is that?
cards.note: Lemons, limes and pickles are sour. Sour makes your mouth water.

cards.q: You eat a pretzel. Which taste do you get?
cards.note: Pretzels, chips, olives and soy sauce are salty. Salt also hides in soup and cheese.

cards.q: You bite a cookie. Which taste is that?
cards.note: Sugar, honey and ripe fruit taste sweet. Babies like sweet best, and that is normal.

cards.q: Kale and other leafy greens have a strong taste many grown-ups like. Which taste is it?
cards.note: Bitter is the taste kids often need the most tries to like. Many grown-ups love it.

cards.q: Pinch your nose shut and eat a bite of apple. What happens to the taste?
cards.note: Most of what we call flavor is really smell, which is why food tastes dull when you have a cold. Let go of your nose and the apple flavor rushes back.

cards.q: You try a new food and are unsure about it. How many tries can it take to like a new food?
cards.note: Taste buds learn: the first bite is a stranger, and by the tenth it is a friend. Keep offering, no pressure.

cards.q: A new food is on your plate. What does a polite bite look like?
cards.note: One polite bite means trying a small taste. After that you can say no thank you to more.

cards.q: Your friend's lunch looks and smells different from yours. What is the kind thing to say?
cards.note: Everyone's taste buds are different, so do not yuck someone's yum. Curious and kind is the way.

cards.q: Tacos, sushi and pasta come from different...?
cards.note: Tacos come from Mexico, sushi from Japan, pasta from Italy. Trying them is like a tasty trip.

cards.q: Your family's dinner and your friend's dinner are different. What does that show?
cards.note: Every family has its own foods and traditions. Different is interesting, never wrong.

cards.q: Carrots and crackers go crunch. What do we call the way a food feels in your mouth?
cards.note: Crunchy, soft, smooth, chewy and crispy are textures. Some kids like crunchy best.

cards.q: Mashed potatoes and yogurt feel smooth and soft. Is that a taste or a texture?
cards.note: Taste is sweet or salty; texture is how food feels. You can like a food's taste but need time to get used to its texture.

cards.q: You grow a tomato plant and pick the tomatoes yourself. How does that change eating them?
cards.note: Kids who grow or cook a food are much more likely to taste it. Try a pot of cherry tomatoes or herbs.

cards.q: A new food is hard to try plain. What can make it easier?
cards.note: Dip broccoli in ranch or hummus, or pair a new food with an old favorite. Small tricks help.
